profile:
A 61-year-old man was referred to hepatobiliary surgery for multiple giant hepatic hemangiomas discovered 5 years earlier on routine examination. In June 20XX, CT showed new multiple lung nodules, a right axillary tumor, and the known hepatic lesions; he was referred for evaluation of the axillary mass.

Laboratory studies showed a normal soluble interleukin-2 receptor level (391 U/mL) and normal carcinoembryonic antigen (2.6 ng/dL), but an elevated thyroglobulin level (226 ng/mL).

FDG–PET/CT demonstrated faint uptake in the thyroid gland, no uptake in the lung nodules, intense uptake in the right axillary tumor (SUVmax 5.1), and decreased uptake in the hepatic lesions.

Cervical ultrasonography revealed irregular, hypoechoic masses with indistinct borders in both thyroid lobes, with suspected capsular invasion in the right lobe and right cervical lymphadenopathy. Breast ultrasonography was normal.

Ultrasonography of the axilla showed a 30 mm lobulated, well-defined, hypoechoic mass with internal heterogeneity and no enlarged surrounding lymph nodes. Contrast-enhanced CT of the axilla confirmed an oval mass with high attenuation, poor contrast enhancement, no chest‐wall invasion, intact subclavian artery, and absence of the dorsal thoracic artery.

Additional findings included bilateral pulmonary nodules up to 7 mm, hepatic nodules with peripheral arterial phase enhancement spreading centrally in the portal phase (consistent with cavernous hemangioma), a left renal angiomyolipoma, a left adrenal adenoma, and a subcutaneous lipoma.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed that the right thyroid tumor was class IV, the left thyroid tumor class V, the left cervical lymph node class V, and the right axillary tumor class III with epithelial-like cells in a mesenchymal background; thyroid transcription factor-1 was negative in the axillary lesion.

He was diagnosed with papillary thyroid carcinoma and an unspecified right axillary mesenchymal tumor. The differential diagnosis for the axillary lesion included lymph node metastasis from papillary thyroid carcinoma and occult breast cancer. The patient underwent total thyroidectomy, cervical lymph node dissection, and resection of the axillary tumor.

A 60-year-old postmenopausal woman with a history of total abdominal hysterectomy 20 years earlier for fibroids presented with a 1-year history of clitoral enlargement, hirsutism, deepening of voice, decreased libido, and increasing abdominal girth. Baseline renal and hepatic chemistries, TSH, and lipid panel were unchanged from 1 year prior except for mildly elevated LDL. Transvaginal ultrasound showed an anechoic, nonvascular, cystic left adnexal lesion measuring 10.5 × 5.9 × 6.2 cm. CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed the cystic left adnexal mass and demonstrated no adrenal mass or other intra-abdominal abnormalities. Initial hyperandrogenism workup revealed a free testosterone of 4.2 pg/ml (normal) but a total testosterone of 264.3 ng/dl (elevated), with DHEA-S 29.2 μg/dl, CA-125 5 U/ml, and inhibin-A 1 pg/ml all within normal limits. Three months later, the cyst was unchanged but symptoms persisted. On referral to endocrinology, repeat labs showed free testosterone 4.7 pg/ml, total testosterone 276 ng/dl, FSH 41.7 IU/L, LH 26.6 IU/L (postmenopausal range), suppressed 8 am cortisol of 1.0 μg/dl, and normal DHEA, DHEA-S, and estradiol. Repeat ultrasound showed slight increase of the adnexal mass to 11.7 × 5.5 × 8.3 cm. A multidisciplinary team recommended laparoscopic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

A 42-year-old woman was referred to the emergency department after an out-of-hospital brain MRI was interpreted as suspicious for a right middle cerebral artery (MCA) aneurysm and late subacute subarachnoid hemorrhage in the right Sylvian fissure. She reported chronic, intermittent headaches responsive to analgesics and short-term memory problems of unclear duration. On examination, she was in good general condition with only moderate headache; the remainder of her medical and family histories was unremarkable.

Review of her MRI revealed a lesion in the right Sylvian fissure with a dilated right MCA passing through it. The lesion was non-homogeneously hyperintense on T1-weighted spin echo, T2-weighted fast spin echo, and FLAIR sequences; susceptibility-weighted imaging showed hypointensity with blooming artifacts, and diffusion-weighted imaging showed no diffusion restriction.

Emergency head CT angiography demonstrated an unruptured fusiform aneurysm of the right MCA at the M1–M2 junction with trifurcation of the M2 branches. A well-defined, non-enhancing, extremely hypodense lesion measuring 10 × 13 × 13 mm (−90 to −100 HU) was noted in the right Sylvian fissure, encasing the distal M1 and proximal M2 segments; there was no evidence of blood or calcification.

An 8-year-old girl with a history of bilateral sporadic retinoblastoma diagnosed at 22 months of age (both eyes ICRB group D) initially received nine cycles of systemic polychemotherapy and multiple intravitreal melphalan injections, followed by plaque brachytherapy, cryotherapy, and eventual enucleation of the right eye 9 months after diagnosis. At age 2, she underwent external-beam radiotherapy to the left eye as salvage therapy. Regular ophthalmological follow-up showed no recurrence in the left eye, with best-corrected visual acuity of 20/200. Five years after completion of EBRT, she developed progressive pain and swelling of the right leg and was treated for presumed osteomyelitis with antibiotics, without improvement. On referral, MRI of the right tibia demonstrated an expansive intramedullary lesion with broad surrounding tissue reaction. A core biopsy was performed to further evaluate the lesion.

A 52-year-old white man presented with a 4-year history of recurrent, intermittent rash of symmetrically distributed, red annular patches on non–sun-exposed areas of the trunk and extremities. The lesions gradually expanded in concentric rings with scale over several months, were mildly pruritic, and associated with arthralgias during flares. His only medication was a proton pump inhibitor. Lyme disease testing was negative. Initial treatment with topical and systemic corticosteroids resulted in only temporary improvement. On examination, pink-red, symmetric, concentric annular patches with trailing scale involved 10% to 15% of his body surface area without lymphadenopathy. Laboratory investigations were within normal limits. A punch biopsy and a broad shave biopsy from the leading edge of a lesion showed a superficial perivascular and lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate with exocytosis of small lymphocytes with mild nuclear contour irregularities, minimal spongiosis, vacuolar alteration at the dermoepidermal junction, and papillary dermal fibrosis. Immunohistochemical staining revealed a predominantly CD3⁺ infiltrate with an approximately equal ratio of CD4⁺ to CD8⁺ cells. Periodic acid–Schiff diastase staining was negative for fungi. No perivascular cuffing, interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate, or significant red blood cell extravasation was seen. Loss of CD7 on lymphocytes was estimated to be approximately 40%.

A 25-year-old woman with a history of chronic headaches and Kawasaki disease presented with lethargy, blurred vision, confusion, and headache. Her serum sodium was 127 mmol/L; other metabolic and hematologic studies were normal. Non-contrast head CT showed a 2.2 cm heterogeneous mass in the pineal region without calcification, with resultant obstructive hydrocephalus and transependymal CSF resorption; an external ventricular drain was placed. Subsequent brain MRI demonstrated a mildly lobulated, well-circumscribed mass that was isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on FLAIR, with heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement except for a small nonenhancing anterior component. On the ADC map, the lesion’s mean ADC was 1077.01 ×10⁻⁶ mm²/s (±191.14 ×10⁻⁶ mm²/s), higher than normal brain. MRI of the spine showed no evidence of drop metastases.

A 10-month-old girl with an uncomplicated antenatal course and term birth presented in the neonatal period with abdominal distension at 1 week and two episodes of macroscopic haematuria by 2 weeks. On evaluation then, she was pale, hypertensive (blood pressure above the 99th percentile), and had a palpable mass in the left lumbar region. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a retroperitoneal mass anteromedial to the left kidney. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a renal mass arising from the upper pole of the left kidney without focal invasion or distant metastasis (stage I). At 1 month, she underwent left nephrectomy with mesenteric lymph node excision. Histological examination showed spindle cells arranged in fascicles with scant cytoplasm, moderate pleomorphism, numerous mitotic figures, erratic thin-walled vessels with a hemangiopericytoma-like pattern, and entrapped glomeruli; lymph nodes and surgical margins were free of tumour. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD99 and vimentin with a Ki-67 index of 45%, and negative for desmin, caldesmon, SMA, MyoD1, cyclin D1, CD34, WT1, NSE, cytokeratin, and neurofilament. Molecular genetic studies revealed an EGFR internal tandem duplication with BCOR and pan-TRK negativity, confirming a cellular subtype of congenital mesoblastic nephroma. She was followed clinically with abdominal ultrasound every 6 weeks and remained asymptomatic and normotensive until 10 months of age, when she developed gradual-onset progressive dyspnoea, post-feed vomiting, poor feeding, and weight loss. On examination, she was tachypnoeic with reduced expansion of the right hemithorax, dull percussion, reduced vocal resonance, and diminished air entry. Chest radiography showed an opacity occupying the right hemithorax with mediastinal shift to the left. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a large (8.6 × 6 × 7 cm) heterogeneous enhancing soft-tissue mass with necrotic regions in the right hemithorax, causing mediastinal shift and collapse of the right lower lobe.

A 55-year-old African American woman with a history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis and Rai stage 1 CLL, diagnosed 8 years earlier on routine evaluation, presented with progressive lymphadenopathy, intermittent fevers, a 5-lb weight loss, and worsening respiratory status requiring airway management. Initial CLL had been managed with observation; rheumatoid arthritis therapies had included hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, prednisone, and rituximab infusions. 

On CT imaging, there was a soft-tissue mass in the nasopharynx representing enlarged adenoidal tissue, diffuse palatine and lingual tonsillar hypertrophy with airway narrowing, and bulky cervical, supraclavicular, and axillary lymphadenopathy. PET/CT showed intense FDG uptake in the nasopharyngeal mass (SUVmax 18.7), level IIB cervical chain nodes (SUVmax 20.7), and bulky FDG-avid lymph nodes in the axillary, periaortic/retroperitoneal, and iliac regions. 

Complete blood count revealed leukocytosis (WBC 40.7 × 10^3/mm^3; 24% neutrophils, 75% lymphocytes), mild hypochromic-macrocytic anemia (Hb 11.8 g/dL; MCV 97.6 fL), and normal platelet count. The peripheral smear showed numerous atypical lymphocytes consistent with persistent CLL. Serologic and viral studies were negative, including HIV, hepatitis A/B/C, COVID-19, influenza A/B, RSV, and QuantiFERON-TB Gold. 

CLL prognostic testing revealed CD19-positive lymphoid cells (87% of lymphocytes), ZAP70 positivity 1%, CD38 positivity 20%, unmutated IGHV3-21 status, normal karyotype, and negative FISH for trisomy 12 and deletions of 6q, 11q, 13q, and 17p. Beta-2 microglobulin was 2.27 mg/L. These features indicated unfavorable CLL prognosis. 

At presentation, the leading clinical consideration was Richter transformation of her CLL, and an ultrasound-guided core biopsy of an enlarged cervical lymph node was performed.

A 57-year-old Fitzpatrick III woman with a history of numerous basal cell carcinomas since 2015, cervical polyps, uterine fibroids, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, arthritis, and decreased visual acuity presented with numerous growths on her eyelids for several years. She denied a family history of basal cell carcinoma, although her mother had breast, bladder, and colon cancer and her maternal grandmother had breast cancer. She denied lesions on the genitals, seizures, dizziness, learning difficulties, dental abnormalities, hoarseness, hypotrichosis, hypohidrosis, or macroglossia; her hair turned gray at age 13. On examination, she had numerous 2 to 6 mm pearly papules scattered on the face and bilateral strings of pearly papules along the upper and lower eyelid margins. Dermoscopic examination of the eyelid lesions revealed arborizing vessels, brown-gray globules, and aggregated yellow-white globules in all lesions. Additionally, a dermatofibroma and a plantar verruca were noted. There were no palmar pits, skeletal abnormalities, macrocephaly, or jawline deformities. Four facial papules were biopsied, each showing infundibulocystic basal cell carcinoma with follicular differentiation. A fifth lesion on the forehead demonstrated a collision of a nodular basal cell carcinoma with a blue nevus.

A 60-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of easy fatigability and a persistent, dull, right-sided throbbing headache, which intermittently worsened. During the same period, she noted a nodular growth over her right forehead that measured approximately 2.5 × 2.5 cm; it was initially excised by a local practitioner but recurred and enlarged over 1½ months. She denied changes in appetite, bowel or bladder habits, and had no weight loss. Her surgical history was notable for a total abdominal hysterectomy performed 6 months earlier for multiple uterine fibroids.

On examination, the forehead lesion was fixed, nonpulsatile, and non-tender, with a nodular surface and an overlying scar from prior excision. A second firm, fixed swelling measuring 4 × 4 cm was palpated on the right chest wall. There was no organomegaly. Routine blood tests and serum chemistry were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed a 5 × 4 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass in the right frontal region with destruction of both the outer and inner tables of the frontal bone and compression of the underlying frontal lobe. CT of the chest and abdomen revealed a 5.7 × 4.1 × 3.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the superior/posterobasal segment of the right lower lobe, with invasion of a branch of the inferior pulmonary vein; multiple spiculated nodules in both upper lobes; and a pleura-based soft tissue mass in the right posterolateral chest wall destroying the 10th rib and infiltrating subcutaneous fat.

Fine-needle aspiration was performed from both the forehead and chest-wall nodules. Smears from both sites showed cohesive overlapping clusters of pleomorphic tumor cells with hyperchromatic oval to bizarre nuclei, some embedded in pink matrix material. The features were interpreted as those of a poorly differentiated malignant tumor.

A 51-year-old Caucasian man presented with three weeks of flu-like symptoms followed by headache, ear pain, transient extremity weakness, and bilateral blurry vision. On exam, visual acuity was 20/80 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye; intraocular pressures were normal bilaterally. There were no anterior chamber or vitreous cells. Dilated fundus examination revealed multiple exudative retinal detachments in both eyes. Fluorescein angiography showed multiple pinpoint hyperfluorescent areas with leakage and pooling. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated choroidal thickening and subretinal fluid in both eyes. He declined neurologic evaluation and was diagnosed with VKH syndrome; oral prednisone 60 mg daily was started. Two days later, he returned with dizziness and confusion. Brain MRI demonstrated subcortical white-matter hyperintensities thought to be consistent with VKH. He received three days of IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily), with improvement of neurologic symptoms, visual acuity (to 20/25 OU), and subretinal fluid, and was discharged on prednisone 60 mg daily. One week later, he returned with altered mental status and worsening vision. Repeat retinal imaging showed increased subretinal fluid, and repeat brain MRI revealed progression of subcortical white-matter hyperintensities and new hemorrhagic foci.

A 28-year-old African woman, with three prior full-term pregnancies and recent immigration from East Africa, presented with a large, tender left axillary mass. She first noticed a small, nontender lump 3 years earlier—6 months after placement of a left-arm etonogestrel implant, 8 months after her most recent delivery, and 2 years after arriving in the United States. The mass grew slowly without pain, drainage, skin changes, or neurologic symptoms, and did not interfere with breastfeeding. Six months before presentation, the mass enlarged rapidly and became tender, limiting full adduction of the left arm. Her implant had been replaced 2 months before this acceleration. She denied breast symptoms, trauma, infection, systemic complaints, or other exposures; her only medication was the implant device.

On exam, there was a softball-sized, mobile, nonreducible mass in the left axillary fossa with overlying skin striations; no regional lymphadenopathy; intact vascular, sensory, and motor function; and mild discomfort with arm adduction. Vital signs and the remainder of the examination were unremarkable.

Prior MRI of the left axilla (with and without contrast) demonstrated a 16 × 11 × 11 cm multiloculated subcutaneous cystic lesion displacing but not invading adjacent structures, without intrathoracic communication or lymphadenopathy. MR lymphangiogram—after subcutaneous contrast injection into the interdigital web spaces—showed no lymphatic communication with the mass, although lymphatic drainage led to nodes over the lesion. Echinococcal IgG antibody testing was equivocal. Initial laboratory studies were otherwise unremarkable, without evidence of systemic infection.

A 73-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of a painless swelling on the tongue that had gradually increased in size. She denied dysphagia, odynophagia, speech changes, or breathing difficulty. Her medical history was notable for well-controlled hyperthyroidism. Examination revealed stable vital signs and no lymphadenopathy. Intraorally, there was a 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm pale-pink, round, soft-to-firm, sessile, nonpulsatile, nontender, slightly mobile nodule with intact mucosa on the dorsum of the tongue near the left lateral border. Oral hygiene was good, with a broken lower molar and sharp opposing cusp noted. Routine blood tests were within normal limits. Based on the clinical presentation, a benign fibrous lesion was suspected, and a broad differential diagnosis was considered. After informed consent, an excisional biopsy under local anesthesia was performed.

A 43-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of left hip pain, worse with exercise and hip flexion, which had intensified over the past week. He also reported 2 months of malaise, anorexia, and a 6-kg weight loss in the previous month. He denied trauma and had no comorbidities.

On examination, flexion of the left hip beyond 40°—especially against resistance—elicited pain; there was no motor weakness, but hip flexion provoked numbness in the left lower extremity. The FABER test was positive, and gait was normal.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, and liver and renal function tests, were all within normal limits.

A pelvic radiograph showed no acute osseous abnormalities. Thoracoabdominal CT revealed a 64×29-mm noninvasive mass posterior to the psoas muscle containing amorphous calcifications. On follow-up pelvic radiograph, calcifications within the psoas compartment were confirmed. Abdominopelvic MRI demonstrated a 72×45×50-mm mass arising from the left iliopsoas muscle extending along fat planes; it was T1 hypointense in areas of calcification, T2 hyperintense, lobulated with sharp margins, and showed marked postcontrast enhancement.

A 58-year-old man with known diabetes mellitus presented with a 3-month history of intermittent fever, night sweats, and a 6-kg weight loss. He noted a hard swelling in the right parotid region that had rapidly enlarged over the past 2 weeks. On examination, a right supraclavicular lymph node was palpable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed multiple hypodense liver lesions, bilateral small pleural effusions, a right apical lung nodule, and axillary, mediastinal, peripancreatic, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Skull and spine radiographs showed no osteolytic lesions.

Fine-needle aspiration of the parotid swelling yielded hypercellular smears composed predominantly of large plasmacytoid cells with central to eccentric nuclei, perinuclear halos, less condensed chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and abundant basophilic cytoplasm. Binucleated and trinucleated forms and atypical mitoses were noted, along with mature plasma cells, scattered neutrophils, eosinophils, and apoptotic bodies. 

Based on these findings, the preliminary differential diagnosis included plasmablastic lymphoma, plasmablastic plasmacytoma/myeloma, and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation.

A 60-year-old man with a 20-year history of hepatitis B and 1-year history of liver cirrhosis presented initially with chronic abdominal pain. His alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level was 2494.2 ng/mL (normal <10.9). CT scans showed a 4×3 cm mass in the left liver lobe and multiple pulmonary nodules. He underwent transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) and two cycles of gemcitabine–oxaliplatin, but his liver tumor enlarged and AFP rose to 8683.0 ng/mL. A bean-sized gingival nodule was noted, which had mild pain, discharged “pus” on puncture, and recurred quickly. He received further TACE and sorafenib, with stable disease for 6 months, then disease progression. 

On readmission, he reported breathlessness, progressive weight loss, severe back pain, and right upper quadrant pain. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 91 g/L, platelets 97×10^9/L, albumin 33.4 g/L, AFP 4325.0 ng/mL, AST 66 U/L, LDH 296 U/L, direct bilirubin 9.4 µmol/L, indirect bilirubin 13.2 µmol/L, and normal coagulation. 

Physical examination revealed a 2×2 cm reddish nodule on the alveolar mucosa distal to the upper right first premolar; it was soft, sharply demarcated, centrally ulcerated, swollen, mildly tender, and bled occasionally. Radiography showed no bony destruction.

A 4-year-old Egyptian girl was referred for evaluation of bilateral breast budding and pubic hair of 4 months’ duration, followed by two episodes of vaginal spotting over the preceding 2 weeks. Her medical and birth histories were unremarkable, with no family history of endocrinologic disorders. She was alert, irritable, 115 cm tall (>97th percentile), and weighed 20 kg (90th percentile). Vital signs were normal. Examination revealed Tanner stage III breast development, Tanner stage III pubic hair, estrogenized vulvar mucosa with clear discharge, slight clitoral enlargement, and a firm, ill-defined, nontender suprapubic mass without ascites.  
Abdominal ultrasonography showed an enlarged uterus with a prominent endometrium and a 7.8 × 5.2 cm irregular, inhomogeneous right adnexal mass crossing the midline; the left ovary and other abdominal organs were normal. CT of the abdomen confirmed a large right ovarian mass. Brain MRI showed a normal-sized pituitary and infundibulum with a normal posterior pituitary bright spot. Bone age was 5 years on left hand/wrist radiograph.  
Laboratory studies revealed elevated estradiol (280–375 pmol/L; normal <73), progesterone (5.3 nmol/L; normal 0–1.3), testosterone (38.9 pg/mL; normal 1–5.2), and androstenedione (4.1 ng/mL; normal 0.3–3.1); basal LH and FSH were low (0.4 and 0.7 IU/L) with no response to LHRH stimulation. Total inhibin was 1,069 U/L (normal <100), alpha-fetoprotein 987 μg/L (normal 1–200), and β-hCG, LDH, and ALP were negative. Karyotype was 46,XX.

A 6-year-old boy presented after awakening with nonbloody, nonbilious emesis, lightheadedness, and approximately one minute of eye fluttering with unresponsiveness but no tonic–clonic movements or incontinence. Post-ictally, he had headache, photophobia, and vision changes. He had intermittent morning vomiting for one month but no fevers, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, or prior seizures. Family history was notable for brain tumors in maternal relatives. 

On exam, blood pressure was 161/102 mm Hg, heart rate 90–110 beats/min, temperature 37.9 °C, and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. He was neurologically intact with bilateral upgoing toes. Abdominal exam revealed suprapubic distension without tenderness or organomegaly.

Noncontrast head CT showed a left‐hemisphere hypodense region with artifact. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral parieto-occipital subcortical T2 prolongation and gyral swelling consistent with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. EEG captured subclinical seizures from bilateral occipital regions, which resolved with lorazepam, levetiracetam, and fosphenytoin.

Initial laboratory studies showed WBC 29.7×10^6/mL, hemoglobin 12 g/dL, platelets 265×10^6/mL, BUN 16 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed 30 mg/dL protein without blood. Lumbar puncture yielded 0 nucleated cells, 0 red blood cells, protein 43 mg/dL, and glucose 69 mg/dL. Renal ultrasound revealed bilaterally enlarged (11.6 cm) echogenic kidneys without Doppler abnormalities and a distended bladder. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal without left ventricular hypertrophy. Despite blood pressure control with intravenous nicardipine transitioned to oral agents, the etiology of his hypertension and renal enlargement remained unclear.

A 29-year-old nonpregnant woman presented with a 2-year history of low back pain that had worsened over the preceding 2 months. Her medical history was notable for a laparoscopic myomectomy for uterine leiomyoma 5 years earlier. Physical examination findings were unremarkable.  
Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 3.6 × 2.5 cm hypoechoic solid mass in the posterior right lobe of the liver; the remainder of the abdominal and pelvic ultrasound examinations was normal.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a patchy, slightly low-density area in the peripheral zone of segment VI of the right liver, with heterogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase.  
Laboratory studies, including liver function tests and tumor markers (AFP, CEA, CA19-9, CA125), were within normal limits. Serologies for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C virus antibodies were negative.  
What is your differential diagnosis?

A 4-year-old girl with bilateral congenital glaucoma underwent examination under anesthesia. Three years earlier, she had trabeculotomy and trabeculectomy in both eyes, and two years ago she suffered a retinal detachment in the right eye. The left eye had also undergone three sessions of transscleral cyclophotocoagulation. She was on topical timolol/dorzolamide twice daily, apraclonidine thrice daily, and latanoprost nightly in the left eye. There was no history of intraocular inflammation.

Visual acuity was count fingers in the right eye and no light perception in the left eye. Examination of the right eye revealed a quiet eye, horizontal corneal diameter 11.5 mm, deep anterior chamber, cataractous lens, corectopia, and chronic retinal detachment. Examination of the left eye showed a quiet eye with white conjunctiva, corneal diameter 12.5 mm with a faint diffuse scar, deep anterior chamber, clear lens, and a healthy optic disc (cup–disc ratio 0.5).

Gonioscopy of the left eye revealed several quadrants of densely hyperpigmented, dark brown, raised mounds within the trabecular meshwork, resembling iris tissue. No retrocorneal pigment deposition or iris transillumination defects were noted. Anterior segment OCT showed a deep anterior chamber, open angle recess, slightly posteriorly bowed iris, and confirmed elevated tissue within the angle. No ciliary body or iris masses were seen. Intraocular pressure in the left eye was 11 mmHg, and axial length was stable at 24.70 mm. Six months later, the appearance of the angle structures remained unchanged.

A 36-year-old man was referred to our hospital because of an abnormal finding on screening colonoscopy. He had a history of tuberculosis-related lung destruction with pneumothorax and an 8-year smoking history; there was no other relevant family or medical history. He had no gastrointestinal symptoms. On examination, his vital signs were normal and laboratory tests, including alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9, were within normal limits.

Colonoscopy revealed an approximately 10-mm yellowish, sessile protruding lesion in the proximal ascending colon covered by intact mucosa without a rolling sign or cushion sign. Endoscopic ultrasonography showed a 10-mm homogeneous hypoechoic-to-isoechoic mass mainly in the mucosal layer with irregular extension into the submucosal layer; the muscularis propria appeared intact. On the basis of the EUS features, a colonic carcinoid tumor was initially suspected. Abdominal CT did not detect the lesion or any enlarged lymph nodes. An endoscopic biopsy specimen was consistent with a granular cell tumor, although the possibility of a malignant tumor could not be completely excluded based on the endoscopic evaluation.

A 55-year-old man presented with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and constipation, with milder similar episodes in preceding weeks. His history was notable for obesity, prediabetes, and a 30-pack-year smoking history. On examination, he was tachycardic; the abdomen was diffusely distended, mildly tender, without rebound tenderness, and had overactive bowel sounds. Blood tests, including liver and renal function, lipase, and calcium, were normal; white blood cell count was 14.9×10^9/L and C-reactive protein was 15 mg/L. Stool tests for occult blood and calprotectin, as well as QuantiFERON-TB Gold, were negative. Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed fecalization of the small bowel, dilated proximal segments, and irregular wall thickening of a distal ileal segment with partial luminal narrowing. Upper and lower endoscopies were unremarkable, and the patient improved with conservative management. Follow-up MR enterography demonstrated asymmetrical small bowel wall thickening and adjacent mesenteric lymphadenopathy, with no significant mechanical cause for intestinal obstruction. In light of a possible systemic pathology, contrast CT of the chest was obtained and showed a solid infiltrative right hilar soft tissue density mass invading the mediastinum.

A 58-year-old Japanese man presented with a three-month history of a painless, swollen mass in the right submandibular region. On examination, the right submandibular gland was enlarged, elastic-hard, nonfixed, with several enlarged, elastic-hard, movable lymph nodes. Salivary flow from the right submandibular gland was poor. His medical history was notable only for recurrent gastric ulcer disease. Laboratory studies were normal except for: lactate dehydrogenase 214 U/L (normal 105–210), γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 88 U/L (11–80), triglycerides 199 mg/dL (42–168), leucine aminopeptidase 83 U/L (19–69), and serum IgG 924 mg/dL (870–1700). With consent, serum IgG4 was measured at 16.9 mg/dL (4.8–105); other immunoglobulin subclasses and autoantibodies were not evaluated. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a 2.8 × 2.8 cm homogeneously hyperdense, enhancing mass in the right submandibular region with invasive extension into adjacent tissues and several enhancing lymph nodes. MRI revealed a 3.0 × 3.0 × 4.0 cm mass that was hypointense on fat-saturated T1-weighted images, heterogeneous hyperintense on gadolinium-enhanced T2-weighted images, and mid-hyperintense on fat-saturated T2 images; the submandibular lymph nodes were also hyperintense. PET scan demonstrated intense uptake only in the right submandibular region, with no other lesions. The clinical and radiological appearance suggested malignant neoplasm of the submandibular gland with metastatic spread. An excisional biopsy of a level II lymph node showed reactive follicular hyperplasia, and flow cytometry revealed polyclonal B-cell populations (kappa 40.1%, lambda 27.1%).

A 75-year-old Albanian man with benign prostatic hypertrophy underwent an ultrasound for prostate evaluation, which incidentally detected a focal liver lesion. He denied symptoms, and his physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including liver function tests, α-fetoprotein, and viral hepatitis serologies, were within normal limits or negative. Contrast‐enhanced multidetector CT of the chest and abdomen showed a solitary focal lesion in the right hepatic lobe without cirrhotic changes, other masses, or lymphadenopathy. For further characterization, a 1.5-T MRI of the upper abdomen was performed with T1-weighted in-phase and out-of-phase sequences, T2-weighted images with fat suppression, and dynamic contrast‐enhanced sequences. On MRI, the lesion was hypointense relative to liver parenchyma on T1-weighted images but isointense to spleen; on T2-weighted fat-suppressed images it was moderately hyperintense relative to liver yet isointense to spleen. In the arterial phase after gadolinium administration, the mass showed mild homogeneous enhancement, and in delayed (90-second) images it demonstrated mild perilesional enhancement.

A 52-year-old man presented with progressive right upper limb weakness and sensory disturbance. In 2018, he had right facial paralysis that resolved with corticosteroids; two years later, he noted numbness of the left face and neck. In February 2022, he developed persistent pain and numbness in his right hand, and by June 2022 he was unable to raise his right arm. He was initially treated with two courses of intravenous methylprednisolone (1,000 mg daily for three days) and one course of intravenous immunoglobulin (0.4 g/kg daily), without improvement. The weakness progressed, and his right facial paralysis recurred, prompting referral in July 2022.

On examination, he had right facial paralysis and diffuse right upper limb weakness (Medical Research Council grade 0–1/5) with severe muscle atrophy and areflexia from C5 to T1 distributions. There was severe dysesthesia and hypoesthesia in the right upper limb and mild dysesthesia in the left face and anterior neck. Vitals were normal.

Blood tests showed negative vasculitis-associated immune markers, including antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and an elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor level (1,198 U/mL). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 14 cells/μL and a normal protein level.

Conventional nerve conduction studies demonstrated absent compound muscle and sensory nerve action potentials in the right median and ulnar nerves, with markedly reduced amplitude in the right axillary nerve; studies in the lower limbs were normal. The pattern indicated axonal degeneration involving postganglionic segments.

Nerve ultrasound (18 MHz) of the right median nerve at the forearm showed marked enlargement (cross-sectional area, 54 mm²) with swollen fascicles and perineurium, and a fusiform hypoechoic mass between the nerve and thickened epineurium. The right ulnar and musculocutaneous nerves also showed segmental enlargement with loss of the normal fascicular pattern. Color Doppler ultrasound revealed massive enlargement and increased vascularity of the right brachial plexus and cervical nerve roots. Subsequent MRI confirmed massive swelling of the right median nerve, nerve roots, and brachial plexus. Fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT demonstrated abnormal FDG uptake in these same structures, suggesting neurolymphomatosis.

A 20-year-old woman presented with back pain after a vertebral fragility fracture and reported 7 kg weight gain over 4 weeks, acne, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, and 1 year of oligomenorrhea. Blood pressure was 150/100 mm Hg; height 1.47 m; BMI 22.2 kg/m2. Examination showed thin skin, dorsocervical and supraclavicular fat pads, central obesity, acanthosis nigricans, moon facies, and purplish striae on the abdomen, thighs, and popliteal fossae; she was not hirsute. Secondary sexual characteristics and visual fields were normal. Laboratory studies excluded diabetes and electrolyte abnormalities. An 0800 h plasma cortisol was 808 nmol/L with ACTH <5 pg/mL. A 48-h, 2-mg low-dose dexamethasone suppression test failed to suppress cortisol (post-test 621 nmol/L). Adrenal CT showed a 0.7-cm hypodense left adrenal nodule reported as an adenoma. Dual-energy bone densitometry revealed Z-scores of –4.5 (lumbar spine) and –3.2 (femoral neck).

Her 18-year-old brother presented 3 months later with a 2-year history of purple striae and 4 kg weight gain over 4 weeks. He was normotensive; height 1.63 m; BMI 23.1 kg/m2. He had moon facies and purple striae in axillae, popliteal fossae, and waist but no dorsocervical fat pad or proximal myopathy. Laboratory studies excluded diabetes and electrolyte abnormalities. ACTH was <5 pg/mL. A 1-mg overnight low-dose dexamethasone test failed to suppress cortisol (624 nmol/L), and confirmatory low-dose dexamethasone testing showed cortisol of 513 nmol/L. A 6-day Liddle’s test revealed a paradoxical 6% increase in urinary free cortisol. DXA showed Z-scores of –3.2 (spine) and –2.5 (femoral neck). Adrenal CT revealed a diffusely enlarged left adrenal gland and a nodular right adrenal gland.

A 54-year-old man presented with right flank pain of eight months’ duration. On examination, a palpable mass was noted in the right upper abdominal quadrant. Contrast-enhanced CT showed an enlarged right kidney (20×15 cm) with hydronephrosis, nodular thickening of the pelvic lining, and enlarged hilar lymph nodes; multiple renal stones were also present. The findings were suggestive of urothelial carcinoma with lymph-node metastasis. There was no history of other neoplastic disease or prior hormonal treatment. The patient underwent right nephroureterectomy; residual matted lymph nodes with aortic encasement were left in situ. 

On gross examination, the kidney was cystically dilated, and the pelvicalyceal surface was almost entirely replaced by pale-tan papillary and solid nodules up to 2.5 cm in diameter, with only a thin rim of renal parenchyma remaining. The ureter was uninvolved. 

Microscopically, the tumor showed complex papillary structures lined by neoplastic cells with clear cytoplasm, large round nuclei with distinct nucleoli, and frequent hobnail morphology. Papillary cores contained variable stroma with hyaline basement membrane–like material, and psammoma bodies were present focally. The tumor invaded into atrophic renal parenchyma and peripelvic fat. The entire pelvicalyceal surface was lined by these clear and hobnail cells. No invasive or in situ component of conventional urothelial carcinoma or non–clear cell adenocarcinoma was identified, and no benign Müllerian-type epithelium was seen. 

Immunohistochemical studies showed tumor-cell positivity for cytokeratin 7, HNF-1β, and PAX8, with focal CA-125 expression; stains for RCC marker antigen, CD10, uroplakin III, p63, and CK20 were negative.

A 13-year-old boy presented with a 6-month history of a rapidly enlarging, painless, diffuse swelling of the right midface and parotid region. On examination there was slight deviation of the right oral commissure, trismus, and mandibular asymmetry. There was no clinical or radiographic evidence of regional or distant metastasis. His medical history was notable for an attempted surgical excision in Honduras three months earlier.

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 7×5 cm hyperintense mass on T1-weighted images in the right masticator space, extending into the mandibular ramus, masseter and pterygoid muscles, the parotid gland, and the parapharyngeal space. On contrasted T2-weighted sequences the lesion demonstrated a high signal intensity with a multinodular, infiltrative pattern.

An intraoral incisional biopsy was performed. Histologic examination revealed multiple, well-demarcated nodules of tumor cells immersed in abundant myxoid stroma separated by fibrous septa. The cells ranged from round to elongated forms with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and eccentrically placed round to ovoid nuclei with homogeneously distributed chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli. Occasional spindle, epithelioid, and lipoblast-like cells were present. The mitotic rate was low (approximately two mitoses per 10 high-power fields). Periodic acid–Schiff staining, before and after diastase digestion, confirmed that the cytoplasmic granules represented glycogen.

Immunohistochemical studies showed tumor cells positive for vimentin, neuron-specific enolase, and chromogranin, and negative for AE1/AE3 cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, S-100 protein, desmin, muscle-specific actin (HHF35), CD57, GLUT-1, synaptophysin, p53, p63, GFAP, and podoplanin (D2-40). The Ki-67 proliferation index was 42% in 1 000 evaluated tumor cells.

A 14-year-old boy presented with headache and nausea. On examination he was alert, oriented, and had no focal neurologic deficits. He had no significant medical, family, or medication history. Serum α-fetoprotein and β–human chorionic gonadotropin levels were within normal limits. Brain MRI showed extensive T2 hyperintense edema in the left frontal lobe without a hypointense rim. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI revealed two irregular ring-enhancing lesions adjacent to the anterior horn of the left lateral ventricle—one involving the globus pallidus and the other in the frontal white matter—with no midline involvement. Arterial spin labeling and MR perfusion demonstrated increased blood flow only in the merged lesion area, not centrally. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed peripheral diffusion restriction. Susceptibility-weighted imaging and contrast-enhanced CT identified engorged veins traversing the centers of the lesions. Lumbar puncture yielded cerebrospinal fluid with an opening pressure of 255 mmH₂O, protein 105 mg/dL, normal cell count and IgG index, and five unique oligoclonal bands.

A 39-year-old man presented to his general practitioner for a routine check-up. He had a history of extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma of the nasal type treated with chemotherapy and local radiation and assessed as in clinical remission two months earlier. During the examination, the physician noted a heart rate of 155 beats per minute. An ECG demonstrated a regular wide-complex tachycardia interpreted as a hemodynamically stable ventricular tachycardia with an apical-anterior-lateral exit. 

He was transferred urgently to the emergency department with ongoing VT. On arrival, he developed cardiogenic shock. One synchronized biphasic shock of 100 J failed to terminate the arrhythmia and induced ventricular fibrillation, requiring chest compressions and three defibrillations to restore an unstable sinus rhythm that soon degenerated back into VT. Intravenous antiarrhythmic therapy with ajmaline, landiolol, and electrolyte substitution was initiated, maintaining a ventricular rate of 120–150 beats per minute with brief sinus rhythm intervals.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 3 × 2 cm hyperechogenic zone in the apex of the left ventricle, regional hypokinesia in that area, and a small pericardial effusion. Coronary angiography showed no stenosing coronary artery disease.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of atypical right upper-quadrant abdominal pain, significant fatigue, and weight loss. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, or tuberous sclerosis complex. On examination she had mild hepatomegaly without palpable mass or jaundice. Liver function tests and tumor markers (AFP, CEA) were within normal limits.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a solitary, heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass in the liver with an ill-defined margin; color Doppler imaging demonstrated abundant blood flow at the lesion’s periphery. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a 6.4 × 8.0 cm low-density mass in segment IV with inhomogeneous enhancement in the portal phase. MRI confirmed a lesion that was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed strong heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. There was no lymphadenopathy, portal vein involvement, or other lesions.  
Given the hypervascular nature of the mass, its lack of adipose tissue, and absence of thick-walled vessels, the lesion was initially interpreted as a hemangioma, an atypical hepatocellular carcinoma, or a metastatic focus. Because of the patient’s worsening symptoms and indeterminate imaging findings, a central segmentectomy of the liver with cholecystectomy was performed.

An 11-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a nodule on the palatal mucosa behind the right upper central incisor. Eight months earlier, he had sustained dental trauma with a crown fracture of that tooth without pulp exposure. On examination, there was a sessile‐based nodule, narrow in the anteroposterior dimension, with a smooth surface, slight white coloration, and diffuse posterior erythema; it was non‐tender on palpation. Panoramic and periapical radiographs showed no bone involvement. Thermal sensitivity testing confirmed that the adjacent teeth were vital, effectively ruling out an acute or chronic periapical lesion.

A 43-year-old Japanese man noted a gradually enlarging soft tissue mass in his right thigh since January 2015. He had no significant personal or family history. On examination, a hard, elastic, non-tender, non-pulsatile mass measuring approximately 30 cm in diameter was palpated in the right thigh without overlying skin changes. Laboratory studies were unremarkable. Plain radiography showed a large soft tissue mass without calcification, periosteal reaction, or femoral involvement. MRI revealed that the lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with peripheral, septal gadolinium enhancement. CT imaging confirmed the absence of calcification and no obvious cortical invasion of the femur. Differential diagnoses included malignant myxoid soft tissue tumors such as myxoid liposarcoma, myxofibrosarcoma, and metastatic carcinomas (myoepithelial or neuroendocrine). An incisional biopsy demonstrated a lobulated tumor with a myxoid matrix and atypical spindle-shaped cells forming eosinophilic cord-like structures. Immunohistochemical staining showed S-100 positivity; synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and pan-keratin (AE1/AE3) were negative; Ki-67 labeling index was approximately 10%.

A 19-year-old man presented with a 6-year history of occasional right thigh pain and a 5-year history of right thigh weakness. He denied night pain, and his pain worsened with activity. There was no history of trauma or systemic disease. On examination, the right thigh circumference was approximately 2 cm less than that of the left thigh; hair distribution was symmetric. Hip and knee range of motion were normal. Mild tenderness was noted on palpation of the right thigh.  
Plain radiographs of the right femur showed cortical thickening in the distal posterolateral diaphyseal region.  
Magnetic resonance imaging revealed cortical thickening (approximately 9.5 mm) at the metadiaphyseal level of the distal posterolateral right femur. Adjacent to this area was an ill-defined soft-tissue lesion measuring about 18 × 12 mm that was hypointense on T1-weighted sequences, hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences, and showed marked contrast enhancement.  
Computed tomography confirmed the posterolateral cortical thickening but demonstrated no central nidus.

An 84-year-old woman had an incidentally discovered simple liver cyst one year earlier. She was asymptomatic, and physical examination was unremarkable. Liver function tests were normal, and hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen was 5.0 ng/mL and CA19-9 was 43.5 U/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a well-defined, low-attenuation cystic lesion that increased in maximal diameter from 41 to 47 mm over one year, with an irregularly shaped mural nodule demonstrating progressive contrast enhancement and no biliary duct dilation. Enhanced ultrasonography revealed a 14 mm isoechoic irregular nodule with a distinct feeding artery and gradual enhancement. MRI depicted a homogeneous water-intensity cystic lesion; the mural nodule showed peripheral low intensity and central high intensity on heavily T2-weighted images and contrast enhancement on portal venous–phase T1-weighted images comparable to intrahepatic vessels, with hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging. PET/CT demonstrated no abnormal ^18F-fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the nodule.

A 47-year-old woman with a 19-year history of HIV infection presented with a 5-day history of cough, chest pain, and asymptomatic bilateral cheek swelling. She was afebrile, with normal vital signs. On examination, there were mild bibasilar crackles, bilateral parotid enlargement, and a palpable 3-cm left superior cervical lymph node. Laboratory studies showed a CD4 count of 551 K/mm³ and an HIV-1 RNA load of 16 784 copies/mL. A chest radiograph demonstrated an abnormal contour along the right cardiomediastinal border. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 7.1 × 2.7 × 8.8 cm lobulated, low-attenuation mass draped across the anterior mediastinum without invasion of adjacent structures. The lesion was composed of nonenhancing cystic areas separated by enhancing septations, with average densities of 14 HU in cystic regions and 43 HU in septations.

A 58-year-old woman with no significant medical history noted a left laterocervical mass enlarging over 3 months. CT imaging showed a 25 × 28 × 44 mm laterocervical mass. In September 2019, a core-needle biopsy was reported as paraganglioma. Octreotide scintigraphy revealed uptake in the left cervical region and in the body of the stomach; endoscopic biopsies of the stomach were negative. In October 2019, the cervical mass was resected, and the initial diagnosis was extraosseous Ewing sarcoma. Upon referral, an anatomopathological review described a well-demarcated tumor composed of oval cells with clear eosinophilic cytoplasm arranged in nests separated by thin fibrous septa. Immunohistochemistry was positive for S100, SOX10, synaptophysin, and CD57; negative for Melan-A, HMB45, MITF, CD99, and multiple other markers. FISH detected an EWSR1 rearrangement that next-generation sequencing confirmed as an EWSR1-ATF1 t(12;22) fusion. A diagnosis of malignant gastrointestinal neuroectodermal tumor (GNET) was rendered. In January 2020, PET-CT showed uptake in the left laterocervical surgical bed consistent with local recurrence.

A 40-year-old woman presented with abdominal discomfort. She had undergone laparoscopic myomectomy 8 years earlier and was otherwise healthy with no medications. There was no known family history of endocrine or inherited disorders.

Vital signs were normal, and the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine biochemical tests, including serum calcium and intact parathyroid hormone, were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a multilocular 21 × 19 mm mass in the pancreatic tail. MRI showed the lesion to be low signal on T1-weighted images with heterogeneous high signal at the margins. Doppler endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated increased blood flow in the lesion and identified three additional tumors in the pancreatic body and one in the uncinate process.

EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration of one of the tumors confirmed a neuroendocrine tumor. Serum levels of gastrin, glucagon, insulin, and other endocrine studies were normal.

Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with nonfunctional multiple pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs).

A 42-year-old man presented with acute right lower abdominal pain of two days’ duration, associated with non-bilious vomiting, dysuria, and fever. The pain was aggravated by movement. He denied prior abdominal trauma or surgery and had no history of weight loss, diabetes, hypertension, tuberculosis, or pancreatitis. He worked in construction for 15 years, including daily handling of asbestos for more than 10 years.  
On examination, temperature was 39.0°C, heart rate 120 beats per minute, and blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg. There was distension and guarding in the right iliac and umbilical regions. Chest radiography and electrocardiography were normal. Sputum was negative for acid-fast bacilli.  
Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, white-cell count 6400 per µL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 16 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 51 IU/L, lipase 149 IU/L, amylase 49 IU/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, glucose 146 mg/dL, and PaO2 54 mm Hg. Urine microscopy revealed numerous red blood cells.  
Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined intra-abdominal cyst with clear internal echoes in the pelvis, compressing and displacing the urinary bladder to the left; there was no free fluid. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a solitary, well-defined intraperitoneal cyst in the pelvis containing low-attenuation fluid and surrounded by a 1-cm nonenhancing wall; it compressed the urinary bladder without communication to bowel or bladder. The pancreas and other abdominal organs were normal, and there was no ascites.  
An infected intra-abdominal cyst was diagnosed.

A 13-year-old previously healthy boy presented with three weeks of mild dyspnea, chest pain on exertion, and a newly detected cardiac murmur. He denied syncope, palpitations, fever, weight loss, recent infections, and had no history of central lines or tattoos. Family history was negative for congenital heart disease, cardiomyopathy, sudden death, or thrombophilia.

On examination, he was afebrile, heart rate 95 bpm, blood pressure 96/72 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 100%. He had a grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, normal S1 and S2, no gallops or rubs, and mild hepatomegaly. Peripheral pulses were normal. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 43 U/L, normal renal function, coagulation profile, C-reactive protein, and troponin, but an elevated NT-proBNP of 4019 pg/mL. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. 

Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm, right bundle-branch block with repolarization abnormalities in the right precordial leads, and isolated monomorphic premature ventricular contractions often in a bigeminy pattern. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 3.5 × 4.0 cm rounded, lobulated mass with clear margins and inhomogeneous content, attached by a pedicle to the infundibular septum and causing severe obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract with a peak gradient of 80 mmHg. The right atrium and right ventricle were dilated, with severe right ventricular systolic dysfunction (fractional area change 18.6%). 

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography confirmed a heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue mass occupying the right ventricular outflow tract without evidence of pulmonary embolism.

A 59‐year‐old woman was referred after an incidental finding of a brain mass on CT performed for evaluation of labyrinthitis. She was asymptomatic, with no neurologic deficits. Her medical history included hypertension and diabetes mellitus; there was no history of seizures. Laboratory studies were unremarkable.

Noncontrast head CT showed a well‐circumscribed hypodense mass in the temporal horn of the right lateral ventricle, with tiny hyperdense foci suggestive of prior microhemorrhages. Brain MRI demonstrated a lobulated intraventricular lesion measuring approximately 4.0 × 2.8 × 2.7 cm. On T1‐weighted imaging, the mass was hypointense relative to gray matter; on T2‐weighted imaging, it was heterogeneously hyperintense, with mild adjacent temporal lobe hyperintensity. Susceptibility‐weighted imaging confirmed punctate hypointense foci within the lesion. There was no or only minimal enhancement after gadolinium administration. High‐resolution 3D‐CISS sequences revealed internal cystic components. Short‐echo‐time proton spectroscopy of the lesion showed a partially decreased N‐acetylaspartate peak, a normal choline peak, and an increased myoinositol peak.

A 72-year-old man presented with 4 months of urinary hesitancy, 4 days of gross hematuria, and mild back pain. During a planned transurethral procedure for presumed benign prostatic hyperplasia, a papillary tumor was found over the right half of the trigone and left bladder neck base, with invasion into the prostate. The tumor was excised as completely as possible. 

Histologic examination of the bladder and prostate specimens revealed adenocarcinoma morphologically similar to colorectal carcinoma. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the tumor cells were positive for cytokeratin 20 (CK20) and CDX2, and negative for cytokeratin 7 (CK7) and prostate specific antigen (PSA). β-catenin staining was strongly positive in the membranous and cytoplasmic portions of the carcinoma cells. 

A colonoscopy failed to detect any malignant lesions, aside from a hamartomatous polyp in the sigmoid colon.

A 70-year-old woman presented with a 4-week history of a right-sided neck mass and a sporadic dry cough. The dry cough was unrelated to eating, talking, or movement, occurred in severe fits that sometimes induced vomiting, and was reproducibly triggered by palpation of the neck mass. She also reported intermittent hoarseness but denied dysphagia or velopharyngeal insufficiency. Her medical history was unremarkable, and there was no family history of neuroendocrine tumors.

On examination, there was a 2.5-cm right-sided level II neck mass deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The mass was discrete, mobile, nonpulsatile, and palpation immediately triggered coughing. Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy showed normal true vocal–fold appearance and movement bilaterally, with only prominent retropharyngeal carotid arteries noted. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable except for a mildly hoarse voice.

Laboratory studies, including a complete blood panel and 24-hour urinary catecholamines, were within normal limits. 

CT angiography of the neck demonstrated a 2.4 × 2.2 × 2.2-cm heterogeneously enhancing, irregular mass in the right carotid sheath lateral to the proximal internal and external carotid arteries, with minimal arterial splaying and a central area of lower attenuation suggestive of necrosis. 

MRI of the neck revealed a 2.5 × 1.9 × 3.0-cm mass extending from the inferior margin of the right carotid to the level of the piriform sinuses within the carotid sheath that enhanced intensely after contrast administration.

A 76-year-old man presented with progressive confusion and long-standing blindness of the left eye. His medical history included type II diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolemia; he had no urological complaints. On examination, he was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and neurologically nonfocal except for left-eye amaurosis. 

An axial contrast-enhanced brain CT demonstrated an irregular infiltrative hyperdense mass in the left temporal region with necrotic components, extensive osseous destruction, and extension into the orbit, sinuses, and adjacent musculature; there was left-sided exophthalmos, vasogenic edema, and a mild midline shift. T2-weighted MRI confirmed a hyperintense lesion in the left temporal lobe with osseous involvement. 

Serum PSA was 194 ng/mL.

An 18-year-old male was admitted with psychomotor excitement, polyuria, polydipsia, vomiting, and a seven-month history of progressive right-sided hemiparesis with dystonia. He had two years of poor school performance, anxiety, and emotional lability. Seven months earlier, a nonenhanced head CT was normal.

On examination, he appeared pale with a BMI of 14.4 kg/m2 and blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg with a poor response to fluids. Sexual maturation was Tanner stage 3 with small testes (6 mL) and pubic and axillary hair stage G2. Neurologically, he had right hemiparesis with hyperreflexia and dystonia. Laboratory studies showed polyuria with low urine osmolality, hypernatremia, hypotension refractory to fluid resuscitation, and panhypopituitarism, leading to treatment with hydrocortisone followed by levothyroxine and desmopressin.

Brain MRI revealed a solid, homogeneously enhancing mass in the pituitary and hypothalamus with marked pituitary stalk thickening and absence of the posterior pituitary bright spot. There was T2 hyperintensity in the left internal capsule, corona radiata, caudate nucleus, and bilateral globus pallidus, with mild atrophy of the left internal capsule and ipsilateral cerebral peduncle. Differential diagnoses included nonadenomatous lesions of the pituitary stalk and ectopic germinoma. Chest CT and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme levels were normal. Skull and long-bone radiographs showed no lytic lesions. CSF examination revealed no atypical cells; CSF α-fetoprotein was negative and CSF β-hCG was slightly elevated.

A 70-year-old Caucasian man, a non-smoker, presented with a 3-month history of 12 kg weight loss and recent generalized pruritus and jaundice. Serum biochemistry and abdominal ultrasonography confirmed obstructive jaundice. Contrast CT of the abdomen showed a 4.6×4.1 cm mass in the head of the pancreas without radiologic evidence of distant metastases. He underwent ERCP with stent placement, followed two months later by a pylorus-sparing pancreaticoduodenectomy, with an uneventful recovery.

Gross examination revealed a 5.5 cm lobulated tumor in the pancreatic head extending to the superior mesenteric vessel margin; the entire lesion was submitted for histology. Microscopically, the neoplasm consisted of large nests of basaloid cells with central necrosis and scattered small foci of squamoid differentiation. There was no morphologic evidence of glandular or acinar formation. The tumor showed extensive intravenous and intralymphatic invasion, foci of perineural invasion, extension into the duodenum, ampullary region, pancreatic duct, and peripancreatic fat, and microscopic involvement of the superior mesenteric vessel margin. Metastatic deposits with similar morphology were identified in 6 of 43 regional lymph nodes.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of polyuropolydipsic syndrome (urine output 5 L/24 h) and severe asthenia, without headache, visual disturbances, or focal neurologic signs. Routine blood and urinary ionograms, serum creatinine, and blood glucose levels were normal. Plasma osmolality was 292 mOsm/kg, and urinary osmolality was 138 mOsm/kg. Evaluation of the thyrotropic, corticotropic, and gonadotropic axes was unremarkable; prolactin was slightly elevated at 650 mU/L (reference range 99–495). She was started on oral desmopressin (0.1 mg twice daily), with symptomatic improvement of her polyuria and polydipsia. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed two intensely enhancing parietal lesions (19.3 × 17.5 × 18.2 mm on the right and 7.7 × 8.2 × 9.3 mm on the left), suggestive of metastases, and an 8-mm contrast-enhancing nodular enlargement in the supradiaphragmatic portion of the pituitary stalk, the differential diagnosis of which included a pituitary adenoma versus a secondary lesion.

A 45-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, presented at 37+4 weeks’ gestation after an obstetric ultrasound suggested a teratoma. The initial ultrasound at 37+3 weeks showed a fetal-like echo in the thoracic cavity of the fetus. On repeat examination, there was a live singleton fetus in cephalic presentation with a right retroperitoneal mass of mixed echogenicity. Two parallel fetal-like signals were seen within the mass: one exhibited a weak heartbeat, and the other was acardiac.  
Both parents were healthy, there was no history of twin gestation, and the first child had no congenital abnormalities.  
Ultrasonography revealed:  
• A 4.7 × 2.1 cm cystic-solid mass in the right retroperitoneum with intra-cyst septation and mixed echogenicity adherent to the cyst wall; no head, spine, upper limb, or heart echoes in this mass.  
• Continuous scanning showed one limb with skin covering, a long bone, distal footpad, and toe-like echoes. An umbilical cord–like vascular echo was connected to the mass, but color Doppler showed no blood flow.  
• A second 3.9 × 2.1 cm irregular mass posteriorly, lacking head, spine, or upper limbs; sagittal sections revealed a buttock-like contour, a limb with a proximal long bone and plantar echo, all covered with skin. A faint fetal heartbeat was detected in this mass; color Doppler demonstrated blood flow, and pulsed-wave Doppler showed a two-way arterial spectrum. Continuous fetal movements were observed.  
• The masses compressed the host fetus’s inferior vena cava and abdominal aorta, causing arch-shaped shifting; the intestines were displaced leftward, and the right kidney was displaced into the pelvis. Renal blood flow to the live mass derived from the host fetus’s abdominal aorta.

A 73-year-old man with a history of treated prostate cancer presented with progressive left lower-extremity weakness and numbness over several years, chronic low back pain, and constipation. On examination, there was diminished sensation in the left groin, anterior thigh, and calf; muscle strength was 4/5 in the right lower extremity and 3/5 in the left lower extremity. He had a history of resection of a lumbar spinal tumor in 1992, originally diagnosed as a paraganglioma, followed by radiation therapy in 2002. Surveillance imaging suggested increase in the lumbar lesion over time. Computed tomography of the spine showed expansion of the spinal canal by an isodense soft-tissue mass with accompanying osseous destruction. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated the mass to be hypointense on T1-weighted and T2-weighted imaging, with homogenous enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images.

A 57-year-old woman presented with a several-day history of cough and fever up to 38 °C. Over the same period, she noted changing sputum color, back pain, limb weakness, dysphagia, hemoptysis, wheezing, chest pain, and alterations in bowel habits. She denied weight loss or facial changes. Her past medical and family histories were unremarkable. Vital signs were normal. Examination revealed clear lungs, normal heart sounds, and no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

Chest CT showed a 5.5 cm × 5 cm × 1.8 cm solid mass in the anterior mediastinum with adhesion to but no definite invasion of the pericardium (Masaoka IIb). The mass was completely resected thoracoscopically. Grossly, it was encapsulated, grayish-white to grayish-brown, and had an ill-defined border against surrounding adipose tissue. 

Microscopic examination of hematoxylin–eosin–stained sections revealed multiple epithelial micronodules separated by abundant lymphoid stroma forming lymphoid follicles. No necrosis was seen. Tumor cells infiltrated surrounding adipose tissue at the periphery. Residual thymic tissue lay adjacent to the lesion. The neoplastic epithelial cells exhibited marked pleomorphism with visible nucleoli and mitotic figures ranging from 1 to 9 per 10 high-power fields.

A 43-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of a slowly enlarging swelling on the left side of her jaw that was asymptomatic until two months ago, when she experienced dull, nonradiating pain that intensified during meals and resolved spontaneously. Her medical history was notable for type 1 diabetes mellitus and dyslipidemia under treatment. On examination, there was a hard, non-tender mass adherent to the lower border of the left posterior mandible. Intraoral examination and bimanual palpation of the submandibular gland were unremarkable. Panoramic radiography revealed a well-defined, irregular radiopaque lesion in the left posterior mandible. Ultrasonography showed a normal submandibular gland and duct. Cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated a 19×12 mm radiopaque mass arising from the lingual cortex of the left posterior mandible.

A 57-year-old man with recently diagnosed stage IV non-mucinous adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon (multiple lung, liver, and nodal metastases) underwent palliative ileocolic bypass and was discharged in stable condition. Four days later, he was readmitted with fever and scrotal pain; a scrotal abscess was drained and antibiotics given. During the last three days of this admission, his wife noted that he developed small-stepped gait, slowed movements, clumsiness, and rigid posture. These neurologic signs worsened after discharge. 

On neurologic examination, he was mask-faced with slow eye movements and dysarthria. He had a resting tremor in both hands, bilateral bradykinesia, postural instability, a wide-based, festinating gait with freezing, absence of arm swing, and a bilaterally dystonic posture. Generalized hyperreflexia and plastic rigidity with cogwheeling were present; there were no cranial nerve palsies. Cognition was intact but responses were delayed. Family reported new nighttime urinary incontinence, and he was fully dependent for activities of daily living. He had no prior neurologic disease or hypertension. 

High-dose intravenous corticosteroid therapy was initiated, and an obvious improvement in the neurologic signs was observed.

A 68-year-old woman under follow-up for osteoporosis presented with symptomatic kidney stones, bone fractures, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dysphagia, and dyspnea. Laboratory studies showed a serum calcium level of 8.99 mg/dL (normal, 8.5–10.5 mg/dL), ionized calcium of 4.69 mg/dL (4.64–5.28 mg/dL), parathyroid hormone level of 191.5 pg/mL (10–65 pg/mL), and vitamin D level of 40 ng/mL (20–50 ng/mL), consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism in the setting of a normal serum calcium level. A Tc-99m sestamibi scan demonstrated a focal area of increased uptake in the anterior mediastinum on immediate imaging with decreased activity on delayed images, as well as slight uptake in the lower third of the left thyroid lobe. A subsequent CT scan revealed an 18-mm mass in the upper anterior mediastinum posterior to the sternum. Neck ultrasound identified nodules in the right thyroid lobe. Given the suspicion for an ectopic mediastinal parathyroid adenoma, she was referred for surgical resection.

In the operating room, after induction of general anesthesia with double-lumen intubation, a right uniportal video-assisted thoracic surgery approach was used to resect the mediastinal mass. The lesion was sent for frozen‐section analysis, which showed a nodular pattern composed mainly of epithelial elements mixed with a patchy lymphoid component; the epithelial cells were arranged in solid sheets and nests with occasional pseudoglandular structures, and lymphocytes were mainly at the periphery. These morphological features were interpreted as consistent with an ectopic parathyroid gland. Ten minutes after removal of the mass, the intraoperative parathyroid hormone level was 149.3 pg/mL. At 30 minutes, the parathyroid hormone level had increased to 259.5 pg/mL.

A 6-year-old boy was brought by his parents for evaluation of firm, non-fluctuant swellings of the jaws noticed 2 months earlier. He had no family history of jaw disease. On examination, there was bilateral buccal cortical expansion of the mandible from the deciduous canine to the deciduous molar, with intact overlying mucosa. Panoramic radiography showed a large, well-demarcated lesion extending from the right mandibular ramus to the left ramus, characterized by central heterogeneous mineralization surrounded by a thin radiolucent zone with a sclerotic border; several tooth germs were displaced, and multiple primary tooth roots were resorbed. A CT scan confirmed thinning of the inferior mandibular cortex, alveolar bone expansion, and a displaced maxillary tooth germ projecting into the maxillary sinus. Serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone levels were all within normal limits. Incisional biopsies of the mandibular and maxillary lesions showed fibrous stroma rich in fibroblasts with spherical calcifications; the mandibular specimen had only sparse small calcifications, whereas the maxillary specimen contained more abundant calcified spheres. Direct sequencing of GNAS (Arg201 and Gln227) and HRPT2 genes on lesion tissue showed no mutations.

A 62-year-old Hispanic woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-week history of progressive dyspnea, palpitations, profound weakness, new hot flashes, and right flank pain. Vital signs showed a heart rate of approximately 100 beats per minute and a temperature of 37.7 °C. Examination revealed pale conjunctivae without erythema or exophthalmos, a thyroid gland of normal size without nodules, a systolic tricuspid murmur, decreased basal breath sounds, and tender hepatomegaly extending 5 cm below the right costal margin. Neurologic examination demonstrated hyperreflexia and tremor. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 3054 U/L (122–222), alkaline phosphatase 434 U/L (40–129), elevated total and free thyroxine levels, and suppressed TSH. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed pulmonary hypertension (65 mmHg), right atrial and ventricular dilation, tricuspid regurgitation, preserved left ventricular function, and an atrial septal defect with right-to-left shunt. Contrast-enhanced 18 F-FDG PET-CT demonstrated hepatomegaly (22 cm) with multiple FDG-avid liver masses up to 12 cm (SUVmax 13.5), FDG uptake in the gastric antrum (SUVmax 9.4) without corresponding wall thickening, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, and small pulmonary infiltrates. A technetium-99m pertechnetate thyroid scan showed diffusely increased uptake, and assays for thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin and TSH receptor antibodies were negative. The patient was started on propranolol and methimazole for thyrotoxicosis.

A 41-year-old woman with no prior medical history was referred for evaluation of suspected early breast cancer. She was asymptomatic. On examination, there were no palpable masses in the breasts, axillae, or abdomen. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and serum tumor markers (CEA 1.8 ng/mL, CA15-3 11.4 U/mL, BCA225 30.7 U/mL, NCC-ST-439 1.3 U/mL, soluble IL-2 receptor 322 U/mL), were all within normal limits.

Mammography revealed a high-density mass with clustered microcalcifications in the inferior lateral right breast. Chest CT confirmed a well-enhancing right breast mass without axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology of the breast lesion yielded class V cells, consistent with malignancy.

As part of staging, abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass with internal blood flow signals arising from the splenic periphery. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 40-mm well-circumscribed splenic lesion with less enhancement than the surrounding parenchyma in the arterial and portal phases, becoming isodense in the delayed phase. MRI of the abdomen revealed a lesion isointense to the spleen on T1- and T2-weighted images, with slow centripetal enhancement reaching parity with the spleen at 10 minutes post-contrast. PET-CT showed no significant FDG uptake in the splenic lesion.

The preoperative differential diagnoses for the splenic mass included benign vascular neoplasms (hemangioma, lymphangioma, littoral cell angioma, hamartoma, inflammatory pseudotumor), angiosarcoma, solitary splenic metastasis of breast cancer, and primary splenic lymphoma. Given the inability to establish a definitive diagnosis noninvasively, the decision was made to perform a partial mastectomy with sentinel node biopsy and a simultaneous laparoscopic splenectomy for therapeutic diagnosis.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a productive cough of six weeks’ duration. She had no smoking history or prior medical conditions. Initial outpatient treatment with a quinolone antibiotic, a bronchodilator, and expectorants for presumed acute bronchitis failed to improve her symptoms. She subsequently developed low-grade fever and was admitted.  
On admission, temperature was 37.0 °C, blood pressure 115/66 mmHg, heart rate 83 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination revealed coarse crackles bilaterally; no peripheral edema was noted.  
Chest radiograph showed diffuse ground-glass opacities, reticular shadows in both lung fields, and right hilar enlargement. Chest CT revealed multiple small nodules, interlobular septal thickening, irregular bronchovascular bundle thickening, ground-glass opacities, reticular shadows, bilateral pleural effusions, and enlarged supraclavicular, mediastinal, and hilar lymph nodes.  
Abdominal CT demonstrated gallbladder wall thickening, a 3 cm mass in the gallbladder body, a low-density lesion in segment 5 of the right hepatic lobe adjacent to the gallbladder bed, porta hepatis and para-aortic lymphadenopathy, and only slight intrahepatic bile duct dilatation.  
Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14.2×10^3/µL with 17.2% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count 2442/µL), LDH 517 IU/L, CRP 5.27 mg/dL, serum CEA 9.7 ng/mL, CA 19-9 395 U/mL, and CA-125 160 U/mL.  
Based on the CT and tumor markers, gallbladder cancer with liver metastasis versus acute cholecystitis with liver abscess was suspected. Chest CT findings also raised concern for multiple metastatic lung tumors or lymphangitic carcinomatosis. Peripheral eosinophilia prompted consideration of drug reaction, parasitic infection, or malignancy; pulmonary sarcoidosis was considered but serum ACE and KL-6 levels were not elevated.

A 52-year-old self-employed man presented with a 5-year history of “allergic rhinitis and sinusitis” managed without standard therapy and a 3-year history of an indeterminate lung shadow. Over four years he had recurrent upper abdominal pain, anorexia, and 10 kg weight loss. Laboratory testing showed a marked peripheral eosinophilia (peak 64.5 × 10^9 cells/L, 78.2%). 

Serial gastroscopy and biopsies demonstrated moderate chronic gastritis, focal glandular epithelial atypia, and eosinophil-rich exudate. Pancreatic head biopsy showed bloody effusion with eosinophils and neutrophils. Abdominal CT and PET-CT revealed a bulky pancreatic head (interpreted as pancreatitis) and mild gastric wall thickening (inflammation versus lymphoma). Chest imaging showed multiple patchy and cord-like pulmonary opacities and mildly enlarged mediastinal nodes.

On admission for evaluation of the lung shadow and hypereosinophilia, his oxygen saturation was 90% on room air, and he had a scattered erythematous rash on both lower limbs. A bronchoscopy with right lower lobe biopsy showed abundant eosinophils, histiocytes and lymphocytes in the alveolar interstitium, and eosinophilic infiltration of small vessel walls. Immunohistochemical findings were CD3(+), CD5(–), CD4(–), CD8(individual+), CD56(–), CD20(–), CD30(+), Ki-67 30%+, with EBER(–) and negative fungal and acid-fast stains. 

Based on these findings, the provisional differential diagnosis included eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, pending characterization of sinus lesions, and eosinophilic gastritis.
