A 55-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of right-sided abdominal pain. MRI of the abdomen revealed a 9.7 × 9.2 × 8.0 cm right renal mass invading the hepatic lobe. Chest CT demonstrated multiple small bilateral pulmonary nodules. He underwent cytoreductive right nephrectomy with partial hepatic resection. Pathology showed 10 cm clear-cell RCC, Fuhrman grade 4 with sarcomatoid differentiation, lymphovascular invasion, direct liver capsule invasion, negative margins, and pT4 N0 M1 stage.

Six weeks postoperatively, CT showed progression of pulmonary metastases. He was intermediate risk by the IMDC model and started sunitinib. After two cycles, he developed severe right upper-quadrant pain. CT at 12 weeks showed increased bilateral lung nodules, an 8 × 5 cm recurrence at the nephrectomy bed, multiple new liver lesions, and a 3.4 cm heterogeneous filling defect in the right ventricle. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 5.6 × 3.0 cm echogenic mass extending from the RV inflow to outflow tract with mobile components, and a separate 4.0 × 2.2 cm mass in the RV apex; right and left ventricular size and systolic function were normal, ejection fraction 50%, inferior vena cava and pulmonary valve uninvolved.

Cardiac MRI at 1.5 Tesla showed a large RV lesion invading 47 mm of the interventricular septum and extending into the RV outflow tract with no IVC involvement. Further tissue characterization revealed: (a) isointense signal on cine, low intensity on pre-contrast T1-weighted images; (b) high T2 signal intensity with absent first-pass perfusion; and (c) heterogeneous enhancement after contrast.

A 53-year-old woman with no family history of cancer presented with a lump in her left breast. Physical examination revealed a movable, painless, 3 cm nodule between the upper and lower inner quadrants of the left breast, without inflammatory signs or nipple retraction; the axillae were clinically negative. Mammography demonstrated a nodular lesion with irregular contours and peripheral calcification, classified as BI-RADS 4. Ultrasonography confirmed a 32 mm hypoechoic nodule with irregular, polylobed margins in the same location. An ultrasound-guided core-needle biopsy was performed. Histopathological examination showed spindle cell proliferation without hemorrhage or necrosis. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed positivity for cytokeratin AE1/AE3 and smooth muscle actin, a Ki-67 labeling index of 25%, and nuclear p63 expression. The pathology report concluded a spindle cell carcinomatous proliferation.

A 53-year-old man with hypertension presented with five days of intractable vomiting, generalized weakness, ataxia, and severe headaches. On examination, he was lethargic, retching frequently, and had bilateral papilledema with impaired upward and downward gaze; gait could not be assessed safely. CT and MRI of the brain demonstrated hydrocephalus from obstruction of the third ventricle by a 2.5 × 3.0 × 3.2 cm hyperdense, contrast-enhancing mass centered in the pineal region with central calcification and mass effect on an edematous midbrain. 

He underwent endoscopic biopsy with third ventriculostomy and external ventricular drainage, followed by a subtotal resection via a supracerebellar infratentorial craniotomy. Histologic examination showed a highly cellular neoplasm of primitive round cells with finely dispersed chromatin, scant cytoplasm, brisk mitotic activity (20 per 10 high-power fields), focal papillary arrangements, and vague rosettes. Immunohistochemistry revealed strong positivity for synaptophysin, neuron-specific enolase, cytokeratin 8/18, CK AE1/AE3, and CAM 5.2; focal positivity for chromogranin, S100, and neurofilament; negativity for CK7, CK20, epithelial membrane antigen, thyroid transcription factor-1, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and parathyroid hormone; intact INI1; and a Ki-67 index of 60–70%. 

A PET/CT scan showed FDG avidity solely in the pineal region. A small, non–FDG-avid lesion in the left renal upper pole was noted incidentally.

A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with abnormal vaginal bleeding. Hysteroscopy identified and resected a 2 cm polypoid mass in the right lateral uterine wall. Histologic examination of the biopsy showed mucinous adenocarcinoma with glandular and solid architecture, intra- and extra-glandular necrosis, neoplastic cells with pale eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, variable intracytoplasmic mucin, mild to moderate nuclear atypia, and a high mitotic rate with atypical figures. Immunohistochemistry revealed diffuse positivity for CK20, CDX2, and p16; focal positivity for CK7 and PAX8; negative estrogen and progesterone receptors; a wild-type p53 pattern; focal (< 10%) chromogranin A and synaptophysin positivity; and intact MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, and MSH6 expression. A diagnosis of high-grade adenocarcinoma with mucinous features, highly suspicious for metastatic origin, was initially rendered. Subsequent ultrasound demonstrated only a superficial minimal residual endometrial lesion without myometrial or adnexal involvement. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, PET, and MRI were all unremarkable.

A 56-year-old Korean woman noted acute onset of fingertip pain, paresthesia, and color changes. Over 6 weeks, she developed digital ulcerations despite hydroxychloroquine. She was subsequently treated with an angiotensin receptor blocker, amlodipine, fluoxetine, topical nitroglycerin, and an oral prostacyclin analogue without improvement. Four months after onset, she reported malaise, fatigue, night sweats, alopecia, and dry eyes. Physical examination confirmed digital ulcerations; vital signs were unremarkable. Laboratory studies included a panel of markers for autoimmune and inflammatory disease, all within normal limits. To evaluate for malignancy, a CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was obtained and revealed peritoneal carcinomatosis with omental caking. Serum CA-125 was 862 U/mL; CEA and CA19-9 were normal.

A 53-year-old woman had a 3-year history of a burning sensation in her mouth and esophagus, leading to a 50-pound weight loss, followed by the development of skin lesions. On examination, there was diffuse intense erythema of the oral mucosa—most pronounced on the gingiva and cheeks—with a reddish, glazed tongue without atrophy and a crusted cheilitis. There was also diffuse vulvar erythema and an anal marisca. The skin of the trunk, pubis, and limbs showed crusted, hyperkeratotic follicular plaques, open comedones, and papulopustules. Both palms and soles had well-demarcated erythematous plaques. Gastroscopy revealed linear ulcerations of the esophagus. Antifungal therapy with oral fluconazole and amphotericin B solution was ineffective. Laboratory studies showed no vitamin B12 or iron deficiency, and serum zinc levels were normal. Topical and systemic corticosteroids did not help. Colonoscopy was normal. Serum glucagon levels were normal, and pancreas CT and MRI showed no abnormalities. Direct and indirect immunofluorescence studies were negative, and antibodies against desmoglein 1 and 3, envoplakin, and periplakin were undetectable. A thoracoabdominal and pelvic CT scan was normal.

A 32‐year‐old Asian man presented with a 1‐year history of a right neck mass. His past medical history was noncontributory. On extraoral examination, there was a soft, slightly movable mass in the right submandibular region with normal overlying skin; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Computed tomography of the neck revealed a well‐defined, mixed‐density lesion measuring approximately 5 × 3 cm adjacent to the right submandibular gland. Subsequent image segmentation suggested that the lesion contained components of fat, connective tissue, and osteoid. Primary differential diagnoses based on imaging included pleomorphic adenoma of the submandibular gland, teratoma, and osteo/chondroid lipoma.

An 18-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of slowly enlarging gingival overgrowth in the left posterior mandible that interfered with chewing but was painless. Intraoral examination revealed a 3×4 cm exophytic mass extending from the left mandibular second molar to the retromolar pad, buccally into the vestibule and inferiorly to the floor of the mouth. Panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined radiolucency around the impacted left third molar. The lesion and the impacted tooth were excised en bloc. 

Grossly, the specimen included both intraosseous and extraosseous components. Histologic examination demonstrated cords, interconnecting strands, and islands of odontogenic epithelium embedded in a cell-rich, myxoid mesenchymal stroma. The epithelial strands and cords were lined by a double layer of cuboidal cells. The islands exhibited peripheral tall columnar cells with polarized nuclei and clear, vacuolated cytoplasm surrounding central stellate reticulum-like cells. Juxtaepithelial hyalinization was noted around some islands. No hard-tissue (enamel or dentin) formation was seen. The cellularity varied, with focal hypercellular areas and other sparsely cellular, myxoid regions. A thin fibrous capsule partially surrounded the lesion. No cytologic atypia or mitotic figures were observed on multiple sections.

A 46-year-old perimenopausal woman presented with a 4-month history of right axillary swelling that was insidious, gradually progressive, and associated with pain, foul-smelling discharge, and intermittent bleeding. Three months earlier, fine needle aspiration cytology of the axillary mass revealed metastatic carcinoma favoring adenocarcinoma, and she received three cycles of epirubicin and cyclophosphamide without response; the mass enlarged with increased bleeding and ulceration. She had no medical comorbidities or family history of malignancy. Menarche was at age 14, with regular cycles; she had two children (first birth at age 22). 

On examination, her performance status was ECOG 1; vital signs were stable, and pallor was present. Both breasts and the left axilla were unremarkable. In the right axilla there was a 7 cm × 6 cm ulceroproliferative, firm, tender mass with limited mobility, overlying ulceration, and bleeding. A single 2-cm, mobile, firm, nontender level I axillary lymph node was palpable. Other systems were normal. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 6 g/dL. Review of the prior cytology confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma. 

Whole-body FDG-PET showed a large lobulated, heterogeneously enhancing soft tissue mass in the right axillary tail (8.8 × 9.5 × 7 cm; SUV max 27.9) infiltrating skin and subcutaneous tissue of the proximal arm, with FDG-avid right axillary and subpectoral lymph nodes (largest 2.4 × 1.4 cm; SUV max 13.6). Both breasts appeared normal, and no other FDG-avid lesions were identified. 

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the breast and axilla revealed a well-defined, lobulated, heterogeneously enhancing hyperintense lesion (10.6 × 9.7 × 7.6 cm) epicentered in the right axillary recess, probably arising from the axillary tail of the right breast, closely abutting the lateral chest wall muscles and axillary vessels, with a few enlarged axillary nodes; both breasts were unremarkable.

A 50-year-old Caucasian man presented with a dull, long-standing pain in the dorsolateral region of the left chest. He denied trauma, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. On examination, he had limited movement at the waist without motor or sensory abnormalities; the neurological examination was otherwise normal. Laboratory tests—including blood cell count, serum electrolytes, renal and liver function, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein—were all within normal limits. Chest radiographs were unremarkable. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax showed a widening of the left T10 costovertebral joint with scalloping and mild sclerosis of the left aspect of the T10 vertebral body, partially involving the left pedicle and adjacent costal bone. FDG PET-CT revealed no significant tracer uptake at this site. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated non-specific changes at the left T10 costovertebral junction, including bone marrow edema in the T10 vertebral body, pedicle, and adjacent costal bone (low signal on T1-weighted images and high signal on T2-weighted fat-saturated images) with non-specific contrast enhancement and no spinal canal invasion.

A fluoroscopy-guided needle biopsy of the T10 vertebral body yielded fibrous/myxoid tissue with reactive lymphocytes and plasma cells and rare histiocytic elements resembling a non-specific chronic osteomyelitic pattern. A CD1a immunostain was performed to further characterize the lesion.

A 37-year-old woman presented 2 weeks after cesarean section with a 2-week history of cough, dyspnea, and head and neck swelling. Symptoms had begun in pregnancy and worsened over the last few days. The cough was nonproductive, with no hemoptysis. She had no history of cardiac or pulmonary disease or risk factors such as alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drugs.

On examination, heart rate was 110/min, blood pressure 110/75 mmHg, and she was afebrile. There was slight respiratory discomfort but no cyanosis. Lung fields were clear; heart sounds revealed wide fixed splitting of S2 without murmur. There was no clinical evidence of right heart failure.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a severely dilated right atrium and right ventricle, a nonmobile 6.5 cm² mass attached to the right atrial wall, and a secundum-type atrial septal defect measuring 2.44 cm with a left-to-right shunt (QP/QS 2.9). A large extracardiac mass (8.7 × 4.3 cm) anterior to the ascending aorta was also noted.

Chest CT and pulmonary CT angiography demonstrated a lobulated anterior mediastinal soft-tissue mass (105 × 46 mm), suggestive of thymoma, teratoma, thyroid goiter, lymphoma, or germ cell tumor, with extension of thrombosis into the brachiocephalic veins, superior vena cava (SVC), and right atrium, as well as multiple pulmonary nodules. Abdominal and pelvic CT were unremarkable. Serum alpha-fetoprotein was 5000 ng/mL; blood cultures were negative.

At this point, by considering the findings of physical and laboratory examinations, echocardiography, thoracic CT scan, and pulmonary CT angiography, a mediastinal malignancy with cardiac and lung metastasis was at the top of our differential diagnoses. Atrial thrombosis was another potential diagnosis due to the hypercoagulable state because of the post‐partum period and the mediastinal probable malignancy. On the other hand, the absence of fever, negative blood culture, and no history of IV drug abuse made endocarditis vegetation a less likely diagnosis.

A 59-year-old Hispanic man with known neurofibromatosis type 1 presented with a 1-month history of episodic epigastric pain, pruritus, a 15-pound weight loss, and progressive jaundice. On examination he was deeply icteric; pulse 118 /min, respiratory rate 20 /min, blood pressure 116/80 mm Hg, temperature 98.3 °F. The abdomen was mildly distended with an enlarged, non-tender liver and widespread excoriations. His skin showed >10 cutaneous fibromas, multiple café-au-lait spots >1.5 cm, and extensive axillary freckling, meeting criteria for NF 1. 

Initial laboratory studies demonstrated a cholestatic liver profile with normal blood counts. Abdominal ultrasound showed marked intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary dilatation with the proximal common bile duct measuring 17 mm. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 4.5 × 5 × 3.4 cm hypoenhancing soft-tissue mass in the porta hepatis encasing the portal vein and common hepatic artery and extending toward the pancreatic head. MRCP confirmed an abrupt occlusion in the mid common bile duct; the pancreatic duct was normal. Additional imaging identified a 5 cm hypoenhancing splenic mass and a 4.5 × 4.5 × 2.8 cm retroperitoneal hypodense mass.

On hospital day 2, a lipid panel showed total cholesterol >1,000 mg/dL, HDL 19 mg/dL, triglycerides 233 mg/dL, and LDL >1,000 mg/dL; a repeat test confirmed these values. ERCP demonstrated a tight 6 cm proximal CBD stricture with marked biliary dilatation. After biliary sphincterotomy and placement of self-expanding metallic stents, the patient’s jaundice improved and serum cholesterol levels declined steadily.

A 63-year-old woman was referred with progressive generalized fatigue, proximal muscle weakness, insomnia, flushing, hypertension, impaired concentration, memory difficulties, and hypomanic symptoms. She reported a 5-kg weight loss over several months despite features of Cushing’s syndrome. Her history included breast cancer 16 years earlier and a superficial melanoma with no recurrence.

On examination she had moon facies, supraclavicular fat, a buffalo hump, chin hirsutism, and proximal myopathy. Laboratory studies showed a 24-hour urinary free cortisol of 1300 nmol (reference <183 nmol), serum cortisol levels of 600–1000 nmol/L without diurnal variation, and plasma ACTH levels of 30–45 ng/L throughout 24 hours. There was no suppression on 1-mg or 8-mg dexamethasone tests.

An MRI of the sella turcica showed no pituitary lesion. Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling after CRH stimulation demonstrated no central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient and no ACTH increase. Fasting CRH was normal at 3.5 pmol/L. Urinary catecholamines and hydroxyindoleacetic acid were normal. Chromogranin A was mildly elevated.

A CT scan of the neck, chest, and abdomen revealed only slight enlargement of the left adrenal gland with an attenuation of 25 Hounsfield units. A whole-body planar 111In-pentetreotide somatostatin receptor scintigraphy scan demonstrated no uptake typical of an ectopic ACTH source.

A 48-year-old man with no specific medical history presented with a 1-month history of intermittent obstructive abdominal pain initially treated symptomatically with slight improvement. Over time, his abdominal pain worsened and he developed weight loss and asthenia. On examination, he was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and had tenderness in the right iliac fossa; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Viral serologic tests for HIV, HBV, HCV, and syphilis were negative; Epstein–Barr virus serology was positive. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 36 mm long segment of regular, pseudo-stenotic circumferential wall thickening of the terminal ileum, with discrete infiltration of the adjacent mesenteric fat, associated with distension of proximal small bowel and ascending colon.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 3-week history of bilateral mandibular swelling and morning purulent oral discharge. She was otherwise well, with stable vital signs. On examination, there was bilateral facial swelling in the mandibular region, multiple dark brown nevi on the palms and soles (unchanged in size for ≥5 years), and clinical macrocephaly. Intraorally, there was bilateral buccal cortical expansion in the posterior mandible with moderate pus discharge adjacent to tooth 36; teeth were firm and without paresthesia.

Orthopantomogram showed expansile radiolucent lesions in the mandible bilaterally, extending from the first molar region to the coronoid processes, with impacted second and third molars displaced into the coronoid areas and cortical thinning and erosion at multiple sites. A smaller radiolucent lesion with an impacted third molar was seen in the maxilla. 

Incisional biopsy from multiple sites revealed a parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelial lining, six to eight cell layers thick, with surface corrugation and basal cell palisading, and a moderately collagenous fibrous capsule. The mandibular lesions were initially marsupialized; three months later, enucleation specimens showed similar histology plus budding of basal epithelial cells, keratin-filled daughter cysts, odontogenic epithelial islands, and focal crowding with mild atypia of basal and parabasal layers.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the head demonstrated calcifications within the falx cerebri. A chest radiograph was normal.

A 46-year-old woman presented with progressive fatigue and shortness of breath. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (WBC 27×10^3/mm^3) with neutrophilia and monocytosis (monocytes 14%), anemia (hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL), and thrombocytopenia (platelets 96×10^3/mm^3). A bone marrow biopsy showed a markedly hypercellular marrow with myeloid hyperplasia, approximately 4% blasts, and 10% monocytes; cytogenetics were normal, and next-generation sequencing detected pathogenic NPM1 and NRAS mutations and an ETV6 variant of uncertain significance. The findings were interpreted as MDS/MPN unclassifiable, and the patient was started on hydroxyurea. Two months later, a repeat marrow biopsy demonstrated myelomonocytic hyperplasia, trilineage dysplasia, mild reticulin fibrosis, and a karyotype of 47,XX,+21/46,XX, consistent with CMML-2. Despite treatment, monocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukocytosis persisted, with 6% blasts in peripheral blood. CT imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed bilateral axillary, mediastinal, right hilar, and inguinal lymphadenopathy, prominent nasopharyngeal lymphoid tissue, and hepatosplenomegaly.

A 33-year-old Guinean woman with a history of diabetes and prior splenectomy presented with chronic left upper-quadrant abdominal pain and a progressively enlarging mass. On examination, there was a fixed deep mass in the left upper quadrant extending below the costal margin. Carcinoembryonic antigen and CA19-9 levels were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 104 × 77 × 44 mm, rounded, well-defined lesion appearing attached to the gastric wall, with both cystic and solid components and scattered calcifications; there were no signs of local invasion or metastases.

A 64-year-old man presented with two days of worsening pain in the left posterior thigh associated with an enlarging mass. He reported that the mass had been slowly growing for 12 years but had only recently become painful. He denied trauma and was not on anticoagulation. On examination, there was a large, firm, tense, relatively non-tender mass in the left posterior thigh. Strength and range of motion at the knee were full, and sensation was intact distally without paresthesias.

Contrast CT and MRI of the thigh demonstrated a 16.0 × 13.7 × 17.1 cm multiloculated, cystic mass in the posterior compartment with fluid–fluid levels, a thick fibrous rim, and splaying of adjacent muscles; the femoral cortex was abutted without invasion. Proximal and distal segments of the sciatic nerve were visualized, but the nerve was not seen at the mass level. The radiology report favored a chronic hematoma.

Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded 1.8 L of serosanguinous fluid. Cultures were negative. Cytology showed scattered lymphocytes, blood clot, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages without atypical cells, again suggesting chronic hematoma. Within 48 hours, the fluid had reaccumulated.

An open irrigation and debridement with biopsy was performed. Approximately 1.5 L of bloody fluid was evacuated through a rind-like capsule, and small areas of solid hypertrophic tissue at the periphery were sampled. No large bleeding vessel was identified, but diffuse capillary oozing prompted specimen collection for pathology. A vacuum-assisted closure device was placed.

Four days later, repeat irrigation and debridement revealed another substantial blood collection despite the VAC. Two dilated, thrombosed vessels were debrided, and fibrin sealant was applied to all exposed surfaces. Two drains were placed, the hamstring was imbricated to obliterate dead space, and multilayered closure with compressive wrapping was performed.

A 52-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a one-month history of constipation, vague abdominal pain, hematochezia, and a pedunculated sigmoid-colon mass found on rigid sigmoidoscopy. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia; other findings were normal. Colonoscopy revealed a fungating obstructive tumor in the distal sigmoid colon (20 cm from the anal verge). Biopsy suggested a gastrointestinal stromal tumor of uncertain malignant potential. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a 5 cm eccentric, irregularly enhancing sigmoid-colon wall thickening with perirectal lymphadenopathy, consistent with T3/T4a N1 M0 (stage IIIB) disease. She underwent a laparoscopic low anterior resection. Grossly, there was a 3.8 cm × 2.5 cm umbilicated polypoid mass in the distal sigmoid colon infiltrating the mesocolic fat. Histologically, the lesion comprised geographic sheets and nests of uniformly small bland cells infiltrating the muscular wall and fat, with prominent small arterioles, extensive lymphovascular invasion, and regional nodal metastases; mitotic figures and necrosis were absent. Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse positivity for CD10, estrogen receptor, and progesterone receptor; negativity for c-kit, CD34, Dog1, α-smooth muscle actin, S100, desmin, and pan-cytokeratin; and a Ki-67 index of 8%.

A 63-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a progressively enlarging cervical mass. He had no personal or family history of neoplasms. Laboratory evaluation showed a thyroid-stimulating hormone level of 56 µIU/mL (elevated), free T3 of 2.4 pmol/L, and free T4 of 10 pmol/L; antithyroglobulin antibodies were within the normal range. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a 4.5 × 4.0 × 4.5 cm calcified mass in the left thyroid lobe causing tracheal compression and deviation, as well as two smooth, homogeneous nodules in the right thyroid lobe. MRI demonstrated that the epicenter of the left-lobe mass was within the thyroid gland, with no invasion of the adjacent thyroid cartilage. The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with cervical lymph node dissection. Gross examination showed a gray, lobulated, firm mass with calcifications occupying most of the left lobe, and two gray, firm, oval nodules in the right lobe.

A 35-year-old man with no past medical history presented with intermittent fever and myalgia of 1 month’s duration. On examination, his temperature was 39.2°C. Both upper arms were swollen and exquisitely tender, but the overlying skin appeared normal.  
  
Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 20 440/mm3 with a differential of 7% segmented neutrophils, 22% lymphocytes, and 40% blast cells, and a lactate dehydrogenase level of 977 U/L.  

Ultrasonography of the upper arms showed diffusely increased echogenicity and thickening of the triceps and brachialis muscles. MRI confirmed diffuse muscle edema without abscess formation.  

A muscle biopsy of the left triceps and brachialis revealed severe myositis with dense infiltration of mature neutrophils, disruption of muscle architecture, and tissue necrosis. Microbiological cultures and stains for bacteria and fungi were negative, and serologic testing for autoantibodies was also negative.

A 3-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of left thigh swelling. The swelling was insidious, progressive, and painful—worse at night and aggravated by movement—and was accompanied by fever, local warmth, weight loss, and anorexia. There was no abdominal pain.  
On radiographs of the left femur, there was an ill-defined expansile lytic lesion of the diaphysis and distal metaphysis with lamellated (“onion-peel”) and focal sunburst periosteal reactions; no fracture was seen.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 7220 cells/µL, hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, hematocrit 24%, platelets 190,000/µL, C-reactive protein 81.5 mg/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 468 U/L.  
High-resolution ultrasonography of the thigh revealed a vascular soft-tissue mass with spiculated sunburst periosteal reaction.  
A provisional diagnosis of a primary bone tumor was made.

A 73-year-old woman with a history of poorly differentiated caecal adenocarcinoma (T4N2M0) treated by right hemicolectomy, incomplete adjuvant chemotherapy, and radiotherapy to para-aortic lymph nodes, presented three years after radiotherapy with a rapidly enlarging, painless, left-sided neck lump. She had no dysphagia, odynophagia, dysphonia, weight loss, or appetite change. On examination, there was a smooth, nonfluctuant, non-tethered 6-mm level IV lymph node. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function, were normal; carcinoembryonic antigen was elevated at 24.0 mg/L (normal <2.5 mg/L). Ultrasound of the lump showed a 6-mm level IV cervical lymph node with intranodal calcifications, loss of hilar architecture, and increased vascularity. Fine-needle aspiration cytology demonstrated clusters of atypical cells with pleomorphic nuclei and moderate cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical analysis of the cell block preparation showed cells positive for cytokeratin AE1/AE3 and CDX2. Whole-body PET-CT revealed elevated tracer uptake in an 8.4-mm left level IV node and a 7-mm left supraclavicular node, with no further evidence of thoracic or abdominal disease.

An 86-year-old man presented with acute shortness of breath and several months of unexplained weight loss. He reported recent high-impact falls, having undergone right hip hemiarthroplasty for a femoral fracture. On examination he was hypoxic with peripheral edema but had no fever, night sweats, or other constitutional symptoms. Laboratory studies showed elevated alkaline phosphatase and D-dimer levels; hemoglobin was chronically low without an acute drop, and the white-cell count, neutrophil count, and C-reactive protein were normal. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 13 × 12 × 24 cm heterogeneous complex cystic hypoenhancing lesion in the left retroperitoneum posterior to the left kidney, with attenuation values of 9–32 Hounsfield units, displacing the kidney, encasing the renal vasculature and collecting system, and causing mild hydronephrosis. MRI showed heterogeneous T2-weighted hyperintensity with multicystic areas; multiple T1-weighted hyperintense foci consistent with hemorrhage; chemical shift imaging demonstrated microscopic lipid content by signal loss on out-of-phase images in the superior portion of the cystic component; there was diffusion restriction in the peripheral solid regions; and post-contrast fat-saturated T1 images revealed avid enhancement of the thick peripheral walls and internal septations.

A 16-month-old boy presented with sudden-onset difficulty in breathing for 1 day. He had a 3-day febrile illness with coryzal symptoms that resolved 2 days before presentation. There was no history of foreign-body aspiration or trauma. His birth and developmental histories were unremarkable.

On examination, he was afebrile, with moderate respiratory distress (subcostal, intercostal, and suprasternal retractions) and a respiratory rate of 50 breaths per minute. He had a loud expiratory grunt; chest expansion was reduced on the right, dull to percussion, with markedly diminished air entry over the mid and lower zones and no added sounds. Oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Heart rate was 140 beats per minute, and blood pressure was 94/60 mmHg; heart sounds and the remainder of the examination were normal.

A chest radiograph showed a well-demarcated opacity occupying the right mid and lower hemithorax, with mediastinal shift to the left and obscuration of the right cardiac and diaphragmatic borders. Ultrasound of the chest suggested a septate right pleural effusion. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 17,000/mm³ (neutrophils 7300/mm³, lymphocytes 8100/mm³, eosinophils 300/mm³), hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, platelets 607,000/mm³, and C-reactive protein 10.5 mg/L; electrolyte, renal, and liver tests were normal.

He was started on intravenous cefotaxime for presumed pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion. Because of the absence of fever, minimal inflammatory findings, and the atypical radiographic appearance, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax was obtained. The scan demonstrated a large, multiloculated, extrapulmonary cystic lesion occupying the right hemithorax, with leftward mediastinal shift, displacement of right-sided mediastinal structures (including the superior and inferior vena cava), narrowing of the right main pulmonary artery, and compression of the right lung; the lung parenchyma was otherwise normal.

A 72-year-old woman presented with postmenopausal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a mass extending from the uterine body into the cervical canal. Her medical history included appendectomy and cholecystectomy. Laboratory studies showed a cancer antigen 125 level of 113 U/mL (normal 0–35 U/mL), cancer antigen 19–9 of 63.7 U/mL (normal 0–37 U/mL), and lactate dehydrogenase of 277 IU/L (isoenzymes LD1 32%, LD2 33.8%, LD3 20.6%, LD4 7.2%, LD5 6.4%). 

Endometrial biopsy demonstrated spindle-shaped cell proliferation covered by non-atypical epithelium. Immunohistochemical staining of the stromal cells was positive for h-caldesmon, α-smooth muscle actin, STAT6, and MDM2, weakly positive for CDK4, and negative for CD34, CD99, and ALK. 

Pelvic MRI showed an 11 × 5 × 7 cm heterogeneous high-intensity mass within the uterine cavity extending into the cervix without myometrial invasion; it exhibited low signal intensity with areas of slight T1 high intensity, low apparent diffusion coefficient (0.97 × 10^−3 mm^2/s), inhomogeneous post-contrast enhancement, and high diffusion-weighted signal. Whole-body 18F-FDG PET-MRI demonstrated increased FDG uptake in the uterine mass (SUVmax 6.2). 

Differential diagnoses based on the imaging and biopsy findings included uterine sarcoma, carcinosarcoma, and adenosarcoma.

A 61-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of discomfort and a gradually enlarging lump at the base of her right thumb and thenar eminence. Her medical history included osteoarthritis of the right thumb, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia; she was an ex-smoker with moderate alcohol use. Family history was noncontributory.

On examination, there was a mildly tender, circumferential mass extending from the thumb base to the proximal phalanx with no movement at the metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joints; neurovascular function was intact.

A radiograph of the right thumb showed soft-tissue swelling over the dorsolateral aspect without bony scalloping or erosion and degenerative changes at the metacarpophalangeal joint. Ultrasound revealed a multilobulated hypoechoic lesion up to 6 cm surrounding the flexor pollicis longus tendon. MRI demonstrated a 4.6 × 2.9 × 6.7 cm multilobulated mass encasing the flexor pollicis longus tendon and surrounding the first proximal phalanx, metacarpophalangeal joint, and first metacarpal, with intermediate T1 signal, T2 hyperintensity, and heterogeneous postcontrast enhancement.

An ultrasound-guided biopsy showed an atypical cartilaginous lesion with mild-to-moderate cytological atypia abutting bone but without bony infiltration; high-grade malignant features were not identified.

A 70-year-old man was referred with a 6-week history of a left-sided scrotal swelling that was not painful but had increased in size. His medical history included hypertension, eczema, and a right orchidectomy with chemotherapy for seminoma 25 years earlier. On examination, he had a large left hemi-scrotal swelling with an impalpable left testis.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 131 g/L, normal inflammatory markers, lactate dehydrogenase 743 IU/L (elevated), alpha-fetoprotein 4 ku/L (normal), and β-hCG 3 IU/L (upper limit of normal 2 IU/L).

Scrotal ultrasound revealed a grossly enlarged left testicle with heterogeneous echotexture, loss of normal architecture, and chaotic intratesticular perfusion on color Doppler. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated a left testicular soft-tissue mass extending through the left spermatic cord into the left gonadal vein up to the level of the left kidney, with an additional large left suprarenal soft-tissue mass. 

FDG-PET showed intense uptake in the left testicular mass, the extending gonadal-venous soft-tissue, and the left suprarenal mass.

A 12-year-old boy presented with a 5-day history of atraumatic, progressively worsening right hip pain. He and his parents recalled a possible low-energy fall around the onset of pain, but could not definitively link the two. He was initially evaluated at an outside emergency department, where his erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, white blood cell count, and hip radiographs were normal, and he was diagnosed with transient synovitis. The following night he awoke with severe hip pain and was unable to bear weight. He returned to the outside emergency department, was given additional nonsteroidal antiinflammatories, and was referred to an orthopedic surgeon due to concern for septic arthritis.

On arrival at our pediatric emergency department, he reported severe right hip pain that prevented weight bearing and woke him from sleep. He was afebrile. Examination revealed that he held the hip in flexion, abduction, and external rotation. Within a moderate arc of motion he had minimal discomfort, but internal rotation, especially with the hip flexed, reproduced significant pain. He was tender over the medial groin and adductor tendons. His temperature was 37.0 °C. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 6050/mm3, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 42 mm/hr, and a C-reactive protein level of 6.6 mg/dL. Radiographs of the hip showed evidence of an effusion, confirmed by ultrasonography. An ultrasound-guided arthrocentesis yielded grossly bloody joint fluid with a white-cell count of 54 999/mm3, a red-cell count of 7000/mm3, and a negative Gram stain. Given equivocal findings, an MRI of the right hip with and without contrast was obtained. MRI demonstrated a 2.5 × 2.1 × 1.4 cm heterogeneous intra-articular mass in the anterior-inferior joint space that was hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images, with enhancement, a moderate joint effusion, and synovitis.

A 13-year-old boy with a history of asthma presented with a 3-month history of progressive lower extremity weakness and balance problems, resulting in multiple falls and the need to hold onto objects to walk. There was no history of trauma, intercurrent illness, or new medications.  
On examination, he had a positive Romberg sign, weakness of hip flexion and ankle dorsiflexion, intact reflexes, and no dysmetria or tremor.  
MRI of the spine showed a mass centered in the T10 vertebral body, extending into the posterior elements, epidural space, and paraspinal region. The lesion was heterogeneously T2 hyperintense with multiple serpentine T2 hypointense areas (suggestive of flow voids), demonstrated avid contrast enhancement, and showed facilitated diffusion. There was severe spinal canal narrowing with cord compression and T2 hyperintensity within the cord, as well as narrowing of the bilateral T10/T11 neuroforamina. No other spinal lesions were identified.  
Subsequent CT of the thoracic spine confirmed a T10 lesion with thickened, striated trabeculae, scattered areas of osteolysis, asymmetric enlargement of the T10 segmental arteries, and hypertrophy of paravertebral veins. CT of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no additional lesions.  
Given these findings, what is your leading diagnosis and what alternatives should be considered?

A 43-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of painful, blurred vision in her left eye.  
On examination:  
• Visual acuity was 6/6 in the right eye and counting fingers at 1 ft in the left eye; intraocular pressure was 12 mmHg and 6 mmHg, respectively.  
• The left eye had 4+ anterior chamber cells, a 1.7 mm hypopyon, 2+–3+ flare, only mild conjunctival injection, and multiple iris nodules. The fundus view was obscured. The right eye was normal.  
• B-scan ultrasonography of the left eye revealed heterogeneous vitreous echogenicity.  

Initial management and investigations:  
• Intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime plus fortified topical drops were administered. Systemic vancomycin and ceftazidime infusions were given.  
• Vitreous gram stain, KOH preparation, acid-fast bacilli stain, aerobic/anaerobic/mycobacterial cultures, and PCR for bacteria, fungus, and mycobacteria were all negative. Two sets of blood cultures were sterile.  
• Mantoux, pathergy, and anergy tests were negative; chest radiograph was unremarkable; paranasal sinus radiograph showed maxillary sinusitis.  
• Four days later, vision had declined to light perception, and intravitreal amikacin was given for presumed atypical mycobacterial infection.  
• Prednisolone at 1 mg/kg/day was started empirically. One day after starting steroids, the hypopyon increased to 2.0 mm.  

On slit-lamp examination at this time, there was scleral thinning and melting at previous injection sites with prolapsed uveal tissue.

A 33-year-old Chinese woman (G1P1) presented in January 2018 with 8 months of intermittent abdominal discomfort and 4 months of worsening pelvic pain and a palpable lower-abdominal mass. Her history was notable for four prior surgeries for uterine leiomyomas without morcellation (2007, 2010, 2012, and 2015), including myomectomies and a total hysterectomy.

On examination, there was an 8 × 8 cm, non-tender, firm mass in the right lower quadrant of the anterior abdomen. Routine laboratory tests, including tumor markers and sex hormones, were within normal limits.

A core-needle biopsy of the mass showed a spindle-shaped smooth-muscle cell tumor without necrosis or atypia. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for Caldesmon, smooth-muscle actin (SMA), Desmin, estrogen receptor (ER), and progesterone receptor (PR) and negative for SOX-10 and CD117; the Ki-67 index was 5%. Next-generation sequencing of 120 cancer-related genes revealed no germline variants.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated multiple nodules involving the abdominal wall and pelvic cavity measuring 3–7 cm in diameter; the largest lesion measured approximately 78 × 66 × 40 mm. There was no evidence of distant metastasis or intravenous proliferation.

A 74-year–old man with no significant past or family history was referred for evaluation of severe osteoporosis. A DEXA scan revealed T-scores of –3.1 at L1–L4, –4.3 at the left femoral neck, –3.4 at the left total hip, –4.7 at the right femoral neck, –4.1 at the right total hip, and –1.3 at the right forearm. He reported 7 years of generalized body pain and progressive proximal muscle weakness, rendering him bed bound for the past 2 years despite calcium and calciferol supplementation. On exam, he had 4/5 strength in shoulder and pelvic girdle muscles, generalized muscle wasting, severe kyphosis, barrel chest with a flail segment, and used accessory muscles to breathe; vitals were stable.

Laboratory studies showed: serum phosphate 0.39 mmol/L (0.78–1.4), calcium 2.01 mmol/L (2.2–2.56), albumin 46 g/L (35–52), alkaline phosphatase 302 U/L (53–128), PTH 16.8 pmol/L (1.6–6.9), 25-hydroxy-vitamin D 45.2 nmol/L (> 72.5 replete), creatinine 59 µmol/L (64–104), and ESR 4 mm/hour (0–20). Fractional excretion of phosphate was 29% (< 5%), and TmP/GFR was 0.33 mmol/L (0.8–1.35), confirming marked renal phosphate wasting. Full blood count, liver function, thyroid function, uric acid, lipids, serum protein electrophoresis, Bence–Jones proteins, and testosterone were normal; celiac serologies (tissue transglutaminase, antigliadin, endomysial antibodies) were negative. Urine studies excluded Fanconi syndrome (normal aminoaciduria, no glycosuria, normal sodium and potassium excretion).

He was started on phosphate supplementation plus calcitriol and alfacalcidol. Despite normalization of calcium and vitamin D levels, he continued to have low serum phosphate and elevated alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone concentrations.

A 55-year-old Chinese woman was admitted with a 2-week history of fever and 1 week of bilateral thigh edema. Her medical history was unremarkable. On examination, there was marked edema and diffuse induration of both thighs, with prominent dendritic-like telangiectasia overlying the skin. Multiple firm subcutaneous nodules were palpable in the thighs without tenderness. There was no lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or neurologic deficit; her mental status was normal. Her temperature fluctuated between 36.2 °C and 39.2 °C. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 98 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 3971 IU/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 120 mm/h, C-reactive protein 137 mg/L, and β2-microglobulin 2.74 mg/L; other tests, including infection workup, were normal. Bone marrow biopsy revealed hypercellular marrow without abnormal cells. MRI of the thighs demonstrated soft-tissue swelling and thickening. Chest CT revealed a solitary low-density nodule in the left upper lobe; abdominal CT was normal. Brain CT and MRI showed a 3.2 × 1.9 cm extra-axial mass in the left parietal region, suspected to be a meningioma. One week after admission, two biopsies of the indurated skin were performed: the first showed mild epidermal keratosis, and the second revealed small lymphocytes around dermal vessels, suggesting possible vasculitis. She was started on intravenous methylprednisolone 40 mg daily. After one week, her fever resolved, but the telangiectasia rapidly spread to the abdomen, chest, and neck, and new subcutaneous nodules appeared on the right arm.

A 26‐year‐old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive lower-limb weakness. She initially walked with crutches, but by presentation she was wheelchair bound and had bladder and bowel incontinence. She denied trauma, fever, or prior medical comorbidities. On examination, she had a palpable thyroid nodule and hirsutism. Neurologic examination showed increased lower-limb reflexes, clonus, hypertonia, a positive Babinski sign, and paraparesis worse on the right. There was a T4 sensory level, diminished anal sphincter tone, and reduced perianal sensation. Her upper limbs and cranial nerves were intact, and there were no signs of infection or spinal tenderness. Laboratory studies revealed negative CEA, negative antinuclear antibodies, negative HIV, normal thyroid‐stimulating hormone, thyroxine, triiodothyronine, parathyroid hormone, CA-19-9, CA-125, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver enzymes, lactate dehydrogenase, and normal urine electrophoresis with Bence-Jones protein of 0. Surveillance CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no primary lesion. Thyroid ultrasound confirmed a solitary nodule. Spinal CT demonstrated expansile osteolysis and collapse of the T2 and T3 vertebral bodies with residual trabeculae, a sclerotic rim, and segmental kyphosis. Sagittal and axial MRI showed vertebral collapse involving posterior elements, high-grade cord compression, lesions that were T1 isointense to gray matter, slightly T2 hyperintense, and demonstrated gadolinium enhancement. CT-guided biopsy of the thoracic lesion and fine-needle biopsy of the thyroid nodule were performed.

A 48-year-old man of African descent was brought to the emergency department unresponsive after a generalized tonic–clonic seizure. On examination he was comatose with a blood pressure of 178/121 mmHg, heart rate 105 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3 of 15; he required intubation and ICU admission. He had no history of epilepsy, head trauma, recreational drug use, smoking, or alcohol consumption. His medical history was notable for resistant hypertension diagnosed 20 years ago, treated with atenolol 50 mg, spironolactone 100 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, and valsartan 160 mg daily, with poor compliance, and for type II diabetes mellitus treated with a sulfonylurea. Family history was positive for hypertension but negative for renal disease or adrenal tumors. Body mass index was 31. Thyroid and visual-field examinations were normal, and there were no cushingoid or acromegaly features. Initial laboratory studies showed a potassium level of 2.6 mmol/L (normal 3.6–5.1), creatinine 113 μmol/L, metabolic alkalosis on blood gas analysis, urea 5.7 mmol/L, and creatine kinase 2.2 μg/L. Urinalysis was negative for leukocyte esterase and nitrites. A chest radiograph showed no signs of heart failure. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm. Troponin-T and BNP were within normal limits. Calcium was 2.46 mmol/L. CT of the brain showed no lesions, and MRI the next day revealed no mass-occupying lesion; EEG was normal. Repeat potassium remained low at 2.6 mmol/L; plasma aldosterone was 36.2 ng/dL (normal 2.8–15.8), and plasma renin was < 0.081 ng/dL (normal 0.4–2.3). A 24-hour urine collection excluded Cushing’s syndrome and pheochromocytoma. Renal ultrasound and cardiac echocardiography excluded renovascular and cardiac causes of secondary hypertension.

A 32-year-old man presented with excessive tearing of the left eye and mild ocular pain. Over the previous 4–5 months he had noticed progressive left-eyelid drooping and intermittent diplopia. He reported a mild left-sided head trauma 1.5 years earlier but had no other medical history or family history of neurological or autoimmune disease.

On ophthalmologic examination, visual acuity, intraocular pressure, and funduscopy were normal. The left eyelid was ptotic, and there was limitation of adduction, elevation, and depression of the left eye, with a dilated left pupil. No other neurological deficits were found. Fluorescein angiography, indocyanine green chorioangiography, and optical coherence tomography were unremarkable. The patient noted that his ptosis fluctuated during the day, with marked improvement when washing his face with cold water.

To evaluate for myasthenia gravis, an ice pack was applied to the left eyelid for 2 minutes, after which his ptosis improved significantly, with near-complete eyelid opening; the improvement lasted only a few minutes.

A 69-year-old man with a 7-year history of refractory anemia–type myelodysplastic syndrome presented in 2008 with macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, MCV 114 fL), a normal white-cell count, normal platelets, and a low reticulocyte count; B12, folate, TSH, and liver function tests were normal, and bone marrow biopsy showed refractory anemia with blasts <5%. By 2011, his hemoglobin fell to 7.0 g/dL and platelets to 50,000/µL despite normal vitamin and thyroid studies; repeat marrow showed hypercellularity with dysplasia, blasts <5%, and a normal karyotype. He required monthly red-cell transfusions to maintain a hemoglobin >8 g/dL and occasional platelet transfusions. 

In October 2013, he noted painless gross hematuria. His hemoglobin was 7.5 g/dL, platelets 13,000/µL, and coagulation studies were normal. CT urography revealed a 16 mm lobulated lesion near the left ureteral orifice. With transfusional support, cystoscopy demonstrated five superficial bladder tumors; transurethral resection showed low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma without invasion. After resection, transfusion requirements decreased but did not resolve. 

Beginning March 2015, he received intravesical BCG (weekly ×6, biweekly ×4, then monthly ×12). While receiving BCG, his hemoglobin rose to 13.7 g/dL, platelets to 317,000/µL, and he became transfusion independent.

A 51-year-old woman was referred to the ENT clinic with a 2-week history of a painless lump on the right side of her neck. She reported no dysphagia or change in her voice. Her gynaecological history included four full-term vaginal deliveries and previously normal cervical smears; she denied intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and had regular cycles. She smoked 20–30 cigarettes per day. Over the past 3 months she had increasing lethargy and severe back pain that prevented her from working. Five years earlier she had significant weight loss and heavy menstrual bleeding requiring five units of blood; an evaluation for colon cancer was negative, and she failed to attend follow-up at a menstrual disorders clinic.

On examination, there were multiple palpable cervical lymph nodes bilaterally. Neck ultrasonography showed two large supraclavicular lymph nodes and several abnormal nodes in the right carotid chain. A chest radiograph was normal. Fine-needle aspiration of a lymph node yielded squamous carcinoma cells. To locate the primary, clinical examination and endoscopy of the nasopharynx, larynx, and hypopharynx showed no tumour. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, chest, and abdomen demonstrated marked mediastinal and para-aortic lymphadenopathy and bilateral dilation of the collecting systems with proximal ureteral dilatation, suggesting pelvic obstruction. 

^18F-FDG PET-CT showed intense uptake in the right cervical lymph nodes, right paratracheal and anterior mediastinal stations, lower para-aortic and bilateral iliac chains with a photopaenic centre in an obturator node, and a focal area of increased activity in the pelvis, suggesting a lesion within the rectal wall or vaginal vault.

A 60-year-old man, a long-term smoker, presented with a one-month history of marked pain and swelling on the left side of his neck, radiating to the left ear and sternum. He denied fever and dyspnoea. Three weeks earlier, he had been diagnosed with subacute thyroiditis by an outpatient specialist, based solely on neck pain and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 84 mm/h, and was treated with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug without improvement. 

On examination, there was a hard, tender 6 cm mass in the left thyroid region. Laboratory tests showed ESR 77 mm/h, white blood count 8370 cells/µl, C-reactive protein 5.04 mg/dl, thyroid-stimulating hormone 1.31 mIU/l, free thyroxine 1.20 ng/dl, free triiodothyronine 3.33 pg/ml, anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies 21.49 IU/l, thyroglobulin antibodies 395 IU/l, and TSH-receptor antibodies < 0.3 IU/l.

Neck ultrasound revealed an unchanged right lobe and a markedly enlarged left lobe (44 × 61 × 100 mm) almost entirely occupied by a heterogeneous mass (44 × 55 × 70 mm) with numerous calcifications, marked reduction of vascular flow, and invasion into adjacent neck muscles. No pathological lymph nodes were seen.

A 52-year-old Japanese man was evaluated for several months of progressive anorexia. His medical history was notable for sublingual adenocarcinoma treated with resection and radiation 6 years earlier, supraclavicular lymph-node metastasis resection and radiation 5 years earlier, and subsequent lung and bone metastases treated with platinum-based chemotherapy. He was currently receiving nivolumab. He had no history of smoking or significant family illnesses and was taking sertraline. 

On initial evaluation, laboratory testing demonstrated secondary adrenocortical insufficiency and secondary hypothyroidism without evidence of diabetes insipidus. Serum IgG4 was 52.0 mg/dL; angiotensin-converting enzyme, 13.6 U/L; soluble interleukin-2 receptor, 684 U/mL; and T-SPOT was negative. 

Magnetic resonance imaging showed an isointense, homogenously enhancing enlargement of the pituitary gland and stalk with extension into the cavernous sinus and the planum sphenoidale dura, without compression of the optic chiasm. No other intracranial lesions were identified. Autoimmune hypophysitis related to immune checkpoint inhibition was suspected, and the patient was started on glucocorticoids and thyroid hormone replacement. 

One month later, he returned with new right-eye visual impairment (visual acuity 20/200) attributed to invasion of the optic canal. Pulse corticosteroid therapy was administered as a diagnostic treatment. Repeat MRI showed no clear reduction in the pituitary lesion, and he subsequently developed a right oculomotor nerve palsy.

A 73-year-old man with a history of heart failure with recovered ejection fraction (60%), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus presented with 2 days of severe, exertional, pressure-like chest pain rated 9/10. His physical examination was unremarkable. Vital signs were: heart rate 60 bpm, blood pressure 119/58 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm. Initial laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin 16 g/dL, platelet count 380 K/cm3, white-cell count 8.1 K/cm3, creatinine 2 mg/dL, high-sensitivity troponin >5000 ng/L, and B-type natriuretic peptide 2810 pg/mL. He was admitted for management of non–ST–elevation myocardial infarction and started on a heparin drip and antiplatelet therapy. 

On hospital day 2, he developed severe left lower abdominal and thigh pain. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed marked swelling of the left psoas and iliacus muscles with heterogeneous density, consistent with hemorrhage. Anticoagulation and antiplatelet agents were discontinued, and a CT angiogram revealed active contrast extravasation into the left psoas muscle. Interventional radiology performed angiography, which showed no arterial source of active bleeding. After stabilization, his hemoglobin rose to 18 g/dL.

A 22-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of stabbing right upper‐quadrant abdominal pain. He had undergone a rib‐series radiograph and abdominopelvic CT at outside hospitals without abnormal findings and had been treated conservatively with analgesics and physical therapy, but his pain worsened. He denied any medical or trauma history, had no gastrointestinal symptoms, weight loss, or systemic complaints. 
On examination he had dysesthesia, hypoesthesia, and pain over the right T8–9 dermatome radiating from the anterior abdominal wall to the back. His pain was aggravated by sitting or lying and disturbed sleep at night. Manual muscle testing was normal throughout, and deep tendon reflexes were intact in the lower extremities.
Nerve‐conduction studies were normal in all four extremities. Needle electromyography showed abnormal spontaneous activity in the right paraspinal muscles at T8–9 and in the right rectus abdominis. Somatosensory and motor evoked potentials were within normal limits.
Contrast‐enhanced MRI of the thoracic spine revealed a well-enhanced lobulated mass along the right paraspinal area with suspicious extension into the right neural foramen at T8–9.

A 64-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease treated with multiple percutaneous coronary interventions (most recently 2 weeks earlier) presented with sudden-onset precordial chest pain and dyspnoea on exertion similar to his prior angina. The pain was initially relieved by sublingual nitroglycerine but recurred, prompting presentation to the emergency department. On examination, his heart rate was 75 beats per minute, blood pressure 167/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air; his body mass index was 35 kg/m2. Physical examination showed a regular rate and rhythm, clear lungs, and jugular venous pressure of 9 cm H2O. Serial cardiac enzymes were normal (troponin T 0.02 ng/mL, normal 0–0.03 ng/mL), and electrocardiography demonstrated sinus rhythm with right bundle branch block and lateral T-wave inversions unchanged from prior studies. His home medications included aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, metoprolol tartrate, amlodipine, ranolazine, and furosemide. A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a homogeneous, echo-dense intracardiac mass measuring 4 cm × 4 cm, located within or attached to the superior interatrial septum and extending superiorly and posteriorly to the aortic root, moving synchronously with the atrial walls. Right and left atrial sizes and left ventricular size, wall thickness, and systolic function were normal, and no tricuspid regurgitation was seen. There was no mention of a similar mass on a transthoracic echocardiogram performed one year earlier.

A 64-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an abdominal mass incidentally detected on routine examination 6 months earlier. She denied fever, abdominal pain or distension, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, or changes in bowel habits. Her history was notable only for type 2 diabetes mellitus of 10 years’ duration; she had no tobacco or alcohol use. Physical examination was unremarkable. Urinalysis showed leukocytes 2+; fasting blood glucose was 6.97 mmol/L; complete blood count, liver and kidney function tests, and tumor markers were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a dumbbell-shaped, moderately inhomogeneous soft-tissue shadow measuring approximately 3.6 cm × 1.8 cm in the region of the stomach’s lesser curvature, with apparent origin from the gastric wall, and a mesenchymal stromal tumor was suspected. Two months before planned surgery, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed chronic superficial gastritis without evidence of mucosal lesions or malignancy, and colonoscopy showed no abnormalities, ruling out colorectal metastasis. The tumor’s extraluminal location and lack of mucosal involvement reduced suspicion for a primary gastrointestinal lesion. Preoperative three-dimensional reconstruction showed a 4 cm × 2 cm × 1 cm dumbbell-shaped mass encircling the left gastric artery, splenic artery, and splenic vein to guide surgical planning. Preoperative diagnosis: abdominal mass (suspected gastric stromal tumor) and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

A male newborn was delivered at 40 weeks’ gestation by uneventful vaginal delivery to a 28-year-old mother. Birth weight was 3040 g; Apgar scores were 9 and 10 at 1 and 5 minutes. On initial examination, the only abnormality was an irregular, asymmetric, enlarged right testis. Scrotal ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous solid mass in the right testis without retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy; the left testis was descended and external genitalia were normal. Serum alpha-fetoprotein was 97 819 ng/mL (normal for gestational age), and total β-hCG was 31.4 mIU/mL (reference < 5 mIU/mL). At 21 hours of age, a right inguinal orchiectomy was performed. Gross pathology revealed a light-brown, round, solid mass measuring 3.0 × 2.0 × 1.5 cm that sharply replaced most of the testicular parenchyma and displaced the epididymis peripherally.

A 59-year-old man with no significant medical or surgical history presented with a 6-week history of an enlarging, painful mass on the dorsum of his right hand. Six weeks earlier, he had sustained a penetrating injury from a galvanized culvert, resulting in a small laceration. Despite antibiotic therapy for presumed Staphylococcus abscess, the lesion continued to enlarge. On examination, there was a 2.5 × 2.0 cm solid, mobile mass over the dorsal right hand. The lesion was nonpulsatile, nonfriable, nonfluctuant, not adherent to underlying structures, and appeared limited to the cutaneous and subcutaneous tissues. There was no surrounding erythema, no expressible drainage, and no palpable lymphadenopathy. A central area of keratinaceous-appearing material was noted. Radiographs of the hand were unremarkable, and routine laboratory values were within normal limits.

A 70-year-old man with known chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) diagnosed in July 2009 underwent staging studies that revealed a large substernal multinodular goiter (volume ≈82 cm3) on chest CT. In October 2009, an ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy of a thyroid nodule was suspicious for carcinoma; serum thyroglobulin was 936.9 ng/mL. CLL required no treatment at that time.

On January 5, 2010, he underwent total thyroidectomy with removal of 29 regional lymph nodes. Pathology showed a 1.2-mm follicular variant of papillary thyroid microcarcinoma confined to the right lobe, with metastases in 8 of 29 nodes but no extrathyroidal extension or vascular invasion. He was referred for radioiodine ablation.

One month later, before I-131 therapy, he was off thyroid hormone replacement. Investigations included:
– Chest radiograph: normal.  
– Neck ultrasound: bilaterally enlarged lymph nodes in levels I, II, and VI, interpreted as inflammatory.  
– CT of chest and abdomen: enlarged axillary and retroperitoneal lymph nodes, attributed to CLL.  
– CBC (Jan 27): 4.74×10^6 erythrocytes/mm^3; 19,200 leukocytes/mm^3 (72.7% lymphocytes); 265,000 platelets/mm^3.  
– Serum (Jan 23): TSH 63 mIU/L; thyroglobulin 93.4 ng/mL; anti-thyroglobulin antibodies negative.  
– Pretherapeutic I-131 whole-body scan (WBS): tiny thyroid remnant uptake (<1% at 24 h); no definite uptake elsewhere, with very faint questionable activity in both axillae.

On February 2, 2010, he received 7,400 MBq (200 mCi) of I-131. A post-therapy WBS on February 6 showed expected cervical uptake and new, definite uptake in both axillary regions and small foci in the inguinal regions. SPECT/CT of the chest localized radioiodine concentration to enlarged axillary lymph nodes, particularly one in the left axilla.

Chief complaint: 39-year-old nulligravid woman with 8 months of androgenic alopecia, facial acne, and hirsutism.

History of present illness:
 • Progressive scalp hair thinning, acne, and hirsutism (Ferriman–Gallwey score 12).  
 • Over 3 months, 6 kg weight gain in the abdomen and sporadic ecchymoses without trauma.  
 • Oligomenorrhea for 9 months after stopping oral contraceptives.  
 • No changes in libido, muscle strength, or fractures.

Medical history: primary hypothyroidism, obesity (BMI 31.8 kg/m²), hypertension.

Medications: levothyroxine, nebivolol, amlodipine/valsartan.

Family history: mother with thyroid and breast cancer, hypertension, type 2 diabetes.

Physical examination:
 • Androgenic facies, alopecia, clitoromegaly.  
 • Dorsocervical fat pad, axillary acanthosis nigricans.  
 • No abdominal masses; no breast atrophy, proximal myopathy, or striae.  
 • Weight 87.6 kg; blood pressure 140/92 mm Hg.

Laboratory studies:
 • Hemoglobin 18.2 g/dL; erythrocyte count 5.84 ×10^12/L.  
 • Total testosterone 1052 ng/dL (6–82); androstenedione 5.13 ng/mL (0.3–3.3).  
 • DHEAS 246.6 µg/dL (60.9–337).  
 • FSH 0.87 mIU/mL; LH 0.61 mIU/mL.  
 • Normal prolactin, free T4, TSH.  
 • Normal 24-h urinary free cortisol and 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test.

Imaging:
 • Transvaginal ultrasound: 15×15×16 mm well-defined solid, slightly heterogeneous left ovarian lesion; no endometrial thickening.  
 • Pelvic MRI: solid left adnexal lesion with smooth margins and moderate T2 hyperintensity; no ascites or lymphadenopathy.  
 • CT of the adrenal glands: unremarkable.

A 64‐year‐old woman presented with headache and fever for 1 week. She described diffuse pain over her calvarium without focal neurologic deficits. Body temperature was 38.7 °C. Examination revealed no lymphadenopathy, no palpable breast masses, and no abdominal masses. Laboratory studies showed:
• Hemoglobin 7.0 g/dL (normocytic anemia), MCV 89.3 fL  
• White‐cell count 12 000/mm3 (neutrophils 61.7%, lymphocytes 26.7%, monocytes 10.8%)  
• Platelet count 325 000/mm3  
• Alkaline phosphatase 158 IU/L (normal 32–91)  
• Lactate dehydrogenase 292 IU/L (normal 98–192)  
• D-dimer 6570 ng/mL (normal 0–500)  
Coagulation times were normal. Chest radiograph showed no pulmonary lesions. A noncontrast CT scan of the head showed multiple osteolytic lesions in the skull compared to films 6 years earlier. A CT scan of the chest and abdomen demonstrated mixed osteolytic and osteosclerotic lesions throughout the skeleton but no clear primary tumor. Serum immunofixation electrophoresis showed no monoclonal protein; immunoglobulin G, A, and M levels were normal. Tumor markers revealed CEA 8.1 ng/mL (normal 0–5) and CA 15-3 163.2 IU/mL (normal 0–31.3), with CA 19-9 and CA-125 within normal limits.  
Bone marrow aspiration from the right posterior iliac crest revealed scant hematopoietic precursors among clusters of oval neoplastic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and granular cytoplasm, some forming rosette‐like structures. Biopsy after decalcification showed metastatic adenocarcinoma composed of round to oval tumor cells in ovoid clusters, cribriform nests, and microacinar patterns filling the marrow. A metastatic adenocarcinoma was considered the most likely diagnosis.

A 19-year-old unmarried woman was found to have hypertension (200/120 mmHg) six months earlier, when she was hospitalized for a febrile illness. She has been on losartan 50 mg twice daily without blood-pressure control. She denies muscle weakness, polyuria, nocturia, weight gain, bruising, acne, hirsutism, episodic headaches, or rheumatologic symptoms. There is no family history of early hypertension or intracerebral hemorrhage. She takes no other medications or supplements.

On examination, her BMI is 22 kg/m2. Pulse is 88 beats/minute and regular. Cardiovascular examination is unremarkable; there are no radio-radial or radio-femoral delays, murmurs, or bruits. Fundoscopy shows silver wiring of retinal vessels; other systems are normal.

Laboratory studies:
• Potassium 2.8 mmol/L (3.5–5.2) despite replacement  
• Sodium 136 mmol/L (135–145)  
• Bicarbonate 24.8 mEq/L (22–26)  
• Overnight dexamethasone suppression test <11 nmol/L (normal <50)  
• Aldosterone 49.7 ng/dL (1.76–39.2)  
• Plasma renin concentration 1275 μIU/mL (2.8–32.9)  
• Plasma renin activity 106.3 ng/mL/hr  
• Aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) 0.5 (<10 suggests secondary aldosteronism)  
• TSH, 24-h urinary metanephrines, creatinine, ESR, and urine microscopy all normal  

Cardiac echocardiogram shows normal biventricular function without coarctation. Renal ultrasound shows normal renal size and parenchyma; renal artery Doppler is normal. CT angiogram excludes renal artery stenosis but reveals a 1.2 × 1 cm well-defined, exophytic, iso-dense lesion in the lower pole of the left kidney with delayed contrast enhancement.

A 22-year-old man with no significant medical or family history presented with a 2-week history of progressive abdominal distention associated with generalized abdominal pain, myalgia, fatigue, decreased oral intake, nausea, and unintentional weight loss. On examination, his vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination revealed distention with shifting dullness; cardiopulmonary, skin, and scleral examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed:  
- White-cell count 10.6 × 10^9/L  
- Hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL  
- Platelet count 557,000/µL  

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated moderate ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, and a 4.7 × 3.3 cm lobular omental mass in the lower pelvis. A diagnostic paracentesis yielded 3.2 L of grossly bloody fluid with a low serum–ascites albumin gradient. Ascitic-fluid analysis showed:  
- Red-blood-cell count >900,000/µL  
- Total nucleated cells 3,382/µL (41% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes, 0% eosinophils, 1% monocytes, 28% other cells)  
- Negative bacterial cultures  
- Cytology revealing mononuclear cells of possible mesothelial origin, inflammatory cells, and histiocytes in a hemorrhagic background

A 62-year-old Indian man with recently diagnosed p16-negative posterior oropharyngeal wall squamous cell carcinoma (stage IVb, T3N3bM0) and comorbid hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and ischemic heart failure (ejection fraction 23% with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator) underwent elective feeding gastrostomy. His thyroid function was normal at initial cancer staging. Three weeks later, he developed fever, tachycardia, and stridor. Flexible nasolaryngoscopy showed near-complete oropharyngeal obstruction; an emergency tracheostomy was performed. Examination under anesthesia revealed rapid progression of the tumour into a circumferential oropharyngeal stricture. Despite 17 days of piperacillin-tazobactam, his fever persisted (maximum 39.6 °C) and heart rate remained 110–120 bpm. Extensive cultures (blood, urine, sputum, gastrostomy site), HIV and cryptococcal tests, echocardiography, and brain CT were negative. Laboratory studies showed C-reactive protein 243.3 g/L and a white-cell count of 18,400/mm3 (75.1% neutrophils). Chest radiography demonstrated a small right pleural effusion. Neck CT revealed worsening pharyngeal disease with invasion into bilateral thyroid lobes and new bilateral lung nodules. On examination, there was central neck tenderness without a palpable goiter. Thyroid function tests showed triiodothyronine 8.0 pmol/L (reference 3.5–6.0), free thyroxine 54 pmol/L (reference 8.0–16.0), and thyroid-stimulating hormone 0.01 mIU/L (reference 0.45–4.5). Antithyroid peroxidase, thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, and thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin antibodies were negative. Thyroid ultrasonography showed reduced vascularity without abscess formation.

A 37-year-old man presented with severe, localized right maxillary pain. He had no facial swelling or tenderness on examination. His history was notable for dental implants placed in the missing right maxillary premolar and molar region; although these implants were loaded, functional, and had an intact periodontium, an implant-related complication was initially suspected. 

A panoramic radiograph demonstrated severe marginal alveolar bone loss around the implants and inferior extension of the maxillary sinus floor. Adjacent maxillary sinus mucosal thickening was noted. 

The patient localized his pain to just below the right orbital rim and reported that it was severe and predominantly nocturnal. A CT scan revealed a small (3.5 mm diameter), well-defined, corticated, spherical radiolucency within the superior anterior wall of the right maxillary sinus, just below the infraorbital rim and medial to the infraorbital foramen, causing minimal bony expansion. The lesion’s CT attenuation was similar to soft tissue. 

These findings suggested a benign bone neoplasm, and an excisional biopsy was planned.

A 54-year-old woman was referred by her dentist for sudden onset of pain in the right mandible and numbness of the right chin. Her medical history was notable for an early breast carcinoma diagnosed in 2008 (pT1a N1a, estrogen- and progesterone-receptor positive, HER-2 negative) treated with wide excision, axillary lymphadenectomy, adjuvant chemotherapy (3 cycles of FEC-100 and docetaxel), radiotherapy, and subsequent letrozole (2 years) and tamoxifen (5 years). In the same year, she underwent a total nephrectomy for a stage T1a clear-cell renal carcinoma. In October 2015, pulmonary and osteoclastic bone metastases from breast cancer were identified, and treatment with monthly zoledronic acid began in January 2016; she also received exemestane followed by fulvestrant after disease progression. 

In June 2016, she noted right mandibular pain and chin numbness, without involvement of the lower lip. Examination revealed no cervical lymphadenopathy. Intraoral inspection showed a firm bony elevation in the region of the right first and second premolars; the lower right second molar was tender to percussion but pulp sensibility was intact. A panoramic radiograph was unremarkable. Cone-beam CT and PET-CT were obtained; the PET-CT demonstrated bony radiolucent areas in the right mandibular ramus suggestive of osteoclastic lesions. Skeletal scintigraphy revealed diffuse metastases in the spine, ribs, pelvic bones, sacrum, proximal femur, and right mandibular ramus. MRI of the head was performed to evaluate possible trigeminal involvement and showed a small lesion in the right cavernous sinus, interpreted as a hemangioma or leiomyoma, with no apparent role in the patient’s neuropathy.

A 30-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of paroxysmal, acid-like pain and swelling of the waist and legs, worsening over the past 2 weeks and impairing ambulation. Physical examination was unremarkable. Pelvic X-ray showed patchy and nodular high-density shadows in both ilia, ischia, pubic bones, and upper femurs. CT bone-window images revealed uneven, elevated bone density lesions in the thoracic vertebrae below T10, bilateral ribs, scapulae, lumbar vertebrae, and sacrum. MRI demonstrated diffuse abnormal signal shadows in the pelvis, sacrum, L3–L5 vertebral bodies, and bilateral femurs. Whole-body SPECT showed extensive sclerotic lesions with diffusely increased bone metabolism and focal areas of reduced density with increased uptake in the left ninth rib axillary segment, the sixth and tenth thoracic vertebrae, and regions of both femurs and right tibia. Bone marrow aspiration and urine protein electrophoresis were normal. HLA-B27 was negative. Tumor markers revealed a mildly elevated neuron-specific enolase (19.03 μg/mL) with other markers within normal limits. Endocrine evaluation showed a slight increase in parathyroid hormone; parathyroid CT demonstrated only small, low-density nodules near the right thyroid lobe. Given nondiagnostic findings, a CT-guided left iliac bone biopsy was planned.

An 88-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer and stage III chronic kidney disease was admitted with one week of severe weakness, anorexia, and jaundice. He was diagnosed with prostate cancer 8 months before admission, with an initial PSA level of 4280 ng/mL, skeletal and lung metastases, and no liver metastases on contrast CT. He began androgen-deprivation therapy with bicalutamide and leuprolide, but his PSA rose rapidly from 357 ng/mL to 3030 ng/mL over several months. One week before admission, bicalutamide was stopped and enzalutamide was initiated. Other medications included leuprolide, finasteride, doxazosin, metoprolol, omeprazole, ferrous gluconate, multivitamin, psyllium, and a nutritional supplement. He denied transfusions, travel, alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drug use and had no personal or family history of liver disease.

On admission, he was afebrile, pulse 91/min, blood pressure 105/47 mm Hg (MAP 66), and visibly jaundiced without hepatosplenomegaly or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory tests showed total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 654 IU/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 988 IU/L, albumin 4 g/dL, and INR 1.2. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography showed nonobstructing cholelithiasis without cholecystitis or biliary ductal dilatation, with normal portal and hepatic vasculature and no lymphadenopathy. Because of his renal impairment, contrast CT was deferred. Noncontrast MRI and MRCP demonstrated normal liver parenchyma with mild reactive hepatic hilar lymphadenopathy, small benign liver cysts/hemangiomas, nonobstructing pancreatic cysts, and no biliary obstruction or metastatic lesions.

A 7-year-old girl presented with 4 months of progressive lower-limb weakness and spasms. There was no history of trauma, fever, or neurologic symptoms such as blurred vision or speech changes. On examination, she was afebrile and fully conscious. A firm, slightly tender 3×5 cm mass was palpated in the right supraclavicular region. Neurologic examination revealed quadriplegia (Medical Research Council grade 2–3/5), right worse than left, generalized hyperreflexia with sustained clonus, and extensor plantar responses; the jaw jerk was normal. Findings localized the lesion to the cervical spinal cord.

Routine chest radiography showed a widened mediastinum, clear lung fields, and no bone involvement. Hematologic studies, including a complete blood count, peripheral smear, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the entire spine demonstrated a well-circumscribed, T2-hyperintense extramedullary lesion with a dumb-bell appearance at C6–T1. The lesion caused severe canal stenosis, widened the right C6/7 and C7/T1 neuroforamina, displaced the cord postero-laterally to the left, and extended peripherally along the C6/7 nerve root into the right supraclavicular region.
