There was increased T2 signal within the spinal cord from C3 to C8. Vertebral alignment was normal, with no bony destruction or marrow abnormalities.

A 50-year-old multigravida woman presented with a 10-day history of intermittent, diffuse lower abdominal pain, more pronounced on the right. She had a known history of uterine leiomyomas. There were no urinary or gastrointestinal symptoms. Vital signs were stable, and she was afebrile. On examination, she had focal tenderness in the right lower abdomen. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 10 000 per mm3, hemoglobin 12 g/dL, C-reactive protein 0.6 mg/L, and a negative pregnancy test. Transabdominal ultrasound was inconclusive because of a large abdominopelvic mass with marked posterior attenuation; the patient declined transvaginal ultrasound. Because of persistent pain, an MRI was obtained. On MRI, a solid abdominopelvic mass was seen arising from the region of the right uterine cornua via a broad pedicle. T2-weighted images demonstrated flow voids at the uterine attachment (“bridging-vessel sign”). The mass was isointense to myometrium on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images without diffusion restriction. After gadolinium administration, most of the mass showed no enhancement, but there was a thin enhancing rim and a small eccentric zone of heterogeneous enhancement near its uterine attachment. The pedicle was thickened and twisted in a spiral fashion. The right ovary was enlarged with heterogeneous T2 signal and peripheral follicles (“string of pearls”), and areas of T1 and T2 hyperintensity in the ovarian stroma suggested hemorrhage. The right pelvic ureter was kinked at the twisted pedicle, causing ipsilateral ureterohydronephrosis.

A 7-year-old female presented with a 12-month history of progressive bilateral neck swelling, intermittent fever, night sweats, and weight loss. She had no known tuberculosis exposure or similar family history. On examination, she was pale and undernourished (BMI 10.24 kg/m2) with multiple rubbery, mobile, non-tender lymph nodes in the submandibular, submental, and posterior cervical regions (largest 4 × 3 cm), as well as inguinal nodes; no hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (14.57 × 10^9/L) with neutrophilia, microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL; MCV 64.7 fL), and thrombocytosis (974 × 10^9/L); ESR was 36 mm/h, CRP 641.8 mg/L, and ferritin 256 ng/mL. Peripheral smear demonstrated hypochromia, anisocytosis, microcytosis, rouleaux formation, and no blasts. Gene-Xpert testing on lymph node aspirate and sputum was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, as was urine LF-LAM. Chest radiography revealed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. CT imaging of the neck, chest, and abdomen showed generalized lymphadenopathy without extranodal masses. She was started empirically on anti-tuberculous therapy.

A 65-year-old man with a history of low-risk prostate cancer managed by active surveillance was referred for restaging when his prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level rose to 26.6 μg/L in 2022. He had no significant comorbidities aside from prior cholecystectomy. Initial prostate biopsy in 2013 showed high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia at a PSA of 6.2 μg/L. A repeat biopsy in 2015 revealed Gleason 3+3 adenocarcinoma in 1 of 14 cores; digital rectal examination was unremarkable, and the cancer was staged as T1c. Surveillance over the next eight years included biennial biopsies that were negative for malignancy. 

When his PSA increased to 26.6 μg/L, a 3-Tesla multiparametric MRI of the prostate identified two PI-RADS 4 lesions (12 mm in the right transition zone and 6 mm in the right peripheral zone). Repeat biopsy detected Gleason 3+3 adenocarcinoma in 2 of 15 cores without perineural invasion, and his prostate volume was estimated at 86 mL. He experienced postbiopsy urinary retention and developed a left lower-limb deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, which were treated with apixaban. He otherwise had no symptoms of metastatic disease.

For staging, CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no nodal or visceral metastases. A 99m-Tc bone scan demonstrated moderate focal uptake in the right frontal calvarium. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a 2.5 cm sclerotic lesion in the right frontal bone corresponding to the area of uptake, suspicious for a solitary sclerotic metastasis.

A 74-year-old Japanese woman noted a tender lump in her right breast and was referred after a core needle biopsy raised suspicion for metaplastic carcinoma. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. On examination, there was a hard, tender 25-mm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast and a palpable right axillary lymph node. Mammography demonstrated an indistinct mass on mediolateral oblique and craniocaudal views. Ultrasound showed an 18 × 16 mm irregular hypoechoic lesion with suspected ductal extension toward the nipple and multiple enlarged level I–II axillary lymph nodes. Contrast-enhanced MRI identified a 17 × 17 mm indistinct mass with surrounding non-mass segmental enhancement extending 74 mm toward the nipple without chest wall or skin invasion. Clinical and imaging findings strongly suggested invasive carcinoma with axillary metastases.

Core needle biopsy of the breast lesion revealed oval and spindle-shaped mononuclear cells admixed with multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells, stromal hyalinization, lymphocytic infiltration, and focal hemorrhage without necrosis. The multinucleated giant cells stained strongly positive for CD68; mononuclear cells were weakly CD68-positive and negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2. Few non-epithelial atypical cells were seen in a breast duct, but no atypical epithelial cells were identified. Fine-needle aspiration of an axillary lymph node yielded only normal lymphocytes. To address the discrepancy between the clinical suspicion of malignancy and the benign-appearing biopsy, a vacuum-assisted ultrasound-guided biopsy was performed again, yielding identical histologic and immunohistochemical findings.

A 56-year-old woman with a 23-year history of thyrotoxicosis treated intermittently with antithyroid drugs presented with recurrent symptoms two weeks after total thyroidectomy. On initial evaluation she had bilateral exophthalmos, an enlarged thyroid with nodules, and an elevated TSH-receptor antibody level of 3.86 IU/L (normal < 1.00 IU/L). A Tc-99m thyroid scan had shown diffusely increased uptake with one hyperfunctioning nodule in the right upper pole and a hypofunctioning nodule in the right midlobe. Histopathology of the 57.7 g thyroidectomy specimen confirmed Graves’ disease and benign nodules.

Two weeks after surgery, she developed symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. Thyroid-function testing confirmed elevated free T4 and suppressed TSH. A radioiodine uptake in the thyroid bed was 0.2 % (reference, 15 %–45 %). An I-131 whole-body scan demonstrated intense radiotracer uptake with a “star” artifact in the pelvic region. SPECT/CT of the pelvis revealed an 8.5 × 7.2 cm mixed cystic–solid mass with internal calcification in the right adnexa. The plasma cancer antigen 125 level was 48.55 U/mL (reference, 0–35 U/mL).

A 60-year-old man presented with a six-week history of sharp, left-sided chest pain worsened by inspiration and lying down. He also reported progressive back pain exacerbated by walking, constipation, and lower-limb weakness and numbness suggestive of spinal cord compression. He had no history of smoking or significant past medical conditions. On examination, vital signs were stable. There was abdominal distension without hepatomegaly, minimal lower-limb weakness, and otherwise normal cardiovascular and respiratory findings.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 138 g/L, white-cell count 5.14×10^9/L with a normal differential, platelets 256×10^9/L, normal renal function, and normal serum calcium. Contrast MRI of the spine revealed widespread skeletal lesions with at least three large thoracic paraspinal soft-tissue deposits, including one at T4/T5 causing significant cord compression. A chest radiograph demonstrated a left upper-lobe opacity. Contrast CT of the chest confirmed a 75 mm lobulated mass in the left upper lobe with invasion into the chest wall (involving the left third rib and adjacent muscle), a mild to moderate left pleural effusion, and CT evidence of vertebral and pelvic bony lesions.

A 16-year-old male presented with a 3-month history of a gradually enlarging mass over the left lower back and pain in the right pelvic region and bilateral lower back that worsened with activity and radiated into the lower limbs. He had no history of trauma or surgery.

On examination, there was a well-circumscribed, soft, compressible subcutaneous swelling over the left lower back and two vague masses palpable in the bilateral iliac regions.

Ultrasonography of the lower back and abdomen demonstrated sizable multiseptated cystic lesions containing echogenic fluid within both psoas muscles, extending into the subcutaneous tissues and abutting the inferior poles of both kidneys.

Noncontrast CT of the abdomen showed a large multilocular cystic mass involving the bilateral psoas muscles, the left extensor muscles, and the left posterolateral abdominal wall, with attenuation values of +20 to +27 HU and calcifications in the walls and septa but no fatty components. Multiple sharply marginated osteolytic lesions were noted in the lumbar and sacral vertebrae.

MRI revealed multiloculated lesions in both psoas muscles extending to the left extensor muscle and posterolateral abdominal wall, with low signal on T1-weighted images, high signal on T2-weighted images, no restricted diffusion on DWI, and peripheral capsular and septal enhancement after gadolinium administration. Lesions extended into the lumbosacral spinal canal and intervertebral foramina, compressing the cauda equina nerve roots.

Chest CT demonstrated interstitial thickening with nodules in the lung fields, no pleural effusion or mediastinal adenopathy, and well-circumscribed osteolytic lesions in the thoracic vertebrae.

An 11-year-old girl presented with an 18-month history of progressive abdominal distention. She had no pain, gastrointestinal, urinary, respiratory, or constitutional symptoms. She reached menarche one year earlier; menstrual cycles were infrequent, with the last period two weeks before presentation. There was no history of menorrhagia or dysmenorrhea. On examination, she was in no distress with normal vital signs. Her weight was 64.5 kg (>95th percentile); she was otherwise thin. There was no clubbing, pallor, icterus, edema, or lymphadenopathy, and no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Abdominal examination showed a uniformly distended abdomen from the pelvis to the xiphisternum with full flanks; fluid thrill was positive, and there was no tenderness or palpable mass. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Urine dipstick was negative for proteinuria. Laboratory studies—including CBC, peripheral smear, serum electrolytes, renal function, and liver function tests—were within normal limits. Tumor markers (CA-125, CEA, alpha-fetoprotein, beta-hCG), uric acid, and LDH were all within normal limits. A transabdominal ultrasound was reported as massive ascites. MRI of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a large, homogeneous, well-defined unilocular cystic abdominopelvic mass measuring 39 × 29 × 18 cm, occupying the entire abdomen and pelvis and bulging into the anterior abdominal wall; no septations or solid components were seen.

A 53-year-old otherwise healthy man presented with a 4-month history of swelling of the right foot and ankle. He denied trauma, fevers, weight loss, or claudication. On examination there was non-pitting edema of the right foot and ankle without erythema or warmth. Duplex ultrasound of the leg veins excluded deep vein thrombosis. Radiographs of the ankle and serologic tests were unremarkable, with no evidence of arthritis. One month later, because of progression of the edema to the entire leg, a CT scan of the pelvis and groin was performed and revealed a hyperechogenic structure in the right groin compressing the common femoral vein and causing focal venous narrowing. Duplex sonography confirmed a 3 cm mass dorsal to the common femoral vein. MRI of the groin showed a 26×24×54 mm lesion that was mildly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, isointense to muscle on T1, and demonstrated slight contrast enhancement. A fine-needle biopsy revealed proliferating spindle cells but did not provide a definitive diagnosis.

A 49-year-old man presented with vague pain in the left mandibular area and lower-lip paresthesia of several weeks’ duration and occasional low-grade fevers. He was edentulous. On examination, there was a firm mass of the left edentulous mandibular ridge covered by intact mucosa. Cone-beam CT showed an ill-defined radiolucent lesion extending from the left alveolar crest to the inferior alveolar canal, with buccal cortical plate invasion. An incisional biopsy yielded tan, soft to elastic tissue fragments. Histologically, the lesion consisted of sheets of malignant small to medium-sized round cells with hyperchromatic, occasionally clefted nuclei, prominent nucleoli, scant cytoplasm, frequent mitoses, perineural invasion, and crush artifact. Immunohistochemistry revealed tumor cells positive for CD45, CD20, C-MYC, CD10, and BCL-6; scattered CD3 positivity; and negative staining for CD5, BCL-2, Cyclin D1, CD19, TdT, and MPO. The Ki-67 proliferation index was >95%, and in situ hybridization for Epstein–Barr virus was negative.

A 5-year-old mare was evaluated for a mass over the right distolateral femur that had been present for approximately 3 months and had slowly increased in size. Over the same period, the mare developed right hind–limb lameness of increasing severity. On examination there was a firm, smooth, subcutaneous nodular mass, 4 × 5 cm, adherent to but not ulcerating the skin. The mare resented local palpation but had no other abnormalities on general physical examination. In-hand trot on a hard surface showed a 3/5 right hind–limb lameness. Radiographs of the distal right femur were unremarkable. Ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, homogeneous subcutaneous mass with moderate echodensity. Regional lymph nodes were normal on palpation and ultrasound.

A 55-year-old man presented with lower urinary tract symptoms characterized by hesitancy, poor urinary stream, and urgency. He denied flank pain, colicky pain, haematuria, weight loss, or constitutional symptoms. His medical history was unremarkable, and he had no prior genitourinary disease. He was afebrile, with stable vital signs, and a physical examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a serum prostate-specific antigen level of 5.1 ng/ml and a serum creatinine concentration of 86 μmol/l. Urine microscopy demonstrated no haematuria or atypical cells. Transrectal ultrasound–guided prostate biopsies revealed benign prostatic hyperplasia.

An abdominal ultrasound performed to evaluate his lower urinary tract symptoms incidentally revealed an exophytic lesion in the right kidney measuring approximately 3.0 × 3.2 × 4.2 cm. The lesion was homogeneous and hypoechoic with a well-defined margin, located at the lateral border of the ventral mid-zone of the kidney. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen confirmed a soft-tissue mass in the same location, measuring up to 2.17 cm in maximum diameter, with a small area of calcification; the lesion was exophytic and situated away from the renal hilum.

A 53-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 2-week history of headache and vertigo. She was alert and oriented, with mild truncal ataxia and gait unsteadiness; nystagmus was absent. Noncontrast CT of the head demonstrated a hyperdense 30 × 31 × 36 mm mass in the anteromedial cerebellar hemispheres adjacent to the medial tentorium cerebelli, with mild ventriculomegaly. Contrast-enhanced CT showed the lesion abutting the lower surface of the medial tentorium between the vein of the cerebellomesencephalic fissure and the declival vein and compressing the dorsal brainstem, causing aqueductal stenosis. With a presumptive diagnosis of tentorial meningioma, she was scheduled for MRI 10 days later. By that time, her symptoms had worsened, and she required assistance to walk. MRI revealed an extra-axial tumor with broad attachment to the medial tentorium, hypointense on T1-weighted images, mixed intensity on T2- and diffusion-weighted images with corresponding hypointensity on the ADC map, extensive perilesional edema, and intense gadolinium enhancement measuring 40 × 41 × 46 mm. Cerebral angiography showed no obvious feeding vessels or tumor blush from the internal carotid, external carotid, or vertebrobasilar systems. The serum level of soluble interleukin-2 receptor was 470 U/mL (normal range, 157–474 U/mL).

A 63-year-old woman with metastatic myoepithelial carcinoma of the left parotid gland, type 2 diabetes (managed with metformin until recently), hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and hypothyroidism presented for routine chemotherapy infusion and was found to have a preinfusion serum glucose level of 30 mg/dL. She reported several episodes over the past week of morning and evening confusion and tremulousness after fasting several hours; finger-stick glucometers confirmed values in the 30s and symptoms resolved with sugar-containing foods, fulfilling Whipple’s triad. Metformin had been discontinued after hypoglycemia began. On admission, renal function was normal. Liver enzymes were stably elevated, with normal bilirubin, INR, and a mildly decreased albumin. During a hypoglycemic episode (glucose 33 mg/dL), laboratory evaluation showed insulin <1 μU/mL (reference 3–25), C-peptide <0.5 ng/mL (reference 1.1–4.3), β-hydroxybutyrate <1.0 mmol/L (reference <3), and random cortisol 23 μg/dL (reference morning 8–25). Thyroid studies showed TSH 8.3 mIU/L (reference 0.3–4.7) and free T4 0.80 ng/dL (reference 0.80–1.70), and her levothyroxine dose was increased. Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) was 15 ng/mL (reference 41–279), and IGF-2 was 147 ng/mL (reference 180–580), yielding an IGF-2:IGF-1 molar ratio of 10.

A 33-year-old Thai man with a heavy smoking habit presented with a 3-week history of left eyelid droop without other complaints. Visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally; intraocular pressure and ocular motility were normal. Examination revealed mild ptosis of the left upper eyelid and anisocoria, with the left pupil measuring 2 mm versus 3 mm on the right in bright light, and 2.5 mm versus 4 mm on the right in dim light. Both pupils reacted briskly to light without an afferent defect. Anhidrosis was noted on the medial aspect of the left forehead. A 10% cocaine test increased the pupillary difference to 2.5 mm (6.0 mm on the right, 3.5 mm on the left) and produced right upper-eyelid retraction. Neurologic examination was otherwise unremarkable. A provisional diagnosis of left-sided, painless, isolated Horner syndrome was made, and MRI and MRA of the neck and brain plus CT of the chest were scheduled.

A 69-year-old man presented with a several-year history of purple spots on both feet that gradually increased in number and size. He had well-controlled hypertension for 10 years. Dermatologic examination revealed multiple purple-colored plaques and papules, 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter, some with crusted surfaces on the dorsum of the feet and around the ankles. He had no systemic symptoms, lymphadenopathy, or visceral involvement. Laboratory and serologic tests, including HIV-1 serology, were unremarkable. A punch biopsy was obtained from a lesion on the dorsum of his foot.

Histopathological examination of hematoxylin and eosin–stained sections showed a dilated, blood-filled vascular proliferation lined by flattened endothelium, extending from the papillary dermis under hyperkeratotic epidermis to the reticular dermis in a lobular pattern. A few thick-walled vessels were interspersed within predominantly thin-walled vascular spaces. Hemosiderin pigment was noted in vessel walls and surrounding stroma. Chronic inflammatory cells were present, and focal areas of immature vascular structures forming clefts, containing extravasated erythrocytes, and mild endothelial cytologic atypia were identified, especially in the papillary dermis. No spindle cell proliferation was observed.

A 9-year-old Limousine beef cow, non-pregnant and 4 months postpartum, was referred for a 10-day history of moderate hyperthermia (39.5–39.6 °C), dry feces, decreased rumination and appetite, an arched back, and attenuated heart and lung sounds. Initial treatment with amoxicillin and dexamethasone produced no improvement.

On arrival, the cow was depressed but in fair body condition (BCS 3.5/5) and weighed 738 kg. She exhibited complete inappetence (rumen-fill score 2), a persistently arched back, dewlap edema, and bilateral jugular distension with a positive jugular compression test. Mucous membranes were pale. Vital signs: heart rate 105 bpm, respiratory rate 44/min (costo-abdominal breathing), rectal temperature 38.7 °C. Right-sided pulmonary auscultation was attenuated; cardiac auscultation revealed a duplicated S1, loud on the left and attenuated on the right. Rumination was absent. A wither-pinch test elicited pain. External lymph nodes: moderate enlargement of the right superficial cervical node. Rectal and urine exams were unremarkable; feces appeared normal.

Laboratory studies showed normal plasma fibrinogen, mild hypoalbuminemia, increased total protein (chronic inflammatory syndrome), leukocyte count at the upper limit with neutrophilia, and lymphopenia. 

A right-sided thoracic ultrasound revealed a 30 cm × 25 cm echogenic mass severely compressing the right heart, reducing right ventricular size, and an adjacent anechoic pleural fluid collection; the pericardium and valves appeared normal. Reticular ultrasonography showed normal structure but absent contractions. Pleural fluid, aspirated under ultrasound guidance, was moderately cloudy, orange-brown; analysis indicated a non-specific septic exudate.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of a progressively enlarging mass in the right lower para-umbilical area of the anterior abdominal wall. She had normal vital signs and no systemic symptoms. On examination, there was a 7 × 6 cm firm, irregular, subcutaneous mass; the abdomen was otherwise soft and non-tender with no intra-abdominal masses or palpable lymphadenopathy. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory studies were within normal limits. CT of the abdomen showed a mass confined to the abdominal wall. A chest radiograph was normal. 

She underwent wide local excision with clear margins. Grossly, the specimen measured 13 × 10 cm with 11 cm of subcutaneous fat; the tumor was a well-defined, nonencapsulated, grayish-yellow mass measuring 7 × 6 cm with necrotic foci and no involvement of overlying skin or muscle. 

Microscopically, the lesion comprised irregular nests of large cells with round to oval pleomorphic vesicular nuclei, abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, eosinophilic globules, variable nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, scattered mitotic figures (4 per 10 HPF at ×200), and focal necrosis. The nests were separated by fibrous bands. 

Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated strong positivity for S100, vimentin, and CD68; stains for cytokeratin, smooth muscle actin, desmin, and myogenin were negative. The Ki-67 proliferation index was 3–5%. PAS stain highlighted the cytoplasmic granules and globules.

A 50-year-old non-smoker Caucasian woman with no past medical history presented with chronic mild right upper quadrant abdominal pain for one year. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver function tests, and alpha-fetoprotein level, were within normal limits. Viral hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. An abdominal ultrasound showed a 15 mm homogeneous hyperechoic nodule in segment VI of the liver. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a well-circumscribed 17 mm nodule in segment VI that was moderately hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on T1-weighted images, and hyperintense on diffusion-weighted images with apparent diffusion coefficient restriction. The lesion demonstrated arterial-phase enhancement, washout in the portal and delayed phases, capsule enhancement, and a signal drop on opposed-phase imaging, indicative of fat content.

A man in his 20s with no prior hearing disorder was referred to the ENT clinic after two episodes of sudden left-ear hearing loss occurring within three months of receiving his second dose of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine. On day 1 after vaccination, he developed progressive left-ear hearing loss lasting 10 days. Treatment with pseudoephedrine and fluticasone nasal spray for suspected allergic otitis media yielded no improvement. He then took cetirizine 10 mg daily from day 9 to 24, with near-normal hearing on an audiogram performed on day 26 (normal pure-tone averages, bilateral type A tympanograms, masked bone conduction). On day 31, he experienced recurrent left-ear hearing loss unresponsive to a 5-day course of cetirizine. A high-dose oral prednisone regimen (60 mg/day for 7 days followed by taper) was given for presumed Meniere’s disease but failed to improve his hearing. Sequential audiograms on days 44 and 60 demonstrated progressive low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear and a marginal decline in word recognition. Videonystagmography on day 76 showed 93% left-ear caloric weakness and 50% directional preponderance to the right; optokinetic testing revealed asymmetrical, reduced left-sided responses. Additional blood tests—including complete blood count with differential, rheumatoid factor, comprehensive metabolic panel, and lipid profile—were all within normal limits, and anti–SARS-CoV-2 antibodies were positive.

A 47-year-old woman presented with a 4-year history of wheezing and productive cough, initially diagnosed as late-onset asthma. Despite standard asthma therapy, her symptoms worsened, with new episodes of left chest pain and dyspnea. She had no relevant past medical or family history. On examination, breath sounds were bilaterally vesicular but decreased at the left lung base. A chest radiograph showed marked volume reduction of the left lung. Computed tomography of the chest revealed a rounded lesion at the carinal region, partially obstructing the ostium of the left main bronchus.  

Rigid bronchoscopy demonstrated a mobile polypoid lesion with a smooth, shiny, non-friable surface that obstructed the left main bronchus; the lesion was removed endoscopically. Grossly, the oval, encapsulated mass measured 2.3 × 1.7 × 1.5 cm, had a fibroelastic consistency, and a smooth, homogeneous brownish cut surface.  

Microscopic examination showed a low-grade mesenchymal neoplasm composed of spindle cells in small, loose fascicles, with alternating hypercellular and hypocellular areas. Hypocellular regions contained dense collagen bands and focal myxoid change. Focal aggregates of mature adipose tissue were present. Blood vessels were irregular with a “staghorn” configuration. Mitotic activity was 2 per 10 high-power fields.  

Immunohistochemical stains revealed that the neoplastic cells were negative for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), S100 protein, smooth muscle actin, and desmin, and were positive for CD34, CD99, and BCL2.

A 44-year-old Mediterranean man presented with a 9-month history of intermittent palpitations and exertional dyspnea classified as New York Heart Association Class II. He had no cardiovascular risk factors, no family history of cancer or heart disease, and no other comorbidities. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits, heart sounds were unremarkable, and there were no skin lesions. A 12-lead ECG showed normal sinus rhythm at 62 bpm, with normal PR and QRS intervals.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a hyperechoic epicardial mass measuring 6 × 4 cm in the region of the inferior vena cava extending toward the right atrium and coronary sinus. Contrast-enhanced CT angiography demonstrated a hypodense heterogeneous mass measuring 7.5 × 6 × 5 cm, and it was suggested to represent a paraganglionic mass vascularized by the distal right coronary artery. Coronary catheterization could not exclude feeding vessels from the right coronary artery.

A conservative watch-and-wait approach was initially adopted. Six months later, cardiac MRI with contrast showed a prolonged T1 relaxation time of approximately 1751 ms (native myocardium ∼1240 ms; left ventricular blood 1774 ms), suggesting similarity to blood signal. T1 mapping showed isointensity to myocardium, T2 mapping showed a homogeneous hyperintense mass, and late gadolinium enhancement was heterogeneous. There was no significant change in size.

A 13-year-old Sudanese girl presented with a 2-day history of colicky abdominal pain, absolute constipation, and vomiting of all ingested food. Since age 5, she had recurrent nocturnal abdominal pain exacerbated by spicy foods, frequent yellowish diarrhea, dyspepsia, and daily loud audible bowel sounds. She is the seventh of 10 siblings, with two of her siblings and four nephews having died in early childhood. 

On examination, she appeared ill, in pain, and tachypneic, with a low-grade fever. Her abdomen was distended and tender. Laboratory investigations were within normal limits. 

Supine abdominal radiography showed a tubular gas-filled structure originating in the right iliac fossa, crossing obliquely upward to the left hypochondrium. Erect abdominal radiography revealed multiple air-fluid levels. A diagnosis of acute intestinal obstruction was made, and the patient was taken for emergency exploratory laparotomy.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 6-week history of dull right upper-quadrant abdominal pain. She was first diagnosed at 16 months of age with a 9 × 8 cm multiseptated cystic mass in the right hepatic lobe on ultrasonography and MRI, consistent with mesenchymal hamartoma of the liver. Resection was planned but deferred, and serial sonographic surveillance continued until age 10 years, after which she was lost to follow-up. On current presentation, vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed mild right upper-quadrant tenderness without rebound or guarding. Laboratory evaluation showed normal liver enzyme levels except for a γ-glutamyl transpeptidase of 40 IU/L (reference, 8–35 IU/L). Serum tumor markers were: α-fetoprotein 1.13 ng/mL (0.89–8.78 ng/mL), carcinoembryonic antigen 1.3 ng/mL (0–5 ng/mL), and CA 19-9 1075 U/mL (0–37 U/mL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated interval growth of the right-lobe cystic mass to 12.9 × 8.3 cm and a new 6 cm peripheral enhancing region within its posterior aspect, with enlarged hepatoduodenal and portocaval lymph nodes. MRI and ^18F-FDG PET revealed heterogeneous internal signal intensity and focal hypermetabolism within the lesion, findings that could not exclude malignant transformation.

A 38-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension. She noted her abdomen, initially tennis-ball size, gradually increased to soccer-ball size. She had no prior medical illnesses, was a lifelong non-smoker without secondhand-smoke exposure, and had no occupational carcinogen exposure. She was nulliparous with regular 28-day menstrual cycles. 

On examination, there was a huge, immobile suprapubic mass equivalent to a 30-week pregnancy. Chest examination revealed reduced air entry and vocal resonance with stony dullness over the left lower lung zone. Breast examination was normal, with no palpable masses; there was no lymphadenopathy and no other abnormalities on systemic review.

Transabdominal ultrasonography showed a 20 × 20 cm solid-cystic ovarian mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a large solid-cystic pelvic mass filling most of the lower abdomen, bilateral ovarian cysts, left hydrosalpinx, a solid irregular lesion in the left upper lung lobe, ipsilateral pleural effusion, and multiple small bilateral lung nodules.

A 65-year-old woman with metastatic malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor on a clinical trial agent and no known germline mutations presented with 6 weeks of nausea, progressive gait imbalance, and falls. On examination, she had no focal deficits beyond gait ataxia. MRI of the brain showed nonenhancing T2 FLAIR hyperintense white matter abnormalities in deep structures. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed a normal cell count and protein, cytology with atypical lymphoid cells, and flow cytometry with an abnormal mature B-cell population that could not be further characterized. CSF viral studies, CSF oligoclonal bands, and both CSF and serum paraneoplastic panels were negative. A whole-body PET scan showed no evidence of new disease, and ophthalmologic examination was normal.

Her clinical trial drug was held, but over the next month she developed intermittent diplopia, neck-extensor weakness, and worsening inability to ambulate. Repeat MRI demonstrated new contrast-enhancing lesions in the corpus callosum. Repeat CSF again showed atypical cells and an abnormal B-cell population, with persistently normal cell count and protein. The differential diagnosis included an inflammatory or autoimmune process, a drug-related process from her MPNST treatment, or a new neoplastic process. Given the deep location of the lesions, brain biopsy was initially deferred, and she received high-dose methylprednisolone for presumed autoimmune or drug-related disease.

Over the next several months, her MRI findings fluctuated, and she underwent a stereotactic brain biopsy of an enhancing lesion that showed gliosis with mild–moderate parenchymal and perivascular mixed inflammatory infiltrate. Genomic testing of the biopsy sample was nondiagnostic. She was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin and a prednisone taper, but her symptoms continued to worsen. She then underwent plasma exchange followed by additional intravenous immunoglobulin and rituximab, without clinical or radiographic improvement.

An 85-year-old man was admitted after three episodes of collapse with transient loss of consciousness at home. He reported only mild, diffuse abdominal discomfort and no trauma. His medical history included severe aortic stenosis, type 2 diabetes, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and a prior duodenal ulcer bleed. Medications were aspirin, bisoprolol, omeprazole, and ramipril. He was a former smoker (quit 35 years prior) with minimal alcohol intake and lived independently.

On examination, he was afebrile with an oxygen saturation of 100% on room air, blood pressure of 80/40 mmHg, and remained hypotensive despite aggressive fluid resuscitation. Cardiac exam revealed an ejection systolic murmur; jugular venous pressure was not elevated and there was no peripheral edema. The lungs were clear. Abdominal exam showed mild epigastric discomfort without peritoneal signs. Rectal examination was normal.

Initial laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL (reference 13–18), white cell count 11×10^9/L, and platelets 136×10^9/L; coagulation profile, renal function, and liver function tests were within normal limits. Chest radiograph was unremarkable and ECG showed left ventricular hypertrophy. He was admitted to a monitored unit given concerns for syncope related to aortic stenosis. An urgent echocardiogram demonstrated aortic stenosis but no critical obstruction, with an ejection fraction >55% and good biventricular function.

A repeat full blood count revealed a hemoglobin of 4.9 g/dL, and he was transfused with blood products. Given the possibility of a dissecting thoracic aneurysm extending into the abdomen, he was transferred to the ICU and underwent an urgent contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen, which showed normal thoracic and abdominal aortas without dissection but revealed a large volume of free intraperitoneal fluid and areas of low attenuation in the right hepatic lobe consistent with metastatic lesions.

A 20-year-old Japanese woman presented with a slowly enlarging subcutaneous nodule on her left forehead, first noticed at age 15. On examination, a firm, poorly mobile 7-mm nodule was palpable beneath the skin. Ultrasonography showed a well-defined, dome-shaped, solid subcutaneous mass (~7 mm) without vascular flow on Doppler; there was apparent continuity with the frontal bone, though the interface with subcutaneous tissue was unclear. MRI of the head demonstrated a 7-mm lesion within the frontalis muscle that was uniformly low signal on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences, with no obvious connection to the frontal bone. Noncontrast CT revealed a high-attenuation nodule beneath the frontalis muscle, measuring approximately 7 mm, with a small zone of decreased attenuation separating it from the underlying bone. Based on these findings, benign entities such as calcifying epithelioma and skull osteoma were considered in the preoperative differential.

A middle-aged man with no past medical history presented with a 2-month history of left-sided sciatica-like pain progressing to lower back discomfort, without bowel or bladder symptoms. HIV testing was negative. CT of the lumbar spine showed a lytic lesion in the left half of the L2 vertebral body and pedicle. MRI demonstrated a T1 hypointense, T2 isointense, contrast-enhancing lesion of the left half of the L2 vertebral body and pedicle. He underwent posterior spinal fixation with lateral extracavitary approach cage fusion and decompression. Intraoperatively, the lesion was fleshy, fibrous, and highly vascular. Histopathology revealed plasmacytoma; immunophenotyping was CD138 positive with a high MIB-1 index. Bone marrow aspirate showed no increased plasma cells, no clonality, and normal cytogenetics. Serum protein electrophoresis and serum-free light chains were negative for paraprotein or light-chain excess; the blood count was normal, and myeloid markers were negative. He received 45 Gy in 25 fractions to the L2 region, with complete pain resolution and stable implant positioning on follow-up imaging.

Six months after radiotherapy (8 months after the initial diagnosis), he developed acute numbness and weakness of both lower limbs over 2 days, accompanied by bladder dysfunction. Examination indicated a T6 myelopathy. CT of the thoracic spine revealed a lytic lesion with collapse of the T4 vertebral body. MRI showed a T1 hypointense, T2 isointense, contrast-enhancing T4 vertebral lesion with collapse and an anterior epidural soft-tissue mass compressing the spinal cord; additional contrast-enhancing lesions were seen in the pelvic bones and ribs. Repeat myeloma workup remained negative. Due to progressive neurologic deficits, he underwent posterior spinal fixation with lateral extracavitary approach cage fusion and decompression at T4. The lesion appeared similarly fleshy, fibrous, and highly vascular. Biopsy of the T4 lesion was interpreted as plasmacytoma by one center, whereas a second center reported a malignant lymphoproliferative disorder with B-cell predominance. Immunohistochemical stains were positive for CD138, CD20, and CD3; negative for CD56; and showed a high MIB-1 labeling index. Comparison with the original L2 specimen demonstrated identical histological and immunophenotypic features.

A 29-year-old woman presented with lower abdominal pain. She had undergone laparoscopic myomectomy at age 25, during which uterine leiomyoma fragments were removed with surgical scissors in a collection bag. Four laparoscopic scars were noted; the mass was not palpable. Laboratory studies, including serum CA 19-9 (≤1.2 U/mL), CEA (0.6 ng/mL), CA-125 (9.5 U/mL), and sIL-2R (206 U/mL), were within normal limits, as were other routine tests. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-defined 38 × 32 × 42 mm pelvic mass with central enhancement in the early phase and peripheral enhancement in the late phase, with a feeding vessel from the second sigmoidal artery and no evidence of invasion or metastasis. T2-weighted MRI demonstrated high signal intensity at the tumor margins and low signal centrally, while T1-weighted images showed heterogeneous low signal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic, heterogeneous mass with a clear capsule and pulsatile internal blood flow. FDG PET–CT showed nodular uptake in the pelvis (SUVmax 3.2) without distant lesions. Colonoscopy was unremarkable. The preoperative differential diagnosis included schwannoma, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, leiomyoma or leiomyosarcoma, desmoid tumor, and solitary fibrous tumor. Because it was difficult to differentiate benign from malignant, surgical resection en bloc was planned without breaching the capsule.

A 17-year-old previously healthy male presented with acute altered mental status. Initial blood glucose was 1.8 mmol/L; he received IV dextrose and improved, but his glucose then rebounded to 12.1 mmol/L over 3 hours with reactive hyperglycemia. His history was notable only for ADHD treated with dextroamphetamine-amphetamine and a family history of autoimmune thyroid disease. Thyroid‐stimulating hormone was normal. Urine screening was presumptively positive for THC; sulfonylurea screen was negative.

He was admitted NPO with glucose checks every 1–2 hours. After a 10-hour fast, glucose fell to 2.1 mmol/L; a critical sample showed insulin 158.35 pmol/L, C-peptide 1.09 nmol/L, and suppressed beta-hydroxybutyrate, indicating endogenous hyperinsulinism. Other hormonal studies (ACTH, cortisol, growth hormone) were appropriate for the clinical context. He received additional dextrose and maintained euglycemia on dextrose-containing fluids. After resuming a general diet, glucose ranged from 2.9–9.1 mmol/L.

Given reactive hyperglycemia and family history, pancreatic autoantibodies (insulin, IgG islet cell, IA-2, GAD) were obtained and all returned positive, leading to a diagnosis of stage 1 type 1 diabetes. He was discharged with self-monitoring of blood glucose, glucagon training, and nutrition education.

On outpatient follow-up, TrialNet screening confirmed multiple islet autoantibodies. An oral glucose tolerance test showed 1-hour glucose 12.0 mmol/L and 2-hour glucose 11.1 mmol/L, consistent with stage 2 type 1 diabetes. Over the next month, he gained weight, discontinued frequent SMBG, and CGM revealed prolonged fasting hypoglycemia alongside postprandial hyperglycemia. Hemoglobin A1c rose from 4.7% to 5.5%. A screening abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable, raising concern for an additional etiology of his hypoglycemia.

A 16-year-old boy noted a progressively enlarging lump at his posterior left knee over one year. MRI revealed a 13 cm mass in the left posteroinferior thigh, centered in the semitendinosus muscle and extending to the biceps femoris. Fine-needle aspiration showed a heterogeneous population of ovoid to tapered spindle cells with densely eosinophilic cytoplasm and occasional multinucleated cells; no lipogenic differentiation was seen. Immunohistochemistry was positive for desmin and myogenin and negative for CD68, keratin, S-100, SOX-10, HMB-45, and Melan-A. FISH for a FOXO1 13q14 rearrangement was negative. A diagnosis of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma was made, and the patient received 10 weeks of vincristine/irinotecan chemotherapy per protocol ARST0531. 

The tumor was then completely excised. Grossly, it was a mixed cystic and solid mass with a thin white capsule. H&E sections revealed diffuse sheets of round cells with eosinophilic rhabdomyoblastic cytoplasm and large nuclei. Throughout the tumor, a subset of cells exhibited a spectrum of cytoplasmic vacuolation, from small vacuoles to multiple vacuoles indenting the nucleus, resembling adipocytes or lipoblasts. These vacuolated cells were positive for adipophilin, Oil Red O, and S-100 protein; the vacuoles were negative with periodic acid–Schiff stain, with or without diastase. Immunostaining for desmin was positive in the vacuolated cells, whereas myogenin was negative in their nuclei. There was cystic change, scattered histiocytes, extracellular hemosiderin, low mitotic activity (1 mf/10 hpf), and no coagulative necrosis.

A 21-year-old man was admitted after minor head trauma, at which time depressive symptoms and behavioral changes were noted. He reported a 4-week history of mild spastic hemiparesis and right-sided hypesthesia. On neurologic examination, there was left-sided weakness with increased tone and diminished sensation on the right.

Conventional brain MRI showed left-hemispheric, diffuse T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the basal ganglia, insular region, amygdala, and left cerebral peduncle, with mild atrophy in these regions. There was no contrast enhancement, no solid mass, no cystic lesions, and diffusion- and perfusion-weighted images were unremarkable. 

A comprehensive diagnostic workup—including extensive laboratory studies, neurophysiological testing, cerebrospinal fluid analysis (with normal β-HCG and AFP levels), and cerebral angiography—revealed no evidence of metabolic or genetic leukoencephalopathy, autoimmune or infectious inflammation, vasculitis or vasculopathy, or a specific tumor entity. 

Proton MR spectroscopy with both 2D chemical shift imaging and single-voxel techniques demonstrated in the lesion a decreased N-acetylaspartate/creatine ratio, a slight increase in choline/creatine ratio, and a markedly elevated myoinositol concentration (up to 13–14 mM) compared with contralateral tissue. Myoinositol levels exceeded values typical of degenerative or inflammatory diseases, and a slight mobile lipid peak was present.

A 74-year-old Asian woman presented with several months of right knee pain without antecedent trauma. Her medical history was notable for papillary thyroid carcinoma treated by resection 5 years earlier, with no recurrence. On examination, there was mild tenderness over the medial femoral condyle without erythema or warmth; the range of motion was slightly reduced.

Radiographs of the right knee demonstrated a 4.0 × 4.5 cm osteolytic lesion within the medial femoral condyle without cortical breach or periosteal reaction. MRI showed the lesion to be hypointense on T1-weighted images, low-to-intermediate signal on T2-weighted images, and avidly enhancing after gadolinium; there was no extraosseous extension.

An open biopsy revealed clusters of oval to spindle-shaped epithelial cells with squamous differentiation, set within a bland fibrous stroma. The epithelial nuclei were uniform with a low mitotic rate, and reactive bone formation surrounded the clusters.

A 40-year-old man presented with a four-week history of a rapidly growing nodule at the site of a scratched surgical scar on his right elbow. His oncologic history included a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor of the right forearm in 2003 treated with surgery (negative margins), radiation, and chemotherapy, and a recurrence over the biceps in 2015 treated with resection (positive margins) and additional radiotherapy. He had no personal or family history of neurofibromatosis. On examination, there was a 2.0 cm violaceous nodule with a 1 cm red, friable papulonodule centrally located on the previous surgical scar. Histopathologic examination of the nodule showed mixed hypercellular and hypocellular areas composed of atypical spindled and epithelioid cells in a myxoid stroma. The Ki-67 proliferation index was high, PHH3 staining revealed more than 30 mitoses per high-powered field, and S-100 immunostaining was focally positive. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the right forearm demonstrated a complex, dumbbell-shaped soft-tissue mass measuring approximately 5.4 × 4.3 × 3.5 cm that displaced the ulnar nerve medially and splayed the flexor muscles and tendons, with no evidence of distant metastases.

A 50-year-old woman presented with a left breast mass of 1 year’s duration. She first noticed a 1.5 cm firm lump in the upper quadrant of her left breast without pain, skin changes, or nipple discharge. The mass had grown slowly. She had no relevant family history and no systemic symptoms. On examination, there was asymmetry of the breasts with a firm, ill-defined 3.5 cm × 3 cm irregular mass at the 12 o’clock position, 4 cm from the nipple, fixed to deep tissues. A small amount of cloudy, light-yellow discharge was expressed from a single duct on the left; no axillary lymphadenopathy was present. 

Diagnostic imaging included:
- Mammography: partially obscured high-density mass measuring 2.0 cm × 1.7 cm with indistinct margins.  
- Ultrasound: heterogeneous hypoechoic solid mass, 30 mm × 13 mm × 20 mm, indistinct borders, with internal blood flow (BI-RADS 4C).  
- Contrast-enhanced breast MRI: oval, spiculated, heterogeneously enhancing mass (2.3 × 2.2 × 2.8 cm), isointense on T1-weighted imaging, hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging and diffusion-weighted imaging, with restricted diffusion on the ADC map. The dynamic enhancement curve showed rapid initial uptake followed by a persistent enhancement pattern (type I time-intensity curve).

A 50-year-old Chinese woman with a history of Graves’ disease presented with one week of dyspnea and cough without fever, chest pain, or hemoptysis. She was a non-smoker, with no weight loss or appetite change. Physical examination revealed a BMI of 17 kg/m2, blood pressure 172/102 mmHg, heart rate 97 bpm, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Chest examination showed reduced air entry on the right. Cutaneous examination disclosed bilateral small erythematous papules on the cheeks and nasolabial folds. There was no clubbing or lymphadenopathy.

A chest radiograph demonstrated a large right pneumothorax without mediastinal shift and diffuse reticular-nodular opacities in the left lung. A right‐sided chest tube was inserted with subsequent lung re-expansion and removal of the tube.

High-resolution CT of the chest revealed multiple round thin-walled cysts throughout both lungs, mild interlobular septal thickening, and numerous tiny (<4 mm) randomly distributed ground‐glass and solid nodules. Abdominal CT showed multiple fat-density lesions in both kidneys consistent with angiomyolipomas.

A 50-year-old Caucasian man presented with several months of vague upper abdominal discomfort that progressed to postprandial stabbing pain and intermittent night sweats. He reported an unintentional weight loss of 1.5 kg without anorexia. Four months earlier, a small tubular adenoma in the sigmoid colon had been resected during an otherwise normal colonoscopy. His medical history was unremarkable, with no family history of cancer.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. Findings were notable for hepatomegaly and a single prominent right axillary lymph node; the remainder of the exam was normal.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• C-reactive protein 40 mg/L (reference <5.0)  
• Lactate dehydrogenase 300 U/L (reference ≤250)  
• Mild elevations in liver enzymes  
• Normal carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)  
• Markedly elevated cancer antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) at 14 968 kU/L (reference ≤34)

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed multiple lesions in the liver and lungs, as well as enlarged axillary, infradiaphragmatic, and hilar lymph nodes. 18F-FDG PET-CT confirmed widespread metastatic involvement of the liver, lungs, kidneys, adrenal glands, skeletal muscle, bone, and lymph nodes but showed no identifiable primary lesion.

Ultrasound-guided biopsy of a liver lesion demonstrated adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining of the liver specimen was positive for CK7 and CK19, negative for CK20 and TTF1, and variably positive for SATB2. Mismatch-repair proteins were intact. Upper endoscopy and endoscopic ultrasound of the esophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum, pancreas, and biliary tract revealed no primary tumor.

A 26-year-old immunocompetent woman presented with a 3-month history of progressive shortness of breath, facial and upper-limb swelling, and mild lower-limb edema. She denied weight loss, night sweats, or fever. On admission, blood pressure was 85/60 mm Hg, heart rate 116 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, temperature 36.3 °C, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Examination revealed facial swelling, jugular venous distention of 6 cm above the sternal angle, upper-limb swelling, mild lower-limb edema, distant heart sounds, a diastolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border, and decreased breath sounds with dullness to percussion at both lung bases.  
Chest radiograph showed bilateral pleural effusions, a widened mediastinum, and hilar congestion. Electrocardiography revealed sinus rhythm, a Q wave in V1, and low‐voltage QRS complexes without electrical alternans. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large right atrial mass obstructing the tricuspid valve and severe pericardial effusion. Pericardiocentesis yielded 1000 mL of serous fluid, with glucose 86 mg/dL, negative acid‐fast bacilli stain, and no malignant cells. Bilateral thoracenteses removed 1 L of serous transudative fluid from each side.  
Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a rounded right atrial mass measuring 6.3 × 6.4 cm obstructing the tricuspid valve. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a large soft-tissue filling defect nearly occluding the right atrium and distal superior vena cava, a 7 × 4 cm anterior mediastinal mass, and a heterogeneous 13 × 13 × 7.5 cm pelvic mass likely arising from the right adnexa.

A 23-year-old Caucasian man presented with 5 months of persistent epigastric pain, intermittent nausea, nonbloody emesis, and a 20-lb weight loss. His vital signs were notable only for a heart rate of 97 beats/min. Examination revealed conjunctival pallor and epigastric tenderness. Laboratory studies showed iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 5.8 g/dL, MCV 67.8 fL, iron < 10 µg/dL, ferritin 2 ng/mL) and a hemoccult-positive stool; carcinoembryonic antigen, cancer antigen 19-9, and α-fetoprotein levels were normal. HIV and EBV PCR were nonreactive. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a markedly thickened heterogeneous loop of jejunum in the left hemiabdomen with mesenteric adenopathy and small-volume pelvic ascites. Push enteroscopy revealed a single ulcerated, malignant-appearing mass measuring 45 mm × 45 mm in the proximal jejunum; biopsy showed a high-grade malignant neoplasm, and fluorescence in situ hybridization was normal. PET–CT confirmed a hypermetabolic, multilobulated, ill-defined mass involving multiple jejunal loops.

A 35-year-old man in a drug rehabilitation center presented with a 4-month history of headaches and one seizure the day before admission. He reported a 2-month history of gradual, painless, progressive visual loss that acutely worsened in the days before hospitalization. He had no history of immunodeficiency, autoimmune disease, or malignancy and denied ongoing substance abuse. On examination, he was afebrile, normotensive, and fully conscious. Neurologic assessment showed bilateral visual acuity reduced to light perception on the right and hand motion on the left, with mild to moderate bilateral optic disc swelling. Pupils were mid-size, isochoric, and reactive to light.

Noncontrast head CT revealed bilateral temporal-lobe hypodensity with loss of gray–white differentiation extending into the occipital lobes and centrum semiovale, with mild left uncal herniation but no mass lesion or hemorrhage. Empiric IV aciclovir was started for presumed herpes simplex encephalitis, and corticosteroids with mannitol were administered for raised intracranial pressure. Lumbar puncture showed clear cerebrospinal fluid, an opening pressure of 38 cm H₂O, mild glucose elevation, and otherwise normal cell counts and chemistry. CSF PCR for HSV and blood and urine toxin assays, as well as HIV and hepatitis B and C serologies, were negative.

Brain MRI showed bilateral T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the temporal lobes, insular regions (worse on the left), with extension into the corpus callosum, centrum semiovale, left basal ganglia, left thalamus, optic chiasm, and periventricular occipital white matter. The lesions were mildly expanded, with no diffusion restriction on DWI, no enhancement on postcontrast images, and no hemorrhagic foci on SWI.

Ophthalmologic testing with optical coherence tomography revealed increased retinal nerve fiber–layer thickness consistent with disc swelling, and visual evoked potentials showed absent bilateral waveforms.

A 46-year-old healthy woman was referred for evaluation of a painful soft-tissue mass on the right plantar midfoot. She first noticed the swelling 2–3 years earlier; it had enlarged and become increasingly painful over the past 4 months, and she described walking on a hard stone. There was no history of trauma or family history of similar problems. On inspection, the overlying skin was normal without signs of infection. Examination revealed bilateral planovalgus feet with bilateral hallux valgus (worse on the right), and a tender, subcutaneous mass on the right plantar midfoot associated with sensitivity and numbness.  

To provide temporary relief, she received an ultrasound-guided injection of 80 mg depo-medrone and 1 ml of 1% lignocaine into the second metatarsophalangeal region. Plain radiographs showed no bony injury or malignancy. Ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined, hypoechoic tender lesion within the plantar subcutaneous tissue, measuring approximately 17 × 7 × 11 mm, extending deep to but not arising from the plantar fascia. Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a 2 cm × 5 mm tubular oblique lesion in the plantar subcutaneous fat and ruled out sinus tarsi syndrome or internal derangements. She was provided with orthotic medial arch support and referred to a sarcoma multidisciplinary team, which found no radiologic features of sarcoma. Despite these measures, she continued to experience sharp, stabbing pain (10/10) and elected to proceed with surgical excision biopsy.

A 24-year-old Bangladeshi man from a rural area presented in early 2008 with progressive bilateral dimness of vision (worse on the left), headache, nausea, and left-sided deafness. Despite evaluation by ophthalmologists, his vision deteriorated to complete blindness. On referral, he was normotensive, nondiabetic, and had no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, leukocyte count 8.8 × 10^9/L, and ESR 14 mm at 1 hour. Chest and sinus radiographs were normal. Audiometry revealed normal hearing on the right and no response on the left ear except for vibrotactile sensation. MRI of the brain demonstrated hypointense lesions adjacent to the cavernous sinus and retroocular region of the right orbit, findings suggestive of an inflammatory lesion or neoplastic mass (e.g., meningioma). An endoscopic endonasal transethmoidal biopsy yielded fragmented soft tissue, chronic inflammatory cells, and a single focus of oval cells forming a whorled pattern. The lesion was reported as an inflammatory pseudotumour with a differential diagnosis of lymphoplasmacyte-rich meningioma.

A 15-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute lightheadedness, diaphoresis, and palpitations in the evening after a 7-hour fast. He had experienced recurrent episodes of dizziness for 2 months without weight change. Point-of-care blood glucose was 1.5 mmol/L, and his symptoms resolved after IV dextrose.

He had no family history of insulinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. Vital signs were normal. On abdominal examination, there was a large, firm, palpable mass in the left upper quadrant.

Serum testing during hypoglycemia showed an inappropriately elevated insulin level of 13.34 μU/mL (normal <3 μU/mL) and a C-peptide level of 2.2 ng/mL (normal <0.6 ng/mL). Serum intact parathyroid hormone, calcium, and prolactin levels were all within reference ranges.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined, lobulated, hypervascular mass measuring 12 cm in the pancreatic tail with areas of low attenuation and calcifications. There was no pancreatic duct dilatation, no hepatic lesions, and no significant lymphadenopathy.

A 37-year-old white woman with no past medical history presented with 4 months of progressive dyspnea and back pain. Four months earlier, chest radiography and CT at an outside facility had shown right upper lobe consolidation, and she was treated for presumed pneumonia. Two months later, bronchoscopy with BAL and transbronchial biopsy revealed chronic inflammation without malignancy. On re-presentation, she complained of neck pain and was tachypneic on exam. Contrast CT of the chest showed near-complete collapse and consolidation of the right upper lobe with enlarged subcarinal and station 6 lymph nodes. Spine MRI demonstrated a 50% compression fracture at C7 and diffuse lytic vertebral lesions. CT of the abdomen revealed a solitary 1.5-cm hypodense lesion in the right hepatic lobe. A transthoracic biopsy of the right upper lobe showed interstitial fibrosis and lymphocytic infiltrates without malignancy. EBUS with transbronchial lymph node sampling and BAL cytology demonstrated poorly differentiated neoplastic cells but was insufficient for immunostains. A CT-guided liver biopsy revealed an undifferentiated epithelioid neoplasm forming nests and cords within a hyalinized sclerotic stroma, with eosinophilic cytoplasm and round‐to‐ovoid nuclei. Initial immunohistochemical stains showed weak synaptophysin positivity, membranous CD99, GATA-3 positivity in a subset, and weak PAX-8. The tumor cells were nonreactive to ER and SATB2 and negative for pankeratin, CK7, CK20, MOC-31, TTF-1, WT-1, HMB45, Melan-A, SOX-10, S100, Inhibin, SMA, MyoD1, CD117, CD45, CD30, and CD34. On expert review, the cells were reactive for MUC4, with preserved BRG1 and INI1 expression and negative claudin-4, ERG, CD31, CAMTA1, P40, ETV-4, and NUT.

A 58-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of gradually increasing lower abdominal pain and irregular vaginal bleeding. She was postmenopausal (age at menopause, 56), with no significant medical, surgical, or family history. She had no history of HPV vaccination.

On examination, she was pale and underweight. Abdominopelvic CT without contrast showed an enlarged uterus. Laboratory evaluation revealed a white blood cell count of 32,200/mm3, a C-reactive protein level of 17 mg/dL, and hemoglobin of 5.5 g/dL; 6 units of red blood cells were transfused. Tumor markers were elevated: SCC antigen, 5.3 ng/mL (normal ≤2.5); CA-125, 112.7 U/mL (normal ≤35).

Speculum examination demonstrated a large bleeding tumor occupying the vaginal canal; bimanual exam revealed an enlarged, fixed uterus with the fundus midway between the symphysis pubis and the umbilicus. Contrast-enhanced CT showed multiloculated, thick-walled cystic lesions in the uterus and pelvic fluid suggestive of an abscess. Empiric antibiotics were begun.

Pelvic MRI revealed an 11×9-cm mass with central necrosis confined to the cervix; the endometrial cavity was spared and distended with fluid. There was no parametrial, vaginal wall, or rectal involvement on MRI; bladder mucosal invasion was not excluded.

Colposcopy-directed biopsy of the cervical lesion showed endometrioid adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemistry was diffusely positive for vimentin and estrogen receptor, almost negative for progesterone receptor, and patchy positive for p16. Tests for high-risk HPV (16 subtypes) and microsatellite instability were negative. Cystoscopy confirmed intact bladder mucosa.

A 13-year-old previously healthy girl presented with fever, bilateral foot pain, and a mottled purpuric rash. Over the prior 6 months, she had intermittent episodes lasting 2–3 days, improving with ibuprofen. In the weeks before presentation, she developed fatigue, hip and calf pain attributed to sports, and an episode of abdominal pain with diarrhea and emesis. She denied headaches, visual changes, oral ulcers, or other systemic symptoms. Family history was negative for autoimmune disease. 

On examination, temperature was 39.2 °C, heart rate 90 bpm, respiratory rate 20 bpm, blood pressure 114/62 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She had blanchable, retiform violaceous patches with areas of true purpura on her lower extremities and duskiness of the right second toe. Cardiac, pulmonary, joint, and neurologic examinations were otherwise normal.

Laboratory studies showed elevated creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, C-reactive protein, and transaminases. A skin biopsy of a purpuric lesion demonstrated subtle ischemia, vascular congestion, purpura, and focal eccrine gland necrosis without evidence of vasculitis. Direct immunofluorescence was negative. An extensive work-up—including hepatitis panel, cryoglobulins, lupus anticoagulant panel, cardiolipins, beta-2-glycoprotein, complements C3 and C4, antistreptolysin O titers, anti-DNAse B, and aldolase—was unremarkable. Abdominal and renal Doppler ultrasonography showed no abnormalities.

A 41-year-old woman presented with a 2–3 cm hard, irregular lump in the lower outer quadrant of her left breast. She had no hormonal symptoms, weight loss, or family history of breast cancer. Three-year-old bilateral mammograms were normal. Current imaging showed an asymmetrical density on the left mammogram (BI-RADS M4), and tomosynthesis confirmed an ill-defined 28 mm mass. Ultrasound demonstrated a suspicious ill-defined lesion (U4) with normal axillary nodes. An image-guided core biopsy revealed a grade 2 invasive carcinoma interpreted as apocrine carcinoma (B5b); ER and HER2 were negative. 

The patient underwent wide local excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy. Grossly, there was a well-defined pale tumour measuring 22 mm. Microscopically, the neoplasm was well demarcated with foci of papillary architecture, comprising large tall cells in solid nests with central fibrovascular cores and luminal histiocytes. The cells had eosinophilic cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei, and cystic spaces contained luminal eosinophilic secretions. Notably, in several areas the nuclei of the tall columnar cells were located at the luminal surface rather than the basement membrane (“reversed polarity”). Focal luminal calcifications were present. No lymphovascular invasion or lymph node involvement was identified.

Immunohistochemical studies showed strong CK7 positivity, ER and HER2 negativity, and no myoepithelial layer around lesional structures on p63 and CK5 stains. GATA3 demonstrated moderate nuclear positivity; CK5 was patchy; calretinin was positive; and TTF1 was negative.

A 33-year-old Moroccan man presented with a left-sided laterocervical mass of four months’ duration. He had no personal or family history of note and denied smoking, alcohol use, irradiation, fever, chills, or weight loss. On examination, the left parotid gland was enlarged and firm, with cervical lymphadenopathy; no overlying skin lesions were observed. Ultrasonography and CT revealed a solid mass in the parotid gland. A biopsy showed a poorly differentiated carcinoma. The patient underwent excision of the tumor. The resected mass measured 21.5 × 9 × 6 cm, with a cut surface that was firm, tan-gray, and lobulated, measuring 6 × 5.5 × 5 cm, with apparently normal salivary gland tissue at the periphery. On histologic examination, the tumor was lobulated, with nests of large foamy cells containing centrally located nuclei and vacuolated clear cytoplasm surrounded by smaller basaloid cells, and areas of squamous islands with keratin pearl formation. Periodic acid–Schiff staining was negative in the foamy cells. Immunohistochemical studies showed expression of EMA, pancytokeratin, and p63 in all neoplastic cells and focal β-catenin, with negative staining for CK5/6, CEA, S100, CD10, vimentin, melan A, and CD45.

A 19-year-old previously healthy male presented with chest pain and fever. Initial evaluation revealed an enlarged cardiac silhouette on chest radiograph, ST-segment elevation in leads aVF and III on ECG, and a 2.2 cm pericardial effusion on transthoracic echocardiography. He was diagnosed with acute pericarditis and treated with ibuprofen and colchicine; colchicine was continued after discharge. One month later, echocardiography showed persistent pericardial effusion (0.7 cm) and ongoing fatigue. Seven months after initial presentation, he experienced recurrent pericarditis with effusion and asthenia, prompting cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR). CMR demonstrated a 54×42 mm mass adjacent to the epicardial surface of the basal and mid anterior left ventricular wall that was hypointense with a peripheral hyperintense rim on T2-weighted images, hyperintense on T1-weighted images, and showed peripheral gadolinium enhancement with a nonenhancing central core; diffusion-weighted imaging showed no signal increase. Contrast-enhanced cardiac CT confirmed a hypervascular mass with a central hypodense scar and showed that the proximal left anterior descending artery coursed through the lesion without chamber invasion. Laboratory testing revealed marked elevations of plasma and urine 3-methoxytyramine and increased chromogranin A levels.

A 30-year-old woman with an 11-year history of chronic occipital headaches and a family history of cancer presented with a 1-year history of increasing difficulty with speech and reaching high notes when singing. She also reported progressive difficulty swallowing, left-sided facial spasms, left-sided hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness. On examination, she had deficits of cranial nerves VIII through XII on the left side. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the head revealed a 2.6 cm mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass causing scalloped expansion of the left jugular foramen, with intracranial extension into the cerebellopontine angle and extracranial extension into the carotid space. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging showed a 3.8 × 3.5 × 3.5 cm dumbbell-shaped lesion with a “salt & pepper” appearance on T2-weighted images, avid postcontrast enhancement, mass effect on the left medulla and anterior inferior cerebellum, and obscuration of left cranial nerves VII through XII. The left cervical internal carotid artery just proximal to the petrous segment was asymmetrically narrowed, and the left internal jugular vein was not visualized.

A 50‐year‐old woman on maintenance hemodialysis for end‐stage renal disease (initiated in 1987) presented during routine dialysis with several months of pruritus and productive cough. Her history was notable for hypertension and prior parathyroidectomy for hyperparathyroidism; she remained dialysis‐dependent. 

On examination, vital signs were stable. Skin turgor was normal without rash or ecchymoses. There was no jugular venous distention, lymphadenopathy, or palpable neck masses. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral rales without wheezing.

Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, creatinine 8.4 mg/dL (0.5–0.9), parathyroid hormone 1891 pg/mL (10–69), and calcium 10.3 mg/dL (8.6–10.2). Thyroid‐function tests (TSH, free T4) and thyroglobulin were within normal limits.

A chest radiograph revealed bilateral pulmonary opacities. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated multiple well‐defined nodules in both lungs, the largest measuring 1.35 cm. A 99mTc‐MIBI scan showed dominant uptake in the pulmonary lesions. Neck ultrasound identified a multinodular goiter but no discrete parathyroid glands, and CT of the neck failed to localize any parathyroid tissue.

What is your differential diagnosis?

A 65-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of fatigue. Laboratory studies showed alkaline phosphatase 1,805 IU/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 2,007 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 47 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 81 IU/L, with normal bilirubin, platelet count, albumin, INR, and creatinine. Tests for viral hepatitis, autoimmune liver disease, serum IgG4 (41 mg/dL), and CA19-9 (121 IU/mL) were unremarkable. MRI/MRCP demonstrated subtle multifocal short-segment intrahepatic biliary dilation, mild perihilar duct wall thickening with enhancement, and a normal extrahepatic biliary tree. Abdominal CT revealed bilateral perinephric fat stranding and diffuse large-vessel inflammation. Lower-extremity radiographs showed diffuse sclerotic changes of the long bones. Positron emission tomography/CT showed no abnormal uptake in the vasculature or bone but revealed an FDG-avid left hilar mass; biopsy of that mass disclosed low-grade follicular lymphoma. A tentative diagnosis of primary sclerosing cholangitis was made, and the patient was treated with ursodeoxycholic acid, with modest improvement in pruritus. Over the next 4 months, he was hospitalized three times for suspected cholangitis, with a total bilirubin fluctuating around 2 mg/dL. Sixteen months after symptom onset, he noted dome-shaped skin lesions on his face, hands, and legs and developed worsening jaundice (total bilirubin 10.7 mg/dL). ERCP demonstrated a common hepatic duct stricture with nonfilling of the right intrahepatic duct system; the hilum was dilated and a plastic biliary stent was placed. Biliary brushing and biopsy from the stricture showed benign reactive tissue.

A 9-year-old boy with no significant medical history presented for dental evaluation of carious teeth and a two-month history of painless swelling in the right posterior maxilla. On examination there was a non-tender, expansile swelling of the right maxillary posterior region associated with carious primary maxillary canine and first and second molars. Panoramic radiograph showed a well-corticated, unilocular radiolucent lesion measuring approximately 4 × 3 cm from the distal aspect of the permanent right lateral incisor to the mesial aspect of the permanent right second premolar. Aspiration of the cystic cavity yielded golden-yellow fluid. Based on the patient’s age, lesion location, and radiographic appearance, both an inflammatory dentigerous cyst and unicystic ameloblastoma were considered in the preoperative differential.

A 65-year-old woman presented with several weeks of peri-umbilical and epigastric discomfort, anorexia, 10-pound unintentional weight loss, and night sweats. Her medical history included treated hypothyroidism, hypertension, chronic hepatitis C infection (genotype 1a), and a low-grade rectal neuroendocrine tumor resected in 2012 with negative re-excision margins in 2017. Physical examination revealed mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without palpable masses or hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests showed elevated serum chromogranin A at 450 ng/mL (normal < 93 ng/mL), α-fetoprotein (AFP) of 2198 ng/mL (normal 10–20 ng/mL), and AFP-L3% at 86.6%. Liver enzymes were mildly elevated (AST 72 U/L, ALT 86 U/L). 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed two hepatic lesions: a 2.2 × 2.1 cm peripherally enhancing mass with central hypodensity in segment 4, and a 1.4 × 1.0 cm low-density lesion in segment 7, with prominent portacaval lymph nodes. MRI with gadolinium confirmed a 2.7 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm T2-hyperintense lesion in segment 4 with peripheral rim arterial phase enhancement and persistent venous phase enhancement; the smaller lesion was too small for enhancement characterization. FDG-PET showed avidity in the segment 4 mass (SUV 6.6) only. Gallium-68 dotatate PET showed no uptake in the liver or lymph nodes. 

A CT-guided core biopsy of the segment 4 lesion demonstrated a high-grade malignant tumor with neuroendocrine morphology and synaptophysin positivity; Ki-67 index was 30%. Non-cirrhotic liver parenchyma was confirmed on biopsy. No extrahepatic disease was found on chest CT. The main differential diagnoses considered at this point were metastatic neuroendocrine tumor versus a primary hepatic malignancy, most likely hepatocellular carcinoma.

A 44-year-old man with a history of colonic diverticulitis presented with acute abdominal pain. On examination, his abdomen was distended with right lower quadrant tenderness. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed small-bowel loops dilated up to 4.3 cm in diameter, with a transition point in the mid-lower abdomen concerning for moderate enteric obstruction and asymmetric wall thickening of some ileal loops, along with a few borderline mesenteric lymph nodes. Diagnostic laparoscopy identified a nonperforated Meckel diverticulum in the mid-ileum that appeared prominent, inflamed, and indurated. 

Histologic examination of the resected diverticulum showed a true diverticulum lined by intestinal mucosa without ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue. Microscopy revealed extensive infiltration of sheets of small lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm (monocytoid B-cells) forming lymphoepithelial lesions in the mucosa and submucosa and focally involving the serosal adipose tissue. In some areas, there were nodular proliferations with occasional reactive germinal centers and an expanded marginal zone. Immunohistochemical studies demonstrated that the lymphocytes were positive for CD20 with weak coexpression of CD43 and positive for BCL-2, and negative for CD10, Cyclin-D1, CD3, and CD5. The reactive germinal centers were BCL-2–negative and BCL-6–positive, with no evidence of follicular colonization by tumor cells. In situ hybridization for kappa and lambda showed scattered polyclonal plasma cells, and the Ki-67 proliferation index was less than 5%.

A 34-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with 5 weeks of progressively worsening pain localized to the distal left leg. She had no history of trauma. On examination, there was tenderness along the lateral aspect of the distal left leg without palpable swelling, erythema, or other abnormalities. Routine laboratory studies were unremarkable.

Plain radiographs of the left ankle showed a well-demarcated geographic osteolytic lesion in the distal fibular metaphysis, with suspected medial cortical disruption. Unenhanced CT confirmed posteromedial cortical discontinuity with extension into adjacent soft tissues, without periosteal reaction or internal mineralization. A technetium-99m bone scan demonstrated a solitary focus of increased uptake in the distal left leg.

MRI of the lesion revealed a metaphyseal mass with both solid and cystic components, posterior cortical destruction, extraosseous extension, and surrounding inflammatory changes. The lesion was isointense to muscle on T1-weighted images and predominantly hyperintense on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, with peritumoral edema. After gadolinium administration, there was avid enhancement of the solid nodular components.

These findings raised concern for telangiectatic osteosarcoma; therefore, the patient was referred for tissue sampling.

A 47-year-old Japanese woman with no breast symptoms was referred after screening mammography revealed clustered pleomorphic calcifications in the left breast. Her mother had bilateral breast and ovarian cancer. On examination, there was no palpable mass or nipple discharge. Serum tumor markers (CEA, CA15-3, NCC-ST-439, BCA225) were within normal limits. Breast ultrasound showed a 13×12×7 mm irregular, hypoechoic mass with clear margins and internal high-echogenic foci in the left breast.
