MRI demonstrated a 14×11×12 mm lesion with early arterial enhancement in the same region. PET-CT revealed focal uptake (SUVmax 3.54) in the left breast without abnormal uptake elsewhere. Core-needle biopsy of the mass showed ductal carcinoma in situ, nuclear grade 2, negative for ER, PgR, and HER2, with a Ki-67 labeling index of 32.4%. Given her family history, hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome was considered, but the patient declined genetic testing. The patient elected to undergo total left mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy.

A 62‐year‐old woman presented with angular stomatitis and intermittent mild-to-moderate abdominal pain for 6 months. She was found to be severely anemic (hemoglobin, 6 g/dL) but denied hematuria, postmenopausal bleeding, or gastrointestinal bleeding; occult blood in stool and red cells in urine were negative. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Renal ultrasonography demonstrated left hydronephrosis; all other abdominal organs appeared normal. Intravenous pyelogram showed an opacity in the left renal region exerting mass effect on the pelvi‐calyceal system. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 9.0 × 7.5 cm solid, enhancing soft‐tissue mass with focal necrosis, inseparable from the medial left kidney, displacing the kidney laterally and compressing the collecting system. At exploratory laparotomy, a radical nephrectomy specimen measured 17 × 12 × 8 cm. The cut surface showed a well‐circumscribed, lobulated, firm, gray‐white mass (10 × 9 × 8 cm) in the lower pole, with a whorled appearance, focal necrosis, and myxoid degeneration, displacing the pelvis. Microscopically, the tumor was composed of interlacing fascicles and whorls of spindle cells with moderate eosinophilic cytoplasm, oval-to‐cigar‐shaped nuclei with moderate pleomorphism, 20–25 mitoses per 10 high‐power fields, and approximately 20% of the tumor showing hemorrhage and necrosis; no epithelial component or perinephric infiltration was identified. Immunohistochemical analysis showed diffuse strong positivity for smooth muscle actin, desmin, and vimentin; epithelial membrane antigen was focally positive, while pancytokeratin and high‐molecular‐weight cytokeratin were negative.

A 47-year-old Asian woman was transferred with a two-month history of episodic chest pain, dyspnea, bilateral lower-extremity swelling, cyanosis, and transient loss of consciousness. Two years earlier she had undergone an abdominal hysterectomy for uterine fibroids. Two months before transfer she had a brief loss of consciousness; two weeks before she noted gradual pleuritic chest pain and leg edema; and one day before she developed shortness of breath and a nonproductive cough. She had no known risk factors for thromboembolism.

At the outside hospital she appeared cyanotic and hypotensive, with a heart rate of 110 bpm, systolic blood pressure of 70 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 34 breaths per minute, and dusky skin. An electrocardiogram and serum troponin were normal. Arterial blood gas on 100% oxygen showed pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 22 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 506 mm Hg. The leukocyte count was 12.9×10³/μL; other hematologic, renal, liver, and coagulation studies were within normal limits. A head CT scan was normal. Venous duplex ultrasonography revealed a right proximal deep venous thrombosis, and unfractionated heparin was started.

On transfer, a CT scan of the chest identified a 3.1-cm hypodense filling defect traversing the right atrium into the right ventricle, with small bilateral pleural effusions and atelectasis but no pulmonary embolism. Abdominal CT showed distension of the inferior vena cava with a similar-density lesion and subtle linear enhancement. Pelvic CT revealed a 6.2×3.9-cm lobulated pelvic mass inseparable from the internal iliac vein. Transthoracic echocardiography in the apical four-chamber view demonstrated a 3.5×3.0-cm tissue-density mass filling the right atrium to the plane of the tricuspid annulus.

A 73-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a slow-growing mass of the left mandible noted over the past 15 months. His medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension. On intraoral examination, there was a painless bony expansion of the buccal aspect of the left posterior mandible; the overlying mucosa was intact, and no tooth mobility was present. Palpation of the neck revealed no lymphadenopathy. A panoramic radiograph showed a multilocular radiolucent lesion, measuring approximately 6.0 × 3.5 cm, extending from the ascending ramus to the periapical region of the left canine and involving the inferior alveolar canal. CT scans demonstrated a large expansile lytic lesion of the left mandibular body with cortical destruction. Ultrasound of the neck showed only reactive lymph nodes on the left. A contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of distant metastatic disease.

A 42-year-old woman presented with a painless, pigmented growth on the left anterior maxillary gingiva for 3 months. The lesion began as a pinpoint spot and gradually enlarged, extending to the palatal gingiva. She reported no systemic illness or head and neck trauma. Vital signs were within normal limits.

Extraoral examination revealed a tender, firm left submandibular lymph node fixed to the mandible and a separate 3 × 3 cm firm, non-tender, mobile right cervical lymph node. Intraoral examination showed a 2 × 3 cm sessile, rough-surfaced, black pigmented lesion on the left maxillary attached gingiva near the central and lateral incisors, extending to the hard-palate rugae and causing displacement of those teeth.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, biochemical tests, and urinalysis, were within normal limits. Intraoral periapical and panoramic radiographs demonstrated a radiolucent area with displacement of the left central and lateral incisors. Neck ultrasonography revealed a highly vascular mass with a low-velocity waveform indenting major vessels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck showed a well-defined, heterogeneously enhancing hypodense nodule in the left premaxillary region without bony erosion, and a 34 × 32 mm necrotic left level II cervical lymphadenopathy compressing the internal jugular vein.

An 11-year-old spayed female Golden Retriever was referred for evaluation of an incidentally detected hepatic mass. Five days earlier, she had pollakiuria and mild abdominal discomfort; abdominal ultrasound then showed a 5.2 × 5.0 cm round hypoechoic mass in the left lateral liver lobe and a smaller hypoechoic lesion near the right middle lobe. Urinalysis was notable only for struvite crystals and mild proteinuria; empirical amoxicillin resolved her urinary signs. CBC and serum chemistry were within reference limits. 

Her only chronic issues were bilateral elbow osteoarthritis and cruciate ligament injuries, for which she was receiving tramadol, amantadine, meloxicam, and supplements. On presentation, she was bright, alert, obese (BCS 8/9), with a left forelimb lameness. Abdominal palpation and peripheral lymph nodes were unremarkable. Repeat abdominal ultrasound confirmed a 4.5 × 5.7 cm heterogeneous, well-vascularized hypoechoic mass in the left lateral liver lobe. Thoracic radiographs were normal.

Ultrasound‐guided fine‐needle aspiration of the hepatic mass yielded a mixed lymphoid population: predominantly intermediate‐sized lymphocytes (12–15 μm, indented nuclei, coarse chromatin, pale blue cytoplasm) and fewer small lymphocytes (8–12 μm, condensed chromatin). There was a lymphoglandular background, few hepatocyte clusters with mild hydropic change, and no expanded lymphocytes in adjacent parenchyma. The cytology was most consistent with lymphoma, and marked inflammation was deemed unlikely.

Flow cytometry on the aspirate demonstrated predominantly small CD3+ T cells (mixed CD4+ and CD8+), about 5% small CD21+ B cells, and 15% CD45+ MHC class II+ leukocytes lacking lineage markers. PCR for antigen receptor rearrangements (PARR) revealed a reproducible clonal immunoglobulin heavy‐chain rearrangement and polyclonal T‐cell receptor rearrangements.

An 80-year-old man with a 13-year history of immunoglobulin G kappa smoldering myeloma presented with a 2-year history of dusky, erythematous, indurated patches on the lower abdomen and back and a hyperpigmented plaque on the right upper calf. Six years earlier, he had similar lesions initially diagnosed as tumid lupus that partially improved with topical corticosteroids and fully resolved after 9 months of lenalidomide therapy. On examination, indurated dusky patches were noted on the trunk and a firm hyperpigmented plaque on the calf. A biopsy of the right calf showed dermal sclerosis with hyalinized collagen bundles extending into the subcutis and absence of CD34+ dermal dendrocytes in sclerotic zones. A biopsy of the back revealed dermal sclerosis with abundant interstitial mucin confirmed by colloidal iron stain and diminished CD34+ dendrocytes in the sclerotic zone. Laboratory studies confirmed persistent IgG kappa monoclonal gammopathy; all other tests were normal. Whole-body CT showed no evidence of systemic mucinosis. At that time, a morphea/lupus erythematosus overlap syndrome and mixed connective tissue disease were considered in the histopathologic differential diagnosis.

A 48-year-old man with an 8-year history of type 2 diabetes managed with oral agents and a 30–pack-year smoking history, but no known exposure to tuberculosis, was referred for worsening low back pain. Four months earlier, he developed diffuse abdominal pain with altered bowel habits and insidious inflammatory low back pain, accompanied by night sweats and a 36-kg weight loss over 6 months without fever. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy without mediastinal or pulmonary lesions. A surgical biopsy of a retroperitoneal lymph node revealed rare epithelioid granulomas without caseous necrosis. Acid-fast bacilli were not detected in sputum, but an interferon-gamma release assay was positive, and the patient was started on a 6-month course of anti-tuberculous therapy.

After 4 months of treatment, he reported progressive low back pain radiating to the buttocks, now constant and disturbing sleep. On examination, he had lumbar spinal tenderness without neurologic deficit or palpable superficial lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine and pelvis were unremarkable. MRI demonstrated an L4 vertebral body lesion (T1 hypointense, T2 and STIR hyperintense), disruption of the inferior L4 cortex with adjacent disc involvement, and a 46 × 32 mm paravertebral soft-tissue collection extending into the left psoas, along with persistent retroperitoneal lymphadenopathies.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of pain and swelling on his back. Over time, he developed numbness and weakness in both lower limbs, hypoesthesia, constipation, and difficulty squatting. Neurologic examination showed bilateral lower-limb strength of 4/5 and hypoesthesia below the xiphoid level. Babinski and Romberg signs were positive. He had no prior trauma, surgery, or relevant family history.

On examination of the posterior chest, there was a deformity with a gibbous lump and a post-biopsy scar from an incisional biopsy performed 2 months earlier, after which the mass enlarged and became more painful. Tenderness was present along the midline, and hypoesthesia was noted at the T4 level; otherwise, sensation and movement were intact.

Conventional radiographs of the thoracolumbar spine showed a lytic-sclerotic expansile lesion on the right posterolateral aspect of T5–T6, with normal alignment and other vertebrae appearing unremarkable. A CT scan revealed an expansile sclerotic mass measuring 4.85 × 5.03 × 11.87 cm with a chondroid matrix, involving the right posterolateral T5–T6 vertebrae, transverse process, costovertebral junction, and ribs 5–6, with surrounding soft-tissue swelling and calcification. MRI of the thoracolumbar region showed an inhomogeneous mass with sharp margins and necrosis, extending from T4 to T8, infiltrating intradurally and intramedullary up to T4–T5, causing spinal canal stenosis and obliteration of posterior ligaments; anteriorly it bordered the aortic arch and entered the thoracic cavity.

Based on these imaging findings, the leading consideration was a primary bone tumor, with differential diagnoses of chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, and osteochondroma.

A 16-year-old girl presented with a one-week history of persistent low-grade fever and slight cough treated with ibuprofen. A general practitioner noted an increase in abdominal girth from a giant palpable mass and referred her urgently. She reported progressive abdominal enlargement for one year, associated with intermittent mild pain; her menstrual cycles were normal. On examination, she was afebrile; there was a giant, tense, relatively mobile abdominal mass with a regular surface, an umbilical hernia, and a brown-black lesion on the right thorax. 

Abdomino-pelvic ultrasound showed a thin-walled, multilocular cystic mass occupying nearly the entire abdomen and pelvis, with transonic fluid and multiple septa; the ovaries were not visualized, and there was no free fluid. MRI demonstrated a well-defined 115 × 224 × 350 mm cystic tumor originating from the right ovary, multiloculated, containing some T1-hyperintense loculi, with moderate mural and septal enhancement after gadolinium; the suggested diagnosis was ovarian cystadenoma.

Laboratory results revealed hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL, hematocrit 29.4%, platelets 656 × 10^3/µL, CRP 26.45 mg/dL, D-dimers 1.21 mg/L, ALP 213 U/L, ferritin 480 ng/mL, iron 28 µg/dL, AST 70 U/L, ALT 77 U/L, GGT 353 U/L. Endocrine studies, including thyroid function, were normal. Tumor markers CEA, AFP, β HCG, LDH, and CA 19-9 were normal; CA 125 was elevated at 124.7 U/mL. Urine culture and nasal and pharyngeal swabs were negative, and chest radiography was normal.

On hospital day 3, she developed high-grade fever (up to 39.5 °C) unresponsive to intravenous antibiotics and antipyretics, without localizing symptoms. Otorhinolaryngeal, respiratory, digestive, urinary, and cutaneous sources were excluded; blood cultures and SARS-CoV-2 testing were negative. Intracystic hemorrhage or infection was suspected, but abdominal ultrasound showed unchanged cyst contents. A pediatric oncology consultation raised concern for paraneoplastic syndrome and sepsis, and she received meropenem, gentamicin, and metronidazole; her temperature normalized after 2 days. Given a presumptive diagnosis of serous or mucinous cystadenoma, surgical removal of the cyst was planned.

A 25-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue, treated 16 months earlier with hemi-glossectomy and chemoradiation, presented with a 1-month history of progressively worsening severe, sharp, constant right shoulder and chest pain, associated with right arm numbness, productive cough, and dyspnoea on exertion. The pain was exacerbated by right arm movement. She denied trauma or travel.

Her medications included pembrolizumab and recent head and neck radiation. She had a 1.5-year smoking history (0.5 pack per day), social alcohol use, and no significant family history of cancer aside from a grandmother with brain cancer.

On examination, she appeared frail with weight loss. Vital signs: heart rate 86 bpm; blood pressure 121/74 mm Hg. Pulmonary auscultation revealed coarse rales and rhonchi in the left lower lung field. Cardiac examination showed a regular rhythm without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. She had tender right supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and swelling with erythema over the right suprascapular area.

Laboratory studies showed haemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, haematocrit 28.8%, total calcium 10.5 mg/dL, ionized calcium 1.51 mmol/L. Admission ECG demonstrated ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads and T-wave inversions in the anterolateral leads. Troponin I peaked at 0.29 ng/L (normal <0.05 ng/L). Chest radiograph revealed a left lower lobe infiltrate, progression of a known left upper lobe cavitary lesion, and a new right clavicular lesion.

Differential diagnosis at this point included acute coronary syndrome, myocarditis due to pembrolizumab, and Takotsubo cardiomyopathy in a cancer patient.

A 28-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 1, with a history of a loop electrosurgical excision procedure two years earlier for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia 3 and adenocarcinoma in situ, was found on routine prenatal Pap smear to have atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance with positive HPV co-testing. Postpartum colposcopic cervical biopsies revealed necrosis and hyalinization, and endocervical curettage demonstrated atypical trophoblastic cells of the chorionic intermediate trophoblastic type. A transvaginal ultrasound showed no retained products of conception. She underwent hysteroscopy with dilation and curettage: both endometrial and endocervical specimens displayed a similar atypical trophoblastic proliferation. Serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin and human placental lactogen were both undetectable. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging showed no evidence of gestational trophoblastic disease. Desiring future fertility, she elected close surveillance. Four months later, a repeat dilation and curettage showed no trophoblastic disease. Six months after that, Pap smear and endocervical curettage were again negative. Approximately six months later, endocervical curettage once more demonstrated atypical trophoblastic disease. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and repeat pelvic MRI revealed no evidence of malignancy or metastasis, and β-hCG remained below 1 mIU/mL. Given these persistent atypical findings and negative systemic evaluation, she opted for definitive surgical management.

A 61-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, stroke, and hypothyroidism presented with altered mental status, nausea, multiple episodes of nonbloody, nonbilious vomiting, and dizziness. She reported a three-month history of intermittent night sweats, diffuse body aches, and 10 lb of unintentional weight loss. She denied fever, chills, respiratory symptoms, excessive dairy or antacid use, recent travel, or sick contacts. Her medications included vitamin D supplements, last taken three months earlier. 

On admission, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed dry oral mucosa and multiple painless, mobile, firm lymph nodes measuring 2–3 cm in the left anterior cervical region, right axilla, and right inguinal area. 

Initial laboratories showed: microcytic anemia, monocytosis, acute kidney injury with a prerenal pattern (BUN/creatinine ratio > 20), hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, and a serum calcium level of 16.5 mg/dL (corrected to 16.7 mg/dL). She was started on intravenous saline, calcitonin, and bisphosphonates. 

Further evaluation of her hypercalcemia revealed:  
• PTH at the lower limit of normal  
• PTHrP within normal range  
• 25-hydroxyvitamin D at the high end of normal  
• 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D elevated

A 69-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of mild lumbar and right hip pain without fever, chills, or weight loss. On examination, lumbar flexion was 60°, extension 10°, lateral bending 10° bilaterally; mild tenderness was noted near the L4 spinous process. Neurologic testing, including cervical reflexes, femoral nerve stretch, and straight leg raise (45° on the left, 50° on the right), was unremarkable except for hypoesthesia of the left lateral leg. Routine tumor markers (CA 19-9, CEA, AFP, NSE, and others) were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the lumbosacral region revealed a well-demarcated, homogeneous soft-tissue mass (3.2 × 7.5 cm) within the right multifidus muscle. Noncontrast attenuation was 55 HU, with heterogeneous enhancement (arterial phase 61–85 HU; venous phase 67–95 HU) and a central low-density area. The mass compressed but did not infiltrate the sacrum; the adjacent bone showed compressive sclerosis without destruction.

MRI showed an intramuscular lesion from L4 to S3. On T1-weighted images, the mass was isointense to muscle with patchy hypointense areas. STIR images demonstrated slightly hyperintense signal with patchy low-signal foci. Post-contrast sequences revealed heterogeneous enhancement with lamellar nonenhancing regions.

At surgery, the tumor was found within the right multifidus muscle, firm, poorly circumscribed, infiltrating surrounding muscle but without bone destruction. Grossly, it measured 7.5 cm, was yellowish-gray and slightly firm.

Histologic sections showed large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, marked nuclear pleomorphism with prominent nucleoli, and approximately 2 mitoses per 10 high-power fields; there was no definite invasion of nerves, vessels, or bone. Immunohistochemical stains were positive for S100 protein, SOX-10, MDM2, and Bcl-2, and negative for Desmin, MyoD1, Myogenin, CD99, Synaptophysin, CK-pan, CD34, ERG, and CD163. The Ki-67 proliferation index exceeded 10%.

A 25-year-old man presented to the emergency department with sudden, severe headache radiating to the right ear and associated nausea. He denied trauma, violent sneezing, cervical massage, or abnormal movements. He had no prior medical or surgical history, and his family history was unremarkable. Vital signs were within normal limits. On physical examination, the right tonsil was displaced toward the midline. A peritonsillar abscess was suspected, and contrast-enhanced CT of the neck was performed. CT showed a hypoattenuating, slightly enhancing mass in the right carotid space, splaying the internal and external carotid arteries, with obliteration of the parapharyngeal space and extension into the nasopharynx and superior retropharyngeal space. MRI of the neck demonstrated an infiltrative lesion within the right carotid sheath extending to the jugular foramen. The lesion was of intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted images, high signal on T2-weighted images, and exhibited slight homogeneous enhancement. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed marked restricted diffusion with an apparent diffusion coefficient of 458×10⁻⁶ mm²/s. No cervical lymphadenopathy was identified. The initial differential diagnosis included idiopathic inflammation, such as IgG4-related disease, and lymphoma.

A 46-year-old woman presented for preoperative evaluation before a planned hysterectomy. She reported a 2-year history of dry cough and an unintentional 10-lb weight loss over the past year. Her medical history was unremarkable; she was a non-smoker with no history of cancer, recent travel, or significant occupational exposures. On examination, she was afebrile and denied dyspnea or shortness of breath on exertion. Pulmonary-function testing showed mild nonspecific restrictive and obstructive defects. A preoperative chest radiograph demonstrated innumerable nodular opacities throughout both lungs without lymphadenopathy or osseous lesions. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest revealed innumerable soft-tissue–density lesions of varying sizes throughout the lungs, the largest measuring 4 cm in the right infrahilar region, with no mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy, pleural effusions, or bone lesions. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a large central pelvic soft-tissue mass measuring 17 × 15 × 13 cm with a necrotic component and multiple thin enhancing septations, as well as a 6.5-cm exophytic right adnexal lesion; there was no fat attenuation, calcification, lymphadenopathy, or osseous involvement.

A 43-year-old man noticed a slowly enlarging, firm mass in his right upper thigh over four months. He denied systemic symptoms such as flushing, diarrhea, or wheezing. Physical examination revealed a 3×3 cm firm mass involving the right sartorius muscle. The mass was excised en bloc.

Histopathology showed skeletal muscle and subcutaneous tissue infiltrated by polygonal cells arranged in packets separated by fine fibrovascular stroma. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrated strong, diffuse positivity for synaptophysin, chromogranin, cytokeratin, Bcl-2 protein, and neuron-specific enolase, and negativity for S100, desmin, and epithelial membrane antigen. Electron microscopy revealed polygonal cells with deeply indented nuclei and abundant neurosecretory granules in the cytoplasm. A 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid level was elevated at 92 nmol (reference range 9–31 nmol/24 h). Metaiodobenzylguanidine and octreotide scans showed no abnormal uptake outside the surgical site, and contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable.

A 56-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of right lumbar pain, intermittent hematuria, and weight loss. He is a chronic smoker (11 pack-years) with an otherwise unremarkable medical history. On examination, there was a palpable right flank mass appreciated bimanually. Routine laboratory studies were normal. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a 25 × 11 × 8 cm heterogeneous mass replacing the right kidney and extending into the right renal vein lumen, with compression of the inferior vena cava; no other intra-abdominal abnormalities were noted. Chest CT showed multiple nodular lesions suggestive of metastatic disease. The patient underwent a right radical nephrectomy with resection of the thrombus in the right renal vein.

A 30-year-old right-handed man presented with acute weakness of the right upper limb that progressed over 2 days to involve the right lower limb. He denied headache or seizures. On examination, he had right upper-motor-neuron facial paresis, right hemiparesis (MRC grade 2/5 in the hand, 3/5 in shoulder, toes, ankle; 4/5 in knee and hip), right hemihypoalgesia, diminished right tendon reflexes, and a right Babinski sign. Other cranial nerves and the fundus were normal. His NIH Stroke Scale score was 12, and his modified Rankin Scale grade was 4. 

Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a left fronto-temporo-parietal hypodense area consistent with an MCA-territory infarction. MRI of the brain demonstrated a 4.1 × 4.0 × 3.5 cm solid right parasellar lesion extending into the right sphenoid sinus and greater wing of the sphenoid, expanding the cavernous sinus, and attenuating the right internal carotid artery. A smaller left parasellar extension was noted. There was no suprasellar extension; the pituitary stalk and optic chiasm were normal. The lesion enhanced uniformly and strongly after gadolinium administration.

Magnetic resonance angiography revealed absence of both internal carotid arteries, with the anterior and middle cerebral arteries supplied via enlarged posterior communicating arteries; vertebral and basilar arteries were normal. Digital subtraction angiography confirmed occlusion of both ICAs at their origins, faint left terminal ICA flow via ophthalmic collaterals, and a parasellar blush from the right internal maxillary artery; external carotid, common carotid, and subclavian arteries were normal. 

Thyroid, reproductive, growth, cortisol, and prolactin hormone levels were within normal limits. Automated perimetry showed mild generalized depression of retinal sensitivity bilaterally with significant visual field defects. Transesophageal echocardiography and the coagulation profile were unremarkable.

A 70-year-old woman presented with acute intractable nausea and vomiting, mild epigastric pain, vertigo, generalized fatigue, and mild headache. She had a history of type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and a 23-pack-year smoking history. On examination, she was alert and oriented but demonstrated amnesia, recalling 0 of 3 words despite denying memory problems.

Brain MRI showed subtle increased T2 signal intensity in the bilateral hippocampi on FLAIR sequences. Video EEG demonstrated clusters of nonconvulsive seizures originating in the left hemisphere with spread to the right, each lasting about one minute and recurring every 5–10 minutes; the patient associated these electrographic seizures with her episodes of nausea.

Lumbar puncture revealed WBC 2 cells/µL, RBC 5 cells/µL, glucose 102 mg/dL, total protein 38 mg/dL, IgG 1.9 mg/dL, and three oligoclonal bands not present in serum. CSF testing was negative for HSV DNA, EBV DNA, Lyme antibodies, VDRL, and Tropheryma whipplei PCR. CSF antiglial nuclear antibody (AGNA/Sox-1) titer was 1:16 (reference <1:2). Additional CSF autoimmune panels (including NMDA-R, VGKC, GABA-B-R, AMPA-R, ANNA-1/2/3, PCA-1/2/Tr, amphiphysin, CRMP-5-IgG, GAD65) were negative. Serum autoantibody testing (including ANCA IgG; anti-SS-A/Ro; anti-SS-B; ANA; anticardiolipin; anti-TPO) was also negative.

A 29-year-old man presented with several years of incomplete bladder emptying. He denied dysuria, hematuria, incontinence, weight loss, or bone pain.  
On CT urography, there was a 13.4 × 10.6 × 13.0 cm thick-walled, predominantly cystic pelvic mass with solid-enhancing mural nodules located inferior to the bladder. No lymphadenopathy or distant metastases were noted. He was started on tamsulosin and referred for further evaluation.  
An ultrasound-guided needle biopsy of the mass showed bland smooth muscle cells with no cytologic atypia, no necrosis, and mitotic activity <1/50 high-power fields, consistent with leiomyoma. Active surveillance with a CT in 3 months was recommended.  
Three months later, he presented with urinary retention requiring catheterization. Repeat CT showed slight increase in tumor size. His AUA symptom index was 35. Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) performed 2 weeks later again showed leiomyoma.  
Over the next 2 years, his PSA remained 1.13 ng/mL, and his creatinine rose to 1.4 mg/dL. MRI of the pelvis demonstrated a well-marginated, complex solid, cystic, and septated mass with multiple enhancing areas and restricted diffusion, appearing to communicate with the bladder neck.  
The patient opted for surgical excision of the mass.

A 65-year-old Namibian man was referred for evaluation of anemia, thrombocytopenia, and back pain. Seven months earlier, he developed insidious low back pain that gradually worsened, radiated to the lower limbs, and was aggravated by walking and relieved by rest. Four months before admission, he noted exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and palpitations. He also reported weight loss, fevers, malaise, and urinary symptoms including straining, frequency, and dysuria. He had no history of trauma, cough, gastrointestinal symptoms, smoking, or alcohol use.

On examination, he appeared pale and mildly wasted. The right shoulder joint was swollen, tender, and had a limited range of motion. There was percussion tenderness over the thoracic and lumbar spine without deformity. Digital rectal examination revealed an asymmetrically enlarged, nodular, and hard prostate with diffuse firm areas. Other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed a normocytic, normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 5.4 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (42×10^9/L), a reticulocyte count of 101 500 cells/µL (index 1.1), hypercalcemia (2.9 mmol/L), elevated alkaline phosphatase (509 IU/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (547 IU/L). Renal and liver function tests were normal. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed no M-protein, and urine was negative for Bence Jones proteins. Urinalysis showed mild proteinuria and microscopic hematuria; urine culture grew Escherichia coli sensitive to cefuroxime. The prostate-specific antigen level was >100 ng/mL.

Radiographs of the right humerus demonstrated osteolytic lesions. Computed tomography of the spine, pelvis, and femur showed multiple osteolytic lesions. A lateral skull radiograph was normal.

A 58-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of 8 months of progressive shortness of breath, intermittent fever and chills, productive (non–blood-stained) cough, and a 25-kg unintentional weight loss over 6 months. She had no night sweats, dysphagia, or hoarseness. Her medical history was notable only for hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. She was a passive smoker, denied tuberculosis exposure, and had no family history of malignancy or pulmonary disease. She had been empirically treated with antituberculosis therapy at another center without improvement.

On examination, she was afebrile (37.8 °C), blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, pulse 84/min, respiratory rate 12/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Lung auscultation was clear, and no thyroid nodules, neck masses, or cervical lymphadenopathy were palpable.

Laboratory studies showed TSH 0.08 mU/L (normal 0.35–4.9), free T4 0.7 ng/dL (normal 0.76–2.24), and serum calcitonin 128 pg/mL (elevated). Other blood tests were normal.

Chest radiography revealed diffuse bilateral 1–3 mm nodular infiltrates with a miliary pattern. Noncontrast chest CT showed innumerable small nodules with a random distribution and a confluent mass in the right lung. Smears and cultures for acid-fast bacilli were negative, Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR was negative, and blood cultures were sterile.

A 90-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of a gradually enlarging left-sided nasal mass. He had no prior sinus disease or surgery. On examination, a voluminous mass was prolapsing through the left nostril, causing complete obstruction of the left nasal cavity and deflecting the nasal septum to the right; there was no cervical lymphadenopathy or facial deformity. Nasal endoscopy via the right naris revealed a smooth, grayish mass filling the left choana and extending into the nasopharyngeal space, displacing the septum. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a homogeneous mass completely occupying the left nasal cavity and extending to the nasopharynx, displacing the medial wall of the left maxillary sinus; erosion of the nasal septum and the left lamina papyracea was noted, along with complete opacification of the left maxillary sinus.

A 26-year-old previously healthy Caucasian man presented with a 3-week history of dry cough and progressive dyspnea. He reported dizziness, retrosternal chest pain, and one febrile episode. Physical examination was notable only for hypophonetic heart sounds. Chest radiography showed an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a large pericardial effusion without signs of tamponade. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed multiple rounded hepatic lesions, all hypodense and hypovascular, the largest measuring 3 cm in segment IVa. Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia and elevated inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 95 mm/h; C-reactive protein, 92 mg/L); liver and thyroid function tests were normal. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C viruses and HIV were negative; rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody tests were also negative. An ultrasound-guided percutaneous liver biopsy showed lobular necrosis and perisinusoidal fibrosis without granulomas or neoplastic cells. During hospitalization he developed fever, night sweats, and weight loss, and was started on empiric therapy for extrapulmonary tuberculosis with corticosteroids. Two months later, pericardial effusion had resolved but liver lesions persisted. He was readmitted in hemorrhagic shock due to bleeding from the hepatic lesions, underwent unsuccessful embolization of the right hepatic artery, and died shortly thereafter.

A 31-year-old non-smoking woman presented with 5 months of dull upper back pain radiating to both shoulders. The pain worsened when upright and improved when supine. She had no history of asbestos exposure. Physical examination and routine laboratory tests were unremarkable.

Chest CT showed nodular pleural thickening on the right, including a 1.5 cm extrapleural mass in the apicoposterior segment, multiple subpleural nodules in the right middle and lower lobes, and lytic lesions in the T5 and T12 vertebral bodies. A bone scan demonstrated focal uptake at T5 and a linear uptake in the left seventh anterior rib.

Thoracoscopic wedge resection of the right lower lobe revealed multiple subpleural whitish-tan plaques up to 1.2 cm in diameter. Histologically, the tumor arose from the pleura with intraparenchymal extension, composed of epithelioid cells with rounded nuclei, scant cytoplasm, intracytoplasmic vacuoles, a hyalinized stroma, few mitoses, and areas of hemorrhagic necrosis; margins were clear.

Immunohistochemistry showed the tumor cells were negative for cytokeratin, calretinin, desmin, and S-100 protein; diffusely positive for α-smooth muscle actin and vimentin; weakly positive for factor VIII and CD31; and focally positive for CD34.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of lethargy, weight loss, cough, and night sweats. He had no personal or family history of tuberculosis. He was born in Turkey and had lived in France for 30 years. On admission, temperature was 37.2 °C, heart rate 80 bpm, respiratory rate 20 /min, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no palpable peripheral lymphadenopathy.

Chest radiography showed mediastinal enlargement without pulmonary infiltrates. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed large mediastinal and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and a hypodense splenic collection. Complete blood count, renal, and liver function tests were within normal limits; HIV serology was negative. Acid-fast bacilli were identified in a sputum sample, and molecular analysis did not suggest antibiotic resistance. A standard four-drug antituberculous regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) was initiated, with some clinical improvement.

Two weeks later, the patient experienced recurrent fever and marked asthenia. Repeat blood cultures and bronchoalveolar lavage were negative. A second CT scan showed a decrease in mediastinal lymph-node size but persistence of the splenic lesion, which remained enlarged and necrotic in appearance.

A 44-year-old man presented in January 2014 with a solitary yellowish plaque on the right temple that had been stable for 5 months and was mildly itchy on touch. His history was notable for a superficial spreading melanoma excised from the right upper leg in 2012; there was no history of pediatric cutaneous mastocytosis. Physical examination revealed a solitary plaque on the right temple without other skin lesions or systemic abnormalities. Laboratory studies showed a normal serum tryptase level (2.9 μg/L; normal <11.4 μg/L). 

A punch biopsy of the lesion revealed diffuse sheets of epithelioid cells in the dermis without epidermal involvement. The cells had abundant, finely granulated cytoplasm and slight nuclear polymorphism, with scattered spindle-shaped and bilobed/multilobed nuclei. Mitotic activity was low (up to 1 mitotic figure/mm2). Giemsa stain highlighted metachromatic granules. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD117, tryptase, and MiTF; CD30 showed heterogeneous positivity; a few cells were CD25 positive; CD2 was negative. Next-generation sequencing of the lesion showed no KIT mutations (exons 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, 17).

In July 2014, the lesion was excised. The histopathologic features were similar but with increased nuclear pleomorphism, up to 9 mitotic figures/mm2, and a Ki-67 index of 29.5%. CD117 and tryptase staining demonstrated small clusters of mast cells extending into the resection margin. No clinical or imaging evidence of systemic disease was found. 

Based on these findings, a provisional diagnosis of mastocytoma was made.

A man in his 70s was admitted with a 1-week history of abdominal fullness, jaundice, and anorexia. His medical history was notable for cutaneous melanoma diagnosed in 2017 (stage IIIc, SOX10 and S100 positive) treated with local excision and 1 year of adjuvant nivolumab, and multiple myeloma diagnosed in 2021 treated with bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone. One month before admission, he was found to have inguinal lymphadenopathy and recurrent melanoma, for which he was started on temozolomide.

Two months before admission, an abdominal CT scan showed multiple sub-centimeter hypoattenuating hepatic foci. Two weeks before admission, liver function tests were mildly elevated, and an abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an increase in size and number of the previously noted hepatic cysts. On admission, liver tests were: alanine aminotransferase 427 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 323 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 568 U/L, total bilirubin 9.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 7.5 mg/dL, and γ-glutamyl transferase 339 U/L.

Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography revealed innumerable, mildly complex cystic liver lesions markedly increased in size and number compared with prior imaging. The lesions demonstrated diffusion restriction, internal fluid-fluid levels, and thin septations; they were hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed no enhancement on postcontrast sequences.

A 63-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of right-sided chest pain that had gradually worsened. He reported mild chest congestion with a mild cough but denied haemoptysis, dyspnoea, or fever. On presentation, his arterial oxygen tension was 84 mmHg and oxygen saturation was 95% on room air. Electrocardiography showed a left anterior fascicular block. A noncontrast CT of the chest demonstrated a suspicious filling defect in the right pulmonary artery. Computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA) revealed filling defects in the right pulmonary artery and its upper branch, with possible focal pulmonary infarction. Laboratory studies showed a D-dimer level of 0.49 mg/L (reference range 0.02–0.80 mg/L), with normal complete blood count, hepatic and renal function tests, serum electrolytes, cardiac biomarkers, autoantibodies, and coagulation parameters; there was no evidence of internal bleeding. The patient was treated with low-molecular-weight heparin for 2 weeks. On transfer to the respiratory department, the D-dimer level remained normal. Autoantibody testing, tumour markers, mycological examination, and T-spot were all normal. Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremities showed no deep vein thrombosis. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 66%, normal chamber sizes, normal pulmonary-artery pressures, and no visible thrombus in the main or branch pulmonary arteries. Considering these atypical clinical and imaging features, (18)F-PET/CT was suggested.

A 16-year-old boy presented with headache, convulsions, blurring of vision, and vertigo. His vital signs were stable, and he was fully conscious and oriented. Pupils were 2 mm bilaterally and equally reactive. There were no cranial nerve, motor, or sensory deficits. He had scattered melanocytic nevi over his back since birth, none larger than 1 cm, and no family history of melanoma. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the brain revealed a heterogeneous high-density mass in the anterior left temporal lobe with contrast enhancement. MRI of the brain showed a T1-hyperintense and T2-hypointense mass in the left temporal lobe with perilesional edema, no dural attachment, and mild heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. The imaging prompted consideration of a hemorrhagic brain tumour.

A 32-year-old Persian woman presented with 3 weeks of progressive abdominal pain. A colonoscopy performed elsewhere revealed a cecal mass and a presumptive diagnosis of colon cancer. She was referred with new‐onset ascites, dyspnea, weakness, and malaise. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no medications or family history of malignancy.  
On examination, she was tachycardic, tachypneic, and hypoxic; breath sounds were decreased at both lung bases without rales. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.31, PCO2 21.6 mm Hg, and PO2 98 mm Hg.  
Laboratory studies on admission revealed: WBC 7.1 × 10^3/μL, hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, platelets 91 × 10^3/mm^3; serum creatinine 5.6 mg/dL, potassium 5.6 mEq/L, calcium 10.9 mg/dL, and uric acid 18.1 mg/dL.  
Contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen showed a cecal mass, omental infiltration, hypodense lesions in the right hepatic lobe, and bilateral pleural effusions.  
Thoracentesis yielded 400 mL of sanguineous fluid containing 11,200 WBCs (80% neutrophils), pleural fluid LDH 15,930 U/L (serum LDH 9900 U/L).  
Her electrolyte abnormalities (hyperuricemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperkalemia) met the Cairo and Bishop criteria for tumor lysis syndrome, but the presence of hypercalcemia and very high LDH in pleural fluid was considered atypical for TLS arising from a solid tumor.

A 45-year-old man presented in December 2010 with one month of left‐eye proptosis and diplopia but no pain or redness. His medical history was notable for HIV and hepatitis B virus infection since 1986, complicated by cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In July 2006, he underwent orthotopic liver transplantation for end‐stage liver disease with concurrent HCC; native‐liver histology had shown a tumor thrombus in the right portal vein branch. In December 2008, he had partial resection of the transplanted liver for recurrent HCC. He began sorafenib in 2009 but received it irregularly due to diarrhea. In December 2009, he developed new liver and pulmonary recurrences; he underwent transarterial chemoembolization of liver lesions and surgical resection of left‐middle‐lobe pulmonary metastases, followed by systemic liposomal doxorubicin. In July 2010, further liver and lung recurrences prompted chemotherapy with 5-fluorouracil and later capecitabine.

On examination, his visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally. The left eye had 6 mm of proptosis with inferior displacement and superior sulcus fullness. A firm mass was palpable in the superior orbit, inseparable from the orbital rim. Left‐eye motility was limited on upward and leftward gaze. Serum α-fetoprotein was 3750 ng/mL. Computed tomography of the orbits showed an extraconal mass involving the superior and lateral walls of the left orbit, with destruction of orbital bone, incorporation of the lateral rectus muscle, and calcifications.

A 34-year-old woman presented with a 6-year history of a painless swelling of the lower jaw, initially 1 cm in diameter on the left, which gradually enlarged to involve both sides of the face. She reported only difficulty in chewing. On examination, there was gross facial asymmetry with fullness of the cheeks and lower lip and obliteration of the mentolabial sulcus and nasolabial folds. A well-demarcated, hard, lobulated, nontender swelling measured approximately 8×6×5 cm over the left cheek and a diffuse hard, lobulated, nontender swelling extended from the left mandibular ramus to the right mandibular body, obliterating the inferior border. No cervical lymphadenopathy was present.

Intraorally, a diffuse, hard, lobulated swelling extended from the left to the right retromolar regions, with bilateral buccal, labial, and lingual cortical expansion and intact mucosa. A provisional diagnosis of a benign fibro-osseous lesion of the mandible was made, and the differential diagnoses included fibrous dysplasia, ossifying/cementifying fibroma, and central giant cell granuloma (non-aggressive).

Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, serum protein, calcium, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase levels, were within normal limits.

Panoramic radiograph showed a well-defined mixed radiopaque and radiolucent lesion from the left ramus to the right angle of the mandible, measuring about 11×7 cm, with a “cotton-wool” pattern of calcification, concentric growth producing a ball-like outline, and bowing—but no erosion—of the inferior mandibular border. Occlusal radiograph revealed buccal and lingual cortical plate expansion with lingual displacement of teeth. Posterior–anterior mandible view confirmed a mixed radiopaque–radiolucent expansile lesion extending from the left ramus to the right mandibular angle. Axial and 3D CT scans demonstrated a large (11.8×7.0×7.3 cm) expansile lesion of the right and left mandibular bodies and left ramus, with mixed sclerotic and lucent areas and central low-density foci.

A 15-year-old spayed female domestic shorthair cat was examined for a routine checkup. Physical examination, complete blood count, and serum biochemistry were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 9 × 7 mm heterogeneous hypoechoic nodule at the periphery of the quadrate liver lobe. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology showed numerous grouped epithelial cells with moderate to marked anisocytosis and anisokaryosis, round nuclei with reticular to coarse chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and poorly basophilic cytoplasm. A presumptive diagnosis of epithelial neoplasia (carcinoma) was made, and metastatic disease was considered. Serial monitoring showed progressive growth of the nodule to 1.73 × 1.34 cm over 4 months, with a transient rise in AST and ALT. Laparoscopic liver biopsy was then performed; histopathology suggested lymphocytic cholangitis, and symptomatic treatment normalized transaminases, but the nodule continued to enlarge. Whole-body CT showed a diffuse heterogeneous liver parenchyma, especially in the quadrate lobe, without any other abnormalities. A partial lobectomy of the quadrate lobe was performed. Histopathology of the excised mass revealed multilobulated epithelial cells forming follicular structures containing dense eosinophilic, colloid-like material, merging into tubular and solid proliferations with nuclear crowding and mitotic figures. Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse cytoplasmic positivity for thyroglobulin in most neoplastic cells. Thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentrations were within reference intervals. Re-evaluation of the CT images revealed no abnormalities in the orthotopic thyroid gland and no nodular lesions elsewhere.

A 37-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of pain in the toes of her left foot. The pain was persistent, worse with movement, and associated with numbness, tingling, and a bluish-pale discoloration of the left toes. She had no prior medical history or medication use. On examination, heart rate was 102 beats/min; left femoral pulsation was weakened, distal pulses were absent, and the left toes were dry, cold, and pale. Motor function was intact, but sensation was reduced in the left foot. Electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, and transthoracic echocardiography showed no abnormalities or intracardiac thrombus. Doppler ultrasound demonstrated triphasic flow in the right superficial femoral artery, and a thrombus in the left common femoral artery with poor distal flow. Laboratory studies revealed a platelet count of 812 × 10^3/μL; other routine blood tests were normal. Peripheral blood smear showed marked thrombocytosis with giant platelets, leukocytosis, and immature granulocytes. A JAK2 mutation assay was obtained.

A 31-year-old man presented with a 6-day history of severe headache and vomiting. He reported a progressive loss of vision in his left eye and decreased libido over the preceding two years. He denied any rhinorrhea, trauma, or prior neurosurgery. On examination, he was alert, febrile (38.0 °C), and had complete blindness of the left eye without other cranial-nerve deficits; no nasal discharge was noted.

Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level of 305 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L), a leukocyte count of 13,000/μL, serum sodium 131 mEq/L, and blood glucose 127 mg/dL. Hormonal assays revealed a prolactin level of 9000 ng/mL (normal 2.5–11 ng/mL) with additional findings consistent with panhypopituitarism.

Computed tomography of the head demonstrated a large sellar mass with erosion of the sellar floor and extension into the sphenoid sinus. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a suprasellar and infrasellar lesion extending into the cavernous sinuses, encroaching on the third ventricle, and compressing the optic chiasm, without evidence of intratumoral hemorrhage.

A lumbar puncture yielded purulent cerebrospinal fluid containing 11,900 white blood cells/μL, 2,680 red blood cells/μL, protein 6.3 g/L, glucose 39 mg/dL, and lactate 81 mg/dL.  
What is your differential diagnosis?

A 65-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a two-week history of left lower extremity swelling and pain that improved slightly with leg elevation and NSAIDs. She denied shortness of breath, recent trauma, fever, chest pain, or unexplained weight loss. Her medical history included inflammatory polyarthritis (on methotrexate and adalimumab), hyperlipidemia, hypertension, asthma–COPD overlap, osteopenia, and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation managed with warfarin (therapeutic INR). She had a three–pack-year smoking history, quitting 40 years prior.

On examination, the left lower extremity had pitting edema; peripheral pulses were strong, and the abdomen was soft and nondistended. Laboratory studies showed hypokalemia (2.8 mEq/L), which was repleted, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm/hr, and a C-reactive protein level of 30.1 mg/L. Doppler ultrasound of the left leg was negative for deep venous thrombosis. Computed tomography angiography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large heterogeneous left pelvic retroperitoneal mass centered at the left iliac chain, measuring 8.7 × 6.9 × 8.5 cm, with probable compression or occlusion of the adjacent iliac vein. Based on imaging, the differential diagnosis included sarcoma, lymphoma, ovarian neoplasm, or germ cell tumor.

A 62-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of progressive gingival enlargement and bilateral tender submandibular lymphadenopathy. Her medical history was notable only for 10 years of hypertension treated with antihypertensive medications. Intraoral examination showed generalized maxillary and mandibular gingival enlargement of firm consistency covering two-thirds of the teeth, without bleeding or purulence. Teeth exhibited generalized attrition and Grade-3 mobility of the mandibular second molars, which were tender to percussion. Extraoral examination revealed bilateral tender, mobile submandibular lymph nodes. A panoramic radiograph demonstrated generalized alveolar bone loss, severe resorption around the mandibular second molars resembling floating teeth, and periapical radiolucencies in the maxilla. Complete blood counts and biochemical tests were within normal limits except for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included drug-induced gingival enlargement, idiopathic gingival enlargement, and inflammatory gingival enlargement, the latter of which was considered unlikely given the firmness of the tissue. An incisional biopsy was performed from the mandibular anterior facial gingiva and submitted for histological evaluation.

A 53-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with a headache. Neurologic examination revealed that he was alert and had no motor or sensory deficits, but he noted narrowing of the left lower visual field quadrant. Noncontrast CT of the head showed a 5-cm, well-circumscribed, high-density mass in the right parietal region without calcification. MRI demonstrated an extra-axial lesion that was iso‐intense on T1-weighted imaging, uniformly very low in signal on T2-weighted imaging, and showed marked enhancement after gadolinium administration. There was no diffusion restriction after correction for a T2 blackout effect. The mass was separate from the ventricles and was associated with a large anterior cyst whose contents had a signal different from cerebrospinal fluid; the cyst wall did not enhance, consistent with a peritumoral cyst, and there was surrounding edema. The tumor contacted the dura mater convexity and the falx cerebri but lacked an obvious attachment or dural tail sign. Time-resolved MR angiography (4D-TRAK) showed no tumor staining or feeding vessels, suggesting low vascularity. Routine blood tests, including tumor markers, were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no extracranial source of malignancy.

A 22-year-old Chinese woman was referred for evaluation of oligomenorrhea. Menarche was at age 12 with previously regular 30-day cycles. Over the past year, she noted spotting two to three times weekly. She denied weight gain, hirsutism, Cushingoid features, or thyroid symptoms. She denied medications or exogenous androgens.

On examination, blood pressure was 128/70 mm Hg, BMI 18.1. She had mild facial acne, deeper voice, and mild clitoral enlargement (10 × 5 mm); there was no hirsutism by Ferriman–Gallwey score. Abdominal, cardiac, respiratory, thyroid, and neurologic examinations were normal.

Initial laboratory evaluation showed:
– Total testosterone 5.35 nmol/L (154.3 ng/dL) [reference 0.48–1.85 nmol/L]  
– 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17OHP) 18.9 nmol/L (623.7 ng/dL) [follicular phase 0.3–3.3; luteal phase 2.9–15.2 nmol/L]

A transabdominal pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a normal uterus and a left ovarian cyst measuring 18.2 × 16 mm, interpreted as a simple physiological cyst; the right ovary was normal.

A 28-year-old normotensive woman reported a 2-year history of paresthesia over the left side of her chest. Over the past 8 months, she noted partial ptosis of her left eyelid and anhidrosis of the left face. On neurologic examination, the left pupil was dilated and nonreactive to light, consistent with Horner’s syndrome. Sensory testing revealed hyperesthesia in the left D2 and D3 dermatomes; the remainder of the neurologic examination was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervicodorsal spine demonstrated, at the D1–D2 level on the left, a large paravertebral extrapulmonary mass that was heterogeneously enhancing on short-T1 inversion recovery images, extended into the neural foramen, and compressed the thecal sac. T2-weighted images showed multiple flow voids within the lesion and heterogeneous signal intensity.

A 30-year-old G1P1 woman presented with a vaginal mass first noted at the time of a vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery 4 years earlier. She reported no change in size until 1 month of worsening watery yellow–pink discharge, occasionally blood-tinged, and entry and deep dyspareunia. She denied bowel or urinary symptoms, fevers, weight loss, or systemic complaints. On examination, there was copious serosanguinous fluid in the vaginal vault. A well-circumscribed, smooth, cystic structure approximately 4 cm in diameter was palpated along the posterior vaginal wall, with a 0.5×1.0 cm exophytic lesion overlying it, draining serosanguinous fluid. On bimanual and rectal examination, the mass was separate from the cervix and located in the rectovaginal septum; there was no rectal invasion. Biopsy specimens showed fibrous tissue with acute and chronic inflammation and squamous debris, without a definitive diagnosis. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed a complex vaginal mass inseparable from the cervix, measuring 5.1×3.8×5.4 cm, with minimal peripheral vascularity on color Doppler. MRI demonstrated a 4.7×4.8×4.9 cm mass arising from the posterior vaginal wall, separate from the cervix, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on T1-weighted images, and on postcontrast sequences showing wall enhancement, absent internal enhancement superiorly, and bulky, nodular hyperenhancement inferiorly, consistent with a complex cystic mass.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of right lower back and abdominal pain. He had a 10-year history of poorly controlled diabetes. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed CA 19-9 of 99.98 μmol/mL, creatinine 73.5 μmol/L, and split glomerular filtration rates of 34.9 mL/min bilaterally. Renal ultrasound revealed a 0.9 × 0.8 cm round hypoechoic mass in the mid-to-lower parenchyma of the right kidney with no internal blood flow. CT angiography demonstrated a 1 cm nodular iso-dense lesion in the mid-right kidney abutting the capsule, with continuous, obvious but inhomogeneous arterial-phase enhancement and no prominent feeding vessels. Thyroid ultrasound showed bilateral TI-RADS 3 nodules.

A 21-year-old Irish woman presented with a 3-week history of an enlarging, firm, painless right-sided neck mass. She denied dysphagia, stridor, fevers, weight loss, and hypercalcemic symptoms except mild constipation and two presyncopal episodes with exercise. Her medical history was unremarkable. Family history included sudden cardiac death in a maternal grandmother, two maternal aunts with hyperthyroidism and goitres, and early-onset hypertension in her mother.

On examination, vital signs showed a heart rate of 112 bpm and blood pressure of 116/80 mm Hg. There was a firm, non-tender swelling in the right thyroid lobe without lymphadenopathy. Thyroid and renal function tests were normal: serum creatinine 64 μmol/L and eGFR 124 mL/min/1.73 m2. Corrected serum calcium was elevated at 3.96 mmol/L (2.2–2.6), phosphate 0.35 mmol/L (0.8–1.5), and albumin 49 g/L. She received IV fluids and bisphosphonates; calcium fell to 2.46 mmol/L in 3 days. 

Neck ultrasound revealed a 5×4 cm solid and cystic nodule in the lower pole of the right thyroid lobe. Two days later, intact PTH was 138.4 pmol/L (1.6–6.9). Six days after presentation, calcium had rebounded to 2.73 mmol/L, vitamin D was low at 35 nmol/L, and alkaline phosphatase rose from 143 to 240 IU/L. A chest radiograph was unremarkable. 

Differential considerations included parathyroid adenoma, parathyroid hyperplasia, parathyroid carcinoma, or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. Tc-99m sestamibi single-photon emission CT/CT demonstrated a 7–10 cm tracer-avid lesion posterior to the right thyroid lobe. Twenty-four–hour urinary calcium was elevated at 9 mmol (2.5–7.5), and prolactin, urinary catecholamines, and metanephrines were normal.

A 60-year-old man with a history of nodular cutaneous melanoma (left subcostal region, pT4a, Breslow thickness 8.3 mm, Clark level IV) underwent wide excision and axillary lymph node dissection (no nodal metastases), followed by six cycles of dacarbazine and IL-2. Four months after chemotherapy, CT showed multiple liver lesions and small pulmonary nodules; thoracotomy yielded only fibrotic tissue. Six months later, he developed recurrent subcutaneous masses, skeletal pain, and widespread metastatic lesions on bone scintigraphy, CT, and PET. He received interferon and temozolomide but developed worsening asthenia, pain, nausea, and vomiting. A CT scan revealed a confluent upper abdominal mass indistinguishable from gastric corpus and pancreas. Upper endoscopy demonstrated a 3 cm hard mass at the gastro-fundal junction covered by fibrin. Histology showed an undifferentiated neoplasm with fused tumor cells. Immunohistochemical stains for melanoma markers (S100, HMB-45, Melan A, tyrosinase), carcinoma (CK), gastrointestinal stromal tumor markers (CD-34, c-Kit), and lymphoma (LCA) were all negative, except for weak, focal vimentin expression.

A 76-year-old Japanese man with a 40 pack-year smoking history was referred after an abnormal chest radiograph at a routine exam. He reported no respiratory symptoms. Laboratory studies revealed elevated squamous cell carcinoma antigen (24.5 ng/mL; normal <1.5), cytokeratin 19 fragment (10.3 ng/mL; normal <3.5), carcinoembryonic antigen (7.3 ng/mL; normal <3.5), and surfactant protein D (299 ng/mL; normal <110). Chest radiograph showed an irregular opacity in the right lower lobe. Chest CT demonstrated a large area of consolidation with air bronchograms in the right lower lobe and bilateral reticular opacities with honeycombing. FDG-PET/CT revealed high uptake in the right lung lesion (SUVmax 9.38 at 1 hour; 13.03 at 2 hours). Bronchoscopic examination showed no endobronchial lesion. Transbronchial lung biopsy and bronchial brushing yielded cytology interpreted as squamous cell carcinoma, but occasional ciliated epithelial cells and mucin-containing columnar cells without atypia were also noted.

A 22-month-old Caucasian girl presented with low-grade fever, cough, decreased activity, poor oral intake, and bilateral jaw-line swelling. She was born at term without complications; her maternal aunt had autoimmune disease. Vaccinations were incomplete (no MMR, varicella, or fourth DTaP). History included recurrent otitis media (with tubes) and eczema. Initial tests showed positive mumps IgM; elevated IgM, IgG, IgA, IgE, and IgG subclasses; positive rhinovirus and enterovirus; negative CMV, HIV, and hepatitis panels. She was leukopenic with cold-agglutinin autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Exam revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly and small mobile cervical nodes. EBV serologies indicated acute infection, with plasma EBV load 9 000–20 600 copies/μL. Flow cytometry showed reduced B, T, and NK cells. Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics and symptomatic improvement, chest radiography and CT demonstrated persistent bilateral perihilar and right middle lobe infiltrates. One month later, she was readmitted with febrile neutropenia, rash, elevated soluble IL-2, but did not meet five of eight HLH criteria. Lymphocyte proliferation studies showed poor response to PHA but normal response to pokeweed mitogen.

A 22-year-old man presented with one month of mid–thoracic back pain and progressive difficulty walking. Over 48 hours in the hospital, he developed spasticity in both lower extremities and worsening weakness to grade 2–3, consistent with paraplegia. He had no history of trauma or prior neurologic disease. Vital signs were normal, and routine hematologic studies were within normal limits. MRI and CT of the thoracic spine revealed a well-defined, lytic, expansile mass measuring approximately 25 × 18 × 33 mm arising from the posterior elements of the T7 vertebra, including the left facet joint, invading the transverse process and lamina, and protruding into the spinal canal with compression of the cord. Intravenous contrast produced homogeneous enhancement of the lesion.

A 45-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of fever and a 7-day history of cough, dyspnea, and a painful swelling over the right side of her neck. She had a 10 pack-year smoking history and no significant past medical or family history. On examination, multiple firm, palpable right cervical lymph nodes were noted, and prominent dilated veins were visible on the right anterior chest wall. No other abnormalities were detected on systemic examination.

Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 13,000/mm3 with 510 eosinophils/mm3, an IgE level of 779 IU/mL, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 120 mm/hr, and a positive C-reactive protein. Tests for HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, antiphospholipid antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, protein C and S, antithrombin III, factor V Leiden, and homocysteine were all within normal limits or negative. Two-dimensional echocardiography revealed a mild pericardial effusion. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable. Sputum studies, including acid-fast bacilli smear, GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Gram stain, KOH mount, and cultures for pyogenic bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungi, were negative.

Neck ultrasonography demonstrated multiple necrotic right cervical lymph nodes and thrombosis of the entire right internal jugular vein. A chest radiograph revealed right middle lobe collapse and consolidation. A CT venogram of the neck and chest showed multiple heterogeneous lymph nodes in the cervical, pretracheal, and mediastinal regions; thrombus in the right internal jugular, subclavian, brachiocephalic veins, and superior vena cava; compression of the right internal jugular vein by an enlarged lymph node; extensive collateral venous channels; a small right pleural effusion; and mild pericardial effusion.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology of a right cervical lymph node yielded few lymphocytes and histiocytes, with no granulomas or malignant cells. Staining and GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and cultures were negative.

A 59-year-old man was followed for mild bilateral renal cystic disease when surveillance imaging showed interval enlargement of an endophytic right interpolar Bosniak III cyst measuring 1.9 × 2.0 × 1.6 cm. He was asymptomatic, with no hematuria or flank pain. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type II diabetes, and gout; his baseline glomerular filtration rate was 77 mL/min. He had a 22–pack-year smoking history but no family history of genitourinary malignancy. Laboratory studies were normal. He elected to undergo a robot-assisted right partial nephrectomy without complication. 

Gross examination revealed a well-circumscribed renal mass composed of multiple cysts ranging from closely packed small tubules to larger simple cysts within fibrous stroma; focal papillary architecture was noted. On light microscopy, the cysts were lined by predominantly a single layer—and occasionally multiple layers—of cells with variable eosinophilic cytoplasm resembling oncocytic cells. In some areas, cells exhibited a hobnail appearance and focal intracytoplasmic vacuoles. Nucleoli were prominent (grade 3). Ovarian-type stroma was absent.

A 28-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of pingueculae in both eyes. She reported a 5-year history of progressively enlarging bilateral conjunctival growths with mild foreign-body sensation in the left eye. She denied trauma, prior ocular surgery, allergies, or significant environmental exposure. Her past medical history was unremarkable, and there was no family history of cancer. Visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye. Slit-lamp examination revealed well-circumscribed, white, gelatinous, non-inflamed subepithelial nodules at the nasal and temporal limbus bilaterally (1.5–3.5 mm), without feeder vessels, along with peripheral corneal vascularization and prominent corneal nerves. The remainder of the ocular examination was unremarkable. Excision and cryotherapy were performed on the largest left nasal limbal lesion. Histopathology showed a circumscribed unencapsulated subepithelial lesion composed of enlarged neural bundles with equal proportions of neurofilament-positive axons and S100-positive Schwann cells, consistent with a conjunctival neuroma. Subsequent examination of the oral mucosa revealed similar gelatinous nodules on the tongue. Further systemic examination showed no Marfanoid habitus or facial dysmorphism.

A 70-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation on enoxaparin, liver cirrhosis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and a history of venous thrombus presented with a 5-day history of left arm weakness, numbness in the left fourth and fifth digits and medial palmar surface, and confusion. She reported chronic vision loss in the right eye but denied headache or trauma. On examination, she was alert; oriented to person, place, and time; and disoriented to situation. Visual acuity was reduced in the right eye. Muscle strength was 4/5 in the left triceps, wrist flexors, wrist extensors, and finger flexors, and 3/5 in the left finger extensors. The left triceps reflex was absent. Sensation to pinprick and light touch was decreased in the left fourth and fifth digits. There was no dysmetria or dysdiadokokinesia. Head CT without contrast showed a 1 cm hyperdense round lesion in the suprasellar cistern.

On hospital day 2, she developed a pupil-sparing right third cranial nerve palsy, which progressed the next day to a dilated, nonreactive right pupil. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the brachial plexus and spine was unrevealing. Gadolinium-enhanced brain MRI revealed enhancing lesions with heterogeneous signal intensity in the suprasellar, pineal, and right periatrial regions, without evidence of acute ischemic stroke. One week later, repeat brain MRI demonstrated interval enlargement of these lesions and focal right frontoparietal dural thickening. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast showed multiple thyroid nodules concerning for metastases. Two serial lumbar punctures yielded lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and an elevated IgG index but no malignant cells or other inflammatory or infectious markers.

A 37-year-old woman was referred for management of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Her only prior surgery was a remote cholecystectomy, and her cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. An attempted pulmonary vein isolation ablation was aborted because of an extremely thick interatrial septum, and her atrial fibrillation was managed medically with propafenone.

Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed a sheet-like, clot-like mass lining almost the entire left atrium and extending into the left atrial appendage. A cardiac magnetic resonance study showed a sessile, sheet-like mass adherent to the septal side of the left atrial cavity, measuring 4.7 × 1.3 cm; it was isointense to myocardium on pre-contrast T1, mildly hyperintense on T2, and hyperintense on Short-T1 Inversion Recovery. These features were interpreted as most consistent with an atrial myxoma.

The patient underwent open surgical excision of the mass. Intraoperatively, the lesion was very fibrotic and densely adherent to the left atrial wall, extending toward the mitral leaflets and into the pulmonary vein orifices. A frozen section showed dense fibrous tissue with areas of fibrin undergoing organization, chronic inflammation, and reactive‐appearing stromal cells. No myxoma cells were identified, and the tissue was thought to represent an organizing thrombus.

Sixteen months later, she presented with severe back pain. Spinal MRI revealed aggressive lytic pathologic fractures of the T10 and L1 vertebral bodies with an associated paravertebral soft-tissue mass. Vertebral body biopsies demonstrated a malignant spindle cell tumour suggestive of smooth muscle differentiation; the tumour cells were positive for desmin and smooth muscle actin. Mammography, Papanicolaou testing, and CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis did not reveal a primary malignancy.

A 43-year-old Hispanic woman with a history of left-leg monoparesis from poliomyelitis, long-standing diabetes mellitus, hypertension requiring three agents, nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy, proteinuria, and osteoporosis was evaluated for suspected Cushing’s syndrome. She first underwent evaluation 13 and 5 years earlier, including inferior petrosal sinus catheterization, without localization of an ACTH source. Three years ago she presented with an 18-month history of polymenorrhea, and examination showed moon facies, buffalo hump, prominent supraclavicular fat, purple striae on arms and abdomen, truncal obesity, an umbilical hernia, and proximal muscle wasting. Laboratory evaluation revealed urinary free cortisol 186.5 μg/day, morning serum cortisol 21.8 μg/dL, midnight serum cortisol 16.1 μg/dL, serum cortisol after a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test 16.6 μg/dL, and plasma ACTH 32.6 pg/mL. An 8 mg high-dose dexamethasone suppression test showed cortisol suppression to 2.69 μg/dL (84.8%). Thyroid function was normal. Two pituitary MRIs were reported as normal. Abdominal CT revealed a 68 × 60 × 76 mm bilobed intra-abdominal mass protruding through the umbilicus, adjacent to a small-intestinal loop, with unenhanced attenuation of 3, 7, and 45 HU rising to 6, 16, and 88 HU postcontrast, raising the possibility of a mesothelioma. Pelvic ultrasound confirmed uterine fibroids but no ovarian masses. Exploratory laparotomy was planned.

A 23-year-old Sri Lankan female law student presented with multiple episodes of nonbilious, nonprojectile vomiting over two days, associated with burning chest pain and regurgitation. She reported a 3-year history of similar cyclical vomiting episodes—each lasting 4–5 days with 4–6 daily episodes—followed by symptom-free intervals. These episodes were managed as gastroesophageal reflux disease with proton-pump inhibitors and prokinetics without full investigations. She denied abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, or bulimic behaviors; there were no signs of an eating disorder. She had reduced appetite, generalized weakness for 3 years, and secondary amenorrhea since age 20. She had psychosocial stressors, including a recent breakup. On exam, BMI was 16 kg/m^2, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, pulse 78 beats/min, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
- Serum sodium 110 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, chloride 74 mmol/L (repeatedly low)  
- Serum osmolality 223 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality 266 mOsm/kg; urine Na+ 14 mmol/L  
- Random serum cortisol 105 nmol/L (measured at 1 a.m.)  
- TSH 0.209 µIU/mL, free T3 1.32 pg/mL, free T4 0.98 ng/dL  
- FSH 1.4 mIU/mL, LH 0.4 mIU/mL  
- Serum prolactin 90.8 ng/mL after dilution  

She was euvolemic, denied polydipsia or polyuria, and had a normal urine output.

A 39-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of discomfort in both eyes. Fundoscopic examination revealed bilateral papilledema, and neuro-ophthalmologic testing showed mild visual field defects. She had no headaches, diplopia, focal weakness, or sensory disturbances, and her neurologic examination was otherwise normal. She was overweight (BMI 27.2 kg/m2), with an unremarkable medical and family history and no current medications. Lumbar puncture demonstrated an opening pressure of 500 mmH2O with normal cerebrospinal fluid composition. Noncontrast CT of the head showed no space-occupying lesions or hydrocephalus, only an incidental arachnoid cyst in the left middle fossa. MR imaging revealed a 2.5 cm lesion in the right sigmoid sinus that was isointense on T1- and T2-weighted images and showed homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. CT venography then demonstrated subtotal occlusion of the dominant right sigmoid sinus caused by a well-defined, homogeneous, hypodense mass.

A 29-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of progressive vision loss in her left eye. She had a 15-year history of headaches with documented bilateral optic nerve head swelling and possible optic disc masses. At age 14, she had been diagnosed with pseudotumor cerebri and underwent an extensive negative work-up, including left optic nerve sheath fenestration, without improvement. On presentation, visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/150 in the left. Initial genetic testing by whole exome sequencing was negative for mutations in von Hippel-Lindau, hypoxia-inducible factor-2α, neurofibromatosis, and tuberous sclerosis genes. Over the next several years, she received monthly then biweekly alternating intravitreal bevacizumab and aflibercept injections, along with bimonthly intravitreal steroid implants, with only limited response in the right eye. The optic nerve head lesions progressed to involve the papillomacular bundles. By early 2017, visual acuity had declined to 20/400 in the right eye and no light perception in the left eye.

A 32-year-old woman noted a subcutaneous mass in her left lumbar region that had grown gradually over 5–6 years. She experienced pain and restriction of trunk movement, particularly flexion, extension, and rotation, and was concerned about its appearance. She had no other symptoms, took no medications, and had no family history of similar lesions. Her weight had decreased by about 20 kg on a low-calorie diet, and her body–mass index was 31.8.
