On inspection, there was a large mass altering the silhouette of the left flank; the overlying skin was normal. Palpation revealed a subcutaneous bulk that was painful to touch but mobile over underlying structures. Routine laboratory tests and a lipid profile were within normal limits.

Ultrasound of the left lumbar region showed an oval, echogenic, non-homogeneous image with a fibrolipomatous aspect, measuring approximately 210 × 49 mm. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 22 cm subcutaneous, round mass with regular, sharp borders and a lipomatous signal; there was no evidence of infiltration into the abdominal wall or underlying muscles.

A 43-year-old premenopausal G4P3 woman with no significant past medical history presented with acute right lower quadrant abdominal pain without vaginal discharge, bleeding, or systemic symptoms. Her serum hCG was negative. An abdominal CT scan revealed a 7×4×4 cm soft-tissue and fluid-containing structure with a 2.5 cm rim-calcified component, most likely representing the right ovary with a contained dermoid cyst. A pelvic ultrasound demonstrated a 6.5×3.0×4.5 cm lobulated solid mass, partially calcified (2.8 cm) and partially solid with color flow, located in the posterior cul-de-sac adjacent to but seemingly separate from the right ovary; etiology was thought to be para-ovarian versus bowel. Review of pelvic ultrasounds from 9 years earlier showed a 4.0×2.0×2.0 cm heterogeneous solid-appearing right adnexal mass with areas of increased echogenicity, felt to possibly represent a broad ligament fibroid. Laboratory studies revealed CA-125 10 U/mL, CEA 1.6 ng/mL, and CA 19-9 7 U/mL. The patient’s pain was controlled with NSAIDs, and she was referred to gynecologic oncology for surgical management.

A 77-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of a left breast lump. She had a history of heart disease, treated for 4 years. On examination, there was a 3 × 2 cm firm, mobile, non-tender mass in the outer quadrant of the left breast; the skin, nipple, and areola were unremarkable. There was no axillary or cervical lymphadenopathy; the right breast was normal. Mammography showed a 2 × 2 cm ill-defined mass with irregular margins in the left upper outer quadrant and no microcalcifications; the right breast was normal. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was inconclusive. She underwent a lumpectomy with frozen-section analysis.

On gross examination, the specimen revealed a firm, grey-white, fibrous, unencapsulated nodular tumor measuring 2 × 1.2 × 0.8 cm with infiltrative borders; the closest margin was 0.5 cm from the base. Frozen sections showed a spindle cell proliferation with mild atypia in a sclerotic stroma infiltrating adjacent fat; a low-grade sarcoma was favored, and no axillary staging was performed at that time.

Permanent sections demonstrated an infiltrative spindle cell tumor with prominent sclerosis reminiscent of keloid formation. The cells were arranged in fascicles with tapering nuclei, mild anisonucleosis, and inconspicuous mitoses. Occasional plump epithelioid cells formed small clusters. Interspersed foci of benign ductal hyperplasia and papillary hyperplasia, including a micropapilloma without atypia, were noted. No squamous differentiation or ductal carcinoma in situ was seen.

Immunohistochemistry revealed tumor cells diffusely positive for cytokeratin (CK), CK7, high molecular weight cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, and vimentin. They were negative for gross cystic disease fluid protein, estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, S100, desmin, CD34, and HER-2/neu. Smooth muscle actin and p63 showed focal positivity. Ki-67 labeled fewer than 5% of tumor cells.

A 33 4/7-week, 2.22-kg female neonate was born after spontaneous vaginal delivery following premature rupture of membranes. She had an unremarkable physical examination at birth and passed meconium within 24 hours. Maternal breast milk feeds were initiated by gavage on day 1 of life. 

On day 4, after episodes of bilious emesis, she was made nil per os. Examination showed a distended, tender abdomen without rebound and normoactive bowel sounds; the remainder of her exam, including genitourinary assessment, was normal. Laboratory studies on day 4 revealed a white-cell count of 21.1×10^9/L with 14% eosinophils. 

By day 5, she developed frank bloody stools. Serial abdominal radiographs showed nonspecific bowel gas fullness without pneumatosis. An upper gastrointestinal series ruled out malrotation. Although abdominal distention resolved by day 6, leukocytosis, eosinophilia, and hematochezia persisted. Family history was notable for a sister with milk-protein intolerance who developed hematochezia after milk exposure. 

Broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin and cefepime) were started on day 5. On day 7, ampicillin was replaced with vancomycin after an abdominal ultrasound was performed to evaluate for ischemia, intussusception, and colitis; the ultrasound showed several subcentimeter hypoechoic, hypovascular liver lesions characterized as microabscesses, scattered loops of thick-walled bowel with minimal ascites, a sludge-filled gallbladder, and no biliary ductal dilatation. There was no pneumatosis, pneumoperitoneum, portal venous gas, or complex ascites. 

On day 8, a contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed irregular hypodensities in the anterior right hepatic lobe consistent with microabscesses and demonstrated mild mucosal hyperenhancement and bowel-wall thickening of the rectosigmoid.

A 21-year-old woman presented with a 1-cm tender, red, fluctuant nodule on her right cheek that had persisted for approximately 1 year. She had been treated by a dermatologist with oral azithromycin and intralesional triamcinolone without improvement. Another physician diagnosed an epidermoid cyst and recommended surgical excision, which she declined. Under suspicion of a parotid gland fistula, ultrasound imaging was requested. During a routine dental examination, a panoramic radiograph showed mucosal thickening in the right maxillary sinus adjacent to the palatal root of the right maxillary first molar. That tooth had received poor-quality endodontic treatment 4 years earlier, and the patient reported no history of abscess, pain, or tenderness since. On examination, a firm, cord-like tract was palpable from the mucogingival junction of that tooth, extending through the cheek toward the facial nodule.

A 37-year-old previously healthy man presented with four days of progressive weakness of all four limbs, dysphagia, drooling, nausea, and vomiting. One month earlier, he had received the first dose of an inactivated SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. In the days after vaccination he developed lethargy and intermittent myalgia with partial improvement. He had no recent infection, no known COVID-19 exposures, and a negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR. 

On examination, temperature was 37.0 °C, heart rate 88 bpm, blood pressure 115/80 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 20 /min. He was alert and oriented. Cranial-nerve examination showed bilateral facial paralysis; pupils were 3 mm and reactive bilaterally. There was no sensory level. Muscle strength was 2/5 in all four limbs, reflexes were preserved, and plantar responses were extensor. 

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, WBC 11,600/µL, platelets 305,000/mm3, PT 17.5 s, PTT 37.2 s, INR 1.27, ESR 23 mm/hr, negative CRP, and normal chemistry. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 2 WBCs, 32 RBCs, protein 56 mg/dL, glucose 97 mg/dL (serum glucose 159 mg/dL), and no oligoclonal bands. Chest radiography and ECG were unremarkable.

On hospital day 2, brain MRI revealed poorly marginated T2-FLAIR hyperintense foci in the left cerebral peduncle, bilateral pons, and medulla with slight T1 hypointensity and faint contrast enhancement. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed restricted diffusion in the pons. MR spectroscopy showed elevated choline and myoinositol peaks. Cervical spine MRI was normal.

A 54‐year‐old Hispanic woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and peripheral vascular disease presented with a 3‐day history of severe watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and altered mental status. Her medications included metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril, metoprolol, pravastatin, aspirin, hydrochlorothiazide, and nightly insulin detemir; she had not administered her prandial insulin for the preceding 24 hours due to poor oral intake. In the emergency department, her serum glucose was 47 mg/dL, for which glucagon was administered. She was hypotensive (70/39 mmHg), confused, and disoriented, with dry mucous membranes and decreased bowel sounds. Shortly after arrival, she became unresponsive and developed pulseless electrical activity; return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after 3 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation, including intubation and mechanical ventilation. In the intensive care unit, her blood pressure was 98/37 mmHg on norepinephrine (0.3 µg/kg/min). Laboratory studies showed arterial pH 6.57, serum bicarbonate 2 mEq/L, anion gap 30 mmol/L, osmolar gap 21 mOsm/kg, lactate 16.3 mmol/L, hemoglobin A1c 7.3%, and creatinine 8.07 mg/dL (baseline 0.86 mg/dL two months earlier). A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed only nonspecific gallbladder wall thickening. Vasopressin was added to maintain a mean arterial pressure above 60 mmHg.

A 70-year-old Caucasian man with a history of essential hypertension, peripheral arterial disease, prior non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction with 3-vessel CABG, bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement, and metastatic stage IV lung adenocarcinoma treated with pembrolizumab presented with increased fatigue, weight gain, weakness, and severe hypotension. On arrival, systolic blood pressure ranged from 50 to 70 mm Hg. His baseline serum creatinine was 1.0–1.2 mg/dL; on presentation it was 7.2 mg/dL, with blood urea nitrogen of 78 mg/dL and bicarbonate of 21 mmol/L. Troponin was 2.8 ng/mL. Sodium and potassium were within normal limits. Platelet counts, historically 30,000–100,000/µL, were 77,000/µL on this admission.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a drop in ejection fraction from 55–60 % to 35 %, without regional wall-motion abnormalities or pericardial effusion. Medication review revealed no new nephrotoxins; losartan was held. The patient denied NSAID or herbal use and had no recent contrast exposure. Renal ultrasound demonstrated no hydronephrosis; a Foley catheter was placed. Creatine phosphokinase was 277 U/L. Urinalysis showed 1+ blood, 1+ protein, 0–5 red blood cells per high-power field, and 0–5 white blood cells per high-power field; the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 0.06 g/g. Peripheral smear revealed no schistocytes, and bilirubin levels were normal. Hemoglobin was 10.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 5,100/µL. A fractional excretion of urea was calculated at 46 %.

An 11‐week‐old intact male mixed‐breed dog was referred for severe anemia and suspected babesiosis. Three weeks earlier, he had been transported from Texas. One week after transport, he developed acute lethargy and fever (40.4°C). In‐house CBC showed severe microcytic, normochromic, non‐regenerative anemia (HCT 0.147 L/L; RI 0.373–0.617 L/L) and severe thrombocytopenia (23 × 10^9/L; RI 148–484 × 10^9/L). He received 15 ml/kg pRBC over 4 h and was discharged on omeprazole, sucralfate, and amoxicillin/clavulanate. The next day, PCV was 23%. Eight days later, he was lethargic with PCV 15%; a blood smear was suspicious for Babesia, and clindamycin was started. When he became too weak to stand, he was referred.

On presentation, the dog was nonambulatory, pale, mildly icteric, and splenomegaly was noted. Weight was 5.75 kg; temperature 38.2°C; heart rate 150 beats/min; respiratory rate 60 breaths/min. Point-of-care testing showed PCV 14%, total protein 5.4 g/dL, and compensated metabolic acidosis with lactate 5.2 mmol/L. Ultrasound revealed volume contraction, no effusions or pulmonary B-lines, and subjective splenomegaly. He was blood‐typed (DEA 1.1 positive), cross-matched, and transfused with 14 ml/kg pRBCs. Cytologic evaluation demonstrated intra-erythrocytic piroplasms consistent with Babesia canis. He was treated with IM imidocarb and IV fluids.

After the first transfusion, PCV remained 13% and lactate rose to 8.2 mmol/L. He received diphenhydramine for suspected transfusion reaction and an additional 13 ml/kg pRBCs. Fourteen hours after admission, his respiratory rate exceeded 100 breaths/min; he was placed in an oxygen chamber, then developed diarrhea and hypersalivation treated with atropine. Tachypnea worsened further, necessitating emergent endotracheal intubation. During intubation, a large volume of serosanguineous/icteric fluid was produced through the endotracheal tube. Initial manual ventilation with 100% FiO₂ yielded SpO₂ values of 88%–92%, after which he was transitioned to mechanical ventilation.

A 28-year-old Iranian woman presented with a 3-year history of bilateral vision loss and photopsia. Three years earlier, she had accidentally ingested four 1250 mg boluses of veterinary niclosamide. A few days after ingestion, she noted visual disturbances and was treated empirically with a short course of high-dose oral corticosteroids for presumed bilateral optic neuritis; her vision neither improved nor worsened. Over the next 3 years, her visual symptoms remained stable. She denied other medication use, alcohol, smoking, night blindness, or photophobia. There was no family history of vision loss or retinal disease, and parents were nonconsanguineous. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Best-corrected visual acuities were 20/50 in the right eye and 20/63 in the left eye. Color vision and pupillary reactions were normal. Anterior segment and vitreous examinations were unremarkable; intraocular pressures were normal. Fundus examination revealed pink optic discs, cup-to-disc ratios of 0.2, and parafoveal retinal pigment epithelial atrophy manifesting as bilateral bull’s-eye maculopathy. Fundus autofluorescence demonstrated annular hyperautofluorescence in the parafoveal region. Optical coherence tomography showed parafoveal ellipsoid zone disruption, outer retinal thinning, and relative foveal sparing (“flying saucer” sign). Full-field electroretinography revealed decreased scotopic and photopic amplitudes with normal waveforms in both eyes. Electrooculography showed Arden ratios of 240% (right eye) and 202% (left eye).

A 29-year-old woman with a history of intermittent headaches and a half–pack-per-day smoking habit presented with subacute intermittent right-sided hemi–body numbness and recurrent transient word-finding difficulties. She had an intrauterine device, was not taking oral contraceptives, and reported multiple sexual partners; her last syphilis screen 6 years earlier had been negative. On arrival, her blood pressure was 138/50 mm Hg; during hospitalization it ranged from the 90s to the 130s systolic. Neurologic examination revealed expressive aphasia, dysarthria, and decreased fine-touch sensation over the right forearm. 

Noncontrast head CT showed ill-defined hypodensities in the left posterior parietal lobe with hemorrhagic transformation and additional hypodensities in the left frontal lobe. CT angiography demonstrated focal moderate-to-severe stenosis of the left M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery. Brain MRI with and without contrast revealed numerous diffusion-restricted foci involving both white and gray matter of the left cerebral hemisphere, with correlating FLAIR hyperintensity suggestive of acute to subacute infarcts, some with hemorrhagic transformation; a left basal ganglia focal enhancing lesion with T1 hyperintensity and no diffusion restriction was also noted. 

Routine stroke workup, including transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study, 48-hour Holter monitoring, and laboratory tests (CBC with differential, serum electrolytes, CRP, ESR, and liver function tests), was normal. Given her young age and unusual presentation, vasculopathy versus vasculitis was suspected; HIV and Lyme disease antibody screening, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), proteinase 3 (PR3), myeloperoxidase (MPO), and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies were all negative. She was started on verapamil for concern of reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS). 

Diagnostic cerebral angiography showed a distal left M1 segment stenosis with partial improvement in caliber after administration of 10 mg of intra-arterial verapamil.

A 48-year-old man with moderate haemophilia A, transfusion-acquired HIV (on maraviroc/efavirenz/raltegravir; CD4+ 1200 cells/mm3; undetectable viral load) and treated genotype 1a hepatitis C virus infection (completed ledipasvir/sofosbuvir 2 years earlier) was referred for evaluation of new-onset proteinuria. He has portal hypertensive changes with splenomegaly, oesophageal varices and mild thrombocytopenia (106×10^9/L). He reports one year of foamy urine but is otherwise asymptomatic. Physical examination shows palpable splenomegaly without peripheral oedema.  
Laboratory studies reveal:  
• 24-h urine protein 4.35 g; microscopy 24×10^6 red cells  
• Serum creatinine 98 μmol/L; albumin 51 g/L  
• ANA 1:160, homogeneous; ANCA, dsDNA, anti-GBM negative  
• Serum anti-PLA2R and cryoglobulins negative; SPEP without monoclonal bands  
Renal ultrasonography shows normal-sized kidneys, preserved corticomedullary differentiation, bilateral simple cysts, and no hydronephrosis or calculi.

A 4-month-old boy, born at 36 weeks’ gestation to third-degree consanguineous parents, was referred for clusters of brief events involving right-sided clonic jerks, chewing movements, and blinking that began at age 3 months after a febrile vaccination reaction. These episodes occurred up to 10 times daily, lasted seconds, and resolved spontaneously or with IV benzodiazepines. Parents also noted decreased feeding, loss of head control, and diminished reactivity.

Birth history was notable only for transient neonatal hypoglycemia; Apgar scores were 10 and 10. Growth parameters at presentation were below the 3rd percentile for weight (7.16 kg) and between the 10th and 25th percentiles for length and head circumference. Family history was unremarkable.

On neurologic examination, there was marked axial hypotonia, poor eye contact, weak sucking, and decreased social interaction. Vital signs, routine labs (CBC, liver and renal function), serum ammonia, and lactate were normal. An initial EEG showed recurrent slow waves in the right temporal region and asynchronous left temporo-occipital slow waves, occasionally followed by suppression of background activity; IV pyridoxine produced no change, and levetiracetam led to only partial seizure control.

Brain MRI at 3 months of age demonstrated a thinned corpus callosum, diffuse white matter hyperintensity on T2 and hypointensity on T1, and absence of myelination in the posterior limbs of both internal capsules. Based on imaging, a hypomyelinating leukoencephalopathy of genetic or metabolic origin was suspected. Complete metabolic screening—including plasma amino acids, urinary organic acids, tests for oligosaccharidosis, mucopolysaccharidosis, neurotransmitter defects, pyridoxine and pyridoxal-phosphate deficiency, primary hyperlactatemia, brain glucose transport deficiency, and peroxisomal disorders—was normal. Comparative genomic hybridization array revealed no duplications or deletions.

A 26-year-old woman with a history of unspecified bipolar disorder and recent antipsychotic treatment was brought to the emergency department after 10 days of worsening mental status. Collateral history revealed progressive fatigue, inability to feed herself, and dependence for activities of daily living. On arrival, she was unresponsive; blood pressure was 175/108 mm Hg, heart rate 170 beats per minute, temperature 37.8 °C, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She had adequate urine output but required assistance with toileting. Physical examination showed rigidity of all four extremities, areflexia, inability to follow commands, and warm skin. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 12,000 per mm³ and a creatine kinase level of 6,500 IU/L. A noncontrast CT scan of the head was unremarkable. The initial differential diagnosis included neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant catatonia, encephalitis, and sepsis.

A 43-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of slowly progressive vision loss in both eyes, which had markedly worsened over the past 3 months. He also noted floaters and a rapid decrease in vision in the left eye. His medical history was notable for chronic kidney failure from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (on peritoneal dialysis and erythropoietin) and well-controlled systemic hypertension (blood pressure 115/80 mmHg on beta- and alpha-blockers). He denied diabetes, prior ocular surgery, or significant eye disease; he was allergic to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 12 mmHg bilaterally. Slit-lamp examination showed clear corneas, rubeosis iridis, and mild nuclear sclerotic cataracts. Funduscopic examination revealed engorged, pale retinal arterioles; attenuated venules; diffuse RPE pigmentary changes; small vitreous hemorrhage and subhyaloid hemorrhage sparing the fovea, with neovascularization of the optic disc in the right eye; and old inferior vitreous hemorrhage with fibrovascular proliferation on the optic disc in the left eye.

Fluorescein angiography demonstrated a leopard-spot pattern of choroidal hyperfluorescence, optic-disc neovascular leakage, and peripheral capillary nonperfusion in both eyes. Spectral-domain OCT showed posterior vitreous detachment with hyperreflective intraretinal flecks, and visible hyperreflective arterial vessel walls. Enhanced depth imaging OCT revealed thickened choroidal vessel walls and lumenal enlargement.

The working diagnosis was bilateral proliferative retinopathy from an occlusive retinal vasculopathy. Laboratory studies showed normocytic normochromic anemia, elevated creatinine (12.9 mg/dL), elevated alkaline phosphatase, and hypoalbuminemia. Syphilis serologies and tuberculosis testing were negative. ANA, RF, anti-Sm, antiphospholipid, ANCA subtypes, complement levels, anti-DNA, anti-RNP, anti-Ro, and anti-La antibodies were all negative. A thrombophilia panel for factor V Leiden, protein C and S deficiencies, and antithrombin III deficiency was negative. Carotid and orbital Doppler ultrasonography showed mild carotid and vertebral artery stenosis with reduced flow in the ophthalmic and central retinal arteries.

A 31-year-old right-hand–dominant man originally from Afghanistan presented with over 3 months of progressive right wrist pain. Seven years earlier he had immigrated to the United States; during the current illness he moved between Florida and Canada. Initial wrist pain followed minor lifting trauma. He was first diagnosed with a wrist sprain and treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, then with primary osteoarthritis without improvement. He re-presented with continued pain and new fluctuance over the volar wrist.

On admission he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers; HIV testing was negative. Radiographs of the right wrist demonstrated diffuse destruction and osteopenia of the proximal and distal carpal rows with scattered cystic changes of the distal radius, ulna, and carpal bones. Physical examination revealed an erythematous, desquamated, fluctuant lesion on the volar right wrist, pain with small arcs of motion, and hyperreflexia of the upper extremities but otherwise intact neurovascular status.

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the wrist showed diffuse T2-weighted enhancement of the carpal bones and a subcutaneous fluid collection communicating with the radiocarpal joint. Synovial aspiration yielded grossly purulent fluid, which was sent for cytology, Gram stain, aerobic, anaerobic, fungal, acid-fast cultures, and crystal analysis. A chest radiograph was unremarkable for pulmonary disease, and MRI of the cervical spine showed no syrinx. He was admitted for presumed septic arthritis and taken for open irrigation and debridement of the wrist, during which extensive purulence, synovitis, severe bony erosion, and cartilage loss were encountered. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics were initiated.

A 13-year-old white female was referred for evaluation of right ear and mastoid pain of 16 months’ duration. She described a constant, dull, throbbing ache rated 6–7/10 on a numeric scale, with 8–10 daily paroxysms of sharp pain rated 9/10, each lasting 1–2 minutes and awakening her once or twice nightly. No specific triggers or relieving factors were identified.

Prior workup by two otolaryngologists, a neurologist, her primary care physician, and a dentist included a brain MRI with and without contrast, a head and neck CT, and panoramic and dental periapical radiographs; all studies were reported as normal. She had been treated empirically for presumed ear infection with NSAIDs and multiple courses of oral antibiotics, and underwent placement of a tympanostomy tube without any pain relief.

Her medical history included asthma, seasonal allergies, and chronic migraine without aura managed with topiramate and other medications. She denied mood or substance-use issues.

On examination, cranial nerves II–XII were intact. Gentle cutaneous stimulation of the posterior wall of the right auditory canal elicited a familiar, sharp 9/10 pain that subsided after about 1 minute, returning to her baseline dull ache. The tympanostomy tube was in place without signs of inflammation. Palpation of the right trapezius, paracervical, and temporalis tendon was tender but did not reproduce her ear pain. A diagnostic anesthetic block of the right temporalis tendon relieved local tenderness but did not alter the ear pain. A repeat brain MRI with and without contrast was then obtained.

A 29-year-old Indigenous Australian man presented with severe (8/10) epigastric pain radiating to his back. He had a history of asthma, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, and known hypertriglyceridemia; he had been hospitalized three years earlier for hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis (triglycerides 39 mmol/L). He was a current smoker and denied alcohol use.  
On arrival: temperature 36.5°C, heart rate 64 bpm, blood pressure 138/83 mmHg, respiratory rate 11/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. He appeared clinically dehydrated.  
Initial blood tests were lipemic; after resuscitation, results showed triglycerides 24.1 mmol/L (reference <1.70), cholesterol 8.4 mmol/L (<5.5), lipase 119 U/L (8–78), white blood cell count 12.3×10^9/L (4–12), corrected calcium 2.29 mmol/L (2.22–2.53), creatinine 68 μmol/L (63–111), and random glucose 21.3 mmol/L. No ketonuria was detected.  
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT performed 24 hours after symptom onset demonstrated fatty liver but no features of pancreatitis.  
Given the absence of imaging evidence of pancreatitis and only mildly elevated lipase, it was considered that his abdominal pain might represent a “hyperlipemic abdominal crisis,” although pancreatitis could not be ruled out.

A 20-year-old Filipino man with systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed 6 months earlier and maintained on hydroxychloroquine presented with sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, fatigue, dry cough, fevers, and a chronic progressive rash. He denied recent travel, sick contacts, high-risk sexual activity, intravenous drug use, smoking, or alcohol use. On examination, his temperature was 100.8 °F, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, heart rate 118 bpm, and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. Skin assessment revealed hyperpigmented to violaceous, scaly plaques with excoriated papules on the extremities, back, and chest.

Laboratory studies showed leukopenia, anemia, non-nephrotic proteinuria without active sediment, elevated troponin and N-terminal pro-BNP, high inflammatory markers, hypocomplementemia, and positive ANA with anti–Smith, RNP, chromatin, SS-A, double-stranded DNA, pANCA, and MPO antibodies. Initial chest radiograph was normal. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Transthoracic echocardiogram at admission showed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction. He was treated with intravenous antibiotics and high-dose corticosteroids for presumed sepsis and SLE flare.

On hospital day 5, after clearance of bacteremia, he developed worsening dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hemoptysis. Chest radiograph and CT of the chest showed bilateral pleural effusions, dense basal consolidations, pulmonary nodules, possible left subsegmental pulmonary emboli, and pericardial effusions. Repeat transthoracic echocardiogram revealed an LVEF of 25%, moderate global hypokinesis, a small pericardial effusion without tamponade, right atrial pressure of 15 mmHg, and mild pulmonary hypertension (43 mmHg). Cardiogenic shock was favored over septic shock.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of altered sensation on the right side of her body, beginning in the lower leg as pins and needles with hyperalgesia and progressing proximally. The leg symptoms resolved before similar sensations appeared in the right arm, tongue, and face. There was no left-sided involvement, no identifiable trigger, and no systemic symptoms. One month after resolution of dysesthesia, she developed true vertigo and was referred for neurologic evaluation.

On examination, she was alert and slightly anxious. Visual acuity and fields were normal, with no diplopia, nystagmus, or internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Pupils were equal and reactive. Cranial nerves were intact except for right-sided facial sensory loss. Motor strength was 5/5 in all limbs, tone and reflexes were normal, and plantar responses were downgoing. Proprioception and cerebellar testing were normal. She had a normal tandem gait but swayed briefly on Romberg testing. She had no significant past medical history, took no medications, and had no vascular risk factors.

Two months after the onset of vertigo, MRI of the brain and cervical spine demonstrated bilateral periventricular T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions, some ovoid and radiating perpendicular to the corpus callosum, and additional lesions in the left medulla and upper cervical cord. 

Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, electrolytes, and thyroid function. Tests for Borrelia, syphilis, HIV, anti-myeloperoxidase, and anti-proteinase 3 were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed an opening pressure of 15 mmHg, normal protein and glucose, and oligoclonal bands detected in CSF but absent in serum.

A 72-year-old man presented with a 3-year history of progressive anorexia, general malaise, and a 15 kg weight loss that left him unable to walk. His medical history was notable only for intestinal volvulus surgery at age 14 years. On admission, he was alert; temperature was 36.9 °C, blood pressure 124/86 mmHg, pulse 60 beats/min. He appeared cachectic (BMI 16.4 kg/m2). Neurologic, respiratory, cardiac, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed:
- Hypoalbuminemia (2.1 g/dL) and low total protein (4.9 g/dL)
- Elevated C-reactive protein (2.75 mg/dL)
- Elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor (1,950 U/mL) and interleukin-6 (20.7 pg/mL)
- Hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL; other values notable for normal LFTs and renal function.

Abdominal CT demonstrated thickening of the small-intestinal mucosa and intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy. Upper endoscopy revealed yellow-white, shaggy mucosa in the duodenum; biopsy specimens showed no specific abnormalities. The patient received intravenous hyperalimentation without improvement. Given the high sIL-2R and IL-6 levels and lymphadenopathy, oral prednisolone (25 mg daily) was initiated, leading to improved appetite and weight gain. He was discharged on day 33. One month later, he lost his appetite again and was readmitted for further evaluation.

A 64-year-old man presented with haematuria and urinary retention after his long-term catheter, placed for benign prostatic hyperplasia, fell out 2 days earlier; he had not passed urine for 24 hours. His history included benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension, treated with ramipril; he was an ex-smoker and did not consume alcohol. On examination he was diffusely tender in the lower abdomen, had an enlarged prostate on digital rectal examination, and a temperature of 37.8 °C. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 179 mg/L, a white-cell count of 8.5×10^9/L with neutrophils of 7.3×10^9/L, urea of 13.9 mmol/L, creatinine of 222 µmol/L, and blood glucose of 14 mmol/L; a subsequent HbA1c measurement was 7.8%. Urine dipstick revealed blood, nitrates, and white cells. Blood cultures were sterile after 5 days; urine culture showed heavy mixed growth without a definitive organism. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis, an incidental 2.7 cm renal cyst, and heterogeneous echogenicities around the bladder consistent with gas. On day 3, CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a thick-walled bladder, a large right-sided bladder diverticulum containing a gas–fluid level with intramural gas, and extraluminal free gas in the pelvis and right paracolic gutter.

An 86-year-old man was brought to the emergency department for abrupt-onset altered mental status, auditory hallucinations, repetition of words and phrases, and intermittent agitation followed by somnolence. His medical history included Alzheimer’s dementia diagnosed one year earlier, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, osteoarthritis, syringomyelia status post laminectomy, and peripheral arterial disease. Home medications were memantine (started 1 month earlier at 5 mg twice daily), metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, and meclizine 12.5 mg every 8 hours as needed.

On arrival, blood pressure was 197/79 mm Hg, heart rate 97 beats/min, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation > 95% on room air. Laboratory testing, including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, lipase level, ethanol level, and drug toxicology, showed no significant abnormalities. An electrocardiogram demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with occasional premature ventricular contractions and a normal QTc interval. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed only chronic microvascular changes and diffuse age-related parenchymal volume loss without acute lesions.

On examination, the patient was alert but oriented only to self, experienced auditory hallucinations, and repeated questions verbatim. There was no nystagmus, tremor, or rigidity. An urgent EEG did not show epileptiform activity. Neurology and psychiatry were consulted, and he was admitted to the intensive care unit for observation.

A 41-year-old Japanese woman with a history of Wilson disease and orthotopic liver transplantation at age 21 presented in January 2018 with several months of insomnia followed by persecutory delusions (“I am being watched”) and auditory hallucinations (“I hear a voice telling me what to do”). She exhibited bizarre behaviors, such as attempting to strip her parents because she believed they were infected. In early March 2018, she was involuntarily hospitalized for psychomotor agitation and psychotic symptoms.

On examination, she had jaundice and bilateral lower-limb edema. Laboratory tests showed WBC 3650/µL, hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, hematocrit 26.1%, platelets 76 000/µL, prothrombin time 19.7 seconds, albumin 2.7 g/dL, total bilirubin 10.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.6 mg/dL, AST 56 U/L, ALT 54 U/L, ALP 1193 U/L, cholinesterase 85 U/L, BUN 20.8 mg/dL, CRP 0.90 mg/dL, serum copper 47 µg/dL (normal 68–128), ceruloplasmin 13 mg/dL (normal 21–37), tacrolimus level <2.0 ng/mL, and mycophenolate mofetil level <0.4 µg/mL. Chest radiography revealed cardiomegaly.

Acute graft rejection due to nonadherence with tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil was diagnosed, and she received two days of methylprednisolone. A psychiatric liaison team administered risperidone up to 4 mg/day orally and intravenous haloperidol for agitation.

Brain MRI showed only a small high-intensity focus in the corpus callosum; there was no evidence of pathological copper deposition. There was no abnormality in copper metabolism, and tacrolimus trough levels had not increased prior to symptom onset and remained low thereafter. No other medical condition or substance use disorder was identified.

Therefore, schizophrenia was suspected, although the duration of psychotic symptoms had not yet met DSM-5 criteria.

A 52-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of microscopic hematuria and a rise in creatinine from a baseline of 59 to 94 µmol/L. Over three months, she had developed a bilateral petechial rash on her lower extremities, intermittent right knee swelling and pain, and a two-year history of subjective fevers and night sweats. A short course of oral prednisone produced transient improvement in her rash and systemic symptoms, but these recurred on tapering. She was restarted on prednisone 30 mg daily one week before nephrology consultation for concern of vasculitis or connective tissue disease.

Her medical history included a left femoral crossover graft (2005), gastroesophageal reflux, dyslipidemia, depression, and at least six months of microscopic hematuria with normal cystoscopy. Medications were rabeprazole, ASA, simvastatin, citalopram, and bupropion. On exam, she had palpable petechiae on her lower extremities and warm moderate effusions in the right knee and ankle; vital signs were normal.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 102 g/L, WBC 11.1×10^9/L, creatinine 94 µmol/L, ESR 115 mm/hr, CRP 94 mg/L, and rheumatoid factor 176 IU/mL. Urinalysis had trace protein, 58 RBCs/HPF with acanthocytes, and 7 WBCs/HPF. ANCA, C3, and C4 were normal. A skin biopsy demonstrated leukocytoclastic vasculitis with dermal capillary IgM and C3 deposition. Knee arthrocentesis was noninfectious and noncrystalline.

Serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, and syphilis were negative; blood cultures were negative. SPEP showed no monoclonal protein; cryoglobulins and anti-CCP were negative. Kappa and lambda light chains were modestly elevated. ANA was weakly positive with RNP 1.1 AI, dsDNA was negative, and lupus anticoagulant was normal. Twenty-four–hour urine protein was 0.32 g. Renal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys.

Because her creatinine and symptoms initially improved on prednisone, biopsy was deferred. Upon prednisone withdrawal, her creatinine rose to 111 µmol/L and symptoms recurred, prompting a renal biopsy. Light microscopy revealed diffuse global mesangial hypercellularity. Immunofluorescence showed trace mesangial IgG and kappa, 1+ IgM, lambda, and C1q, and 2+ C3. Electron microscopy demonstrated mesangial electron-dense deposits. These findings were thought to be consistent with mesangial proliferative lupus nephritis, although her clinical and serologic profile was atypical.

She was treated with prednisone and azathioprine, then mycophenolate mofetil, hydroxychloroquine, and rituximab in various combinations, each time showing creatinine improvement on steroids and relapse on tapering. Given her atypical clinical features and inability to wean prednisone, the lupus diagnosis was reconsidered. Repeat transthoracic echocardiogram, CT of the abdomen and pelvis, and blood cultures showed no infectious focus. She was referred for further infectious evaluation.

A 52-year-old Filipino man was referred for evaluation of progressive shortening of his fingers. Over 30 years ago, he noticed “map-like” hypopigmented patches on both hands and wrists with tingling in cold weather. Over the past 20 years, he observed gradual shortening of his fingers without pain, pruritus, or ulceration. He reported one episode of bluish discoloration of a left finger that resolved spontaneously. One year before presentation, he developed bilateral ankle and foot swelling, a sensation of skin thickening over the extremities, and occasional hand tingling. Three months ago, he noted inversion of his feet causing difficulty walking. He denied systemic symptoms such as fatigue, weight loss, morning stiffness, gastrointestinal or genitourinary complaints. His medical history was notable only for remote burn injuries to his left hand and right arm; family history was negative for similar extremity abnormalities. He quit smoking several years ago and drank alcohol in moderation. For 30 years, he worked as a painter, laborer, and cleaner at construction sites, including a five-month stint at a PVC factory where he cleaned containers and transferred chemicals without gloves.

On examination, he had hypopigmented patches on the hands, wrists, knees, and ankles without telangiectasias or salt-and-pepper changes. Oral aperture was three fingerbreadths without perioral furrowing. Bibasal crackles were heard in the lungs; cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. There was non-pitting edema of the lower extremities. Multiple finger contractures were present. The remaining fingers showed no skin thickening or sclerodactyly. Sensation was reduced by 50% up to the knees, and there was muscle atrophy of the hands.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 83 g/L, white blood cell count 13.3 × 10^9/L (85% neutrophils), platelets 173 × 10^9/L, creatinine 86.7 μmol/L, BUN 4.7 mmol/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, potassium 2.44 mmol/L. Chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion, and right lower-lobe infiltrates. Chest CT confirmed bilateral pneumonia with right loculated pleural effusion and emphysematous and bronchiectatic changes. Renal ultrasound indicated chronic kidney disease. Echocardiography demonstrated a dilated cardiomyopathy (EF 38%) and moderate pulmonary hypertension. Radiographs of the hands revealed complete resorption of distal phalanges of multiple digits, fusion of phalanges, cortical sclerosis, and subchondral cystic lucencies. Foot films showed lytic and erosive changes of the metatarsals and tarsal bones.

A 30-year-old right-hand–dominant Polynesian man (BMI 42.6) with a history of crystal-proven gout and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presented with progressive right forearm, hand, and shoulder swelling and pain. Four days after two days of light weight exercise, he noted moderate forearm swelling and pain unrelieved by his usual oral anti-inflammatories. Four days later, during a long car trip, his right shoulder pain and forearm/hand swelling worsened. In the emergency department he received IV ketorolac, oral prednisone, and tramadol. The next morning he was admitted for presumed severe acute gout flare and emerging compartment syndrome of the right forearm and hand.

He was afebrile, blood pressure 140/73 mm Hg, heart rate 89 bpm. Examination showed tense volar forearm compartments, reduced finger sensation, decreased capillary refill, and severe pain with passive finger stretch, with overlying erythema suggestive of cellulitis.

Laboratory studies revealed serum uric acid 7.7 mg/dL, leukocytosis (13 800/μL), normal initial blood glucose (84 mg/dL), and mildly elevated CK (245 U/L). Tests for rheumatoid factor, HIV, and blood toxicology were negative. CT of the right upper extremity demonstrated fluid in the olecranon bursa and elbow joint; MRI of the shoulder was unremarkable. Aspiration of the elbow joint yielded monosodium urate crystals and a white-cell count of 91 650/mm3; wrist aspiration showed calcium pyrophosphate crystals with no bacterial growth. CT angiogram and Doppler ultrasound excluded vascular pathology.

With clinical signs of compartment syndrome and compartment pressures of 20–24 mm Hg in the volar forearm and 45–48 mm Hg in the carpal tunnel and palm, urgent fasciotomies of the volar compartments and carpal tunnel were performed. Intraoperatively the volar forearm muscles were tense, bulging, and contractile; there was no necrosis, pus, or odor. Small 0.25–0.5 mm tophi were noted in the synovial sheaths of the flexor tendons. Wounds were dressed with negative-pressure therapy.

A 28-year-old woman with Turner syndrome (karyotype 45,X/46,X,+mar), diagnosed at age 16 for amenorrhea, was referred after abnormal brain MRI. She denied alcohol, tobacco, or drug use and had no family history of neurologic disease. On arrival, her temperature was normal, blood pressure 180/130 mm Hg, and heart rate 89 bpm. She was obese (BMI 27.3 kg/m2). Neurologic examination showed no focal deficits. She had had sudden-onset severe headache with a recorded blood pressure of 240/140 mm Hg. Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. Diffusion-weighted MRI demonstrated restricted diffusion in multiple lesions involving different vascular territories. Cerebral MRA and carotid ultrasound revealed no extracranial or intracranial arterial stenosis. Chest radiograph and ECG were normal. Laboratory tests showed a fasting glucose of 219 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1C 11.0%, and LDL cholesterol 189 mg/dL.

A 66-year-old man with sleep apnoea and a history of junctional tachycardia ablation presented with acute dyspnoea shortly after undergoing urgent percutaneous coronary intervention for an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. His medications included aspirin, clopidogrel, bisoprolol, atorvastatin, and ramipril. Initial examination prior to PCI was unremarkable, and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed no valvular abnormalities. Coronary angiography revealed a complete occlusion of the distal right coronary artery, which was stented without difficulty, despite a shepherd’s crook configuration of the proximal vessel.

Soon after the procedure, he developed shortness of breath and a short decrescendo early diastolic aortic murmur. NT-pro–brain natriuretic peptide was 1784 pg/mL. Chest radiograph was normal, and CT angiography excluded dissection and pulmonary embolism. Repeat TTE showed new moderate-to-severe aortic regurgitation (vena contracta 0.6 cm; jet >50% of outflow tract; pressure half-time 340 ms) with an abnormal mobile structure on the aortic valve. Left ventricular ejection fraction was 45% with inferior wall hypokinesis.

Transoesophageal echocardiography identified a 17 mm fine, filamentous mobile lesion attached to the non-coronary cusp, causing a coaptation defect and severe eccentric regurgitant jet. The valve was tricuspid without root dilation. There was no clinical or laboratory evidence of infective endocarditis. After multidisciplinary discussion, the patient was referred for surgical evaluation.

A 44-year-old man presented in December 2020 with acute onset of fever and rash two days after completing a 14-day home isolation for RT-PCR–confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, during which he had remained asymptomatic. He described mild, intermittent fevers with chills and developed a non-blanching, non-pruritic, maculopapular rash on his abdomen that rapidly desquamated into annular plaques with satellite lesions. He reported extreme fatigue, several episodes of vomiting and diarrhea without abdominal pain, and denied headache, myalgia, arthralgia, bleeding, mucosal involvement, or any respiratory symptoms.

On arrival, he was hypotensive (84/52 mmHg), tachycardic (137 beats/min), and febrile (38.2 °C). The lower extremities were cool, distal pulses were undetectable, and capillary refill was prolonged. His respiratory rate was 20 breaths/min with oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. Cardiac auscultation revealed tachycardia with distant heart sounds; lung fields were clear. Neurologic examination was normal.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with a left shift, neutrophil predominance, and anemia; inflammatory markers were markedly elevated (see Table 1). A chest radiograph and electrocardiogram were obtained. He received bolus intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics but developed acute pulmonary edema during resuscitation, prompting initiation of inotropic support and transfer to the ICU with noninvasive ventilatory assistance. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed global left ventricular hypokinesia, moderate systolic dysfunction, dilation of all four chambers, mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, pericardial effusion, and an ejection fraction below 30%.

A 37-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive skin thickening, initially on his torso and then spreading diffusely, accompanied by a 20–30-lb weight loss and fatigue. He denied Raynaud’s phenomenon, dyspnea, or wheezing. His blood pressure at presentation was 100–110 mmHg systolic, with a serum creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL. He had a history of treated hepatitis B without active disease.

Serologic studies showed a negative antinuclear antibody, negative anti–Smith and anti–ribonucleoprotein antibodies, and low-level anti–topoisomerase I (3–4 AU/mL). Nailfold capillaroscopy was suggestive of systemic sclerosis, and a skin biopsy was read as suspicious for morphea versus systemic sclerosis. Echocardiography revealed no pulmonary hypertension or pericardial effusion. He was started on mycophenolate mofetil.

An IgG λ monoclonal protein of 1.1 g/dL was detected. Bone marrow biopsy showed 10% λ-restricted plasma cells without high-risk cytogenetics besides 1q and 5q gains, monosomy 13, and 14q deletions. Three months after presentation, for unclear reasons, he was started on high-dose prednisone (60 mg daily). Shortly thereafter, his systolic blood pressure increased to 140–150 mmHg and serum creatinine rose to 1.1 mg/dL. He developed blurry vision; ophthalmologic examination revealed cotton-wool spots. He received two intravitreal injections of bevacizumab (1.25 mg each).

One week after the injections, he was admitted with severe hypertension (systolic blood pressures 200–220 mmHg), a rise in serum creatinine to 1.4 mg/dL, and new proteinuria (urine protein-creatinine ratio 1 g/g). Renal ultrasound with Doppler showed normal-sized kidneys and no evidence of renal artery stenosis. Given the abrupt hypertension, worsening renal function, proteinuria, recent corticosteroid exposure, and intravitreal VEGF blockade, scleroderma renal crisis was suspected, and a complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy related to VEGF inhibition could not be ruled out. A renal biopsy was planned after blood pressure control.

A 65-year-old man was brought to the emergency department because of progressive fatigue, diffuse myalgia, and altered mental status. His medical history included chronic ischemic heart disease status post coronary-artery bypass grafting, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease.  

On arrival, he reported several days of worsening leg and shoulder pain with an inability to walk independently. Vital signs showed hypotension, and an electrocardiogram revealed atrial fibrillation, a left bundle-branch block, ST-segment depression, and peaked, high T waves. Laboratory tests demonstrated a troponin T level of 532 ng/L (normal < 14 ng/L) and NT-proBNP of 5579 ng/L (normal < 125 ng/L). A temporary pacemaker was placed because of bradyarrhythmia.  

Urgent coronary angiography showed severe three-vessel atheromatous disease with an 80% stenosis in the left anterior descending artery and sub-occlusive lesions in the right coronary artery, which was successfully stented. During the procedure, he developed cardiogenic shock, treated with vasopressors and inotropic support. Arterial blood gas analysis disclosed a metabolic acidosis (pH 7.26) and a serum potassium concentration of 7.5 mmol/L.  

He was admitted to the intensive care unit. Further laboratory results included a creatine phosphokinase level > 22,000 U/L (normal 39–308 U/L), a myoglobin level > 30,000 μg/L (normal < 72 μg/L), aspartate aminotransferase 1406 U/L (normal < 50 U/L), lactate dehydrogenase 1969 U/L (normal 50–250 U/L), blood urea nitrogen 304 mg/dL (normal 10–71 mg/dL), and serum creatinine 6.58 mg/dL (normal 0.67–1.17 mg/dL).

A 78-year-old woman presented with acute vision loss and headache. Her ocular history was notable for pseudophakia in both eyes, dry macular degeneration, and open-angle glaucoma treated chronically with latanoprost 0.005% nightly in both eyes; three weeks earlier she was started on Simbrinza™ (brimonidine 0.1%/brinzolamide 0.1%) twice daily in both eyes. She also had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

On examination, visual acuity was 20/400 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye. Pupils were equally reactive without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressures were 24 mm Hg OD and 23 mm Hg OS. Slit-lamp examination revealed quiet anterior chambers that were shallow in the periphery. Indentation gonioscopy showed closed angles in both eyes. Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrated iridocorneal apposition with 360° choroidal effusions in both eyes. Manifest refraction revealed a myopic shift of 3 diopters in each eye.

A 55-year-old man (160 cm, 65 kg) with hepatitis B–related cirrhosis and previous esophageal varices underwent laparoscopic subsegmental resection of segment 7 for hepatocellular carcinoma under combined general and epidural anesthesia. His postoperative course was complicated by refractory abdominal pain, managed with patient-controlled epidural, morphine infusion, celecoxib, loxoprofen, and tramadol. He was discharged on postoperative day 10 but readmitted for a wound infection, which resolved with antibiotics. On postoperative day 15, he was referred to the pain clinic for severe recurrent upper abdominal pain unrelieved by tramadol and loxoprofen.

At the first pain clinic visit, his Numerical Rating Scale score was 2 at rest and 8 with movement. He described constant aching with posture-induced paroxysms in the right epigastric region. Rotation and lateral bending provoked severe pain, yielding a positive Carnett’s sign. Examination revealed a hypersensitive tender spot with underlying muscle stiffness forming a taut band in the right lateral subcostal area; palpation reproduced radiating pain to the epigastrium. Clinical criteria for a myofascial trigger point were met.

After initial relief with a blind mepivacaine injection into the tender spot, pain recurred 19 days after the first visit. We localized the tender area approximately 5 cm from the nearest port site on the right upper abdomen and performed B-mode ultrasonography with an 11–3 MHz linear probe. Imaging demonstrated a 5 mm diameter hyperechoic spot surrounded by a hypoechoic area within the internal oblique abdominal muscle. The surrounding muscle fibers were continuous with no loss or abrupt discontinuation as seen at port sites, and the echogenic focus lay within the muscle fibers rather than along a vertical nerve path.

A 40-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 2-month history of exertional dyspnea and had New York Heart Association class II symptoms. He had been therapeutically anticoagulated for 5 months for a presumed diagnosis of CTEPH based on imaging at a local hospital. Repeat CT pulmonary angiography showed extensive proximal narrowing of both the right and left pulmonary arteries with concentric soft-tissue thickening, and occlusion of the right upper-lobe and left apical segmental branches. Full blood count and renal function were normal. C-reactive protein was 77 mg/L, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 79 mm/hr. Tests for antinuclear antibodies and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. MRI pulmonary angiography confirmed smooth plaque-like focal intimal thickening in both proximal main pulmonary arteries. Because of concern for pulmonary artery sarcoma, an 18F-FDG PET/CT was performed and showed intermediate uptake in the distal right main pulmonary artery. Right-heart catheterization revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 32 mmHg with a cardiac index of 2.0 L/min/m2.

A 69‐year‐old woman with multiple myeloma complicated by an L4 vertebral fracture began localized radiotherapy and systemic therapy with lenalidomide (25 mg Days 1–21), bortezomib (1.3 mg/m2 Days 1, 4, 8, 11), and dexamethasone (20 mg on scheduled days) in a 28‐day cycle, along with enoxaparin for thromboprophylaxis. Nineteen days after treatment initiation, she presented with a 12‐hour history of right upper‐quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and general fatigue. She denied chest pain, dyspnea, muscle pain, or fever. She reported pruritus since Day 8 and an erythematous, pruritic rash over her chest, abdomen, and back for one week. 

On examination, blood pressure was 114/54 mmHg, heart rate 76 bpm, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Abdominal palpation revealed tenderness in the right hypochondrium with guarding. Skin examination showed an extensive erythematous rash. Cardiorespiratory examination was unremarkable without rales, edema, or elevated jugular venous pressure. 

CT of the abdomen excluded acute intra‐abdominal pathology. Laboratory tests showed C‐reactive protein 47.4 mg/L (normal <5.0), lactate dehydrogenase 718 U/L, creatine kinase 2122 U/L, N‐terminal pro‐BNP 1440 ng/L, and high‐sensitivity troponin T 5.47 µg/L (normal <0.013). Repeat troponin after 1 hour was 5.40 µg/L. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with convex ST elevation in leads I and aVL and reciprocal ST depression in II, III, and aVF. 

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, normal ejection fraction, no regional wall motion abnormalities, and a localized posterolateral pericardial effusion measuring 8 mm without hemodynamic compromise. Global longitudinal strain was subtly reduced in the anterolateral segments.

A 52-year-old woman presented to the emergency department 10 days after receiving a third dose of the Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine with pain in both eyes, numbness in both legs, difficulty walking, and dysuria. She had no prior similar episodes or cognitive impairment. PCR tests were negative for SARS-CoV-2, adenovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and HIV. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed elevated total protein at 101.3 mg/dL but was otherwise unremarkable. A T2-weighted spinal MRI revealed an intramedullary hyperintense lesion extending from T2 to T12. On hospital day 2, muscle strength in both lower extremities deteriorated to the point that no voluntary movements were observed. Brain MRI demonstrated hyperintense lesions in the optic chiasm and optic nerve, and visual evoked potentials showed central conduction delay.

A 72-year-old man was admitted with a 1-day history of right flank pain and massive gross hematuria with clot retention. He was a heavy smoker and denied any history of trauma, recent medical intervention, known urinary stones, bleeding disorders, or use of anticoagulants. On examination, his blood pressure was normal. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal serum biochemistry, and normal coagulation parameters. A rinsing urinary catheter was placed, and the hematuria resolved over the next few days. Ultrasonography of the kidneys and bladder was unremarkable. 

Subsequently, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a small soft-tissue filling defect within the right renal pelvis that did not significantly enhance in the arterial phase and was not associated with dilation of the collecting system. There was no evidence of calculi. 

Urine cytology was negative for malignant cells. Cystoscopy with placement of a right ureteral catheter was performed to obtain selective upper-tract urine cytology and to perform a retrograde pyelogram. Upper-tract cytology was negative, and the retrograde study revealed no filling defect in the right renal pelvis or calyces.

A 40-year-old Nepali woman from the far western region presented with sudden onset left-sided weakness and difficulty speaking for 6 hours. Seven days earlier, she developed moderate-to-high–grade continuous fever without chills, accompanied by headaches, nonbilious vomiting, and generalized weakness. Despite 4 days of over-the-counter treatment, symptoms persisted, and during the last 3 days she developed shortness of breath and cough with mucoid sputum. She denied vision changes, altered mentation, chest pain, abdominal pain, or dysuria.

On examination, she was confused with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14 (E4 V4 M6); temperature 102 °F; blood pressure 80/50 mmHg; heart rate 123/min; and oxygen saturation 78% on room air. She was pale and icteric, with bilateral chest crepitations. Head-to-toe inspection revealed a brownish-black scab on the right buttock. Pupils were equal and reactive; plantar responses were normal; and there was no neck rigidity.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed an acute right frontal lobe parenchymal hemorrhage with vasogenic edema and mild mass effect. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and features of pulmonary edema. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed diffuse gallbladder wall thickening, borderline splenomegaly, and right-sided pleural effusion.

Laboratory studies on admission included: leukocyte count 13,200/µL (neutrophils 88%); hemoglobin 10 g/dL; platelets 460,000/µL; serum creatinine 1.7 mg/dL; total bilirubin 6.2 mg/dL (direct 2.7 mg/dL); AST 228.6 IU/L; ALT 72.3 IU/L; ALP 619.9 IU/L; arterial blood gas pH 7.26, pCO₂ 31 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 15.8 mmol/L, lactate 5.54 mmol/L.

Serological tests for dengue, leptospirosis, and Brucella were negative. Thick and thin blood smears for malaria and PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 were negative. Sputum AFB staining and culture were negative for tuberculosis, and HIV serology was negative.

A 20-year-old woman was referred for constant right proximal thigh pain that had progressed over 8 years. She had no other medical conditions, menarche at age 13, and no family history of bone disease. The pain was worse at night, somewhat relieved by activity and cold baths, and required daily NSAIDs, paracetamol, and weak opioids. She had a leg-length discrepancy managed with shoe inserts and was on sick leave due to her symptoms. At age 11 she had hip joint pain with an ultrasound-guided aspiration revealing sterile fluid; pain resolved. Six months prior, she was hit by a car at knee level, with no fracture diagnosed, after which her thigh pain worsened.

On examination, there were no skin lesions, café au lait spots, erythema, heat, or swelling over the right thigh. Leg lengths were slightly unequal but within normal limits.

Magnetic resonance imaging and PET–CT showed significant increased cortical thickness of the right femoral diaphysis with partial medullary obliteration and an uneven sclerotic surface. A Tc-99m bone scan demonstrated increased uptake in most of the right femoral shaft. Biochemical bone markers, including alkaline phosphatase, were normal. Genetic screening in blood for the GNAS1 R201 mutation and for SQSTM1 mutations was negative. Bone biopsy of the lesion revealed thickened bone trabeculae with preserved lamellar structure, accentuated cement lines, and no fibrosis, inflammation, alcian positivity, malignancy, or neoplasia.

A previously healthy 3-year-old boy presented with a 3-day history of drooping of both upper eyelids and a 2-day history of unsteady gait with sleepiness and reduced activity. He had no seizures, visual blurring, limb weakness, swallowing or breathing difficulties, or bladder dysfunction. On examination, he was alert (GCS 15), with bilateral ptosis; vision, extraocular movements, pupils, light reflexes, and fundoscopy were normal. Other cranial nerves were intact. He had a broad-based ataxic gait and bilateral dysmetria on finger-nose testing. There was no dysarthria, nystagmus, involuntary movements, or Romberg sign. Limb tone and power were normal, tendon reflexes were present, and plantar responses were flexor. There were no signs of fatigability, sensory loss, or meningeal irritation. Vital signs, cardiovascular, and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed normal complete blood count, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, and calcium; ESR was 22 mm in the first hour. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 2 polymorphonuclear cells/mm3 and 20 lymphocytes/mm3, with protein 55 mg/dL and negative oligoclonal bands. Electroencephalogram and noncontrast CT of the brain were normal. MRI of the brain demonstrated high signal intensities in the subcortical white matter of the parietal and occipital lobes, midbrain, cerebellar vermis, right cerebellar hemisphere, and right caudate and lentiform nuclei, without diffusion restriction or contrast enhancement.

A 50-year-old Chinese woman with a 9-month history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) was admitted for fever and relapsing abdominal pain over the same period. Initial SLE had been diagnosed on the basis of fever, recurrent abdominal pain, bloating, leukopenia, positive antinuclear and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies, anti-Smith and anti-RNP antibodies, and polyserositis, and responded to prednisolone and mycophenolate mofetil. As steroids were tapered, she redeveloped fever (38.5°C), abdominal pain, hair loss, dry mouth, and reduced defecation; she denied photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthralgias, or Raynaud’s phenomenon. Examination was notable only for tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Her history included osteoporosis and a tuberculous infection treated with rifampicin and isoniazid for 3 months without relief of abdominal pain. Laboratory studies showed leukopenia (WBC 2.56 × 10^9/L), anemia (hemoglobin 102 g/L), normal ESR, CRP, and procalcitonin, and negative blood cultures. Immunologic tests revealed rheumatoid factor 153 IU/mL, low complement C3 (0.71 g/L), positive ANA (1:320), and positive anti-Smith, anti-dsDNA, and anti-RNP antibodies; a TB-spot test was positive. A PET-CT scan showed no abnormalities. After exclusion of infection, intestinal tuberculosis, and malignancy, SLE-related mesenteric vasculitis and intestinal obstruction were considered. Treatment with methylprednisolone (120 mg/day for 11 days), cyclophosphamide, gastrointestinal decompression, and nutritional support resolved her fever and normalized her WBC count, but her incomplete intestinal obstruction and decreased bowel movements persisted. An abdominal X-ray showed multiple air-fluid levels. Enteroscopy demonstrated a small intestinal ulcer with luminal stenosis. Contrast CT of the small intestine revealed segmental dilatation with wall enhancement and multiple air-fluid levels.

A 54-year-old woman presented in 2023 after discovering a firm, movable, nontender mass in her right breast. She had no systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or dyspnea. She underwent breast-conserving surgery with sentinel lymph node biopsy; pathology showed invasive carcinoma, ER 5%, PR negative, HER2 0+, Ki-67 45%, pT2N0M0, with a close margin (<1 mm at 3–6 o’clock). She received one cycle of docetaxel and then, at our institution, five cycles of docetaxel (120 mg/m2 q3w) plus cyclophosphamide (600 mg/m2 q3w) and pembrolizumab (200 mg q3w). After the fifth cycle, she noted numbness in her hands and edema of her lower limbs, followed by swelling and fibrotic changes of the skin on both lower extremities. On examination, there was bilateral leg skin induration without sclerodactyly, Raynaud’s phenomenon, or dysphagia. Laboratory testing revealed negative antinuclear antibodies. A skin biopsy of the lower leg demonstrated perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and thickened collagen bundles.

A 16-year-old male presented to the emergency department alone with an initial complaint of “homelessness.” Shortly after arrival, he collapsed and had a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure that lasted approximately five minutes. He did not meet criteria for status epilepticus. On examination, there was blood in his mouth without any visible trauma, and his oxygen saturation was 72% on room air. He was promptly intubated for airway protection, and approximately 10 mL of blood was suctioned from the endotracheal tube. 

Laboratory studies on admission showed: WBC 8300 K/µL, hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, platelets 222 K/µL, CRP < 0.5 mg/dL, ESR 9 mm/hr, PT 14.4 sec, PTT 28 sec, INR 1.1. Serum ANA, ANCA, and anti-GBM antibodies were all negative. Blood and sputum cultures remained negative. A transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.

Chest radiography demonstrated diffuse hazy opacities and right upper lobe partial atelectasis. Chest CT revealed bilateral, diffuse ground-glass opacities, more pronounced in the apices with peripheral sparing, and consolidation in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe. Based on these imaging findings, the differential diagnosis included pulmonary edema and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH).

Additional history revealed that he had been diagnosed with a seizure disorder two years earlier and was taking levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. Five months ago, he had a similar episode of hemoptysis (5–10 mL) immediately following a seizure that required hospitalization. At that time, CT of the chest showed similar ground-glass opacities, bronchoscopy revealed frank blood in the airways, and bronchoalveolar lavage showed no hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Rheumatologic evaluation was notable only for an ANA titer of 1:160 and a low-positive anticardiolipin IgM (20 MPL), with normal complement levels; this was deemed clinically insignificant given the absence of systemic autoimmune features. On the current admission, repeat ANA testing was normal.

A 25-year-old previously healthy man was brought to the emergency department after becoming unconscious at home; a capillary glucose measurement was <2 mmol/L. He recovered with intravenous dextrose infusion and was admitted for further evaluation. Over the preceding 2 months, he had recurrent episodes of palpitations, dizziness, light-headedness, and sweating, often late after meals or after prolonged fasting; capillary glucose values had reached as low as 3.5 mmol/L and improved with dextrose. He denied seizures. Symptoms transiently improved with daily high-dose oral dexamethasone but recurred after discontinuation. He also reported unquantified weight gain and 1 month of erectile dysfunction. He had no family history of insulinoma or diabetes and denied exogenous insulin use. He admitted to using injectable anabolic steroids, growth hormone, oral amino acids, and fat-burner supplements for bodybuilding over the previous 2 months. 

On admission, weight was 66 kg, height 170 cm, BMI 22.8 kg/m2, blood pressure 125/75 mm Hg, pulse 65 beats/min. Examination was unremarkable.

After 24 hours of a supervised 72-hour fast, he developed neuroglycopenic symptoms with a capillary glucose of 2.5 mmol/L. Laboratory evaluation during hypoglycaemia showed: serum insulin >301 µIU/mL, C-peptide 681 pmol/L, proinsulin 2.7 pmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 27.8 µmol/L, and anti-insulin antibody titer >100 IU/mL. Full blood count, liver, renal, and thyroid function tests were normal. ACTH and random morning cortisol levels were normal. MRI of the abdomen (including the pancreas) and the sella turcica showed no abnormalities.

A 32-year-old man, a US service member, was referred for chronic neuropsychiatric and vestibular symptoms years after deployment to East Africa. Two weeks after starting mefloquine 250 mg weekly for malaria prophylaxis, he developed anxiety and vivid dreams, progressing over two months to disequilibrium and confusion. He continued mefloquine for six months; four months into deployment he experienced enemy gunfire but reported no change in symptoms after this trauma. On return, he had emotional lability (anger, irritability), difficulty concentrating, anhedonia, short-term memory loss, word-finding difficulty, persistent “sea legs,” and episodic vertigo (4–5 times daily, 20–30 min), relieved by eye closure, without autonomic symptoms. He also had constant “spinning” dizziness, falls, insomnia with vivid dreams and nightmares, and daily headaches without aura or photophobia. He denied significant environmental exposures, illicit drugs, or head trauma; alcohol use occurred during deployment but was later limited.

He was diagnosed with anxiety and PTSD by psychiatry and treated with prazosin, clonazepam, lorazepam, venlafaxine, diazepam, clonidine, and psychotherapy, with partial improvement in mood but persistent vestibular and sleep symptoms. Physical examination showed mild right cervical lymphadenopathy and balance loss on rising and tandem gait; neurologic exam was otherwise normal.

Laboratory studies were notable for negative infectious and heavy metal panels, normal inflammatory markers, and normal endocrine and tumor markers. Neck ultrasound–guided lymph node biopsy showed benign reactive tissue. MRI of the brain and internal auditory canals were unremarkable. Vestibular evaluation demonstrated hyperactive vestibulo-ocular reflex gains and abnormally low phase on rotary chair testing, consistent with a central vestibulopathy.

An 8-month-old child presented with progressive head enlargement since birth, global developmental delay (developmental age equivalent to 3 months), and cranial bruits. The occipitofrontal circumference was 54 cm (normal 43–45 cm). Brain MRI showed a well-circumscribed, markedly T2-hypointense midline lesion dorsal to the third ventricle with aqueductal obstruction, resulting in dilation of the lateral and third ventricles and a normal fourth ventricle. Digital subtraction angiography confirmed a mural type vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation with feeders from both posterior cerebral arteries and the left anterior cerebral artery. The child underwent transarterial embolisation via Onyx injection into the posteromedial choroidal branches of the right posterior cerebral artery, achieving occlusion of the venous sac. On day 3 post-embolisation MRI showed minimal reduction in sac size, mild peripheral rim enhancement, and no internal restricted diffusion. One-month follow-up MRI demonstrated a residual aneurysmal sac with thick peripheral mural enhancement, marked restricted diffusion, and persistent hydrocephalus.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of worsening generalized abdominal pain and distension, accompanied by a 17-kg weight loss over 5 months. She reported no fever, cough, hemoptysis, or night sweats and had no prior history of tuberculosis or known TB contacts. An ultrasound at an outside hospital suggested ovarian malignancy with septations and irregularities.

On examination, vital signs were normal. The chest was clear; there was moderate ascites without peripheral edema. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL (low MCV), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 95 mm/h, normal AST and ALT, and reduced serum albumin. A CA-125 level drawn 7 days later was 792.1 U/mL.

Two days after admission, 540 mL of serous ascitic fluid was removed. Analysis revealed a lymphocyte-predominant exudate (300 cells/mm3; SAAG 0.98 g/dL), with no organisms on culture or Gram stain, negative cytology for malignant cells, and a negative Gene Xpert test for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The ascitic fluid adenosine deaminase level was 54.6 IU/L.

An initial chest radiograph showed clear lung fields with minimal left pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated diffuse peritoneal thickening, diffuse small-bowel wall thickening, multiple non-specific retroperitoneal lymph nodes (average 1.2 cm), minimal pelvic and perihepatic fluid, and otherwise unremarkable solid organs.

Patient is a 40-year-old man with a history of reactive arthritis, Graves’ disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, mitral valve prolapse, and Gilbert’s disease who presented with one month of progressive jaundice, fatigue, lightheadedness, and exertional dyspnea. He described dark urine and dark brown to black stools. He denied fevers, chills, or recent transfusions and had no history of hepatitis, alcohol or intravenous drug use. His medications included etanercept, methimazole, niacin, and aspirin; he had discontinued metformin and pioglitazone more than one month before symptom onset. Family history was notable for autoimmune hemolytic anemia in his mother and anemia of unknown cause in his maternal grandmother. On examination, he was jaundiced with scleral icterus; vital signs showed heart rate 102 beats per minute and normal blood pressure, respiratory rate, and temperature. There was no lymphadenopathy. The thyroid gland was non-tender without enlargement or exophthalmos. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed mild hepatomegaly without splenomegaly. A vesiculobullous rash was present on the plantar surface of the right foot. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 5.8 g/dL, hematocrit 18.7%, MCV 107.5 fL, reticulocyte count 23.4%, total bilirubin 13.6 mg/dL (direct 0.6 mg/dL), LDH 369 U/L, and undetectable haptoglobin. Hepatitis serologies, antinuclear antibody, cold agglutinins, cryoglobulins, and HIV were negative. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Peripheral smear showed spherocytes and bite cells without schistocytes. Direct antiglobulin test was positive for IgG and negative for C3; indirect antiglobulin test was negative. G6PD level and thyroid-stimulating hormone were normal. Lumbar spine radiographs showed sacroiliac joint ankylosis. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed probable anterior mediastinal enlargement, mild splenomegaly, and multiple small hypodensities in the liver and kidneys.

A 24-year-old Hispanic man was brought to the emergency department after a witnessed tonic–clonic seizure with urinary incontinence, which resolved after intravenous lorazepam. He had a remote history of seizures but was not on antiepileptic medications. On arrival he was postictal, afebrile, tachycardic (124 bpm), and had a blood pressure of 144/66 mmHg. Initial laboratory studies showed a lactate level of 17 mmol/L that normalized rapidly. A routine urine toxicology screen was positive for cannabinoids and benzodiazepines and negative for cocaine, phencyclidine, opiates, and amphetamines.

On hospital day 1, he developed abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, and progressive agitation with confusion. His serum lipase was normal, but the serum creatinine rose from 1.4 mg/dL on admission to 4.3 mg/dL and continued to increase. Several hours later, he became hypoxic with an arterial oxygen saturation of 70%, febrile to 38.9°C, tachycardic at 140 bpm, and hypertensive at 163/104 mmHg. He failed a trial of noninvasive ventilation and was intubated. A chest radiograph showed bilateral alveolar infiltrates. Despite high–fractional inspired oxygen, his oxygenation improved only with high positive end-expiratory pressure.

Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics were started. Bronchoscopy revealed normal airways and clear secretions; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was obtained. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30% with global wall-motion abnormalities, suggesting cardiac dysfunction and fluid overload as contributors to his respiratory failure. The causes of his acute kidney injury and congestive heart failure remained unclear. He underwent three sessions of hemodialysis, after which his oxygenation, urine output, and creatinine level improved. He was extubated on hospital day 8.

A 54-year-old Caucasian woman presented with 5 days of nausea, vomiting, and fatigue.
