She reported a 1-month history of poor appetite, fatigue, 6-kg unintentional weight loss, occasional vague abdominal pain, and recent tanning of her skin. Her medical history was notable for 17 years of hypothyroidism, initially well-controlled on levothyroxine until she switched to animal thyroid extract several months earlier. One week before presentation, she began trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) 160 mg twice daily for a sinus infection.

On examination, she appeared ill and dehydrated. Supine blood pressure was 131/80 mm Hg with heart rate 81/min; standing blood pressure was 107/67 mm Hg with heart rate 96/min. Skin and mucous membranes were dry, capillary refill was 3 seconds, and there was mild epigastric tenderness without guarding. Neurologic examination was normal.

Laboratory studies revealed sodium 101 mmol/L, chloride 73 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, CO2 16 mmol/L, BUN 20 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, and normal liver function tests, calcium, phosphorus, glucose, albumin, and lipid panel. Plasma osmolality was 225 mOsm/kg (normal 275–295), urine sodium 128 mmol/L, and urine osmolality 128 mOsm/kg. Hyperglycemia and other causes of nonhypotonic hyponatremia were excluded. She was diagnosed with hypotonic hypovolemic hyponatremia with elevated urine sodium and osmolality and no history of diuretic use. According to the diagnostic algorithm, adrenal insufficiency was considered and adrenal function tests were ordered.

A 58-year-old man with a 12-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and poor glycemic control presented four years ago with involuntary, irregular movements of the right upper and lower limbs two weeks after a fall. At that time, his blood glucose level was 712 mg/dL. A noncontrast CT scan of the brain showed no acute abnormalities. Brain MRI on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences demonstrated a tiny hyperintense lesion in the left basal ganglion. His hemichorea resolved spontaneously the next day, and he had no residual neurologic deficits.

Four years later, he returned with a two-week history of involuntary movements involving his right upper limb and jaw, which abated during sleep. Neurologic examination revealed normal strength and sensation in all extremities. Laboratory studies showed a blood glucose level of 671 mg/dL without ketoacidosis, a normal serum creatinine concentration, and an HbA1c of 17.3%. A CT scan of the brain demonstrated increased density in the left basal ganglia. Subsequent MRI revealed increased signal intensity in the left basal ganglion on T1-weighted imaging.

A 71-year-old normotensive man with a 50–pack-year smoking history was referred by his primary care physician for severe hyponatremia (serum sodium, 117 mMol/L). He reported no active complaints or neurological symptoms. On examination, he appeared euvolemic, had feminine facial features, and was notably short (height, 149 cm). Blood pressure was 131/70 mmHg. Initial laboratory studies showed mild metabolic acidosis (serum bicarbonate, 19 mEq/L), normal potassium, BUN 13.1 mg/dL, creatinine 1.27 mg/dL, and GFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m2. Serum osmolality was 245 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality, 309 mOsm/kg; and urine sodium, 68 mEq/L. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest was obtained and ruled out lung malignancy as a source of ectopic ADH.

A 53-year-old man presented with facial swelling. A chest radiograph showed a large mass projecting over the right lung field. CT of the chest demonstrated an enormous anterior mediastinal mass contiguous with the posterior sternum and right ribs, occluding the superior vena cava and compressing the heart. Routine blood tests, tumor markers, and acetylcholine receptor antibodies were all normal or negative. Bronchoscopic biopsy revealed features of a carcinoid tumor. 

He underwent en bloc excision of the mass, including resection of the superior vena cava with graft insertion, resection of the right phrenic nerve, and diaphragm plication. Histologic examination identified an atypical carcinoid of the thymus (intermediate-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma), with invasion into fat, pleura, lung lymphatics, and metastases in a hilar node and a cervical thymic node.

One month postoperatively, chest CT showed poststernotomy changes, a right basal fluid-filled cyst, bilateral atelectasis, and pleural thickening. An I-123 MIBG scan was negative for residual or recurrent disease. One year later, follow-up CT revealed no mediastinal recurrence, persistent linear atelectasis in both lower lobes, and elevated right hemidiaphragm. A bone scan showed increased uptake in the posterior arch of the right eighth rib. 

To further evaluate his status, a somatostatin receptor scintigraphy with In-111-DTPA-D-Phe^1-pentetreotide was performed. The scan demonstrated an area of abnormally increased radiotracer concentration in the mediastinum, raising the question of residual tumor, recurrence, or an inflammatory process.

A 72-year-old man presented for routine follow-up of sigmoid colon cancer. Two years earlier, he had undergone laparoscopic sigmoidectomy for a pStage I, moderately differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma with submucosal and venous invasion. His father died of gastric cancer. 

He was asymptomatic, with no abdominal pain, palpable masses, or lymphadenopathy on examination. Laboratory studies showed:
- Lactate dehydrogenase 239 U/L (elevated)
- Creatinine 1.14 mg/dL (elevated)
- Carbohydrate antigen 19-9 41 U/mL (elevated)
- Other serum biochemistry and tumor markers within normal limits
- Urine cytology: no atypical cells (class II)

Enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a 30 × 13.7 mm soft-tissue mass involving the left ureter at the level of the common iliac bifurcation; the lesion had grown from 16.7 × 10.3 mm over 17 months. There was no hydronephrosis or lymphadenopathy. FDG-PET–CT showed focal uptake in the same region (SUVmax 8.93) and no other abnormal accumulations. Ureterography and colonoscopy were unremarkable.

Given the slow growth and significant FDG uptake, concern arose for lymph node recurrence or peritoneal seeding of colon cancer, and a decision was made to proceed with laparoscopic excisional biopsy of the mass.

A 4-year-old boy was evaluated for a 1-year history of a slowly enlarging mass in the right cheek. He reported no pain, tenderness, dysphagia, dysphonia, dyspnea, trauma, or systemic symptoms. No relevant medical, family, or psychosocial history was noted.

On examination, there was a 3 × 2 × 1 cm firm, non-tender, non-fluctuant, non-pulsatile mass on the right cheek, extending from the right oral commissure to the pterygomandibular raphe. The overlying mucosa was normal in color, margins were distinct, and the lesion was freely mobile between the buccal mucosa and skin. Aspiration yielded no fluid. No submandibular or submental lymphadenopathy was present.

Ultrasonography confirmed the presence of a soft-tissue mass. Contrast-enhanced CT of the right cheek demonstrated a well-defined, hypodense lesion within the muscle layer. Complete blood count and metabolic panel were within normal limits.

A 5-year-old boy was brought with a 40-day history of pain, swelling, and redness in both legs. He had been treated 30 days earlier elsewhere with a 10-day course of oral antibiotics for fever. He had no history of chronic illness or trauma. On examination, both legs showed swelling, erythema, warmth, and purulent discharge from the proximal tibiae. Vital signs were within normal limits except for mild tachycardia. Laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 15,640/mm3, C-reactive protein 5.29 μg/mL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 63 mm/h. Serologic tests for Brucella and Salmonella and purified protein derivative tests for tuberculosis, previously negative twice, were again negative; chest radiograph was normal. Radiographs of both tibiae showed cortical destruction and periosteal reaction at the proximal tibiae and distal left tibia. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated bone-marrow edema throughout both tibiae, purulent debris within the medullary canals and metaphyses, and adjacent pyomyositis. Radionuclide bone scanning revealed increased technetium uptake in the metaphyses of both tibiae.

A 26-year-old Caucasian man with a history of diabetes mellitus presented with a two-month history of diffuse headache, progressive nausea, and vomiting. He denied fever, chills, or photophobia. He was born in Mexico and had lived in California for eight years. On examination, his temperature was 37 °C; he had mild neck stiffness, but neurologic and ophthalmologic examinations were otherwise normal. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 6500/mm3 (75% neutrophils, 15% lymphocytes, 8% monocytes), serum glucose of 90 mg/dL, and normal electrolytes and liver–renal function tests. Noncontrast head CT revealed dilated lateral and third ventricles consistent with hydrocephalus. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 400 mmHg, 330 white blood cells/mm3 (14% neutrophils, 45% lymphocytes, 38% monocytes, 3% eosinophils), protein 84 mg/dL, glucose 43 mg/dL, and 3 red blood cells/mm3. Gram stain and India ink of cerebrospinal fluid were negative, and bacterial, viral, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures were negative. Empiric antimycobacterial therapy was initiated for presumed tuberculous meningitis. MRI of the brain demonstrated hydrocephalus with dilation of the lateral and third ventricles, stenosis of the cerebral aqueduct, absence of meningeal enhancement, and a subtle cystic area in the region of the aqueduct.

An 81-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of a palpable left upper-quadrant mass, dull pain, anorexia, and 5-kg weight loss. His medical history included hypertension and chronic kidney disease. On examination, temperature was 36.7 °C; there was an elastic, soft mass in the left upper quadrant without tenderness and no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, CRP 8.39 mg/dL, creatinine 1.94 mg/dL, BUN 41.6 mg/dL, and elevated interleukin-2 receptor at 2420 U/mL; tumor markers were within normal limits. Plain abdominal CT revealed a 13 × 12 × 8 cm irregular mass arising from the transverse colon, abutting the pancreas and stomach, with mildly enlarged peritumoral lymph nodes; no upstream dilation was noted.

On hospital day 6, colonoscopy showed a circumferential ulcer with thick slough at the splenic flexure and marked mucosal thickening; the lumen was narrowed but not obstructed. Initial biopsy specimens showed only mucosal erosion with moderate inflammatory cell infiltration and regenerative epithelial changes. Surgical exploration was recommended, but the patient sought a second opinion. Thirty-six days after initial CT, repeat CT showed spontaneous regression of the mass and resolution of lymphadenopathy. On day 41, repeat colonoscopy demonstrated a smaller ulcer, improved inflammation, but persistent 30 mm of luminal narrowing with scarring. Biopsy of the periphery revealed granulation tissue with marked infiltration of small lymphocytes, plasma cells, histiocytes, and medium-sized atypical cells; immunohistochemistry showed CD20-positive B cells, some of which were EBER-1–positive on in situ hybridization, suggesting a high likelihood of Epstein–Barr virus–positive mucocutaneous ulcer.

A previously healthy 5‐year‐old girl presented with 9 hours of intermittent, moderate–severity epigastric pain radiating to the right lower quadrant. The pain was unchanged by position and was associated with multiple episodes of nonbloody vomiting. She was afebrile, had normal urination and bowel movements, and reported a similar, self‐limited episode 1 month earlier.

On examination, she was alert, without signs of systemic infection. Abdominal palpation elicited tenderness in the epigastrium; there was no guarding or rebound. Murphy’s sign was positive, and there was no jaundice.

Laboratory studies showed normal hepatic and biliary function tests and an elevated C-reactive protein level of 30.2 mg/L. A supine abdominal radiograph was unremarkable.

Initial abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an enlarged gallbladder (54 × 34 mm) with a 3.2 mm wall thickness, pericholecystic fluid, increased pericholecystic fat, and no gallstones or intraluminal nodules. On repeat ultrasound 24 hours later, the gallbladder measured 53 × 33 mm with a 3.1 mm wall, lacked vascular flow, contained biliary sludge, and showed a cone-shaped hypoechoic structure at the neck; the fundus was displaced to the left of its fossa and moved with patient repositioning.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 53.5 × 22.8 × 31.5 mm gallbladder with an irregular, poorly enhancing wall, an intraluminal hyperdense area suggestive of hemorrhage, a 3 mm hyperdense nodule, fundus deviation to the left of the gallbladder bed, pericholecystic fluid and fat stranding, and focal hepatic perfusion abnormalities.

An 81-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on warfarin, heart failure with moderately reduced ejection fraction, coronary artery disease status post–coronary artery bypass graft, pulmonary hypertension, severe tricuspid regurgitation, obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a thoracic aortic aneurysm presented with one day of numerous grossly bright-red bloody bowel movements. He reported epigastric discomfort that had resolved and denied dyschezia, hematemesis, or lightheadedness. His last colonoscopy was 16 years earlier.

On examination, he was afebrile, blood pressure 101/63 mmHg, heart rate 73 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 90% on home 3 L/min oxygen. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Digital rectal examination revealed bright-red blood and a positive stool guaiac test. He had 3+ pitting edema of the lower extremities.

Laboratory tests showed an international normalized ratio of 3.1, creatinine 1.37 mg/dL (baseline 1.1–1.3), and hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed no source of gastrointestinal bleeding. Intravenous vitamin K was given, but he continued to have hematochezia.

On hospital day 2, he developed small-volume hemoptysis and hematemesis while remaining hemodynamically stable, with rising oxygen requirements to 4–6 L/min. Chest imaging demonstrated a new focal opacity in the left lower lobe, suspicious for pulmonary hemorrhage. Bronchoscopy revealed old blood in the left lower lobe without an identifiable bleeding source. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed erosive gastropathy in the gastric body and antrum, with no active bleeding lesions.

A 56-year-old Puerto Rican man with untreated HIV infection and hypertension presented with 3 months of left upper jaw swelling and pain, difficulty swallowing, a 9-kg weight loss, and nonproductive cough. On examination, temperature was 97.8°F, blood pressure 147/95 mm Hg, heart rate 116/min, and respiratory rate 16/min. He had oral thrush, palpable cervical lymph nodes, a mass in the posterior left maxillary region, and a generalized maculopapular rash on the upper chest and back. Laboratory studies showed an HIV viral load of 162 500 copies/mL and a CD4 count of 27 cells/μL. MRI of the brain revealed a 3.9 × 5.8 × 4.3 cm soft-tissue mass in the posterior left maxilla with erosion into the maxillary sinus. Biopsy of this mass demonstrated sheets of granulomatous tissue with macrophages containing well-demarcated fungal spores. Chest CT revealed hilar lymphadenopathy and bilateral adrenal enlargement (left, 4.8 × 3.7 cm; right, 4.7 × 2.3 cm). Laboratory testing showed hyponatremia (serum sodium 126 mEq/L) and mild hyperkalemia (serum potassium 4.9 mEq/L). A 250-μg cosyntropin stimulation test yielded a baseline cortisol of 7 μg/dL, an adrenocorticotrophic hormone level of 86 pg/mL, and a 60-minute cortisol of 9 μg/dL, consistent with primary adrenal insufficiency. Twenty-one-hydroxylase antibody levels were undetectable.

A 68-year-old woman presented with a dry cough of more than 1 month’s duration, associated with dyspnea, fever, chills, myalgia, and intermittent diarrhea. She had type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and a history of COVID-19 diagnosed by PCR 40 days earlier that required hospitalization and treatment with antipyretics, corticosteroids, anticoagulants, and intravenous fluids. She denied known exposure to tuberculosis. On examination, she had crackles in the right lung, an oxygen saturation of 80% on ambient air, a blood pressure of 118/80 mm Hg, and a pulse rate of 97 beats per minute. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 33 000/mm3 and a C-reactive protein level of 194 mg/dl. A chest radiograph demonstrated a cavitated density in the right upper lobe. Computed tomography of the thorax revealed bilateral diffuse parenchymal densities, two cavities in the right lung (one in the right upper lobe and one in the right lower lobe), and residual ground-glass opacities.

A 36-year-old woman with no prior liver disease presented in August 2008 with a 5-day history of constant, sharp right upper quadrant abdominal pain associated with nausea and fatigue but no vomiting. Initial labs showed an ALT of 42 IU/L. Right upper quadrant ultrasound demonstrated hepatomegaly and steatosis. Two weeks later she returned with worsening abdominal pain, low-grade fevers, nausea, and vomiting. MRI of the abdomen revealed a 2 cm enhancing lesion in the right hepatic lobe. Fine-needle biopsy showed a nonspecific mixed inflammatory infiltrate and steatohepatitis without evidence of malignancy; fungal and mycobacterial cultures were negative, and she was discharged without treatment.

Two months later she presented again with worsening right upper quadrant pain and fever. Abdominal CT revealed a 4.8 × 4.7 cm mass in the right hepatic lobe suspicious for malignancy, prompting a partial right hepatectomy. Histopathology revealed florid necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with pseudotumor formation; immunohistochemical stains for mycobacteria, fungal organisms, and cytomegalovirus were negative. Her symptoms initially resolved.

In April 2009, she experienced recurrent right upper quadrant pain with low-grade fevers. An extensive evaluation—including serologies for acute viral hepatitis, toxoplasmosis, HIV, Entamoeba histolytica, Borrelia burgdorferi, Bartonella spp.; testing for urinary Histoplasma and Blastomyces antigens and cryptococcal antigens; and tuberculin skin testing with Quantiferon—was entirely negative. A random liver biopsy showed mild steatosis and nonspecific chronic inflammation; special stains and cultures remained negative.

In July 2009, she again developed right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and fevers up to 102.4 °F. CT of the abdomen revealed multiple low-attenuation lesions in both hepatic lobes. On transfer, she was afebrile with RUQ tenderness; labs showed AST 93 IU/L, ALT 74 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 193 IU/L, and total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL. Blood, urine, and stool cultures were negative. ANA was 1:40 and anti-mitochondrial antibody was negative. On hospital day 3 she developed a fever of 101.1 °F. A percutaneous liver biopsy revealed extensive granulomatous hepatitis with occasional fibrin rings on a background of mixed micro- and macrovesicular steatosis.

A 64-year-old woman was found unresponsive by her husband in their non–air-conditioned home during a heatwave, with outdoor temperatures above 33°C (90°F). Her medical history included bipolar depression, diabetes mellitus, migraine headaches, and a known seizure disorder. Home medications were:
• Amitriptyline 175 mg daily  
• Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg daily  
• Lurasidone 80 mg daily  
• Benztropine 1 mg three times daily  
• Topiramate extended release 100 mg daily  
• Clonazepam 0.5 mg daily  
• Trazodone 100 mg daily  
• Sitagliptin 25 mg daily  
• Erenumab 70 mg monthly

Emergency medical services noted that she was febrile en route. In the emergency department, her blood pressure was 84/42 mmHg, and rectal temperature was 42°C. Her skin was warm and dry, and her mucous membranes were dry. On neurologic examination she was responsive only to painful stimuli, with no focal deficits, hyperreflexia, or rigidity. Initial laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 11 400 cells/mm3 and a normal creatine phosphokinase level. A screening electrocardiogram was unremarkable.

A 51-year-old Japanese man presented with a 2-month history of painless right vision loss. He had type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral agents without retinopathy and a 60–pack-year smoking history; there was no family history of sarcoidosis. On examination, cutaneous nodules were noted on his back; the neurologic examination was otherwise unremarkable. Visual field testing showed slight enlargement of the right blind spot. Funduscopic examination of the right eye revealed optic disc edema with hemorrhages; best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25. There was no evidence of uveitis. MRI of the orbits with contrast demonstrated enhancement of the right optic nerve; brain FLAIR images showed no demyelinating lesions. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed protein 74 mg/dL, 19 mononuclear cells/µL, glucose 77 mg/dL; there were no oligoclonal bands or elevated IgG index, and bacterial, viral, and fungal cultures were negative. Laboratory studies showed an elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level of 34.2 IU/L with normal serum calcium; antinuclear antibody, interleukin-2 receptor, immunoglobulin G4, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, T-spot, and aquaporin-4 antibody tests were negative. Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed bilateral mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy.

A 44-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of progressive, painless bilateral visual deterioration. She had been prescribed reading glasses one month earlier but noted no improvement. On examination 9 days later, her visual acuity had declined to 6/60 bilaterally. Confrontational testing with a red pin revealed bilateral central scotomas; Goldman kinetic perimetry showed normal peripheral fields. The optic discs appeared normal and were not pale. She could not identify any Ishihara test plates.

Her medical history was unremarkable. She consumed 14 units of alcohol per week and smoked 20 cigarettes daily. She denied weight loss but admitted to a poor diet: breakfast of milk tea and toast; lunch often skipped or a packet of crisps; dinner usually meat and potatoes; green leafy vegetables only once or twice a month.

Physical examination was otherwise normal. Laboratory studies showed:
- Serum folic acid: 1.5 ng/ml (reference 2.5–18)
- Red cell folate: 208 nmol/l (reference 220–620)
- Hemoglobin: 14 g/dl; MCV: 122.8 fl (reference 78–100)
- Vitamin B12: 354 nmol/l
- Thyroid function tests, endomysial and gliadin antibodies: negative

Brain MRI revealed a tiny focus of high T2 signal in the left frontal lobe consistent with a benign perivascular space and no evidence of demyelination.

A 9-year-old Caucasian male with preexisting diagnoses of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and inattentive subtype attention deficit disorder (ADD) presented as an emergency to our inpatient service due to minimal dietary intake. He was detained under Section 2 of the Mental Health Act and admitted to a specialist psychiatric ward for children under 12. At presentation, his most prominent symptoms were refusal of food and fluids, mutism, school refusal, and self‐neglect, including refusal of personal care. His dietary restriction led to severe weight loss with a body mass index of less than 12 kg/m2 (<0.5th percentile), requiring nasogastric tube feeding. His sole method of communication was typing on an iPad, and his personal care was limited to wearing pajamas and a coat for several days without washing or changing. His mother reported incidents of urinary and fecal incontinence. He would not sleep in his bed but instead slept on the floor outside his parents’ bedroom in the “fetal position.” When family members attempted to touch him, he became physically aggressive and hit out at them. In May 2015, his stepfather gave him a haircut that he particularly disliked. Following this event, he became more controlling of his dietary intake and selectively mute with his stepfather, refusing to eat his food or speak to him.

A 51-year-old multiparous perimenopausal woman presented with a painless right breast mass noted on self-examination. The mass had not changed in size since detection, and there was no associated pain, nipple discharge, skin discoloration, or axillary swelling. Her medical history was notable for well-controlled hypertension. On examination, there was a nontender, mobile 2 × 2 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, free from the overlying skin and chest wall, and no axillary lymphadenopathy. Two weeks after detection, a blind core biopsy with a 14-gauge needle yielded inadequate tissue for diagnosis. Three weeks later, a repeat blind core biopsy showed acute-on-chronic nonspecific inflammation with fat necrosis and no evidence of malignancy. Three weeks after the second biopsy, because the mass persisted and the patient experienced some discomfort, a breast ultrasound was performed. B-mode imaging demonstrated a thick-walled anechoic lesion measuring 2.07 × 1.02 × 0.9 cm with a pulsating anechoic center. Color Doppler examination revealed swirling flow within the center of the lesion.

A 33-year-old woman was found unresponsive and diaphoretic by paramedics. A point-of-care blood glucose measurement was 18 mg/dL. She received 12.5 g of intravenous dextrose, regained consciousness, and her glucose rose to 109 mg/dL. 

On arrival at the hospital, she was alert. Vital signs were blood pressure 117/68 mm Hg, heart rate 73 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination showed mild distress, moist oral mucosa, and a nonfocal neurologic examination with normal pupils.

In the emergency department, her venous blood glucose was 15 mg/dL. She received two additional doses of dextrose 50% in water, improving her glucose to 45 mg/dL, followed by an infusion of dextrose 5% in water, which raised her glucose to 96 mg/dL.

Once stable and alert, she reported that the previous evening at 5 pm she took two light blue pills given by a friend for anxiety, believing they were diazepam. She felt unwell overnight with nausea and diaphoresis, awoke at 4 am with tremulousness, improved after a large lunch at 11 am, then used cocaine and consumed three beers before losing consciousness at dinner around 7 pm.

Her history was notable for substance use disorder and anxiety. She denied personal or family history of diabetes or use of hypoglycemic medications. Current medications included methadone; she had no allergies. Social history included daily tobacco use and occasional beer consumption.

Urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines, ethanol, and cocaine. Laboratory studies revealed a blood glucose of 44 mg/dL, insulin level of 47.4 mIU/mL (normal 2.6–24.9), and C-peptide of 5.4 ng/mL (normal 1.1–4.4). Morning cortisol, thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, and insulin antibodies were within normal limits.

A 44-year-old man was referred for evaluation of several weeks of constipation without abdominal pain or fever. He had a history of similar symptoms 10 years earlier with a normal colonoscopy at that time. His only medication was for hypertension. On examination, a hard, palpable mass with local warmth was noted in the lower left to mid‐abdomen. The white blood cell count was 6500/μL and C‐reactive protein was 2.7 mg/dL. Colonoscopy from another hospital showed significant edema of the sigmoid colon mucosa and narrowing of the lumen, preventing passage of the scope. Initial contrast‐enhanced CT demonstrated edematous thickening of the bowel wall from the splenic flexure to the rectum, a thin, cord‐like inferior mesenteric vein, and ectatic mesenteric venous branches, while the inferior mesenteric artery was patent. There were no arterial or venous thrombi, arteriosclerotic changes, or calcifications. Clinically, inflammatory bowel disease and eosinophilic enteritis were suspected, but an endoscopic biopsy showed only mildly inflamed mucosa without significant eosinophilic infiltration. The patient was managed conservatively. One month later, he developed lower abdominal pain for 1 week and self‐medicated with NSAIDs. On examination he had left lower‐quadrant tenderness with guarding and a temperature of 38.0°C. The white blood cell count rose to 18,600/μL and CRP to 20.5 mg/dL. CT angiography was performed to evaluate suspected vascular abnormalities.

A 51-year-old woman with no prior comorbidities presented with altered sensorium of 28 days’ duration. Her initial symptoms included drowsiness, decreased voluntary eye movements, inability to eat or follow commands, absence of spontaneous speech, and bladder and bowel incontinence. After a 5-day hospitalization at a local hospital without improvement, she was transferred to a district hospital, where she tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 and was treated in the ICU. Two days later, she regained spontaneous eye opening but remained emotionally labile with inappropriate speech. After 15 days in the ICU without further improvement, she was referred to our center.

On arrival, she was alert and cooperative. She denied weakness, sensory disturbances, headache, visual changes, seizures, trauma, or other systemic symptoms. She reported an episode of fever and cough 4 days before the onset of neurologic symptoms, treated as an upper respiratory infection. Her past history was notable only for burr hole drainage of a traumatic intracranial hemorrhage 25 years earlier. Vital signs were stable except for blood pressure of 150/90 mm Hg. Respiratory and cardiovascular examinations were normal. Neurologically, she had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12 (E4V2M6), intact memory and comprehension, dysarthria, increased tone and 3+ reflexes in all limbs with preserved muscle bulk and power, flexor plantar responses, normal sensation, no cerebellar signs, no neck rigidity, and intact cranial nerves and facial symmetry.

She was treated acutely with intravenous hydrocortisone (100 mg) and fluids, then started on oral prednisolone (60 mg daily). Given her new-onset encephalopathy, multifocal neurologic signs, absence of prior demyelinating disease, and recent SARS-CoV-2 infection, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis was considered. 

Laboratory studies showed normal renal and liver function tests, negative erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed <5 leukocytes/mm^3 (100% mononuclear), glucose 47 mg/dL, protein 36 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 62 U/L, adenosine deaminase 1.839 U/L, immunoglobulin G 18.90 mg/L, and absent oligoclonal bands. The encephalitis/meningitis panel was negative. India ink staining and polymerase chain reaction tests for neurotropic viruses were negative. Serologic tests were nonreactive for antinuclear antibody, Treponema pallidum hemagglutination, and toxoplasma antibodies. NMO-IgG and MOG-IgG autoantibodies were negative. Malignancy screening, including serum tumor markers, was negative. She was not recently vaccinated against COVID-19. An MRI of the brain and spine was planned for diagnostic confirmation.

A 14-year-old girl presented with 2 days of bilateral painful red eyes and mild blurred vision, following a month of persistent low back pain unrelieved by rest. She had a 2-year history of recurrent inflammatory arthritis and morning stiffness treated intermittently with NSAIDs. Ten days before presentation her joint pain became continuous and more intense, accompanied by daily fever peaks; she received prednisolone 20 mg daily for 3 days and a 5-day course of gentamicin, doxycycline, and rifampicin without improvement.  

She had no significant past medical, travel, or family history. On exam, temperature was 38.5 °C, pulse 105 bpm, respiratory rate 23/min, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, and BMI 20 kg/m2. She had red eyes, tenderness of the right elbow and both ankles, and a swan-neck deformity of the fifth fingers bilaterally.  

Ophthalmic exam: visual acuity 20/20 OU; slit-lamp showed bilateral endothelial and anterior lens precipitates, 3+ anterior chamber cells, few anterior vitreous cells (anterior uveitis); grade 1 optic disc edema bilaterally; normal macula, peripheral retina, vessels; normal IOP.  

Laboratory studies: WBC 12.4 K/mm3 (85% neutrophils), hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelets 340 K/mm3, ESR 50 mm/h, CRP 4.6 mg/L; normal LFTs, creatinine, urea, urinalysis. Negative ANA, RF, HIV, VDRL, HBsAg, anti-HCV, Brucella IgG/IgM, blood cultures; negative tuberculin test. Hand X-ray: proximal interphalangeal joint space narrowing of fifth fingers; chest, pelvis, lumbosacral spine X-rays normal; echocardiogram normal.  

She was diagnosed with enthesitis-related JIA and treated with prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day, with rapid improvement of fever, eye redness, and arthritis. Methotrexate 10 mg weekly was added on discharge.  

Seven days later she returned with a new, generalized persistent tension-type headache, partially relieved by analgesics, and blurred vision. Ophthalmic exam revealed normal visual acuity but grade 3 optic disc edema OU with no anterior chamber or vitreous flare. Vital signs were normal.  
Brain computed tomography (CT) was normal. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 300 mm H₂O; CSF analysis revealed no cells, protein 40 mg/dL, glucose 56 mg/dL (serum 79 mg/dL). Total blood leukocyte count was 10.4 K/mm3 (86% neutrophils), ESR 20 mm/h; other labs were normal.  
MRI of the brain demonstrated mild optic nerve tortuosity, posterior globe flattening, and prominent subarachnoid space around the optic nerves; magnetic resonance venography (MRV) was normal.

A 23-year-old Asian man with no significant medical history presented with sudden onset of diplopia followed by left-sided facial asymmetry for 3 days. He was alert and fully oriented. Visual acuity and color vision were normal bilaterally. Pupils were equal and reactive without a relative afferent pupillary defect. On extraocular-movement testing, there was a complete left conjugate horizontal gaze palsy. On attempted right gaze, the left eye could not adduct past midline and the right eye showed horizontal nystagmus. These deficits did not improve with the oculocephalic (doll’s-eye) maneuver. Prism cover testing showed 30 prism diopters of left esotropia. There was no ptosis and convergence was intact. Funduscopy was unremarkable. Cranial-nerve examination also revealed a left lower motor–neuron facial palsy, with inability to wrinkle the left forehead, lagophthalmos, and flattening of the left nasolabial fold. All other neurologic findings were normal. Brain MRI showed multifocal T2 FLAIR hyperintense lesions without restricted diffusion in the bilateral periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial regions, including the left pontine tegmentum. A focal gadolinium-enhancing lesion with an open ring sign was noted in the left frontal juxtacortical region.

A 23-year-old man from Cameroon presented with acute-onset, right-sided scrotal pain and swelling while in the United States for military training. He denied any current or prior sexual activity, penile discharge, hematuria, fevers, night sweats, weight loss, or cough.  
Initial urinalysis showed pyuria; no urine culture was performed. Urine nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) was negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. He was diagnosed with acute epididymitis and treated with ceftriaxone and doxycycline, with symptomatic improvement. Six weeks later, he had recurrent pain; scrotal ultrasound again showed epididymitis. Repeat urinalysis (no culture) and gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT were negative, and he received a 30-day course of ciprofloxacin, which improved the pain but not the swelling.  
Five months after the initial presentation, he returned with another recurrence. On examination, there was prominent right scrotal swelling and tenderness. Ultrasound demonstrated right epididymitis with possible necrosis, a complex hydrocele, and a focal scrotal abscess. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a complex right scrotal fluid collection, an enlarged heterogeneous prostate, an enlarged juxtaesophageal lymph node, and right apical lung nodular scarring. Although TB was considered in the differential diagnosis, a unilateral orchiectomy was performed because malignancy was also high on the differential given his age.

A 16-year-old girl presented with severe nausea, epigastric pain, decreased appetite, and vomiting. Two weeks earlier, she had an acute episode of nausea, non-bilious vomiting, and diarrhea that resolved in 24 hours. During the preceding week, she experienced intermittent, dull, diffuse abdominal pain and decreased appetite; over several days, emesis progressed from non-bilious to bilious. Pain was sharp, localized to the epigastrium, relieved by vomiting, and worsened with oral intake. She denied fevers, respiratory symptoms, hematemesis, hematochezia, or melena.

Further history revealed a 16-month period of 22-kg weight loss through deliberate fat and meat restriction and excessive exercise. She reported eating ~900 kcal/day, running 3.5 miles three times weekly, doing 1.5 hours of yoga daily, and playing soccer. Her menses had ceased over one year ago. She described herself as a perfectionist and enjoyed praise for her thinness but denied body-image fixation.

On examination, her weight was 39 kg (z-score –2.5), height 161 cm (z-score –0.5), BMI 15 (z-score –2.9), and pulse 45–55 beats/min. She appeared cachectic and in mild distress. Abdominal examination showed diffuse tenderness and hypoactive bowel sounds without masses or organomegaly; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed chloride 95 mmol/L and bicarbonate 36 mmol/L, consistent with contraction alkalosis, amylase 141 U/L, and lipase 164 U/L; CBC and liver tests were normal. A barium swallow with small-bowel follow-through demonstrated an extremely dilated stomach and failure of contrast to pass beyond the third portion of the duodenum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen in the arterial phase showed severe narrowing of the third portion of the duodenum with compression between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta.

A 46-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of new-onset heart failure. She reported exertional dyspnea (NYHA class II) and fatigue. Her history was notable for lichen planus dermatitis treated with immunosuppression several years earlier and TPO antibody–positive hypothyroidism on levothyroxine. One month earlier, she had mild COVID-19 confirmed by RT-PCR, with no hypoxemia or pulmonary involvement, which resolved with outpatient therapy. Three weeks later, she developed severe chest discomfort and shortness of breath. ECG showed ST-segment elevations in leads V2–V6 and troponin-I was elevated, but coronary angiography revealed normal epicardial arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a normal LV size, apical hypokinesia, and an EF of 35–40%; RV size and function were normal. Cardiac MRI showed mildly enlarged LV size (LVEF 35%), a thin and aneurysmal apex, and widespread patchy subepicardial to mid-wall fibrosis in inferolateral and septal segments with subendocardial fibrosis at the apex; the report recommended evaluation for recent viral, autoimmune, or sarcoidosis-related myocarditis.

On exam in January, blood pressure was 115/75 mmHg, heart rate 90/min, oxygen saturation 96%, and bi-basilar crackles were present. Labs showed hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, normal renal and liver function, NT-proBNP 885 pg/mL, normal thyroid tests, and elevated anti-TPO. She was started on guideline-directed heart failure therapy. A few days later, she developed worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, abdominal pain, and nausea. On admission, blood pressure was 85/60 mmHg, heart rate 120/min, jugular venous distention, hepatomegaly, mild ascites, and 2+ pitting edema. Creatinine was 1.7 mg/dL, ALT 46 U/L, AST 40 U/L, total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL, NT-proBNP >18,000 pg/mL, and troponin-I remained elevated. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with low-voltage QRSs, Q waves in leads I, III, aVF, and V1–V6, ST elevations, and T-wave inversions. Echocardiography revealed mild LV enlargement, EF 15–20%, global hypokinesia, apical akinesia, mild RV enlargement with severe dysfunction (TAPSE 10 mm, RV Sm 6 cm/s), moderate to severe mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, a plethoric IVC (23 mm), and TR gradient 25 mmHg. She received IV milrinone and diuretics. Right heart catheterization showed a cardiac index of 1.4 L/min/m2, CVP 16 mmHg, PCWP 17 mmHg, and mixed venous O2 saturation 48%. She was scheduled for emergent endomyocardial biopsy.

A 44‐year‐old previously healthy man presented with chills for 3 days and arthralgias in the knees and hips, preceded by several days of unproductive cough and headache. One week before presentation, he had been treated with a macrolide antibiotic and an NSAID. His medical history was notable only for smoking; there was no family history of cardiovascular disease or long‐term medications. 

On examination, temperature was 38.5°C, heart rate 113/min, blood pressure 126/64 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Auscultation revealed no pericardial rub or crackles; there was epigastric tenderness. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with first‐degree AV block (PQ 210 ms). Laboratory studies demonstrated WBC 13.4×10^3/µL, CRP 16.9 mg/dL, ESR 95 mm/h, and high‐sensitivity troponin T 656.2 ng/L; the differential count showed no eosinophilia. Electrolytes, liver, and kidney function were normal. Blood cultures, serology, and PCR for pathogens were negative; vasculitis‐associated autoantibodies were absent.

Chest radiograph showed mild peribronchial cuffing. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved LV function, a 9-mm pericardial effusion, and slight IVC dilation; coronary CT excluded obstructive disease. He was treated empirically for pneumonia with pericarditis.

Over 2 days he developed worsening dyspnea and congestion, requiring noninvasive ventilation and diuretics. Repeat echocardiography showed an LV ejection fraction of 35%. On hospital day 4, cardiac MRI demonstrated myocardial edema with multifocal subepicardial and subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement and pericardial inflammation.

On day 8 he had syncope from complete heart block, was treated with isoproterenol, but progressed to low‐output state requiring dobutamine and a temporary pacemaker. Right heart catheterization revealed a cardiac index of 1.65 L/min/m^2, mean PCWP 34 mmHg, and LVEDP 29 mmHg.

A total of eight endomyocardial biopsy specimens were obtained from the left ventricle.

A 72-year-old man with a history of stage IIIA non–small cell lung cancer (cT4N0M0) treated 13 months earlier with concurrent cisplatin/docetaxel and radiotherapy followed by 1 year of durvalumab presented for evaluation of an incidental pelvic nodule. Surveillance CT showed a 15-mm, round, contrast-enhancing lesion adjacent to mesorectal vessels. FDG PET/CT revealed solitary uptake in this lesion with an SUVmax of 10.3. There was no other abnormal uptake. Laboratory tests demonstrated normal carcinoembryonic antigen, sialyl Lewis X, squamous cell carcinoma antigen, neuron-specific enolase, cytokeratin fragment, progastrin-releasing peptide, and normal coagulation studies. Total colonoscopy revealed no neoplastic lesions, and urinary cytology showed only nonmalignant urothelial cells. Endoscopic or CT-guided biopsy was deemed infeasible due to anatomical restrictions and risk of complications.

A 36-year-old woman undergoing in vitro fertilization presented for ultrasound‐guided follicular aspiration under short‐term intravenous anesthesia. She denied any history of allergic reactions. Standard monitors included BIS index, pulse oximetry, end-tidal CO₂, airway pressures, blood pressure, and ECG. Anesthesia was induced with midazolam, propofol, and alfentanil, and ventilated on 40% FiO₂ with airway pressures and vital signs within normal limits (ABP 113/68 mmHg; SaO₂ 99%; heart rate 75/min; EtCO₂ 34 mmHg; Pplato 10 mbar; Ppeak 12 mbar).  
Due to a high follicle count (>30), an intravenous infusion of diclofenac sodium (75 mg) was started to prolong postoperative analgesia. Within 1–2 minutes, the patient developed a heart rate >160/min, blood pressure <70/40 mmHg, and frequent premature supraventricular and ventricular contractions. SaO₂ fell to 68% and EtCO₂ to 19 mmHg. There was pronounced oral and nasal secretions, bilateral rhonchi on auscultation, and an increase in Ppeak to 24 mbar and Pplato to 20 mbar. No erythema or urticaria was seen, but lip, periorbital, eyelid, and facial edema developed.  
The diclofenac infusion was stopped, and two doses of intramuscular adrenaline (0.5 mg each) were given. Crystalloid fluids, methylprednisolone, chlorpyramine, and aminophylline were administered intravenously, and the patient was ventilated with 100% oxygen. Airway pressures normalized, and spontaneous breathing returned. Consciousness was regained after 60 minutes. During resuscitation, blood was drawn for serum troponins, D-dimer, and tryptase measurement.

A 56-year-old woman was evaluated for 8 months of symptomatic hypoglycemia associated with syncope, relieved by carbohydrate intake. She had type 2 diabetes managed without medications since 2018 and had undergone Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 3 years earlier. On examination, her body-mass index was 29, and the abdominal examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed a hematocrit of 33.9%, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, plasma glucose 114 mg/dL, c-peptide 4.71 ng/mL, insulin 27.9 μU/mL, and hemoglobin A1c 4.9%. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated a large gastrojejunostomy anastomosis but no pancreatic mass. A selective arterial calcium stimulation test showed a fourfold increase in insulin secretion localized to the gastroduodenal artery. During a supervised 72-hour fast, her glucose level remained above 60 mg/dL. She was discharged on octreotide and a low-carbohydrate diet. Two weeks later, she presented with a blood glucose level of 44 mg/dL. CT of the abdomen again showed no enhancing pancreatic mass but revealed intrahepatic biliary ductal dilation and a pancreatic duct dilated to 4.3 mm concerning for a head mass.

A 51-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus status post pancreas transplant presented for evaluation prior to kidney transplant and right native nephrectomy. She had developed a right ureteral stricture managed by a nephrostomy tube and nephroureterostomy stenting every two months, with progressive decline in right renal function and recurrent complicated urinary tract infections. Her past surgical history included left native nephrectomy at age 2, for unclear reasons. She denied any history of renal calculi. Preoperative contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the abdomen demonstrated an atrophic right kidney with extensive lipomatous proliferation of the renal sinus fat and marked inflammation within the collecting system. A percutaneous drainage tube was in place.

A 63-year-old man with a history of duodenal ulcer repair and mesh insertion for an abdominal incisional hernia was admitted with fever and found to have pus in his abdomen on examination. He had no history of thrombotic events, smoking, drug use, or family history of coagulopathy. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 2.63 mg/dL, fibrinogen 493 mg/dL, and a normal antithrombin III level; blood cultures were negative. He was diagnosed with a mesh infection and received 4 weeks of antibiotic therapy before transfer for abdominal surgical debridement. Preoperative transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 39 mm mass in the left atrium adherent to the atrial septum, an ejection fraction of 56%, and no valvular abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced CT also demonstrated a 39 mm left atrial mass with partial calcification. Brain MRI showed minuscule, scattered cerebral infarctions. Based on these findings, the mass was presumed to be a myxoma and surgical resection was scheduled.

A 55-year-old man with chronic hypertension and gout presented to the emergency department with acute-onset chest tightness and a burning sensation radiating from the chest into both upper extremities, accompanied by sensory impairment at the T4 (nipple) level. Minutes after arrival, he developed bilateral arm weakness. He reported receiving a fourth dose of the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine three weeks earlier. Cardiovascular and vascular etiologies were excluded on initial evaluation.

Over the next few hours, his left lower extremity strength declined from 5 to 2 on Lovett’s scale, followed by progressive weakening of the right lower limb (to 3/5) and both upper limbs (to 3/5). Cervical spine MRI revealed an inflammatory focus centrally at C5–C6 without contrast enhancement; brain and thoracic spine MRI were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed elevated protein (0.91 g/L) and albumin (656.7 mg/L) levels without intrathecal oligoclonal band synthesis. CSF culture and PCR for pathogens were negative. Serum aquaporin-4 antibody was negative. Anti–myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibody titers were 1:10 on October 13 and <1:10 on October 18. A connective-tissue–disorder workup was unremarkable.

A 41-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of daily high-grade fevers, night sweats, a 20-kg weight loss, anorexia, asthenia, progressive lower-limb weakness, and recent jaundice. His history included hypertension managed with captopril, remote heavy alcohol use, and active smoking. On examination, he was febrile (38.0 °C), slightly dehydrated, and icteric; blood pressure was 120/75 mmHg, pulse 106 bpm, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min; BMI was 21.6. No lymphadenopathy was noted. Cardiac exam revealed a mild systolic murmur at the mitral area; lung fields were clear. Abdominal examination showed a liver edge 1 cm below the right costal margin and a tender spleen 5 cm below the left costal margin.  

Laboratory studies revealed: hemoglobin 14.8 g/dL, WBC count 4.78×10^3/mm^3 with normal differential, platelets 91.7×10^3/mm^3; AST 443 U/L, ALT 404 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 719 U/L, γ-GT 368 U/L, total bilirubin 9.6 mg/dL, LDH 1274 U/L; INR 1.69; fibrinogen 67 mg/dL; triglycerides 617 mg/dL; ferritin >16 500 ng/mL. Serologic tests were negative for HIV, CMV (IgG/IgM), hepatitis B and C, syphilis, Schistosoma mansoni (IgM); EBV IgG was positive, IgM negative; toxoplasmosis IgG positive, IgM negative; rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies were negative.  

Upper endoscopy showed enanthematic pangastritis. Transthoracic echocardiography was normal. Abdominal ultrasound and CT demonstrated splenomegaly with multiple hypoechoic areas. Bone marrow aspiration was hypercellular with granulocytic predominance; biopsy showed megakaryocytic hyperplasia and a microgranuloma. Ziehl–Neelsen, Grocott, and PAS stains were negative. Immunophenotyping showed no evidence of lymphoma.  

Despite broad supportive care—including blood product transfusions—the patient remained febrile and developed progressive hepatic failure, acute renal failure requiring hemodialysis, and respiratory failure necessitating mechanical ventilation.

An 18-year-old African-American man presented with a 5-day history of pruritic, maculopapular rash, periorbital swelling, fever, and transaminitis. Five days before presentation, he noted pruritus and rash over his extremities that progressed over several days to involve his chest, back, and face. Thirty-five days earlier, he had begun treatment for new-onset seizures with phenytoin extended-release, 100 mg daily, and levetiracetam, 500 mg twice daily. He had no other significant medical history, drug allergies, or alcohol use. Review of systems was positive for non-productive cough, fever, and tea-colored urine, and negative for chest pain, abdominal pain, shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, chills, or altered mental status.

On examination, his temperature was 40.2 °C, heart rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and blood pressure 110/55 mmHg. He was well developed and nourished, alert and oriented, and appeared uncomfortable but was not in distress. A fine exanthematous rash was present on the face and sun-exposed upper and lower extremities without involvement of the oral mucosa, palms, or soles. There was profound periorbital edema preventing eye opening. The abdomen was soft, non-distended, and nontender, with no hepatosplenomegaly. Neurological examination showed no focal deficits.

Laboratory studies on admission:
• WBC 7.9 × 10^3/mm^3 (60% neutrophils, 8% lymphocytes, 4% eosinophils; absolute eosinophils 0.32 × 10^3/mm^3)  
• Free phenytoin level 0.4 µg/mL (therapeutic 1.0–2.0 µg/mL)  
• Basic metabolic panel within normal limits  
• AST 778 U/L, ALT 1274 U/L  
• Acetaminophen and salicylate levels undetectable  
• Serologies for hepatitis A, B, and C negative  
• Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram normal  
• EBV, CMV, and HIV testing negative  
• Antinuclear antibody test negative

A 28-year-old Polish woman who had lived in the United Kingdom for four years presented with severe ulceration of the perineal area, dysuria, soreness of the mouth, fever, nonproductive cough, and a facial rash. Two weeks earlier she had a flu-like illness and sore throat treated with antibiotics. Three days into the illness she developed burning itching of her genital region refractory to topical antifungal and antibiotic therapy for presumed urinary tract infection. She subsequently developed high fever, vomiting, and a maculopapular rash confined to her face and neck.

Her medical history was notable for von Willebrand’s disease and a caesarean delivery two years earlier; she denied relevant drug or sexual history. On examination, temperature was 38 °C, heart rate 110 bpm, blood pressure 105/60 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. She had crepitations at the left lung base, right upper quadrant tenderness, mild conjunctival injection, and an ill-defined erythematous rash on her face and neck. Oral examination showed erythema at the back of the mouth with a white coating. The perineum exhibited marked erythema, excoriations, and discrete ulcerations causing severe pain.

Laboratory studies revealed lymphopenia (0.26 × 10^9/L), C-reactive protein 49 mg/L, alanine transaminase 342 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 185 IU/L. An infectious disease consult was obtained. Initial differential diagnoses included HIV seroconversion, herpes simplex virus, Behçet’s disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic vasculitis, and Reiter’s syndrome. Viral serologies (including measles IgM and IgG), HIV PCR, anti-streptolysin O titre, complement levels, autoimmune screen, and immunoglobulin levels were ordered. She was started on intravenous acyclovir and high-dose prednisolone.

Within 20 hours she developed type 1 respiratory failure (pO2 9.5 kPa on 10 L oxygen) and required noninvasive ventilation. Chest radiography showed minimal left basal consolidation, although bronchial breathing was noted clinically. The working diagnosis was HIV seroconversion complicated by Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, with consideration also of atypical severe bacterial infection. She received imipenem, teicoplanin, cotrimoxazole, and high-dose methylprednisolone.

By day 4 the facial rash had resolved and oxygenation improved (pO2 13.1 kPa on 40% FiO2). Repeat studies showed negative HIV PCR, negative ASO titre, normal complement and immunoglobulin levels, and a negative autoimmune screen. Steroids were tapered, antibiotics (including cotrimoxazole) were stopped, and by day 10 her symptoms had completely resolved.

An 81-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer and newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia, managed palliatively, presented with bilateral painful skin lesions of the thumbs. On admission she was febrile (38.2 °C). Examination revealed well-demarcated, tender, violaceous plaques on the dorsal and palmar surfaces of both thumbs, with pus at the left thumbnail base. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 19.8 × 10^9/L and a C-reactive protein level of 121 mg/L. She was started on intravenous clindamycin, acyclovir, and fluconazole. Over the next 2 days, the plaques extended to the bases of both thumbs and both index fingers. Wound swabs yielded no growth at 40 hours. Orthopaedic debridement removed necrotic fat tissue; histology demonstrated haemorrhage with fibrinopurulent exudate, florid reactive atypia and epidermal hyperplasia, and an acute inflammatory infiltrate without neoplastic cells. Subsequently, the lesions evolved into haemorrhagic bullae and new lesions appeared on the little fingers. Nonadjacent digit involvement and failure to respond to antibiotics suggested a noninfectious process.

A 7-year-old girl presented with involuntary movements of her upper limbs that were triggered by running. She was born full term, with normal developmental milestones and a history of febrile seizures at age 1 year. There was no family history of endocrine disorders or epilepsy. At age 7 years 2 months, she exhibited involuntary lifting of the left hand, dropping of the right hand behind her back, and flexion of both wrists with running. By 7 years 4 months, these movements increased in frequency, and jerking of the lower extremities occurred upon walking, without alteration of consciousness. An interictal electroencephalogram was normal. On the basis of these findings, carbamazepine was started, and the dyskinesia resolved.

Two months later, she was hospitalized with fever (38.6 °C) and a 3-minute generalized tonic convulsion. On examination, she was 114 cm tall (–1.4 SD), weighed 19.8 kg (–0.8 SD), and had no features of Albright’s hereditary osteodystrophy. Blood pressure was 109/73 mmHg, heart rate 127 beats/min, and SpO2 96% on room air. Laboratory studies showed sodium, glucose, and renal function within normal limits. Serum calcium was 5.5 mg/dL (normal 8.7–10.2), phosphorus 7.6 mg/dL (3.9–5.8), intact parathyroid hormone 343.1 pg/mL (10–65), 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 74.3 pg/mL (20–60), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 13.5 ng/mL (>20). Thyroid function was normal. Brain CT revealed multiple bilateral calcifications in the basal ganglia and frontal cortex. Ophthalmological examination showed cataracts, and electrocardiography demonstrated QT prolongation with QTc 0.496 msec.

A 46-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 1-month history of worsening dry cough and slight loss of appetite without weight loss. She had no significant medical or family history, was a non-smoker, and drank alcohol socially. On examination, vital signs were normal, lung and heart auscultation were unremarkable, there was no peripheral lymphadenopathy or skin lesions, and neurologic findings were non-specific. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed bilateral anterior uveitis. Laboratory studies showed: white blood cell count 5300/µL, hemoglobin 14.7 g/dL, platelets 201 000/µL, C-reactive protein 0.76 mg/dL, serum calcium 9.7 mg/dL, angiotensin-converting enzyme 35.1 U/L (elevated), soluble interleukin-2 receptor 1693 U/mL (elevated), and normal antinuclear antibody. Urinalysis was normal. Blood and sputum cultures were negative. A Mycobacterium tuberculosis–specific interferon-γ release assay was negative, but serum anti-glycopeptidolipid core immunoglobulin A antibody for MAC was positive. Tests for Aspergillus galactomannan antigen, beta-D-glucan, Cryptococcus antigen, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, and HIV were all negative or within normal limits. Chest radiography showed upper mediastinal widening. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT demonstrated enlarged mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes with low-density areas and hepatosplenomegaly. Bronchoscopy revealed edematous bronchial mucosa, but endobronchial ultrasound‐guided needle aspiration yielded insufficient tissue. A surgical biopsy of a mediastinal lymph node was performed. Histology showed epithelioid cell granulomas with marked necrosis. Ziehl–Neelsen staining and PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and MAC on the biopsy specimen were negative.

A 63-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and New York Heart Association class IV symptoms, on maximal medical therapy, was referred after 22 days in an intensive care unit for inability to wean from dobutamine support (INTERMACS III), with evidence of low cardiac output (acute on chronic kidney injury, hepatic dysfunction, and respiratory failure). 

On transfer, he was bed-bound, afebrile, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, heart rate 90 beats/min (on dobutamine), and oxygen saturation 95% on 40% FiO2 by facemask. Cardiovascular examination revealed a 2/6 apical systolic murmur and signs of volume overload with low output. 

His history included a myocardial infarction at age 48 (managed conservatively), coronary artery bypass grafting with left internal mammary artery grafts and left ventricular aneurysmectomy 6 months earlier, stage IV chronic kidney disease (peak creatinine 3.0 mg/dL, eGFR 21 mL/min/1.73 m²), and obesity (BMI 30.4 kg/m²). The most recent angiogram before surgery showed patent left main, mid left anterior descending artery occlusion, atheromatous circumflex and right coronary arteries, and 70% stenosis of the posterior descending artery. 

Laboratory tests on transfer showed B-natriuretic peptide 1328 pg/mL, INR 1.44, albumin 2.9 g/dL, total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL, γ-glutamyl transferase 114 U/L, urea 98 mg/dL, creatinine 2.3 mg/dL, sodium 137 mmol/L, high-sensitivity troponin 79 ng/L, and CK-MB 1.8 IU/L. Chest radiography revealed cardiomegaly and interstitial pulmonary oedema. 

Transthoracic echocardiography was suboptimal. Transoesophageal echocardiography showed a dilated left ventricle (end-diastolic diameter 72 mm), ejection fraction ~20% on dobutamine, and a severe, centrally directed mitral regurgitant jet from A2–P2 attributed to annular dilatation and leaflet tethering (Carpentier types I and IIIb). The MR was considered disproportionate, with an effective regurgitant orifice area of 80 mm² and a regurgitant volume of 76 mL. Systolic pulmonary artery pressure was 60 mmHg. Left atrial haemodynamic tracing demonstrated giant V waves up to 65 mmHg (mean 32 mmHg).

A 44-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a 5-year history of persistent headaches and nausea. Over this period, she noted progressively worsening vision in both eyes and short-term memory loss. She was born in Honduras and continues to travel there regularly; she has no history of fever, night sweats, weight loss, rash, oral or genital ulcers, or sick contacts. Her past medical history is unremarkable; she does not smoke and has no pets.

On examination, her vital signs were within normal limits. Neurologic examination revealed decreased peripheral vision in both eyes; the remainder of the neurologic and general physical examination was normal. Formal ophthalmologic evaluation showed no signs of ocular cysticercosis.

Initial laboratory studies showed:  
• White blood cell count 7000 cells/mcL  
• Hemoglobin 12 g/dL  
• Platelets 333,000 cells/mcL  
• Creatinine 1 mg/dL  
• Glucose 109 mg/dL  
• Aspartate aminotransferase 111 units/L  
• Alanine aminotransferase 149 units/L  
• Morning cortisol 1.1 mcg/dL (low)  
• Adrenocorticotropic hormone 5.8 pg/mL (low)  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a partially calcified suprasellar and parasellar mass with both solid and cystic components, the largest segment measuring approximately 1.0 × 1.3 cm in the right parasellar region.

A 65-year-old Chinese man was first seen 9 years ago for chronic floaters. At that time his visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally. Slit-lamp examination showed multiple peripheral subepithelial corneal opacities in both eyes, with quiet anterior chambers, clear lenses, and an unremarkable fundus. He had no history of corneal injury or family history of corneal disease; his medical history included diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.

Six years after initial presentation, he noted blurred vision in the right eye with a decrease in visual acuity to 20/30. On referral, slit-lamp biomicroscopy revealed bilateral mid-peripheral subepithelial opacities and a central mid-to-posterior stromal haze in the right eye. Fluorescein staining showed mild punctate epithelial erosions and negative staining of some subepithelial opacities. Cataracts were very mild in both eyes, and the visual decline was attributed to progressive corneal opacities.

Anterior segment optical coherence tomography demonstrated a hyperreflective band at the level of Bowman layer and anterior stroma, extending 160 µm centrally and 250 µm paracentrally; the subepithelial opacities protruded toward the surface, causing focal epithelial thinning. Hyperreflective deposits were also seen in the posterior stroma, more prominently in the right eye. In vivo confocal microscopy of both corneas revealed small, discrete hyperreflective epithelial deposits, a heterogeneous hyperreflective anterior stroma masking keratocytes, and highly reflective granular endothelial deposits with preserved cell architecture; corneal nerves were tortuous but without perineural deposits.

Given the presumed diagnosis of a Bowman layer dystrophy or epithelial recurrent erosion corneal dystrophy (ERED), genetic testing of TGFBI and COL17A1 was performed, and no pathogenic mutations were identified. Concern for paraproteinemic keratopathy was raised, and the patient was referred for hematologic evaluation.

An 8-year-old boy born to consanguineous parents was evaluated for markedly delayed development. Antenatal and perinatal history were unremarkable; birth weight was 2.5 kg. At 4 months of age, a white reflex was noted bilaterally; lens aspiration for congenital cataracts yielded no visual improvement. The child has not attained neck control, vocalizes by turning his head to sound, and has a developmental quotient of 3.6%. There is no history of seizures.

On examination, he is wasted and stunted (weight 8 kg [<3rd percentile]; height 95 cm [<3rd percentile]; head circumference 45 cm [<3rd percentile]). Dysmorphic features include microcephaly with plagiocephaly, frontal hypertrichosis, microphthalmia, microcornea, broad nasal root, long philtrum, retrognathia, low-set prominent ears, high-arched palate, and poor dentition. There is bilateral undescended testes and micropenis. Musculoskeletal findings include bilateral simian creases, syndactyly of the second and third toes of the left foot, equinus deformity of the right foot, and scoliosis with left-sided concavity. Neurologic examination shows hypotonia of the upper limbs, hypertonia of the lower limbs, and brisk deep tendon reflexes. Pupils are atonic and unresponsive to light and mydriatics. Brainstem auditory evoked responses and visual evoked potentials were abnormal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed right frontal pachygyria, right ventriculomegaly, and hypoplasia of the corpus callosum with age-appropriate myelination.

A 45-year-old woman from Eastern Nepal presented with a 10-day history of painful erythematous nodules along the radial border of her left hand, forearm, and arm, and a 5-day history of swelling of the left hand. For the preceding 10 months, she had been treated with oral corticosteroids, methotrexate, and hydroxychloroquine for presumed pain in the left arm and forearm. She denied any antecedent trauma.

On examination, there were six tender, warm, erythematous nodules in a linear distribution along the radial border of the left upper extremity, with edema extending from the proximal third of the fingers to the wrist joint. Vital signs were within normal limits.

Laboratory investigations revealed a normal complete blood count, blood glucose, chest radiograph, urine microscopy, and serum cortisol. C-reactive protein was elevated; rheumatoid factor and serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative. Liver transaminases were mildly elevated (1.6× upper limit of normal), and vitamin D level was low. A wound swab culture was sterile, and a microfilaria test was negative.

An incisional skin biopsy was performed and sent for histopathology and tissue culture for bacteria and fungi. Histopathological examination showed lymphohistiocytic infiltrates admixed with neutrophils and activated macrophages forming epithelioid aggregates and ill-defined granulomas, with acid-fast bacilli on staining. A slit-skin smear for Mycobacterium leprae and sputum examination for acid-fast bacilli were negative. Culture of the biopsy specimen yielded no growth.

An otherwise healthy 8-year-old Bajau boy from Malaysia was evaluated for gradually developing pigmentation over his nails and mucosa. Over the past two years, he noted longitudinal and diffuse melanonychia of all fingernails and toenails. Over the past year, he also developed discrete, asymptomatic brown-black macules on the lower lip and tongue and a well-defined pigmented macule on the nasal aspect of the right sclera. He denied fatigue, weight loss, abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, palpitations, or other systemic symptoms. There was no relevant medication history, no consanguinity, and no family history of pigmentary disorders or intestinal polyposis. 

On examination, all 20 nails showed longitudinal melanonychia without dystrophy. There were multiple brown-black macules on the tongue and lower lip, and a single pigmented macule on the right sclera. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies—including complete blood count, serum electrolytes, liver function tests, serum cortisol, and adrenocorticotropic hormone—were all within normal limits. Chest radiograph, abdominal ultrasound, electrocardiogram, and echocardiography were unremarkable. The patient had undergone esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy eight months earlier, both of which yielded normal findings.

A term (39+1 weeks) 3580 g Caucasian girl was transferred on day 1 of life for imperforate anus and a perineal mass. The pregnancy and prenatal ultrasound at 21 weeks were unremarkable. Apgar scores were 9 and 9. Physical examination revealed a soft, skin-covered, midline mass (3 × 1 cm) arising from the perineum posterior to the vagina, a sacral dimple, normal female genitalia, and no anal opening. Neurologic and the remainder of the examination were normal. The infant did not pass meconium on day 1. She was started on ampicillin and gentamicin. 

On day 2, mild abdominal distention developed and flecks of meconium appeared in the diaper. Inspection revealed a small opening in the posterior vaginal vestibule; on probing, meconium passed through a vestibular fistula, partially decompressing the abdomen. 

Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the sacrum and coccyx showed normal bony structures without soft-tissue calcifications. A prone cross-table lateral pelvic radiograph demonstrated a column of air in the rectum and sigmoid colon terminating just below the caudal sacrum. Echocardiogram and ultrasound of the spine and retroperitoneum showed no cardiac, vertebral, or renal anomalies; the spinal cord terminated normally at L2 with normal cauda equina motion and no tethered cord. 

Ultrasound of the perineal mass measured 2.5 × 3.6 × 1.3 cm, with internal vascular flow and possible presacral extension, suggesting a presacral teratoma. Serum alpha-fetoprotein was appropriate for age. MRI revealed a pedunculated, predominantly fat-intensity mass with a single central vessel, no presacral component, and a normal sacrum; the rectum and vagina converged just above the perineum. 

A contrast study through the vestibular fistula demonstrated a long, narrow fistulous tract to a distended colorectal pouch located approximately 3 to 3.5 cm from the skin.

A 17-year-old previously healthy male presented with a one-week history of fevers to 102 °F, drenching night sweats, nonproductive cough, nasal congestion, and chest tightness. One week before symptom onset, he had exposure to a COVID-19–positive contact, and nasopharyngeal PCR testing at symptom onset returned positive for SARS-CoV-2. Over the next seven days, he continued to have fevers, weight loss of 5 lb, and worsening fatigue. On illness day 7, he developed acute shortness of breath, lightheadedness, two episodes of hemoptysis, and recorded an oxygen saturation of 86% at home. He was taken to a community hospital, where he was febrile to 101.2 °F with otherwise normal respiratory rate, heart rate, lung examination, and an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Repeat SARS-CoV-2 PCR remained positive.

Chest radiography revealed a 5-cm left upper-lobe mass and a 3-cm right paratracheal mass. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, electrolytes, liver enzymes, and kidney function. Chest CT demonstrated multiple bilateral cavitary lung lesions, the largest measuring 6.5 cm in the left upper lobe. He was transferred on illness day 8 to a tertiary pediatric center.

On arrival, he was afebrile, with 98% oxygen saturation on room air and an unremarkable examination. SARS-CoV-2 PCR remained positive. Initial laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 2.91 × 10^3/μL, hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, platelets 369 × 10^3/μL, creatinine 0.74 mg/dL, ALT 35.8 U/L, C-reactive protein 4.52 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 55 mm/hr. Urinalysis was negative for blood, protein, and white cells.

Broad infectious coverage with vancomycin and ceftriaxone was initiated, and over 48 hours, testing for HIV, tuberculosis, Aspergillus, Histoplasma, Cryptococcus, and blood cultures were all negative. Echocardiography was normal, and upper and lower extremity Doppler ultrasounds showed no deep venous thrombosis. Evaluation for multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children—including ferritin, D-dimer, fibrinogen, troponin levels, and echocardiography—revealed only mild elevations of ferritin, D-dimer, and fibrinogen but normal troponin, hemodynamics, and down-trending fevers. Concern for MIS-C decreased, and the patient improved clinically. He was discharged home on illness day 11.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of progressive upper‐quadrant pain and postprandial vomiting. The pain became continuous, worsened after meals, and was relieved only by vomiting. She reported a 5-kg weight loss. There was no history of alcohol abuse. On examination, she had severe epigastric tenderness without abdominal distension. Laboratory tests showed an amylase level of 156 U/l (reference ≤100) and a CA 19-9 level of 52 U/ml (reference ≤37); complete blood counts were normal. 

Abdominal ultrasonography revealed normal abdominal parenchyma, a normal gallbladder, and no common bile duct dilation. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was unremarkable. 

Multidetector CT (portal phase) demonstrated cystic lesions encircling the second portion of the duodenum with circumferential duodenal wall thickening, and a soft‐tissue component in the pancreaticoduodenal groove abutting the pancreatic head; the pancreatic head and pancreatic duct appeared normal. Signs of inflammatory change, including fat stranding and fluid, surrounded the groove area. 

Contrast‐enhanced MRI confirmed intramural fluid‐signal lesions within the thickened duodenal wall and sheet‐like tissue in the groove with enhancement patterns similar to the pancreas. MR cholangiopancreatography showed a normal gallbladder and no dilation of the common bile duct or pancreatic duct.

A 77‐year‐old African American woman with hypertension, rheumatoid arthritis, and hypothyroidism presented with a 1‐month history of progressively worsening shortness of breath and a nonproductive cough. She denied fever, chills, chest pain, hemoptysis, leg swelling, weight loss, or appetite changes and reported no sick contacts, allergies, or exposures to hay, dust, or toxic fumes. Her rheumatoid arthritis had been well controlled on oral methotrexate, 2.5 mg daily, for more than 30 years. 

On examination, her temperature was 38.2 °C, blood pressure 116/57 mm Hg, heart rate 106 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Cardiac and lung examinations were unremarkable except for mild tachypnea. 

Laboratory studies showed a white‐cell count of 9400/µL with 18.3% eosinophils, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 111 mm/hr, serum albumin 2.9 g/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase 265 U/L. Brain‐natriuretic‐peptide levels were normal. 

Chest radiography revealed bilateral upper‐lobe hazy opacities with prominent reticulation. Computed tomography of the chest confirmed nonspecific bilateral upper‐lobe opacification. Influenza and respiratory‐syncytial‐virus tests were negative. Sputum cultures (including acid‐fast bacilli), two sets of blood cultures, and a urine Legionella antigen assay were all negative. A (1-3)-β-D-glucan assay was within normal limits. Echocardiography was normal. Pulmonary‐function testing showed no obstruction, normal maximum voluntary ventilation, no restriction, and mildly decreased diffusion capacity.

A 71-year-old man with advanced renal cell carcinoma treated with ipilimumab (1 mg/kg) and nivolumab (240 mg) presented four days after his second infusion with an asymptomatic, sustained mild rise in serum creatine phosphokinase. On the seventh day after infusion, ST-segment elevations were noted on his cardiac monitor. Twelve-lead electrocardiography showed ST-segment elevation in all leads. Laboratory testing revealed elevated inflammatory markers and myocardial biomarkers (creatine kinase MB-isozyme, 23 488 U/L; troponin-I, 100 680 pg/mL; NT-proBNP, 15 964 pg/mL). Echocardiography demonstrated an akinetic apex, a hypokinetic septum, and an ejection fraction of 50% (baseline 72%). Emergency cardiac catheterization excluded relevant coronary disease, and left ventriculography showed that the left ventricular apex was nearly akinetic while the remaining left ventricle was hyperkinetic.

An 82-year-old man with chronic atrial fibrillation and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with a 3-month history of worsening peripheral edema and pleural effusion despite escalating diuretic therapy. He had stable heart failure with preserved ejection fraction for 2 years on bisoprolol, losartan, spironolactone, furosemide, and empagliflozin. Laboratory studies showed total bilirubin increased from 0.9 to 1.7 mg/dL, γ-glutamyl transferase from 32 to 197 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase from 70 to 176 U/L. He developed sialadenitis.  
Electrocardiography revealed chronic atrial fibrillation. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 50%, biatrial enlargement, a septal bounce, and a 40.1% respiratory variation in left ventricular E-velocity. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated partial pericardial calcifications without aortic wall thickening or hydronephrosis. Right heart catheterization showed equal right and left ventricular end-diastolic pressures, a dip-and-plateau pattern, and a systolic area index of 2.5.  
Autoimmune serologies—including anti-nuclear, anti-DNA, P-ANCA, C-ANCA, and anti-RNP-1 antibodies—and C-reactive protein were not elevated. QuantiFERON-TB Gold was negative. His serum IgG4 level was 1168 mg/dL, and a minor salivary gland biopsy showed >10 IgG4-positive cells per high-powered field with an IgG4+/IgG-positive cell ratio of about 40%.
