An 11-year-old previously healthy boy presented with 1 day of severe abdominal pain localizing to the right iliac fossa. He underwent a laparoscopic appendectomy for a perforated gangrenous appendix and was started on intravenous cefuroxime, gentamicin, and metronidazole. 

On postoperative day 5, his C-reactive protein remained elevated at 281 mg/L, and on day 8 he spiked fevers up to 38 °C. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 4 cm × 2 cm hypoechoic fluid collection in the right iliac fossa. Antibiotics were changed to intravenous cefotaxime plus metronidazole. CT on day 13 confirmed the persistent collection, which was drained. Culture of the fluid grew ESBL-producing, carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (resistant to ertapenem but sensitive to meropenem), Enterococcus faecalis, and Enterococcus avium. 

On day 20 postappendectomy, a PICC line was placed and therapy was switched to high-dose intravenous meropenem (40 mg/kg every 8 h) plus teicoplanin. He defervesced and serial imaging showed resolving collection.

On day 7 of meropenem administration (day 27 postappendectomy), he developed a rapidly spreading pruritic, non-tender maculopapular blanching rash with occasional petechiae over his trunk and upper limbs, and fevers up to 38 °C recurred.  
 
Complete blood count on that day showed a platelet count drop to 101 × 10^9/L from 322 × 10^9/L; by day 8 of meropenem it had fallen further to 14 × 10^9/L. Leukocyte and hemoglobin levels were stable. Coagulation studies (aPTT ratio, INR, fibrinogen) were within normal limits. Repeat abdominal CT showed improvement of the fluid collection. The PICC line was removed; line tip and blood cultures were negative, as were stool and urine cultures. Serial viral serologies and molecular tests for Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and parvovirus remained negative.

A 65-year-old Japanese man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted with a 2-week history of progressive dyspnea and productive cough. Several days before symptom onset, vildagliptin (100 mg/day) was initiated for uncontrolled diabetes.  
On admission, temperature 35.8 °C, blood pressure 120/79 mmHg, heart rate 66 bpm, and oxygen saturation 98% on 2 L/min oxygen. On chest auscultation, fine crackles were heard bilaterally; there were no signs of connective-tissue disease.  
Laboratory studies showed elevated serum IgE (4216 mg/dL; normal <400 mg/dL) and KL-6 (9781 U/mL; normal <500 U/mL). Autoantibodies including ANA, anti-RNP, anti-Smith, anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB, anti-centromere, anti-topoisomerase I, and anti–tRNA synthetase antibodies were all within normal limits.  
Arterial blood gas on 2 L/min oxygen showed pH 7.450, PaO2 111.6 Torr, PaCO2 32.1 Torr, and HCO3– 21.8 mmol/L.  
Chest radiography revealed reduced bilateral lung volumes and diffuse reticular shadows. Chest CT demonstrated extensive ground-glass opacities with irregular reticulation in a peribronchovascular and basal-dominant distribution. Pulmonary function testing showed a restrictive pattern with FVC 43.2% of predicted.  
Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid analysis revealed 23% macrophages, 57% lymphocytes, 5% neutrophils, and 12% eosinophils; microbiological studies were negative.  
Transbronchial lung biopsy specimens showed atypical multinucleated regenerative alveolar epithelial cells, infiltration of eosinophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells, and interstitial fibrosis around thickened alveolar walls, consistent with subacute interstitial pneumonia showing organizing pneumonia with an acute alveolar injury pattern.

A 75-year-old man from a nursing home was brought to the emergency department after a fall with a head laceration. Three weeks earlier, he had been hospitalized for a traumatic right-sided parietal skull impression fracture after a fall with transient loss of consciousness; hyponatremia was noted then but untreated. On the current presentation, he reported dizziness without syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, gastrointestinal symptoms, or fever. His history included hypertension (on candesartan) and type 2 diabetes (on metformin); he denied diuretic use and had no known chronic kidney disease.

On examination, blood pressure was 98/50 mmHg, heart rate 82/min, Glasgow Coma Scale 15, and there were no focal neurologic deficits. He had a fresh right-temple laceration requiring sutures. Mucous membranes were dry, skin turgor reduced, and there was no peripheral edema or jugular venous distention; lungs were clear and the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies on admission showed serum sodium 118 meq/L, potassium 3.6 meq/L, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 7 mg/dL, glucose 101 mg/dL, and measured osmolality 226 mosm/kg; thyroid-stimulating hormone was normal. Ten hours after admission, urine sodium was 83 meq/L and urine osmolality 518 mosm/kg. One day later, serum uric acid was 2.6 mg/dL.

Noncontrast CT of the head revealed no acute hemorrhage or edema, but a new right frontal hygroma and a stable posterior fossa Dandy-Walker cyst; the known parietal impression fracture was unchanged. On hospital day 6, with serum sodium at 129 meq/L, an orthostatic test showed supine blood pressure 123/71 mmHg with pulse 83/min, dropping to 75/52 mmHg with pulse 100/min after 2 minutes of standing; the patient became dizzy and the test was stopped. Immediately on returning to supine, vitals returned to 115/75 mmHg and 90/min.

A 68-year-old African American woman underwent routine bilateral screening mammography, which showed a focal asymmetry in the right upper breast on the mediolateral oblique view. She denied breast pain, nipple discharge, skin changes, or history of trauma. Her medical history was notable for chronic kidney disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, irritable bowel syndrome, and gout; she had no personal or family history of breast cancer. Physical examination revealed no palpable masses or tenderness; breast symmetry was consistent with her baseline. Diagnostic mammography with spot compression confirmed the persistent focal asymmetry in the superior right breast, and the lesion was assigned BI-RADS category 4A. Targeted ultrasound demonstrated a complex cyst at the 12:00 position, 8 cm from the nipple, measuring 0.3 × 0.8 × 0.2 cm, with an adjacent simple cyst. An ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the complex cyst was performed. Histologic examination showed a hypocellular proliferation of bland spindle cells admixed with collagenous and focally myxoid stroma; no breast glandular elements were identified. Immunohistochemical staining of the spindle cells was negative for cytokeratin 5/6 and p63, showed negative nuclear but positive cytoplasmic β-catenin staining.

A 63-year-old obese African American woman with asthma, hypertension, congestive heart failure, obstructive sleep apnea, and obesity presented with sudden onset of bilateral facial and tongue swelling and progressive shortness of breath. She had minor fruit allergies but no history of anaphylaxis. Initial vital signs were blood pressure 127/67 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths/minute, and oxygen saturation 100% on 6 L nasal cannula. She received epinephrine, diphenhydramine, and solumedrol for presumed anaphylaxis and was intubated for airway protection. On examination, there was extensive laryngeal edema. The right pupil was dilated and unresponsive; the left pupil was pinpoint but reactive. Emergent head CT showed bilateral effaced sulci with small ventricles and narrowed basilar cisterns, consistent with increased intracranial pressure. Initial arterial blood gas analysis on controlled ventilation (tidal volume 600 mL, respiratory rate 12, FiO2 50%) revealed pH 7.22, pCO2 85 mmHg, pO2 109 mmHg, and bicarbonate 33 mEq/L. A neurosurgeon recommended no surgical intervention. Mannitol was not administered, as there were no clinical or laboratory signs of an osmotic disturbance. The patient remained unresponsive with a dilated right pupil and blurred disc margins bilaterally.

A 78-year-old man with triple-vessel coronary disease status post coronary-artery bypass grafting (LIMA to mid-LAD, SVG to first diagonal, and SVG to second obtuse marginal), heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and hypertension was admitted after a mechanical fall complicated by left chest pain. On examination, he had a hematoma and swelling of the left chest wall but denied cardiac pain or dyspnea. An initial chest CT angiogram was unremarkable except for an incidental abdominal aortic aneurysm. 

Fourteen days later, he developed moderate, pressure-like chest pain and dyspnea. He was mildly tachycardic without hypoxia. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with frequent premature atrial complexes. Laboratory studies revealed a high-sensitivity troponin I level of 140 ng/mL (reference 0–12 ng/mL) and a BNP of 3363 pg/mL (reference 0–450 pg/mL). A pulmonary embolism was suspected; a repeat chest CTA was negative for PE but demonstrated a new hyperattenuating structure in the left pulmonic pericardial recess concerning for a hematoma. 

The differential diagnosis for this pericardial hematoma included left anterior descending artery pseudoaneurysm, mycotic aneurysm, pericardial injury, connective tissue disorder, or malignancy with central hemorrhage. Considering recent left-sided chest trauma, imaging, and negative blood cultures, an LAD pseudoaneurysm was the leading possibility.

A 61-year-old African-American man presented with a four-day history of binocular diplopia, left eyelid droop, and numbness and tingling in both hands and feet. He also reported one month of profound fatigue and progressive proximal weakness, to the point of being unable to ambulate. His medical history was notable for biopsy-proven sarcoidosis treated with steroids in 1970, gout, dyspepsia, and mild obstructive pulmonary disease. He had lost 30 pounds over six months and had a chronic dry cough.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Cranial-nerve testing revealed significant left eyelid ptosis (1 mm aperture), impaired adduction, abduction, and upward gaze bilaterally, partial right III and VI nerve palsies, and almost complete left III and VI nerve palsies. There was subtle bilateral facial weakness, decreased left facial sensation to pinprick, and proximal muscle atrophy with 4/5 strength in the shoulders and hips, 3/5 in lower extremities, preserved distal strength, decreased to absent reflexes bilaterally, and mildly decreased distal leg sensation. The abdomen was diffusely mildly tender; joints were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, normal calcium, electrolytes, renal function, HIV serology, vitamin B12, folate, muscle enzymes, and infectious serologies except mildly elevated AST and total bilirubin. ESR was 66 mm/hr, CRP normal, and urinalysis revealed 3+ proteinuria (normal six months earlier). Head CT was normal.

He was treated with five days of IVIG for a presumed Guillain-Barré–like syndrome. Chest CT showed multiple calcified nodules (some larger than prior studies) and a new right lower lobe infiltrate. Brain MRI/MRA (including orbits with gadolinium) was unremarkable. Nerve conduction studies and EMG revealed a diffuse, predominantly axonal, length-dependent sensory-motor polyneuropathy with myopathic features. Lumbar MRI showed multilevel degeneration. CSF analysis demonstrated albuminocytologic dissociation (protein 105 mg/dL). CT abdomen and pelvis showed minimal free fluid. Fine-needle aspiration of the lung infiltrate showed inflammatory cells and plasma cells without granulomas; cultures were negative. Muscle biopsy showed inflammatory myopathy with fiber atrophy and regeneration without vasculitis. Sural nerve biopsy revealed no acute abnormality but evidence of possible old vasculitis.

A previously healthy woman was admitted with a 20-day history of recurrent headache and fever and a 3-day history of dyspnea. Twenty days before admission, she developed intermittent left occipital headache lasting 2–3 minutes per episode, followed by low-grade fever, sore throat, and dry cough. Initial outpatient treatment provided only transient relief. Fifteen days before admission, fever recurred (to 38 °C), with marked fatigue, persistent dry cough, nausea, and non-projectile vomiting. One week before admission, she noted memory loss, bilateral hearing loss, and limb weakness; urinary incontinence developed the next day without altered consciousness. Three days before admission, dyspnea worsened, and she was transferred to the MICU after rapid progression to severe hypoxemia and lethargy, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation.

Her medical history was notable for hypothyroidism (on levothyroxine) and chronic hepatitis B (on entecavir), with normal thyroid and liver function pre-illness. She had no diabetes, head trauma, psychiatric disease, tuberculosis, or malignancy. She denied smoking, drug abuse, recent travel, tick bites, and any known contact with birds, poultry, or horses.

On MICU admission (day 1): temperature 39.0 °C; pulse 128 beats/min; respiratory rate 20 breaths/min; blood pressure 105/78 mmHg on dopamine infusion; SpO₂ 96.4% on FiO₂ 0.90. She appeared lethargic under sedation. Lung auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds and bilateral wet rales; no murmurs, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, or definitive neck stiffness; Kernig sign was equivocal.

Laboratory results: WBC 6.37 ×10⁹/L (neutrophils 94.7%); CRP 175 mg/L; PCT 6.87 ng/mL; ESR 65 mm/h; lactate 1.3 mmol/L; albumin 29.4 g/L; AST 218 U/L; ALT 97 U/L. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.378, PaO₂ 79.4 mmHg, PaCO₂ 32.8 mmHg, PaO₂/FiO₂ ≈ 88.2. Interferon-gamma release assay was negative. Hepatitis B serologies showed HBsAg+, HBeAb+, HBcAb+; HBV DNA 610 IU/mL. Tests for influenza A and B viruses, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Toxoplasma, rubella virus, and herpes simplex virus were negative. Cryptococcal antigen, galactomannan, and β-D-glucan tests were negative. Autoimmune panels (ANA, anti-ENA, ANCA) were negative. Lymphocyte subsets: CD3 76/mm³, CD4 44/mm³, CD8 28/mm³. 

Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 212 mm H₂O; CSF clear; WBC 6 ×10⁶/L; RBC 124 ×10⁶/L; protein 0.267 g/L; glucose 5.83 mmol/L; chloride 125.9 mmol/L; ADA 1 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. Chest CT showed multiple patchy shadows in both lungs with bilateral pleural effusions. Head CT was normal. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures during febrile episodes were negative.

A 38-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of a nonpruritic rash and 1 year of bilateral knee pain. The rash began as small red macules on the right thigh and progressed to brownish-red papules on both thighs, neck, shoulders, back, chest, abdomen, and arms. Treatments for presumed eczema had no effect. Over the subsequent year he developed firm, smooth, brownish-red nodules (2–8 mm) on the dorsal hands and “gooseneck” deformities of the fingers, with difficulty making a fist. He also reported worsening knee pain, swelling, and limited squatting but denied fever, myalgia, oral ulcers, or weight loss.

On examination, he had densely distributed brown-red maculopapular lesions behind the ears, neck, shoulders, chest, back, waist, abdomen, arms, and inner thighs. Multiple 2–8 mm hard, nontender nodules were present on the dorsal hands, with limited interphalangeal motion and flexion deformities of digits 2–5. Thumb interphalangeal joints were swollen bilaterally. Knee joints were swollen and tender with a reduced range of motion.

Laboratory studies showed normal liver function, biochemistry, lipids, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and tumor markers. ANA, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, ANCA, anti-MPO, and anti-PR3 were negative. Platelet and monocyte counts were normal. Immunoglobulin G and C3 were within reference ranges.

Radiographs of the hands revealed narrowing of interphalangeal and intercarpal joint spaces, reduced bone density, and cystic translucent areas. Left radial–carpal joint space was narrowed. Knee MRI demonstrated degeneration of the menisci, osteochondral injury of the patellofemoral surface, possible synovitis, and joint effusion. Chest CT showed bilateral interstitial inflammation, interlobular septal nodules, fibrous foci in the lower lobes, and cystic foci in the right subscapularis muscle.

A 37-year-old woman underwent uterine curettage for fetal death at 9 weeks and 6 days of gestation. Six days later she developed fever up to 39.8 °C, generalized arthralgia without joint swelling, muscle fatigue, and dyspnea on minimal exertion. Initial laboratory studies showed pancytopenia (moderate microcytic anemia with circulating myelocytes), C-reactive protein elevated, procalcitonin normal, elevated D-dimer and ferritin levels. Vaginal swab grew Acinetobacter baumannii. ECG showed no right-ventricular overload or left-ventricular dysfunction. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 65% and no pericardial fluid. Chest CT angiography revealed no emboli but an 11-mm pleural effusion. Broad-spectrum antibiotics yielded minimal improvement despite sterile blood cultures. Bone marrow biopsy showed reactive changes with cells containing eosinophilic amorphous nuclear material. Further tests revealed hypoalbuminemia, decreased C3 and C4 complement, ANA with granular fluorescence at 1:1280 (anti–SS-A and SS-B positive).  

After 16 days she was transferred to rheumatology, reporting persistent fatigue, arthralgia with 1-hour morning stiffness, dyspnea on minimal exertion, and low-grade fever up to 37.4 °C. Exam showed limb muscle weakness, decreased breath sounds at lung bases, tachycardia (100/min), and bilateral lower-leg edema. Labs: WBC 3.05×10^3/mm^3, hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, platelets 117×10^3/mm^3, ESR 27 mm/h, CRP 199 mg/dL, procalcitonin normal, D-dimer 21 μg/mL, ferritin 953 ng/mL, NT-proBNP 798 pg/mL, triglycerides 268 mg/dL, fibrinogen 142 mg/dL, C3 0.67 g/L. ANA ≥1:10,000, anti-dsDNA 1:3200, lupus anticoagulant slightly elevated, anticardiolipin IgM positive, proteinuria 0.7 g/24 h. ANCA negative, CK normal, Coombs test negative, cultures negative. She met 2018 ACR/EULAR criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (score 24).  

She received heparin prophylaxis, antipyretics, IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 6 days, then oral prednisone 1 mg/kg. Despite this, she developed worsening dyspnea, right-upper-quadrant pain, increased leg edema, and fever. Exam again showed reduced breath sounds at lung bases and epigastric tenderness. Repeat labs demonstrated rising ferritin, fibrinogen falling to 94 mg/dL, further cytopenias, NT-proBNP rising to 4600 pg/mL, and troponin T at the upper limit of normal. CT showed pleural effusions widened to 25 mm and small pelvic fluid; abdominal organs were unremarkable. Echocardiography again showed no right-ventricular overload or left-ventricular dysfunction, with only mild mitral regurgitation. The calculated H Score was 195, corresponding to an 80–88% probability of macrophage activation syndrome.

A 22-year-old Caucasian woman was first evaluated in 2014 for dyspnoea, chronic cutaneous eruptions, and symmetrical polyarthritis. High-resolution chest computed tomography showed pulmonary fibrosis, and lung biopsy led to a diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis in the setting of significant mould exposure. Skin biopsies were consistent with spongiotic dermatitis (eczema). Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated right ventricular dilatation with mild tricuspid regurgitation and normal left ventricular size and function. Right heart catheterization revealed normal pulmonary arterial pressures.

Over the next 4 years, she received methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and intermittent prednisone. In mid-2018, she reported dyspnoea on walking 50 m and four episodes of syncope at rest. On examination, blood pressure was 130/70 mmHg, heart rate 88 b.p.m. (regular), and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Jugular venous pressure was elevated with prominent V waves, and there was a right ventricular heave. A loud pansystolic murmur was audible at the left sternal edge, with pulsatile hepatomegaly and fine crackles at both lung bases.

Electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with a right bundle branch block. Repeat echocardiography demonstrated severe right ventricular dilatation and severe tricuspid regurgitation; left ventricular size and function remained normal, with no significant left-sided valvular disease. Telemetry captured non-sustained ventricular tachycardia at 150 b.p.m. Right heart catheterization again showed normal pulmonary arterial pressures (22/10 mmHg), elevated right atrial pressures (16/14 mmHg), and normal cardiac output and pulmonary vascular resistance. 

Transesophageal echocardiography excluded atrial thrombus and intracardiac shunts. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed no late gadolinium enhancement and excluded congenital anomalies. Cardiac positron emission tomography did not reveal increased metabolic activity. A chest CT demonstrated unchanged pulmonary fibrosis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 75-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease (balloon angioplasty and stenting of the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries 7 years earlier), hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and obesity presented with chest pain. An electrocardiogram during pain showed diffuse ST-segment depression. She received a loading dose of ticagrelor 180 mg and aspirin 325 mg and underwent urgent coronary angiography, which revealed chronic total occlusion of the right coronary artery and severe stenosis of the left main and circumflex arteries. Two drug-eluting stents were placed with excellent angiographic results. Postprocedural left ventricular ejection fraction was 50% with mild mitral regurgitation. A few hours later, telemetry showed Cheyne–Stokes respiration without overt heart failure, marked sinus arrhythmia with sinus tachycardia during apneic phases and severe sinus bradycardia (<30 beats/min) during hyperpneic phases, and cyclical transient complete atrioventricular block with pauses up to 5 seconds. Work-up including electrolytes, creatinine clearance, liver enzymes, and thyroid function was unrevealing.

A 10-year-old female was born full term and noted on day 4 of life to have bilateral congenital cataracts, which were removed by anterior vitrectomy at 5–6 weeks of age, with secondary membranous cataract removal two months later. At 3 months, she was referred for elevated intraocular pressure (30 mm Hg OD); examination revealed a hemangioma lateral to the right eyebrow, a posterior scalp protuberance consistent with a hemangioma, bilateral multifocal congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium, and left microphthalmia. Despite maximal medical therapy, she required a Baerveldt anterior chamber shunt and pars plana vitrectomy in the left eye at 17 months, with additional vitrectomies for inflammation; intraocular pressure has since remained controlled on topical therapy in both eyes.

Cardiac evaluation at 1 month identified an atrial septal defect and possible Wolff–Parkinson–White pattern on ECG. At 11 months, neurology assessment of a 5 × 6 cm parietal scalp vascular lesion raised suspicion for PHACE syndrome. MRI/MRA at 12 and 25 months showed a large right parietal scalp hemangioma (initially 3.9 × 2.3 cm, later involuting to 1.4 cm thickness) and a smaller right frontal scalp lesion, both without intracranial arterial communication, plus an aberrant right subclavian artery. Growth and development were otherwise unremarkable, with no endocrinopathies, hearing loss, or structural brain anomalies.

At 9 years, genetic consultation rendered a definite clinical diagnosis of PHACE syndrome based on two forehead/scalp hemangiomas and the presence of arterial, cardiac, and eye anomalies. During routine ophthalmic follow-up, the combination of congenital cataracts, glaucoma, bilateral CHRPE, and parental report of long dental roots, one missing tooth, and delayed primary tooth loss prompted consideration of an alternative diagnosis and molecular testing.

A 26-year-old man with no history of hypertension or heart disease presented with a 3-day history of upper abdominal pain. He reported epigastric tenderness with rebound and a positive Murphy’s sign. He was afebrile. Laboratory tests showed mild jaundice and a mildly elevated leukocyte count; procalcitonin and C-reactive protein levels were normal. An abdominal CT scan demonstrated a hyperdense gallbladder, mild gallbladder wall swelling, and fluid collections in the chest, pericardial sac, and abdomen. Electrocardiography showed ST-segment depression with T-wave inversion in V1–4 and a prolonged QT interval. The patient was taken to the operating room for an emergency laparotomy; intraoperatively, there was no evidence of bowel perforation, gallbladder enlargement, or cholangitis, but there was ascites and bowel wall edema. Approximately 1000 mL of peritoneal fluid was drained, and the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit.

A 56-year-old man with idiopathic hypertension presented with a 1-month history of right aural fullness and subjective hearing loss. Examination and audiometry confirmed a conductive hearing loss consistent with otitis media with effusion; on placement of a ventilation tube, the effusion was thick and viscid with a red–yellow hue. CT of the temporal bones showed partial opacification of both the middle ear and mastoid cavities; incidental findings suggested chronic rhinosinusitis. Nasal endoscopy was unremarkable and his nasal symptoms were mild. Despite spontaneous extrusion of the first grommet and placement of a larger tube, otorrhea persisted; a swab was negative and a biopsy of the postnasal space showed nonspecific inflammation. MRI with gadolinium demonstrated a large T2-hyperintense, T1-hypointense effusion in the right middle ear and mastoid with patchy mucosal enhancement extending along the Eustachian tube into the nasopharynx and sinonasal cavity. The extensive mucosal inflammation, persistent effusion, and lack of clear infectious or atopic cause raised suspicion for an autoimmune process. Blood tests showed normal RF, ANCA, ANA, serum IgE, CCP, renal and liver function, and ESR; ACE was elevated, as was total IgG (16.21 g/L; normal 6.2–14.4 g/L). A chest radiograph and QuantiFERON Gold test were unremarkable, and repeat ACE testing normalized.

A 68-year-old woman was referred for gradually increased facial hirsutism and deepening of the voice over 6 months. She had entered menopause at age 52 and had an unremarkable family history. Her medical history included hypertension managed with telmisartan and osteoarthritis treated with topical NSAID creams. On examination, blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg, pulse 84 beats/min, and temperature 36.9 °C. She had plethoric facies and terminal hair growth on the upper lip, chin, and upper abdomen (Ferriman–Gallwey score 4). There was no clitoromegaly or temporal balding. The remainder of her examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed polycythemia (hemoglobin 18 g/dL, hematocrit 54%), normal electrolytes and biochemistry, and a serum testosterone level of 25.40 nmol/L (normal range for women, 0.38–1.97 nmol/L). Further testing revealed a 17-hydroxyprogesterone level of 302.57 pmol/L and a cortisol level of 2.7 nmol/L after a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test. Pelvic MRI showed ovarian dimensions of 22×12 mm and 22×14 mm without masses, and adrenal CT demonstrated normal gland size and configuration. Serial measurements on hospitalization days 4, 6, 8, and 10 showed a decline in testosterone levels to 12, 7.4, 4.3, and 2.1 nmol/L, respectively.

A 69-year-old Hispanic woman was referred for progressively worsening blurry vision, right eye greater than left. Her past ocular history included bilateral epiretinal membranes. Medical history was notable for nonspecific joint disease managed with low-dose prednisone and methotrexate, and pulmonary symptoms of unclear etiology for which she was also on low-dose prednisone. 

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left. Intraocular pressures were 13 mm Hg OU. Slit-lamp examination showed nuclear sclerotic cataracts OU (2+ OD, 1+ OS) without cell or flare. Dilated fundus examination revealed 0.5+ vitreous haze OU and mild vessel attenuation OU. Spectral-domain OCT showed preserved foveal contour without sub- or intraretinal fluid. Wide-angle fluorescein angiography demonstrated mild bilateral peripheral perivascular leakage.

Initial laboratory tests including liver function, basic metabolic panel, hemoglobin A1c, angiotensin-converting enzyme, lysozyme, QuantiFERON, syphilis serologies, anti–dsDNA, and chest radiography were within normal limits, except for a positive antinuclear antibody titer of 1:80. Complete blood count showed leukocytosis (11.6 K/µL) and anemia (hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL; previously 10.2 g/dL one year earlier).

Methotrexate was discontinued; the patient was started on mycophenolate mofetil 1000 mg twice daily and prednisone 20 mg daily. Two months later, visual acuity remained stable (20/25 OD, 20/20 OS), but repeat fluorescein angiography showed worsening peripheral perivascular leakage.

A male infant was born at 39 weeks’ gestation via non-elective cesarean delivery for failed induction of labor in the setting of intrauterine growth restriction. Birth weight was 2730 g (<10th percentile) and Apgar scores were 8 and 8. Within the first hour of life the infant developed progressively worsening biphasic stridor, respiratory distress, and hypoxemia with oxygen saturations falling to 60%. He was started on nasal continuous positive airway pressure at 6 cm H₂O with FiO₂ 0.21 and a nasogastric tube was placed. Despite this support, there was continued respiratory compromise, and he was transferred to a tertiary pediatric center.

On arrival, the respiratory rate was 70 breaths/min with marked intercostal recession and tracheal tug; he had a weak cry. A venous blood gas revealed a pH of 7.10 and a PaCO₂ of 75 mm Hg despite escalation of respiratory support. Fibreoptic nasendoscopy performed at the bedside demonstrated a normal supraglottic anatomy and vocal cords but revealed a large subglottic mass causing near–complete occlusion of the airway.

A 51-year-old Caucasian man was admitted with a 20-day history of progressive dyspnea and fatigue without chest pain, cough, or fever. He had a history of Wilson’s disease diagnosed 8 years earlier, treated successfully with D-penicillamine, complicated by well-compensated cirrhosis. Six and a half years later, he was found to have pulmonary hypertension on echocardiography and treated with bosentan and sildenafil.

On examination, he had jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, vascular spiders, a systolic tricuspid murmur, accentuated and split second heart sounds in the pulmonary area, and splenomegaly. ECG showed right-axis deviation and right bundle branch block. Chest radiography revealed a “water bottle”–shaped cardiac silhouette and bilateral hilar enlargement. Echocardiography demonstrated a large pericardial effusion, dilated right heart chambers, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and an estimated RV systolic pressure of 75–80 mmHg (normal <25 mmHg).

Laboratory tests showed leukopenia (3,600/µL), thrombocytopenia (83,000/µL), INR 1.33, and albumin 4.6 g/dL; other liver and renal functions were normal. Viral markers (hepatitis B and C, HIV, EBV, HSV, CMV, Echo, Parvo, Coxsackie, Arbovirus), Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia, and Coxiella burnetii tests were negative. Autoimmune profile and tumor markers were normal. A tuberculin skin test was positive (15 mm induration).

Contrast CT of the chest showed a moderate pericardial effusion with enlarged anterior and posterior mediastinal lymph nodes, left hilar and carinal nodes, and dilation of the portal and splenic veins; abdominal CT confirmed cirrhosis and splenomegaly. Serum ACE level was elevated at 68 IU/L (normal 0–52 IU/L).

A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of an intermittent throbbing headache in the left temporal region that had worsened at night. She also noted bilateral temporal visual field defects. Her medical history was significant only for hypertension of more than 20 years; there was no personal or family history of autoimmune disease. On examination, her temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure 140/108 mmHg, and neurologic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a serum potassium of 3.2 mmol/L, microscopic proteinuria, and a urinary specific gravity of 1.025. She was negative for antinuclear antibodies, immunoglobulin G (IgG), IgM, IgA, and IgG4, and had no antithyroid antibodies. Other biochemical and coagulation tests were within normal limits. Endocrine evaluation revealed deficiencies of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, thyroid axis, and gonadal axis. Chest CT was normal, and ECG showed flattened T waves. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary gland demonstrated symmetrical enlargement with suprasellar “dumbbell” extension, significant homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium, low signal in the anterior pituitary on T1, high signal on T2, a preserved bright spot in the posterior lobe, thickening of an undeviated pituitary stalk, bilateral cavernous sinus encirclement of the internal carotid arteries, and a parasellar dural tail sign.

A 62-year-old woman with a 3-year history of non–insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes and inconsistent metformin use presented with 2 days of involuntary “jerking” movements of her left arm and leg. She reported increased urination and a 14-kg weight loss over the prior month. Her medical history was notable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, peripheral vascular disease, bronchiectasis, resolved hepatitis C, and steatohepatitis without cirrhosis. She smoked 20 pack-years, consumed about 10 alcoholic drinks per week, and had a remote history of intranasal cocaine use. 

On examination, her temperature was 98.1 °F, blood pressure 159/64 mmHg, heart rate 54 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, and BMI 23.6 kg/m2. She was alert and oriented. Neurologic examination demonstrated nonrhythmic, circular, writhing movements of the left upper and lower extremity with intermittent ballistic jerks, consistent with chorea.

Laboratory testing showed: blood glucose 776 mg/dL, HbA1c 15.8%, venous pH 7.37, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, anion gap 13, BUN 16 mg/dL, creatinine 1.48 mg/dL, ALT 17 U/L, AST 20 U/L. A noncontrast head CT revealed asymmetric hyperattenuation of the right lentiform nucleus with sparing of the internal capsule. She was admitted and glucose was controlled with insulin; within 48 hours, the movements were suppressible with concentration. MRI performed 4 days later showed only chronic microvascular ischemic changes without focal basal ganglia abnormalities.

One month later she returned with increased frequency of left-sided chorea and ambulatory dysfunction. Blood glucose was 62 mg/dL and HbA1c 9.9%. She was treated with alprazolam, tizanidine, and haloperidol without improvement. Antinuclear antibody and paraneoplastic autoantibody tests were negative. Ceruloplasmin and copper levels were normal. It was noted that the chorea dissipated when she was not observed, and she was diagnosed with a conversion disorder.

Within 24 hours she returned with persistent chorea (blood glucose 200 mg/dL) and was diagnosed with diabetic hemichorea hemiballismus. Two days later her blood glucose was 40 mg/dL, and repeat MRI showed hyperintensity of the right lentiform and caudate nuclei with corresponding intrinsic T1 hyperintensity.

A 32-year-old Caucasian man with an eight-year history of well-controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus (average blood glucose 150 mg/dL; hemoglobin A₁c 7.5%) presented with a three-month history of an unintended 22-pound weight loss. He denied abdominal pain, diarrhea, changes in diet or exercise, palpitations, heat intolerance, neck soreness, or other thyroid-related symptoms. His diabetes regimen (insulin pump plus pramlintide) and glycemic control were unchanged. 

On examination, he was well-nourished and in no distress. Blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/minute. There was no lid lag, proptosis, thyroid enlargement, tenderness, cervical lymphadenopathy, or tremor. 

Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, electrolytes, liver and kidney function. Thyroid studies revealed a suppressed TSH level of 0.033 mIU/L (reference 0.4–5.0 mIU/L) and a free thyroxine level of 33 pmol/L (reference 7.7–15.4 pmol/L). An anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody was elevated at 13.2 SD (normal <2.0 SD). A thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) assay was undetectable. Serum thyroglobulin was within the normal range.

A 27-year-old gravida 4, para 3 woman was admitted at 32 weeks of gestation with premature rupture of membranes and suspected fetal malformations. Prenatal serologic testing for toxoplasmosis, rubella, syphilis, and HIV was negative. Ultrasonography at 29 weeks showed a reduced left thoracic volume and a large cystic mass occupying the right hemithorax. A cesarean delivery was performed for fetal distress, resulting in a male newborn weighing 2030 g. The infant suffered cardiorespiratory arrest immediately after birth and died at 37 minutes of life. At autopsy, the mediastinum was shifted to the left. The combined weight of the heart and lungs was 38 g. The right lung measured 9 × 7 × 3 cm, was hyperinflated, and contained multiple contiguous cystic spaces up to 7 cm in diameter. The left lung measured 4 × 2 × 1 cm and appeared immature. The heart had a 2 mm atrial septal defect; no other anomalies were identified. Histologic examination of the right lung revealed proliferation of terminal respiratory structures forming cysts lined by ciliated pseudostratified epithelium with polypoid mucosal projections, small cartilage foci in bronchial walls, clusters of goblet cells, and mucinous glands. The left lung showed immature parenchyma with mostly collapsed alveoli and cartilage around the bronchi. The placenta was histologically unremarkable.

A 32-day-old girl was brought with a 4-day history of watery diarrhea (12–13 nonbloody, nonmucoid stools in 24 hours) and fever. There was no vomiting, poor feeding, or respiratory symptoms. She had contact with a COVID-19–positive case 4 weeks earlier. She was born at term, breastfed, and had normal growth parameters.

On admission she appeared toxic, tachypneic, and irritable. Temperature was 38.4°C, pulse 140/min, respiratory rate 30/min, and blood pressure 90/60 mmHg. Signs of dehydration included tenting skin, sunken eyes, and a soft fontanelle. Neurologic exam and development were normal.

Initial labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated ESR, CRP, ammonia, and D-dimer. A venous blood gas revealed metabolic acidosis (pH 7.22, HCO3– 11.5 mEq/L). Blood glucose and liver tests were normal. She received IV fluids and sodium bicarbonate.

On hospital day 2, repeat venous blood gas showed persistent metabolic acidosis (pH 7.26, HCO3– 11.5 mEq/L) with a normal anion gap (11 mEq/L). Chest CT, echocardiography, and an abdominopelvic ultrasound were unremarkable. Urine and stool cultures were negative; blood culture grew Klebsiella pneumoniae. SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR was positive, and COVID-19 IgM was elevated.

By day 4, diarrhea had improved but a venous blood gas still showed hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (pH 7.21, HCO3– 15 mEq/L, Cl– 115 mEq/L). Urine pH was 6.5 with a sodium of 105 mEq/L, specific gravity 1.012, and a positive urine anion gap. Serum potassium was 3 mEq/L, and ammonia was 235 mg/dL.

A 74-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of dyspnea and bilateral chest pain, continuous and worse on exertion; she denied cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Her past medical history included glaucoma, hip arthrosis, and cystocele repair. She was a non-smoker with no relevant exposures. Medications: boric acid and timolol eye drops. Physical examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed WBC 4860/μl, hemoglobin 133 g/l, platelets 205 000/μl, normal PT and aPTT, D-dimer 5360 ng/ml, calcium 2.35 mEq/l, albumin 4.3 U/l, potassium 4.3 mEq/l, CRP 3.4 mg/l, creatinine 0.852 mg/dl, LDH 306 UI/l, and normal liver tests. Chest radiography revealed multiple bilateral nodules. CT pulmonary angiography confirmed bilateral pulmonary emboli and multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, some calcified, the largest measuring 35 mm in the right middle lobe. She was anticoagulated with enoxaparin. Flexible bronchoscopy was normal; bronchoalveolar lavage was nondiagnostic, with no AFB on microscopy and negative cultures for bacteria, nocardia, mycobacteria, and fungus. CT-guided lung biopsy demonstrated amorphous eosinophilic material with surrounding plasma cells and no neoplastic cells. 18F-FDG PET-CT showed intense uptake in all pulmonary nodules (SUVmax 8.8) without hypermetabolic lesions elsewhere. Autoimmune serologies were negative (ANA, ANCA); ACE was normal. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis were normal, but immunofixation revealed an isolated monoclonal kappa IgM. Bone marrow biopsy showed 3% plasma cells and 9% lymphocytes with slightly reduced cellularity. Pulmonary function tests and arterial blood gases were normal.

A 49-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of pain in the right laterocervical region over the carotid bifurcation. The pain was a severe dull discomfort radiating to the ipsilateral ear and was triggered by head and neck movements. He had mild fever, fatigue, and myalgia at the onset but denied migraine or other neurological symptoms.

On examination, he was afebrile and in good general condition. There was localized swelling and tenderness at the right carotid bifurcation, worsened by palpation. No carotid bruits were audible. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy or induration along the jugular vein.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 9910/mm3, C-reactive protein of 0.10 mg%, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 20 mm/h. All other laboratory parameters were within normal limits.

Ultrasonography of the neck demonstrated an asymmetric hypoechoic thickening of the right distal common carotid artery extending into the proximal internal carotid artery. No intimal plaque or stenosis was present, and Doppler studies showed normal flow parameters. The thyroid, parathyroid, and salivary glands appeared normal; no neck mass or cervical lymphadenopathy was seen.

MRI of the neck revealed a thin rim of hyperintense tissue surrounding the right carotid artery on STIR sequences, which showed diffusion restriction on DWI and marked enhancement after contrast administration. There was no significant luminal narrowing.

A 1-year-old boy was brought to the emergency department for altered consciousness. He had no history of fever, upper respiratory symptoms, feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, bloody stools, or known trauma. His past history included prematurity at 29 + 3 weeks’ gestation and stage IA necrotizing enterocolitis. The patient’s parents were young with a history of drug abuse. On arrival his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 3 (E1V1M1). Vital signs: temperature 33.5 °C, heart rate 124 beats/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 58/47 mmHg. Examination revealed a distended, guarded abdomen with absent bowel sounds; there were no skin bruises, and retinal examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 13 g/dL, white blood cell count 30 240/µL (13% neutrophils), pH 6.76, pCO2 22.5 mmHg, HCO3 3.2 mmol/L, base excess –31.6, BUN 16 mg/dL, creatinine 1.07 mg/dL, AST 485 U/L, ALT 366 U/L, Na 133 mmol/L, K 6.1 mmol/L, Cl 100 mmol/L. Chest radiography demonstrated diffusely dilated bowel suggestive of ileus. A long-bone survey showed no fractures. Abdominal CT revealed pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas with poor perfusion of the right-sided small bowel. Noncontrast brain CT showed diffuse cerebral swelling with no subdural or subarachnoid hemorrhage, consistent with hypoxic-ischemic changes and severe edema. Considering the clinical presentation and imaging findings, the working diagnosis was septic shock with acute ischemic bowel.

A 26-year-old man presented with two weeks of progressive lower-limb edema and exertional dyspnea. He had chronic sinusitis and a family history of celiac disease. Two months earlier, he had eaten raw fish without gastrointestinal symptoms. On examination, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, with muffled heart sounds and pitting edema of the legs.

Laboratory tests showed eosinophilia (980/mm^3; normal 0–700), elevated total IgE, and C-reactive protein of 12 mg/dL (normal <5). ECG was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large pericardial effusion with “swinging heart,” ventricular interdependence, a dilated inferior vena cava, respiratory variation of mitral inflow of 25%, and an LVEF of 48%. Contrast CT of the chest and abdomen showed pericardial and pleural effusions and mediastinal lymphadenopathy up to 15 mm. 

He was started on colchicine and ibuprofen. Echo-guided pericardiocentesis drained 1150 mL of serous fluid. Fluid cultures were negative and cytology revealed normal lymphocytes, macrophages, and mesothelial cells, without eosinophils. His LVEF normalized and edema improved, but eosinophilia persisted (940–1100/mm^3) and a residual posterior effusion of 16 mm remained.

Cardiac MRI demonstrated pericardial and subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement and myocardial edema on T2 mapping, with an LVEF of 54%. PET-FDG scan showed intense uptake in the pericardium and mediastinal lymph nodes. 

Extensive testing was performed: serologies for viral and bacterial causes of pericarditis were negative; inhalant allergy tests and skin prick tests were negative; stool studies were normal; serologies for Toxocara canis, Strongyloides stercoralis, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Trichinella spiralis were negative. Echinococcus granulosus IgG was mildly elevated at 1:64 (positive >1:32), and Anisakis simplex IgE was 0.33 kUA/L (positive >0.10). Peripheral-blood and bone-marrow immunophenotyping and cytology showed expansion of normal eosinophils without malignancy. Autoantibodies for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis were negative, and sinus imaging was unremarkable.

A 72-year-old woman was evaluated in the renal transplant clinic for mild left lower quadrant abdominal pain of recent onset and a single episode of vaginal bleeding the prior week. Ten months earlier, she had received a cadaveric renal transplant for focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and was maintained on prednisone, mycophenolate, and tacrolimus. Six weeks before this visit, she completed valganciclovir therapy for cytomegalovirus viremia. She denied fever, changes in bowel habits, or hematochezia. Her medical history included iron deficiency anemia, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and prior hysterectomy with right oophorectomy. 

On examination, she was afebrile. The abdomen was mildly distended, supple, and non-tender, with no palpable masses. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 5.6×10^9/L, hemoglobin 94 g/L, and normal renal function. 

An abdomino-pelvic CT scan without intravenous contrast, using rectal contrast, revealed two nonstenotic, ill-defined moderately dense masses in the mesocolon: one adjacent to the descending colon and the other involving the sigmoid colon in a diverticular segment, which contained a few extraluminal air bubbles. 
A diagnosis of subacute perforated diverticulitis with two phlegmons was proposed, although it was noted that the proximal mass was completely separate from the distal one and contained no air. The differential diagnosis also included a perforated sigmoid neoplasm with a metastatic implant and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease. Colonoscopy was canceled pending further management.

A 56-year-old previously healthy woman presented with persistent fevers and pleural effusions. Three months earlier, she had surgical repair of a left diaphragmatic rupture sustained in a motor vehicle collision. One month postoperatively, she developed bilateral pleural effusions (left greater than right). Thoracentesis revealed an exudative effusion (protein 3.9 g/dL; LDH 205 U/L; albumin 1.7 g/dL; glucose 90 mg/dL; ADA 10.7 IU/L). Bacterial and mycobacterial cultures were negative, and cytology showed no malignancy. Echocardiography was normal.

Despite broad‐spectrum antibiotics, she developed quotidian fevers of 39–40 °C. Serologic testing for Brucella, EBV, SARS-CoV-2, hepatitis viruses, and HIV was negative. Tumor markers (CEA, CA 19-9, CA 125, CA 15-3) and rheumatologic panels were unrevealing. Endoscopic evaluation showed no malignancy. PET/CT demonstrated hypermetabolic mediastinal and cervical lymphadenopathy, intense FDG uptake in the spleen and bone marrow, and persistent pleural effusions.

On admission five months after surgery, she was alert and hemodynamically stable but continued to spike fevers. Examination revealed decreased breath sounds over the left lung; other systems were normal. Chest CT confirmed bilateral pleural effusions and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy. Abdominal CT showed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Empiric meropenem was administered. Blood and urine cultures remained negative.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 16.3 K/μL (92% neutrophils), hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, platelets 533 K/μL, AST 128 U/L, ALT 50 U/L, CRP 260 mg/L, procalcitonin 1.55 ng/mL, LDH 727 U/L, ferritin 3254 ng/mL, ESR 98 mm/h, D-dimer 4.85 μg/mL, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR negative. Repeat thoracentesis again yielded an exudative effusion with reactive mesothelial cells; cultures were negative. Bone marrow biopsy was normal. Autoimmune serologies, vasculitis panels, and QuantiFERON test were negative. Video-assisted thoracoscopic pleural biopsy showed chronic nonspecific pleuritis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 31-year-old Mestizo-Mexican woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of asthenia, adynamia, polydipsia, nausea, vomiting, food intolerance, impaired visual acuity, and abdominal pain. Fifteen years earlier, she had episodes of idiopathic pancreatitis with normal exocrine and endocrine function between ages 12 and 16. More recently, she developed alopecia, malar rash, and oral ulcers; a skin biopsy indicated discoid lupus. One week later she had focal motor seizures and was diagnosed with neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE; SLEDAI 18). Initial therapy included three daily 1-g doses of intravenous methylprednisolone, followed by discharge on chloroquine, levetiracetam, phenytoin, lorazepam, a tapering prednisone regimen (initially 1 mg/kg daily), and monthly cyclophosphamide boluses. Seven days after the sixth cyclophosphamide dose, examination revealed tachycardia (125 beats/min), tachypnea (27 breaths/min), drowsiness, dehydration, a normal body-mass index, and no dermatologic stigmata of insulin resistance. Laboratory evaluation showed: serum glucose 1240 mg/dl, sodium 127 mEq/L, potassium 5.56 mEq/L, chloride 86 mEq/L, arterial pH 7.07, bicarbonate 3.0 mmol/L, urinary ketones 80 mg/dl, effective serum osmolarity 322.8 mOsm/kg, and anion gap 43.56. Liver tests, amylase, and lipase were normal. Fluid resuscitation with 0.9% saline and continuous intravenous insulin infusion was initiated.

A 51-year-old woman with a history of long-term smoking presented with left hip pain. She denied cough, dyspnea, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable aside from hip tenderness. 

Laboratory tests revealed a leukocyte count of 21,200 cells/μL, hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, platelets 337,000/μL, and C-reactive protein 19.5 mg/L. A CT scan of the left hip demonstrated extensive osteolysis of the left acetabulum with suspected pathological fracture, confirmed on MRI. A CT-guided biopsy of the acetabular lesion showed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma, confirming metastatic disease. Immunohistochemical stains were pan-cytokeratin positive; TTF-1 and other lineage markers were negative. 

Subsequent CT imaging of the chest revealed a 2.3-cm right hilar mass encircling the right main bronchus, with enlarged mediastinal nodes and pleural, pericardial, and diaphragmatic metastases; abdominal imaging showed a 2.0-cm left adrenal lesion. Bronchoscopic biopsy confirmed a moderately to poorly differentiated lung adenocarcinoma. Molecular testing revealed wild-type EGFR and a KRAS mutation. 

The patient underwent radiotherapy to the hip lesion and concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin and vinorelbine) to the primary tumor and mediastinum. During treatment, she developed left flank pain due to adrenal mass growth, and her leukocyte count rose to 146,200 cells/μL. Differential showed neutrophils 85%, lymphocytes 1%, monocytes 2%, metamyelocytes 6%, and myelocytes 5%. CRP was 49.3 mg/L and procalcitonin 0.4 ng/mL; she remained afebrile.

Bone marrow aspiration revealed massively increased, left-shifted granulopoiesis up to myeloblasts with displacement of erythropoiesis and normal megakaryopoiesis. Flow cytometry showed mature granulocytic cells with partial CD56 expression and no immature blasts. Cytogenetic analysis showed a normal female karyotype (46,XX). FISH excluded t(9;22) translocation, and PCR was negative for BCR-ABL and JAK2 V617F mutation. A CT-guided biopsy of the iliopsoas lesion, along with repeated blood and urine cultures, were sterile. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics did not reduce leukocytosis or inflammatory markers.

A previously healthy 16-year-old female presented with a four-day history of abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, headache, myalgias, and cough. In the referring emergency department, her temperature was 39.4°C, pulse 154 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, blood pressure 115/61 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 96%. On examination, she was pale and had tenderness in the right lower quadrant without guarding or rebound. 

Initial laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 5.8×10^3/µL with 93% neutrophils, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 102×10^3/µL, C-reactive protein 11 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 26 mm/hr, and procalcitonin 0.50 ng/mL. A pregnancy test was negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated mesenteric edema, an 8-mm dilated appendix, and fat stranding throughout the lower abdomen and pelvis.

She received two intravenous fluid boluses and antipyretics and was transferred to our pediatric hospital. On arrival, the pediatric surgery team felt the presentation was not consistent with acute appendicitis. Further examination revealed mild bilateral conjunctival injection and neck tenderness in addition to right lower quadrant pain. She reported a positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR result one month earlier. Additional tests showed positive SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibody and normal troponin and N-terminal pro–brain natriuretic peptide levels. Given persistent fever, positive SARS-CoV-2 IgG, laboratory evidence of inflammation, and multisystem involvement, she was hospitalized for further monitoring and treatment.

A 61-year-old homeless African American man with hypertension presented with 1 week of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. He had presented 6 days earlier with similar symptoms but left against medical advice. On arrival, he reported intractable nausea, vomiting, fatigue, headache, photophobia, anuria, and myalgia; he denied cough, fevers, chills, or night sweats. He used cocaine regularly but denied alcohol, tobacco, and intravenous drugs. He had no recent travel.

Vital signs: afebrile; blood pressure 177/65 mm Hg; heart rate 77/min; respiratory rate 16/min; oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Examination revealed scleral icterus, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice of the soft palate, and a supple neck. Cardiopulmonary exam showed a heaving, laterally displaced point of maximal impulse with regular rate and rhythm. Abdominal exam disclosed epigastric tenderness without guarding or rigidity, normal bowel sounds, and a negative Murphy’s sign.

Laboratory studies showed: 
• Lipase >3× upper limit of normal  
• Mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic liver injury (elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, AST, ALT)  
• Thrombocytopenia  
• Acute renal failure (creatinine 10.4 mg/dL)  
• Elevated creatine kinase  

Urinalysis revealed hematuria, pyuria, leukocyte esterase, and hyaline casts.

Initial differential: hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).  
• Peripheral-blood smear: thrombocytopenia without schistocytes.  
• ADAMTS13 activity: normal.  
• Stool cultures: negative for Escherichia coli, Shigella, and Salmonella.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia was suspected but anti–platelet factor 4 antibodies were negative. Serologic and PCR testing for CMV, EBV, and HIV were negative. Workup for glomerulonephritis and other autoimmune renal disease (ANA, anti–dsDNA, p-ANCA, c-ANCA, complement levels) was unremarkable. Evaluation for chronic and autoimmune liver disease, including hepatitis panel, QuantiFERON, CMV, EBV, HIV, α₁-antitrypsin, and ceruloplasmin, was negative.

Given elevated lipase and epigastric pain, acute pancreatitis was diagnosed. Investigations for causes of pancreatitis included autoimmune markers (negative), urine toxicology (negative), undetectable blood ethanol level, abdominal CT (only subtle gallbladder sludge vs small stones), and MRCP (unremarkable).

Right upper-quadrant ultrasound demonstrated isolated hepatofugal flow in the right portal vein suspicious for portal vein thrombosis, whereas the left portal vein had normal directional flow.

A 72-year-old Caucasian woman with Sézary syndrome, previously treated with interferon alfa-2b and photopheresis, began romidepsin therapy (14 mg/m2 on days 1, 8, and 15) with bexarotene. Five hours after the second infusion, she noted bright, hot, salmon-pink, nonscaly, edematous nummular patches and plaques in body folds, on the face, upper chest, and back. She described her skin as feeling like a heat rash with minimal pruritus. She had no fever, skin pain, lymphadenopathy, mucositis, arthralgia, transaminitis, neutrophilia, or eosinophilia. Topical desonide and triamcinolone were applied. A punch biopsy showed a neutrophilic infiltrate in the papillary and superficial reticular dermis with mild spongiosis and no epidermal necrosis.

A 77-year-old woman presented with 2 weeks of progressively worsening oral tongue pain, ulceration, and odynophagia leading to dehydration. She reported that her tongue turned blue before ulceration. She denied fevers, chills, malaise, scalp or jaw tenderness, headaches, or vision changes. Initial outpatient treatment with trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, then amoxicillin–clavulanate, followed by acyclovir and fluconazole, did not improve her symptoms. On examination, she had dry mucous membranes and a well-demarcated area of necrosis involving the anterior one-third to one-half of the tongue, which was tender to palpation. Laboratory testing showed a leukocyte count of 22 000/µL, a platelet count of 716 000/µL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 65 mm/h. A CT angiogram of the head and neck revealed an undulated-beaded appearance of the distal internal carotid arteries and vertebral arteries bilaterally. A biopsy of the tongue demonstrated marked acute inflammation and granulation tissue with focal loss of the squamous mucosa; staining showed no fungal elements, and immunohistochemistry showed no cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, or varicella zoster virus.

A 44‐year‐old Hispanic woman with insulin‐dependent diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented with 3 weeks of progressively worsening nonradiating chest pain, fatigue, and exertional dyspnea. She also reported melena, gum bleeding with tooth brushing, nausea, and loss of taste; she denied fevers, chills, hemoptysis, weight loss, neurologic symptoms, or diarrhea. Her mother had myelodysplastic syndrome. 

Vital signs were notable only for a blood pressure of 138/92 mm Hg. On examination, she was obese with conjunctival pallor and multiple ecchymoses on the lower extremities; there was no hepatosplenomegaly and no neurologic deficits. 

Laboratory studies showed:  
• Hemoglobin 5.4 g/dL, hematocrit 16.4%, MCV 116.3 fL, WBC 3.5×10^3/µL, platelets 28,000/µL.  
• Peripheral smear: macrocytes, schistocytes, and teardrop cells; no hypersegmented neutrophils.  
• Troponin I <0.03 ng/mL; total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL; AST 52 U/L; LDH 1647 IU/L; haptoglobin <30 mg/dL.  
• CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis: no splenomegaly or evidence of neoplastic disease.  
• Coagulation studies: PT 11.2 s, fibrinogen 349 mg/dL, aPTT 24.6 s.  

She received two units of packed red blood cells, was started empirically on prednisone and daily plasmapheresis due to concern for TTP, and had hematology consultation on admission day 1. On hospital day 2, ADAMTS13 activity was 85%, an ANA screen was negative, and flow cytometry showed no PNH clone. The patient had no improvement in blood counts or symptoms after two days of plasmapheresis.

A 54-year-old woman with primary open-angle glaucoma and poor adherence to topical therapy was referred for surgical management. She had a history of severe obesity (BMI 37 kg/m2) and well-controlled insulin-dependent diabetes. Preoperative best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Untreated IOPs were consistently in the mid-30s mmHg; with tafluprost, her IOPs were 18 mmHg OD and 16 mmHg OS. Optic discs showed a temporal notch OD and were otherwise unremarkable.  

She underwent an uneventful mitomycin C–augmented trabeculectomy in the right eye. On postoperative day 1, her IOP was 8 mmHg, the bleb was functioning, and the anterior chamber was well formed; fundus examination was normal.  

Two weeks later, she complained of blurred vision in the right eye. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/32, and IOP was 10 mmHg off medications. Fundoscopy revealed multiple superficial, flame-shaped hemorrhages radiating from the optic disc with disc edema and no choroidal effusion. Optical coherence tomography showed macular folding with a small neurosensory detachment. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated macular microaneurysms with dye leakage, peripapillary hemorrhages, and late optic disc leakage without areas of nonperfusion or neovascularization.

A 49-year-old white woman with a remote history of sarcoidosis was referred for evaluation of an incidentally noted nodular liver during laparoscopic ovarian cyst surgery. She reported no fatigue, hematemesis, abdominal pain or distension, ankle swelling, pruritus, jaundice, or encephalopathy. She denied alcohol use. Vital signs were normal. Examination showed no icterus, spider nevi, clubbing, ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, or peripheral edema. Laboratory tests revealed a mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase level, a slightly prolonged prothrombin time, and mild thrombocytopenia. Serologic testing for hepatitis A, B, and C, antinuclear antibody, antimitochondrial antibody, anti–smooth-muscle antibody, ferritin, ceruloplasmin, and α1-antitrypsin were all within normal limits. A percutaneous liver biopsy showed cirrhosis without granulomas and demonstrated sinusoidal dilatation. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an enlarged inferior vena cava but was otherwise unremarkable. Left heart catheterization showed normal coronary arteries. Right heart catheterization revealed a right atrial pressure of 12 mm Hg, pulmonary-artery pressure of 32/15 mm Hg (mean 21), pulmonary-artery wedge pressure of 18 mm Hg, left ventricular end-diastolic pressure of 18 mm Hg, and a cardiac output of 5.2 L/min. Over the next weeks, she developed progressive exertional dyspnea. Pulmonary function testing showed mild restriction; chest radiography was unrevealing. Computed tomographic pulmonary angiography ruled out pulmonary embolism and demonstrated scattered pericardial calcifications. A contrast echocardiogram showed no right-to-left intracardiac shunt.

A 17-year-old male presented with several hours of right lower quadrant abdominal pain associated with nausea and subjective fevers. He had a heart rate of 106 beats per minute, blood pressure of 130/90 mm Hg, and was afebrile. He appeared comfortable at rest. On abdominal examination, he had normal bowel sounds and isolated right lower quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory tests showed a normal white blood cell count, normal C-reactive protein level, and normal creatinine. A point-of-care ultrasound of the right lower quadrant was performed to evaluate for appendicitis and revealed a hyperechoic circular focus with acoustic shadowing within a hypoechoic, non-peristalsing, non-compressible, tubular structure adjacent to the iliac vessels. There was no surrounding mesenteric fat stranding, free fluid, or hyperemia, and the walls of the structure were thinner and lacked the alternating layered appearance typical of intestinal structures.

A 44-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of fever and a 2-week history of cough and dyspnea. His past medical history included cutaneous lupus erythematosus, membranous nephropathy, and a 24-pack-year smoking history. On examination, temperature was 38.0°C, blood pressure 116/51 mmHg, heart rate 97/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air; bilateral rhonchi were noted without rash, joint swelling, or edema. Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (WBC 3,200/μL), normal platelet count, elevated lactate dehydrogenase (1,362 IU/L), C-reactive protein (7.34 mg/dL), ferritin (10,570 ng/mL), and soluble interleukin-2 receptor (4,865 U/mL); evidence of renal and hepatic dysfunction; coagulopathy not meeting DIC criteria; elevated tumor markers CEA (8.8 ng/mL) and SLX (71.7 U/mL); antinuclear antibody with a speckled pattern (160×) and anti-ribonucleoprotein antibody (2×) positivity; and negative blood and sputum cultures, β-D-glucan, and viral serologies for Epstein–Barr virus and cytomegalovirus. Chest radiography showed diffuse reticulated shadows in the lower lobes and a left hilar mass; CT of the chest revealed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities and a left hilar mass without lymphadenopathy or interlobular septal thickening.

A 9-year-old Caucasian girl presented with a 4-month history of gradually increasing swelling of both her upper and lower lips, which was distressing to her and her parents. Prior evaluations included a pediatric dentist, periodontist, and allergist. Her history was notable for excessive thumb sucking, frequent use of nail polish, and playing with homemade slime (glue, saline, shaving cream, glitter). She had mild eczematous skin lesions, vague rhinitis with nasal congestion, occasional postnasal drainage, intermittent headaches, and conjunctival pruritus, all worse in spring. There was no relevant family history, medication use, or known allergies to foods, drugs, or cosmetics. 

Physical examination revealed a symmetrically enlarged, erythematous upper lip, erythematous and edematous maxillary anterior gingiva (especially on the right), and mild lip fissures with cheilitis. Routine blood tests—including a basic metabolic panel, complete blood count with differential, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hepatic function panel, hepatitis A/B/C serologies, C-reactive protein, immunoglobulin panel, complement levels, and relevant autoantibodies—were all within normal limits. The patient had no clinical signs or symptoms of gastrointestinal disease.

A right upper lip incisional biopsy showed submucosal lymphohistiocytic infiltrates with loose perivascular noncaseating granulomas; adjacent salivary gland tissue exhibited lymphocytic infiltrates with occasional germinal centers. Acid-fast bacilli were not seen on a concentrated smear.

An 89-year-old Sudanese farmer presented with 9 days of generalized colicky abdominal pain, distension, anorexia, persistent vomiting, and constipation. The pain began in the left iliac fossa and periumbilical area, became generalized and colicky, was aggravated by eating, and partly relieved by vomiting and analgesia. It was associated with fever, nausea, and anorexia. One day before presentation, the pain became diffuse, constant, and severe, with abdominal guarding, distension, and absolute constipation. He denied weight loss, bleeding, or prior abdominal surgeries; his only past complaint was an episode of left-sided and lower abdominal pain without gastrointestinal symptoms. 

On examination, he was alert and hemodynamically stable (pulse 108/min, blood pressure 130/70 mmHg). His abdomen was distended with full flanks, diffusely tender with guarding, absent bowel sounds, and an empty rectum on digital examination. 

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 22,000/mm^3 (neutrophil predominant), C-reactive protein 189 mg/dL, serum albumin 2.3 g/dL, and a normal carcinoembryonic antigen level. Electrolytes and urinalysis were unremarkable. 

Erect chest and abdominal radiographs demonstrated dilated small and large bowel loops, a cecal diameter ≥ 12 cm, and free subdiaphragmatic air. 

Given the clinical signs of peritonitis, free air under the diaphragm, and radiographic evidence of a large-bowel obstruction, the provisional diagnosis was severe peritonitis due to large-bowel perforation from an obstructing left-sided tumor. The patient was started on intravenous fluids, antibiotics, and human albumin and taken for emergency exploratory laparotomy.

A 58-year-old woman presented with multiple episodes of coffee-ground emesis over 24 hours, preceded by nearly 20 episodes of greenish, nonbloody emesis beginning 3 days earlier. She reported a 7-month history of similar 2- to 3-day episodes of moderate, continuous, dull, midline abdominal pain associated with nausea, anorexia, and a mild headache without visual changes or aura; these episodes required three prior hospital admissions. Between admissions she was symptomatic enough to need assistance with activities of daily living. She denied fever, chills, bowel‐habit changes, weight loss, or skin findings. Her medical history included coronary artery disease treated with a drug-eluting stent 2 months earlier; she was on aspirin and ticagrelor. Prior outpatient therapies (omeprazole, ondansetron, sucralfate, meclizine, scopolamine, topiramate) had failed. 

On examination, her abdomen was soft, mildly distended, and tender in the epigastric and periumbilical areas without guarding or rebound. Initial laboratory studies showed potassium 3.0 mEq/L, glucose 264 mg/dL, anion gap 20 mEq/L, venous pH 7.412, HCO3 18.6 mmol/L, and beta-hydroxybutyrate 2.25 mmol/L. Management for presumed starvation ketosis and possible diabetic ketoacidosis corrected her metabolic abnormalities. Low hemoglobin and coffee-ground emesis raised concern for an upper GI bleed, so aspirin was held and intravenous fluids and antiemetics were administered.

A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a small hiatal hernia and no acute changes in the bowel or mesentery. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed no ulcers, strictures, or active bleeding, and biopsies were negative for malignancy. A gastric-emptying study was normal. Brain MRI demonstrated only a stable chronic cerebellar infarct without new findings. Blood cultures and urinalysis were normal, and chest radiography showed no pulmonary process. Cardiac evaluation revealed a normal ECG and negative troponins.

A 78-year-old woman presented with five days of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and intermittent fevers. She had undergone a difficult laparoscopic subtotal cholecystectomy one month earlier for chronic cholecystitis, with placement and subsequent removal of a Jackson-Pratt drain. Her past medical history was notable for hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux. On examination, she was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and had minimal right upper quadrant tenderness without jaundice. Laboratory studies showed elevated liver-function tests with a normal white-blood-cell count and lipase. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated no collection in the gallbladder fossa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed central intrahepatic biliary ductal dilation and dilation of the common hepatic duct to 1.2 cm. Based on this presentation, the decision was made to perform an endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography.

A 4‐year‐old castrated male mixed‐breed dog was referred for evaluation of an open wound overlying the left orbit. Two months earlier, the dog had undergone bilateral transconjunctival enucleation with silicone orbital implants for uveodermatologic syndrome (UDS) and secondary glaucoma. Prior to surgery, he had received oral mycophenolate and topical anti‐inflammatory and anti‐glaucoma medications. At surgery, unshaped silicone implants were placed in both orbits. The wounds were closed in multiple layers using absorbable polyglactin deep sutures and nylon skin sutures. Oral amoxicillin/clavulanate was administered for 10 days. Skin sutures were removed 14 days postoperatively, and both incisions appeared healed.

Approximately two months after surgery, marked swelling of the left periorbital region developed, followed by a draining tract. The family veterinarian prescribed oral cefpodoxime and referred the dog for further evaluation. On presentation, there was a 7-mm open wound with serosanguineous discharge at the midpoint of the left orbital incision. The right incision was well healed, and a silicone implant was palpable in the right orbit. Palpation of the left orbit revealed a firm spherical structure similar in size to the contralateral prosthesis. A preliminary diagnosis of partial incisional dehiscence with possible infection or suture reaction was made; implant extrusion was not suspected. Surgical exploration was planned, with removal of the implant and sampling for bacterial culture.

Preanesthetic physical examination and point-of-care bloodwork were unremarkable. Following intramuscular hydromorphone and acepromazine, the dog vomited, and a black spherical object consistent with a silicone implant was recovered from the vomitus. The left incision remained unchanged, and palpation still detected a firm orbital sphere. Under general anesthesia, an elliptical incision was made around the previous scar. Dissection revealed an approximately 2-cm firm, pinkish-white mass filling most of the orbital space. The mass was removed en bloc with peri-incisional skin and bisected to rule out a retained surgical sponge; no foreign material was evident grossly. Additional cultures were obtained, the orbit was flushed, and the wound was closed.

A Caucasian man in his early 20s with schizophrenia spectrum disorder and a history of monthly crystal methamphetamine use was transferred to a forensic psychiatric unit for aggression and erratic behavior. He had been on oral ziprasidone for several weeks but stopped it briefly and then restarted at a lower dose. Over the next month, he refused medications, and his behavior worsened. He was switched to oral aripiprazole, with low‐dose clonazepam added. After a requested increase in aripiprazole, his irritability improved. Two weeks later, staff noted that he was wearing a thick pullover despite warm temperatures, was sweating, and refused to speak, responding only by head movements. Concerned about oversedation, clonazepam was reduced. Over the next two days, he developed bizarre persecutory delusions, undressed, paced, and became noncompliant. A single dose of intramuscular zuclopenthixol was given; the next day he was calmer but had increased paranoia, vague suicidal thoughts, slowed movements, and disordered thinking. He was thought to be in a psychotic state with catatonic‐like features. That night, he exhibited ambitendency and mild posturing. His temperature and blood pressure were at baseline; heart rate was 135 beats per minute. Physical examination revealed mild rigidity of the arms. To rule out neuroleptic malignant syndrome, blood was drawn for measurement of creatine kinase.

A 26-year-old man was admitted for evaluation of recurrent hepatitis and persistent cytopenias. One year earlier, he developed acute hepatitis (AST 1750 U/L, ALT 3110 U/L, T-bil 8.9 mg/dL) one month after influenza vaccination; a liver biopsy at that time showed prominent lymphocytic portal infiltration. Six months later he had a second episode of hepatitis (AST 957 U/L, ALT 1970 U/L) accompanied by leukocytopenia and thrombocytopenia; viral serologies (hepatitis A, B, C, E, cytomegalovirus) and autoantibodies were negative, and liver enzymes normalized without treatment, but cytopenias persisted. Seven months later, he presented with fatigue and again had elevated transaminases (AST 434 U/L, ALT 1017 U/L). 

On admission he was afebrile, normotensive, without jaundice or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings included: AST 501 U/L, ALT 1165 U/L, ALP 429 U/L, γ-GTP 103 U/L, T-bil 1.0 mg/dL, albumin 4.5 g/dL, PT-INR 0.96. Complete blood count: WBC 2.35×10^3/μL, neutrophils 0.94×10^3/μL, hemoglobin 14.0 g/dL, reticulocytes 8.0×10^4/μL, platelets 3.0×10^4/μL. Serologies remained negative for HBsAg, HCV IgG, CMV IgM, EBV IgM, antinuclear and antimitochondrial antibodies; immunoglobulin levels were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound and contrast-enhanced CT showed mild splenomegaly but unremarkable liver morphology. 

A transjugular liver biopsy was performed and compared with the specimen from one year earlier. The earlier specimen showed prominent lymphocytic infiltration in portal areas; the current specimen showed disappearance of lymphocytes, replacement by histiocytes, bridging hepatic necrosis in portal regions, and new centrilobular fibrosis.

A 73-year-old man was transferred for evaluation of persistent fever despite 7 days of doxycycline for scrub typhus, diagnosed by an axillary eschar and an indirect immunofluorescence antibody titer of 1:1,280. He had no prior illnesses or medications. He lived in a rural area and worked as a farmer. On admission, his temperature was 36.9°C, pulse 72/min, respiratory rate 21/min, and blood pressure 97/54 mmHg. Examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly, a maculopapular rash on the abdomen, and a 1-cm eschar in the left axilla.  

Laboratory studies showed WBC 2,610/mm3 (41.7% neutrophils, 55.8% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 237,000/mm3, lactate dehydrogenase 1,500 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 675 U/L, AST 245 U/L, ALT 106 U/L, total protein 6.6 g/L, albumin 2.3 g/L, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase 444 U/L, total bilirubin 0.65 mg/dL, total cholesterol 61 mg/dL, ferritin 2,000 ng/mL, fibrinogen 70 mg/dL, triglycerides 138 mg/dL, CRP 85.2 mg/L, BUN 18.4 mg/dL, creatinine 0.67 mg/dL, and uric acid 3.4 mg/dL. Serologies for HIV, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus, Hantaan virus, leptospira, hepatitis A, B, and C were negative. ANA and rheumatoid factor were negative. Blood and urine cultures were negative. A repeat O. tsutsugamushi IgG titer was 1:5,120. Abdominal CT confirmed hepatosplenomegaly.  

Azithromycin was administered for 5 days for possible doxycycline resistance. Four days after admission, the fever persisted and his condition deteriorated. Repeat labs showed WBC 1,800/mm3, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 105,000/mm3, AST 591 U/L, and ALT 365 U/L. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed.
