A 70-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic mitral stenosis status post percutaneous mitral valvotomy in 2012, hypertension, persistent atrial fibrillation, and prior amiodarone-induced hepatotoxicity underwent successful radiofrequency pulmonary vein isolation for symptomatic atrial fibrillation and was discharged off antiarrhythmics. Two days later, she was admitted in atrial fibrillation, converted to sinus rhythm with 360 J, and started on flecainide 100 mg every 12 hours. 

Approximately five hours after the first dose of flecainide, she developed fever (38.7 °C), chills, and a dry cough, and her oxygen requirement increased from 2 L/min by nasal cannula to high-flow nasal cannula. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocytosis of 12 000 cells/mm3. Portable chest radiography showed increased interstitial markings compared with baseline. She received 20 mg intravenous furosemide, and her symptoms initially improved.

Three hours after the second 100 mg dose of flecainide, fever recurred with worsening dyspnea, and her oxygen support escalated to bilevel positive airway pressure. Leukocytosis rose to 16 000 cells/mm3. Computed tomography of the chest demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities predominantly in the upper lobes, multifocal perilobular consolidation in the lower lobes, and mild traction bronchiectasis and bronchiolectasis. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 65–70%, no mitral valve stenosis, and a small, collapsed inferior vena cava; serum brain natriuretic peptide was 186 pg/mL. Flecainide was discontinued.

A 22-year-old man presented with two weeks of right supraclavicular and prelaryngeal pain aggravated by swallowing, along with sweating and palpitations. He had a preceding upper respiratory tract infection. On examination, the right thyroid lobe was enlarged; the nose, larynx, and pharynx were normal. He admitted to regular anabolic steroid use. Vital signs were normal, and he was afebrile. Laboratory tests showed: TSH 0.04 µU/mL (0.10–4.00), free T4 30.7 pmol/L (9.5–24.0), free T3 8.7 pmol/L (3.0–6.3); thyroid antibodies were negative; thyroglobulin 231 ng/mL (0–30); white blood count 11.42/µL (4.4–11.3); CRP 38.5 mg/L (0–5); liver enzymes normal. Thyroid ultrasonography revealed a markedly enlarged right lobe (2.6 × 2.8 × 5.8 cm) with inhomogeneous reduced echogenicity and decreased vascularity, and a 1.11 cm adjacent lymph node; the left lobe was normal. With thyrotoxicosis, unilateral involvement, and absence of fever, subacute thyroiditis was suspected; treatment with prednisolone 50 mg daily and propranolol was initiated, and the patient reported rapid symptomatic relief by phone.

A 37-year-old man with no past medical history developed fever, headache, and a painful left-sided neck swelling while working offshore. He denied cough, dyspnea, chest pain, or recent travel and had no known COVID-19 contacts. On admission: temperature 41 °C, heart rate 115 beats/min, blood pressure 119/76 mm Hg, respiratory rate 12–22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Physical examination revealed a tender, non-fluctuant swelling extending from the left mandibular angle to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and a red area on the posterior palate; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  
ECG showed sinus tachycardia with moderately flattened T-waves. Chest radiograph was normal. Arterial blood gas on room air demonstrated respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.55, pCO2 3.9 kPa, pO2 8.4 kPa, HCO3 23 mmol/L). Laboratory studies revealed CRP 230 mg/L (0–5), procalcitonin 2.1 µg/L (0–0.10), WBC 7.1 × 10^9/L (3.5–11.0), troponin T 90 ng/L (0–15), and NT-proBNP 160 ng/L (0–85).  
Contrast CT of the neck showed left-sided subcutaneous edema with multiple enlarged lymph nodes up to 2.7 cm. Transthoracic echocardiography on admission demonstrated normal ventricular function without hypokinesia. On day 2, echocardiography revealed a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 40%, while CRP rose to 344 mg/L and procalcitonin to 12.9 µg/L, with persistently normal WBC count.

An 86-year-old woman was referred for several months of worsening vision. She had cataract surgery two years earlier and a 25-year history of open-angle glaucoma treated for seven years with brimonidine tartrate 0.1% twice daily in both eyes and artificial tears. She denied contact lens use or lid disorders and had no history of corneal disease. She reported gradual vision decline since her cataract surgery, most noticeable over the past three months, and experienced photosensitivity in both eyes. She had no history of hyperlipidemia or systemic disease.

On examination, best-corrected distance visual acuity was 20/60 in the right eye and 20/70 in the left. Manifest refraction was +0.75–1.00 × 160° OD and +0.50–1.25 × 165° OS; intraocular pressures were within normal limits. Slit-lamp examination revealed dermatochalasis, superficial punctate keratitis, and bilateral peripheral corneal opacities from the 4- to 5-o’clock and 7- to 8-o’clock positions with overlying neovascularization. Crocodile shagreen was noted bilaterally, with no guttata or lattice lines. Dilated fundus examination showed a blunted macular reflex in both eyes and cup-to-disc ratios of 0.65 OD and 0.75 OS.

An infectious and autoimmune workup was performed, including CBC with differential, ESR, CRP, ANA, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, rheumatoid factor, anti-SSA/Ro, anti-SSB/La, PPD, interferon-gamma release assay, chest radiography, ACE and lysozyme levels, MRSA swabs, stool ova and cysts, Lyme titers, syphilis testing, and review by the primary care physician for systemic rheumatologic disease. All test results were negative or within normal limits, and there were no systemic symptoms to suggest autoimmune disease.

A 19-year-old woman presented after an accidental ground-level fall with direct head trauma. She noted a tender, unilateral soft-tissue swelling over the left temporoparietal region extending into the periorbital area, causing facial asymmetry and compromised opening of the left eye. On examination, she was alert, hemodynamically stable, and neurologically intact; facial sensation and motor function were preserved, though her chin deviated leftward with some dental malocclusion. Brain CT showed no intracranial injury but noted deformation of the left zygomatic arch. Further history revealed excision of a tongue neurofibroma in childhood and multiple café-au-lait spots; physical exam confirmed NF1 with a congenital lateral neck mass. Facial bone CT and orthopantomogram demonstrated left mandibular hypoplasia with osseous defects, a thinned zygomatic arch, and an enlarged mandibular canal and mental foramen without signs of infection. CT angiography excluded ruptured aneurysms but revealed a 75 × 45 × 97 mm ill-defined lobulated lesion in the left suprahyoid neck, infiltrating multiple neck spaces and encasing the jugular vein and internal carotid artery. Over the next 6 hours, the facial swelling rapidly increased in size, and the overlying skin became tense with punctate hemorrhagic spots.

A 41-year-old multiparous woman (G6P5) with a history notable only for an open appendectomy at age 12 years presented in active labor. Seventeen hours after admission she had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with 400 mL blood loss and received methylergonovine and misoprostol for uterine atony. On postpartum day 1 she tolerated oral intake, voided, and ambulated. Approximately 11 hours after delivery she developed severe, cramping, generalized abdominal pain. Vital signs were: temperature 36.8 °C, heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 147/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 100% on room air, and blood glucose 98 mg/dL. Examination revealed moderate tenderness in all quadrants without rebound or guarding. Bedside abdominal ultrasound showed a thin endometrial stripe, a well-contracted uterus, and no free intraperitoneal fluid. Hemoglobin was 11.7 g/dL. She was treated conservatively with antacids, soft diet, and analgesics with initial symptomatic improvement. On postpartum day 2 she became intolerant of oral intake, with persistent pain. Electrolytes, liver function tests, amylase, and lipase were normal; white-cell count was 15.2 × 10^9/L. An abdominal radiograph showed mildly distended, gas-filled large bowel loops and absence of gas in the rectum, “possibly due to ileus or early obstruction.”

A 69-year-old woman reported a 5-year history of recurrent febrile episodes every 6–8 weeks. Each episode featured a temperature of 38.5–40 °C lasting up to 7 days, accompanied by sore throat, cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy and pain, headache, myalgia, fatigue, and dysphagia. She was asymptomatic between episodes and could predict their onset. She had a history of childhood tonsillitis treated with tonsillectomy. She worked in black metal analysis for over 30 years.  

During episodes, laboratory studies showed CRP 64 mg/L, serum amyloid A 140 mg/L, leukocytes 2.94 × 10^9/L, and neutrophils 3.19 × 10^9/L; procalcitonin, immunoglobulins, and ANA titres were normal. HIV, CMV, EBV, and other infection indicators were negative, and blood and throat cultures showed no growth. PET-CT demonstrated increased glucose metabolism in the sigmoid colon, but colonoscopy was normal. Pharyngoscopy revealed pharyngitis with white exudate. Ultrasound showed enlarged bilateral cervical, submandibular, and supraclavicular lymph nodes (up to 21 × 6 mm), and a supraclavicular lymph node biopsy revealed reactive hyperplasia. Bone marrow biopsy and cytogenetics were unremarkable. Despite multiple courses of antibiotics, febrile episodes persisted.

A 37-year-old woman with metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer presented with a 2-week history of episodic hemoptysis, odynophonia, and odynophagia. She described awakening choking on blood and a sensation of “water in her throat” with cough. She also had recent rhinorrhea and cough. Her medical history included lung, neck, and bone metastases and chemotherapy-related iron deficiency anemia, menorrhagia, hematochezia, and thrombocytopenia. Initial therapy with docetaxel, trastuzumab, and pertuzumab was changed to trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1), zoledronic acid, and tamoxifen; her last T-DM1 infusion was 26 days before presentation (total of 15 infusions). Nasopharyngolaryngoscopy revealed a friable, excoriated nasal septum; bilateral vocal fold edema with ulceration; epithelial bleeding on supraglottic and glottic surfaces; no submucosal hemorrhage; and no surrounding ecchymosis. CT imaging of the head, neck, and chest showed no parenchymal lung lesions or other sources of hemorrhage. The pulmonology team determined that this was not related to progression of metastatic lung lesions or lung-related hemoptysis.

A 15-week-old male domestic longhair kitten was evaluated for a 1-month history of intermittent generalized tremors and progressive abdominal distension. The kitten was fully vaccinated, dewormed, had not travelled outside the UK, and was fed a constant mixture of three commercial kitten diets according to manufacturers’ recommendations. No treats were given.

On examination, the kitten was bright and responsive, weighed 1.2 kg (body condition score 3/9), and had moderate muscle wasting. Heart rate, respiratory rate and temperature were normal. The long bones were visibly bowed but non-painful on palpation. The abdomen was markedly distended; palpation revealed a faeces-filled colon. Neurologic examination was otherwise unremarkable.

External haematology showed a mild leukocytosis and monocytosis. Serum biochemistry revealed hypocalcaemia (total calcium 1.42 mmol/L; RI 2.3–2.5) with a mildly decreased creatinine and mildly increased alkaline phosphatase. Pre- and post-prandial bile acids and total thyroxine were within normal limits; serum phosphorus and total protein were considered normal.

Further evaluation demonstrated ionized hypocalcaemia (0.78 mmol/L; RI 1.2–1.4), elevated parathyroid hormone (120 pg/mL; RI <40), normal magnesium, normal feline pancreatic lipase immunoassay, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 (75 nmol/L; RI 127–335), and high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (670 pmol/L; RI 90–342).

CT of the chest, abdomen and long bones revealed generalized marked osteopenia with abnormal metaphyseal mineralization and normal physes; the right femur, left shoulder and left stifle were most affected. There was a markedly distended colon with faeces and a subjectively narrowed pelvic canal. No malformation of the pelvic canal bones or pathologic fractures were identified.

A 40-year-old woman was evaluated for a Raynaud-like disorder when a chest radiograph revealed a peripheral 8-cm lesion involving the third right rib with cortical expansion; a concurrent CT scan confirmed this finding. She reported oligomenorrhea since age 26 but was otherwise asymptomatic. Physical examination was unremarkable. 

Further evaluation included 99mTc bone scintigraphy, which showed focal uptake in the rib lesion and the medial condyle of the right femur. MRI of the chest demonstrated an aneurysmal cystic bone lesion at the same rib site. A percutaneous biopsy of the rib lesion revealed numerous osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells without necrosis, mitoses, or histologic features of malignancy, a picture compatible with a giant cell tumor of bone.

Six months later, the lesion was excised with local curettage, including resection of the right pectoralis major and portions of the II, III, and IV ribs. Grossly, the specimen was a well-circumscribed, tan, fleshy mass measuring 6.0 × 4.5 × 2.2 cm, confluent with two rib segments. 

Microscopic examination showed:
- A diffuse distribution of multinucleated giant cells  
- A background of spindle-shaped mononuclear stromal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and oval, non-atypical nuclei  
- No necrosis, hemorrhage, or atypical mitoses (mitotic index 6 per 10 HPF)

A 49-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of headache. Physical, neurologic, and ophthalmologic examinations, including visual acuity, fundoscopy, and visual fields, were unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a sellar cystic lesion measuring 18 × 14 × 14 mm that extended from the suprasellar cistern through the diaphragma sellae to the dorsum sellae and compressed the optic chiasm. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images; in contrast studies, rim-like peripheral enhancement was noted. The normal pituitary gland and stalk enhanced typically and were displaced laterally to the right by the lesion. Computed tomography of the sellar region showed a hypodense cystic lesion with no contrast enhancement. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, routine biochemistry, pituitary hormone levels, and urinalysis, were within normal limits.

A 51-year-old man, former smoker, presented with a palpable mass in the right supraclavicular region. His ECOG performance status was 0, and he denied systemic symptoms. A biopsy of the lymph node revealed TTF1-positive lung adenocarcinoma with a KRAS p.G12C mutation; PD-L1 expression was 80% in tumor cells. Staging CT of the chest and abdomen showed right supraclavicular lymphadenopathy measuring 3.8 × 2.7 cm infiltrating the jugular vein, right hilar and right paratracheal nodes up to 3.8 × 2.7 cm, with tracheal compression; there was no detectable primary lung mass. PET-CT showed hypermetabolism in these nodes (SUVmax 6) without distant metastases, and brain MRI was negative. The disease was staged as cTxN3M0. Pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every 3 weeks was initiated.  

A few days after the first infusion, the supraclavicular mass at least doubled in size, became painful with erythema and edema of overlying skin, and the patient’s ECOG status worsened to 3; he reported hyporexia, asthenia, dysphagia, dysphonia, and syncopal episodes. Over the next three weeks, his symptoms resolved, his ECOG status returned to 0, and the supraclavicular mass visibly regressed. A CT scan performed immediately before the second pembrolizumab dose showed a partial reduction in size of the thoracic lymphadenopathies consistent with a partial response by RECIST 1.1.

A 53-year-old woman, nonsmoker, nondiabetic, and nonhypertensive, presented with a 2-month history of insidious, progressive weakness of all four limbs, accompanied by decreased sensation in the lower limbs and tingling in all extremities. Over the past 4 days she developed urinary retention. Two months earlier, she experienced a one-week history of low-grade fever that resolved spontaneously, after which she noted persistent dull neck pain and gradually worsening quadriparesis. She denied anorexia, weight loss, cough, hemoptysis, or palpable lumps elsewhere.

On examination, mild pallor was present. Neurologic exam revealed spastic quadriparesis (grade 4/5 upper limbs; grade 3/5 lower limbs), hyperreflexia in all limbs, bilateral extensor plantar responses, and hypoesthesia in the lower limbs without a clear sensory level. Mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted.

Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL; white blood cell count 8,000/mm3; erythrocyte sedimentation rate 42 mm in the first hour; blood glucose, renal function, and liver function tests normal; HIV negative.

Chest radiograph showed an expansile lesion of the right fourth rib. MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated altered marrow signal and erosion of C5 to T1 vertebrae, intraspinal extension elevating the posterior longitudinal ligament between C5 and T1, compression of the thecal sac and spinal cord, with preserved intervertebral disc height and signal. MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spine revealed multifocal vertebral marrow signal abnormalities involving T6, T7, T9, T10, L2–L5, and the sacrum, with pedicle involvement at T10 and L5, intraspinal extension at T6 and sacral levels, and large pre- and paravertebral soft tissue masses.

At this stage, the differential diagnosis included metastatic disease versus an infectious etiology such as tuberculosis.

On reexamination, a small, firm, painless, mobile mass was palpated in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. Ultrasonography of the right breast showed a 3.5 × 2.3 cm hypoechoic, heterogeneous lesion with internal echogenic foci and several enlarged right axillary lymph nodes; the left breast was normal.

A 53-year-old Afro-Caribbean woman with no history of cardiac disease presented with 3 weeks of confusion, anorexia, a 20-lb weight loss, and fatigue. She denied fever, headache, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, or edema. In the emergency department her blood pressure was 92/52 mm Hg, heart rate 129 beats/min, and she was lethargic but without focal neurologic deficits. Examination revealed small, painless supraclavicular and inguinal lymph nodes; heart and lung exams were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-blood-cell count of 88 000/μL, creatinine 4.8 mg/dL, and corrected calcium 21 mg/dL. Peripheral smear demonstrated atypical lymphocytes. Additional studies were consistent with tumor lysis syndrome. Imaging revealed diffuse lytic bone lesions and enlarged lymph nodes. Bone marrow biopsy and flow cytometry confirmed a T-cell clonal neoplasm, and HTLV-1 serology was positive, establishing acute adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL). A baseline transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular size and function, with an ejection fraction of 65%.

After stabilization of tumor lysis syndrome, she was started on inpatient EPOCH chemotherapy: continuous infusions of etoposide, vincristine, and doxorubicin, followed by cyclophosphamide and prednisone. Ten hours into the infusion of doxorubicin, etoposide, and vincristine, she developed acute hypoxia (70% on room air), tachycardia (152/min), and tachypnea (40/min), prompting endotracheal intubation and discontinuation of chemotherapy.

An electrocardiogram showed new nonspecific T-wave inversions in leads V2-V3. A bedside echocardiogram revealed apical ballooning with severe hypokinesis of the anterior and anteroseptal walls, mild hypokinesis of other walls, and an estimated ejection fraction of 20%. Chest radiography demonstrated pulmonary edema and an enlarged cardiac silhouette. N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide was 7000 pg/mL (normal <125 pg/mL), and peak troponin was 0.7 ng/mL (normal <0.01 ng/mL). 

She was started on intravenous dobutamine for hemodynamic support.

A 47-year-old woman was admitted with a 10-day history of remittent fevers up to 39°C, fatigue, and sore throat. Initial outpatient treatment with azithromycin followed by garenoxacin yielded no improvement; she then developed muscle pain and lower-extremity edema. 

On admission: temperature 39.7°C; heart rate 135 bpm; respiratory rate 26/min; oxygen saturation 91% on 1 L nasal cannula; mild respiratory failure. Abdominal examination revealed distension, tympany on percussion, and near-absent bowel sounds. Lung auscultation detected wheezing. Both proximal interphalangeal and ankle joints were swollen and tender, with lower-extremity edema. No rash was present.

Despite treatment with sulbactam/ampicillin, fevers persisted above 39°C. Abdominal radiography showed marked colonic gas and upward diaphragms. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated mediastinal lymphadenopathy, dilated colon with fluid levels, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and a small pericardial effusion—without mechanical obstruction. Colonoscopy confirmed no obstructing lesion. A diagnosis of acute intestinal pseudo-obstruction was made on hospital Day 5; nasogastric decompression and metoclopramide yielded no improvement. Clostridium difficile tests were negative, and metronidazole produced no response.

On Day 6 her respiratory status worsened (PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio 177), and she was intubated for presumed ARDS. A salmon-pink, edematous erythema appeared on the trunk and extremities. Discontinuation of all potential culprit drugs failed to improve the rash.

Laboratory studies: WBC 18 560/µL (89% neutrophils); AST 36 U/L; ALT 45 U/L; LDH 430 U/L; ferritin 3551.4 ng/mL; CRP 27.6 mg/dL; ESR 134 mm/h; procalcitonin 0.4 ng/mL; ANA <1:40; rheumatoid factor 29 IU/mL; C3 and C4 normal; blood cultures and viral serologies (EBV, hepatitis) negative.

A 40‐year‐old man with a history of juvenile polyposis syndrome (post–partial colectomy) and alcohol use disorder in remission presented in June 2018 with sudden‐onset right calf pain, swelling, and erythema. Venous ultrasound showed an acute, occlusive thrombus in the right popliteal, tibial, and peroneal veins. He was started on rivaroxaban. One week later, he returned with 3 days of melena. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 5.3 g/dL and MCV 55.7 fL; he received 3 units of packed red blood cells. Anticoagulation was held, and abdominal CT showed transmural thickening of the gastric antral and pyloric walls protruding into the duodenal bulb, multifocal bilateral segmental and subsegmental pulmonary emboli, and a nonocclusive thrombus from the right renal vein into the suprarenal IVC. An IVC filter was placed. Upper endoscopy demonstrated diffusely irregular, raised gastric mucosa throughout the gastric body, resembling a soft carpeted mass. Biopsy revealed prominent foveolar hyperplasia, focal granulation tissue, ulceration, reactive glandular changes, and chronic active inflammation, with no evidence of dysplasia or malignancy. Immunostaining was negative for Helicobacter pylori. A probable diagnosis of Ménétrier disease was established, and he was discharged on high‐dose oral pantoprazole.

A 35-year-old African American man presented with a one-month history of worsening low back and bilateral leg pain, intermittent night sweats, and a 32-kg unintentional weight loss over one year. He denied saddle anesthesia or bowel/bladder incontinence. He was treated empirically for sciatica with prednisone 10 mg daily without relief. He then experienced an episode of leg weakness and was admitted for evaluation. 

On examination, vital signs were stable. There was no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Neurologic examination showed intact strength and sensation in both lower extremities. Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, normal serum electrolytes, and a normal serum calcium level of 8.1 mg/dL. HIV serologies were negative.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine demonstrated multiple enhancing lesions in the T11, T12, L3, and L4 vertebral bodies, right sacrum, and ilium, with retropulsion causing effacement of the lateral recesses at L3–L4 and L4–L5; a small epidural lesion was noted at T5 without significant cord compression. Additional osseous lesions were seen in the sternum and multiple ribs.

Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, mild cardiomegaly, a dilated main pulmonary artery (3.6 cm), hepatomegaly (18.1 cm), splenomegaly (12.4 cm), and multiple enlarged pelvic sidewall, external iliac, and inguinal lymph nodes. Testicular ultrasound was normal. Serum protein electrophoresis, urine immunofixation, β-hCG levels, and fecal occult blood testing were all negative.

A CT-guided core biopsy of a left iliac crest lesion revealed noncaseating and necrotizing granulomas; Grocott’s methenamine silver and Ziehl–Neelsen stains were negative. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial needle aspiration of a mediastinal lymph node demonstrated nonnecrotizing granulomas without malignant cells; fungal and acid-fast cultures were negative. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme was 62 U/L (reference 14–82).

One month later, an excisional biopsy of a left inguinal lymph node again showed necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous lymphadenopathy without evidence of fungal or acid-fast organisms. An ^18F-FDG PET scan revealed extensive hypermetabolic osseous and nodal uptake.

A 21-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus (onset at age 15 years) and hyperlipidemia presented with a 3-month history of gradually worsening difficulty walking. She and her family denied any cognitive complaints. On neurological examination, she was alert and oriented, with no overt encephalopathy. Her speech was normal. There was moderate-to-severe truncal ataxia and appendicular ataxia in both arms and legs. Eye-movement testing showed no square-wave jerks, mild left-beating gaze-evoked nystagmus on extreme left gaze, normal pursuit without saccadic intrusions, and normal saccades. Deep-tendon reflexes were normal throughout. There was no pes cavus.

Laboratory studies revealed an anti–thyroid peroxidase antibody titer of 1:1600 (normal <1:100) and a borderline anti–thyroglobulin antibody titer of 1:40 (normal <1:20). Thyroid function tests were within normal limits. Serum anti–glutamic acid decarboxylase, antinuclear antibody, anti-Ro, anti-La antibodies, and ceruloplasmin were all normal or negative. 

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a protein level of 46 mg/dL, a glucose level of 112 mg/dL (serum glucose 196 mg/dL), 1 white cell per mm3, and 570 red cells per mm3. CSF oligoclonal bands, anti–aquaporin-4 antibodies, and a CSF paraneoplastic panel (including anti-Hu, anti-Ri, anti-Yo, anti–Purkinje cell cytoplasmic antibody type 2 [PCA2], anti-Tr, anti-MAG, anti-Ma, anti-GAD, anti–CRMP5, and anti-amphiphysin) were negative.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was normal without evidence of cerebellar atrophy.

A 60-year-old Japanese woman presented with a one-month history of slightly pruritic, tender subcutaneous nodules in both temporal areas. She denied systemic symptoms, including fever, weight loss, visual changes, or musculoskeletal stiffness. Her medical history was unremarkable for allergic disease or asthma; she was a 20–30 pack-year smoker. Family history was notable only for neurofibromatosis in her son.

On examination, her temperature was 35.7°C, pulse 61/min, and blood pressure 131/71 mmHg. The nodules corresponded to enlargement of the superficial temporal arteries with reduced pulsation. Cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were normal; there was no peripheral edema.

Ultrasound of the temporal arteries showed hypoechogenic wall thickening and luminal stenosis. Initial laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 10,300/μL with 5.4% eosinophils (556/μL); ESR and CRP were within normal limits. Serologic tests including ANA, RF, ANCA, complement levels, and hepatitis serologies were unremarkable. Stool examinations were negative for parasites. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed no ischemic changes.

Over the next three months, her absolute eosinophil count rose to 1,954/μL. She developed coolness and cyanosis of the fingertips and small pruritic nodules on the sides of her fingers. CT of the chest and echocardiography were normal. Color duplex ultrasonography of the hands revealed occlusion of the ulnar arteries and a corkscrew pattern of the digital arteries. Angiography confirmed occlusion of the ulnar artery, palmar arch, and proper digital arteries.

A 25-year-old Samoan man was referred for evaluation of a 2-month history of persistent productive cough and worsening exertional dyspnea. Over the preceding 3 months he had noted subjective fevers and a 5-kg weight loss. He had chronic sinusitis and had been diagnosed with asthma in adolescence; treatment with inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators yielded no improvement. He was a lifelong non-smoker, worked in a mattress factory, and had no known risk factors for tuberculosis or immunosuppression.

On examination, he was afebrile, with an oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. Auscultation revealed coarse crackles predominantly at the lung bases, without wheezing; there were no signs of right heart failure.

A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral nodular interstitial infiltrates in the mid and lower lung zones. High-resolution computed tomography of the chest showed extensive tree-in-bud nodularity in all lobes, most pronounced in the lower lobes, along with bronchial wall thickening and early bronchiectasis. Spirometry revealed a fixed moderately severe airflow obstruction (FEV₁ 55% predicted, FEV₁/FVC 63%).

Sputum cultures grew Haemophilus influenzae; mycobacterial cultures were negative. An autoimmune panel, including rheumatoid factor and cold agglutinins, was within normal limits.

A 77-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of recurrent episodes of transient vision loss in her right eye over the past 6 months. Each episode lasted 2–4 hours and occurred several times per week. She denied any headache or migrainous symptoms. Her past medical history was notable for hypertension, dyslipidemia, and thyroidectomy on levothyroxine; her ocular history was significant only for uncomplicated phacoemulsification with in-the-bag intraocular lens (IOL) implantation in the right eye 16 years ago.  

On initial examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 18 mm Hg OD and 14 mm Hg OS. Humphrey visual field testing (24-2) showed a mean deviation of −2.83 dB OD and −0.05 dB OS. Optical coherence tomography revealed ganglion cell layer thickness of 64 μm OD and 67 μm OS, and retinal nerve fiber layer thickness of 89 μm OD and 87 μm OS. Slit-lamp examination showed mild posterior capsule opacification but was otherwise unremarkable.  

Given the transient monocular vision losses, a vascular workup for amaurosis fugax was performed, including C-reactive protein, MRI of the head and orbits, transthoracic echocardiography, carotid Doppler ultrasound, and 24-hour Holter monitoring; all results were within normal limits.  

On follow-up, IOP in the right eye had risen to 32–38 mm Hg (21–23 mm Hg OS). Gonioscopy revealed blood in the right anterior chamber angle without iris transillumination defects. Cerebral angiography was then obtained. Results were negative for any dural or carotid–cavernous fistula. Ultrasound biomicroscopy of the right eye demonstrated a circumscribed mass contacting the posterior surface of the iris.

A 9-year-old girl was referred for an irregular heart rate noted at an incidental well-child visit. An electrocardiogram showed a prolonged QTc of 485 ms and runs of non-sustained bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. There was no family history of arrhythmogenic disorders, congenital heart disease, or sudden death; the mother and maternal grandmother had syndactyly. Physical examination revealed short stature, low-set ears, mild micrognathia, wide-spaced eyes, dental abnormalities, and left iris heterochromia. Vital signs were age-appropriate. Holter monitoring revealed a ventricular ectopy burden of 40%. Laboratory studies, including a CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, cardiac enzymes, and thyroid function tests, were normal. Exercise stress testing showed no significant increase in ectopy from baseline at higher heart rates. Transthoracic echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a structurally normal heart with no evidence of ventricular dysfunction.

A 58-year-old man with a history of heavy smoking presented with 10 hours of chest pain, dyspnea, and general malaise. Vital signs were notable for a pulse rate of 110 beats per minute, blood pressure of 110/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable, but fine rales were heard up to the mid-lung fields. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm with a QS pattern and ST-segment elevation in leads V1 through V6, consistent with an acute anterior myocardial infarction. He received 300 mg of clopidogrel, 150 mg of aspirin, subcutaneous enoxaparin, intravenous furosemide, and underwent unsuccessful fibrinolysis with tenecteplase. On transfer to the cardiology ward, he was hemodynamically stable. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 20% with akinesis of the apex and anterior and septal walls, a small pericardial effusion adjacent to the anterior and lateral right ventricle, and a 59 × 32 mm hyperechoic structure at the left ventricular apex. Color-Doppler imaging did not demonstrate any flow within this structure.

A 6-month-old term female infant was brought for evaluation of a congenital scalp lesion. The lesion has been present since birth; there is no history of trauma or maternal teratogen exposure. The infant was born at term by uncomplicated vaginal delivery and had a history of a patent foramen ovale diagnosed at birth.

On dermatologic examination, there is a single, oval, midline occipital lesion measuring 0.6 × 0.7 cm with a glistening, translucent surface, absence of hair, and a distinct hair-collar sign. Dermoscopy shows a translucent epidermis, telangiectasia, absence of follicular orifices, and peripheral hypertrichosis. The remainder of the skin exam is normal.

General examination reveals normal growth and developmental milestones with no spinal or limb deformities. Lung auscultation is clear. Cardiac examination discloses a grade 3 holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border without a thrill. Echocardiography demonstrates an asymptomatic small ventricular septal defect.

A 33‐year‐old woman, gravida 5 para 4, with a history of attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, treated hypothyroidism (discontinued in 2005), and previous bilateral carpal tunnel release, presented with many years of bilateral leg pain that worsened with activity and caused nocturnal cramps. She was unable to sleep more than 3 hours at a time without walking to relieve cramping of the first toes into dorsiflexion. At 30 weeks of a pregnancy due on March 23, 2008, her body mass index was 24.1 (68 kg, 168 cm). She rated her leg pain at 120% on a visual‐analogue scale and completed a pain drawing showing diffuse “toothache‐like” pain and radiating lines above the knees.

On examination, palpation elicited excessive tenderness in all muscle compartments of both legs, maximal laterally, with increased tenderness after a 3-minute exertional step test. Arterial pulses were normal in the groins, ankles, and feet, and there were no signs of venous insufficiency. Lumbar CT and MRI were normal. Neurography showed normal nerve conduction. Skin sensitivity was reduced bilaterally in the distributions of the deep fibular, superficial fibular, and sural nerves, with normal sensitivity above the knees. A neurologist excluded common neuropathies, and a physiatrist proposed a tentative diagnosis of bilateral chronic compartment syndrome.

A 20-year-old man fell and struck the back of his head. He reported severe neck and shoulder pain with difficulty raising both arms and in gripping objects. He was alert (GCS 15), with normal vital signs and no signs of head injury or respiratory distress. On cervical palpation, there was tenderness at the upper cervical spine and marked paraspinal muscle spasm. Neurologically, he had weakness of both arms (right worse than left) in the C5–T1 distribution with brisk reflexes but no sensory deficits. The lower limbs had brisk reflexes but normal strength. Cranial nerves were intact. An open-mouth odontoid radiograph and cervical CT scan showed an undisplaced type III odontoid fracture.

A 52-year-old woman with known unrepaired Type II tricuspid atresia with d-transposition of the great arteries, hypoplastic right ventricle, unrestricted atrial and ventricular septal defects, and multi-level pulmonic stenosis presented with sudden-onset severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain without nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or dysuria. Two months earlier, she had flu-like symptoms treated with doxycycline, and she reported poor dentition with no dental care for two years. On examination, her blood pressure was 90/54 mmHg, she was afebrile, heart rate was 80 bpm, and oxygen saturation was 79% on room air. A grade-2 systolic ejection murmur was heard at the left upper sternal border. She had cyanotic fingers bilaterally but no Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, or splinter hemorrhages. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 17.9 g/dL and C-reactive protein 2.2 mg/dL; lactate, white blood cell count, and creatinine were within reference ranges. Computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated an acute right renal infarct; cerebral computed tomography was negative. She was anticoagulated with heparin.

A 25-year-old woman with insulin-treated diabetes mellitus presented 4 weeks after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with a 1-week history of progressive vision loss in her right eye. Vital signs were stable. Visual acuity was 20/80 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Intraocular pressures were 14 mmHg OD and 12 mmHg OS. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed fine keratic precipitates, 3+ anterior chamber cells, and a clear lens. Dilated fundus examination showed 1+ vitreous haze, a hyperemic optic disc, and multiple yellow-white retinal infiltrates. The left eye examination was normal. Fluorescein angiography of the right eye demonstrated diffuse retinal vascular leakage and optic-disc staining. Optical coherence tomography showed a dry macula. 

She was admitted with a provisional diagnosis of right acute nongranulomatous panuveitis, probably representing atypical toxoplasmosis. A uveitis workup—including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, purified protein derivative skin test, chest CT, syphilis and toxoplasmosis serology, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and urine analysis—was entirely negative. Hemoglobin A1c was 6.7%. Empirical therapy with clindamycin, co-trimoxazole, and systemic prednisolone resulted in only transient mild improvement, followed by persistent inflammation. Repeat toxoplasmosis serology remained negative. 

Further history revealed persistent vaginal discharge during the peripartum period without fever. A gynecologic evaluation including a vaginal swab showed heavy growth of Candida albicans. Infectious disease consultation prompted blood and urine cultures, contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and cardiac echography, all of which were unremarkable.

A 42-year-old Sri Lankan shopkeeper with diet‐controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with three weeks of generalized malaise, nightly “feverishness,” evening sweats, anorexia, and 3-kg weight loss. He denied cough, hemoptysis, or tuberculosis contacts. There was nausea without vomiting or abdominal pain and no features of autoimmune disease. He had no significant environmental or travel exposures and no history of recurrent infections.

On examination he was afebrile, mildly pale, with mild nontender hepatomegaly but no lymphadenopathy, rashes, or splenomegaly. Blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg without postural drop. Initial labs showed pancytopenia (WBC 3.0×10^9/L, platelets 120×10^6/L, hemoglobin 10 g/dL), CRP 8 mg/L, ESR 60 mm/h, normal liver and renal profiles, and HbA1c 6.5%. Chest radiograph and echocardiogram were normal. Blood and urine cultures, Mantoux test, and bone marrow biopsy (including fungal and tuberculosis studies) were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild hepatosplenomegaly, para‐aortic lymphadenopathy, and bilateral hypoechoic adrenal masses.

One week later he returned with three days of severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and postural dizziness. He was hypotensive (90/60 mmHg with a 30 mmHg postural drop), tachycardic (100 bpm), and dehydrated. Despite fluids his blood pressure remained low. Labs showed hyponatremia (114 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (5.0 mmol/L), random cortisol 1.3 µg/L, and improved blood counts. An ACTH stimulation test showed persistently low cortisol (<1 µg/L). CT of the chest and abdomen revealed bilateral, well‐defined, homogeneously enhancing adrenal masses (left 6.9×3.7×5.0 cm; right 5.3×3.4×5.4 cm), mild hepatosplenomegaly, and patchy para‐aortic lymphadenopathy.

Ultrasound‐guided adrenal biopsy showed necrosis with plasma cells, lymphocytes, and histiocytes. Gomori–Grocott methenamine silver staining demonstrated numerous fungal spores morphologically similar to Histoplasma.

An 84-year-old woman was admitted with a  one-day history of left lower abdominal pain and nausea without fever. She had a history of hysterectomy, femoral neck fracture repair, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. Her body mass index was 18.2 kg/m2; vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, there was tenderness in the left lower abdomen without peritoneal signs and no Murphy sign. Laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, liver function tests, and biliary enzymes, were all within normal limits. 
A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen at admission showed an enlarged gallbladder with wall thickening but no gallstones, along with prominent small-bowel gas, mild intestinal dilatation, and slight wall thickening. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed an enlarged, thick-walled gallbladder without stones. She was diagnosed with acute enterocolitis or subileus and managed conservatively with bowel rest and intravenous fluids.
Six hours later, she developed sudden severe right upper quadrant pain and vomiting unresponsive to analgesics or antiemetics. A repeat CT scan demonstrated that the gallbladder had become more distended and thickened, had rotated approximately 180°, and had shifted toward the midline; the cystic duct was now located on the right side of the gallbladder.

A 44-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a one‐month history of transient numbness of her right face and arm. She also reported intermittent episodes of left‐arm weakness over several years previously attributed to psychosomatic causes. On neurologic exam, plantar responses were indifferent bilaterally, and deep‐tendon reflexes were brisk. Brain MRI demonstrated multiple T2 and FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter and periventricular regions, with mild linear cortical enhancement in the left parietal lobe. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and laboratory studies for inflammatory or autoimmune disease were unremarkable. A detailed review of the MRI revealed that the lesions were predominantly located in the watershed zone between the anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery territories, without restricted diffusion. Given this watershed distribution, magnetic resonance angiography of the brain was recommended to exclude a cerebrovascular etiology.

A 40-year-old man presented with right upper quadrant pain and fevers up to 38 °C. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 17.9 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein of 425 mg/L, and normal liver-function tests. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated acute cholecystitis with an 8 mm stone impacted at the gallbladder neck and surrounding inflammation involving the duodenum and hepatic flexure. He received intravenous antibiotics, improved, and returned four weeks later for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

Intraoperatively, dense adhesions of the omentum and transverse colon obscured the gallbladder and dissection was converted to open. The gangrenous gallbladder was separated from the duodenum, which showed patchy bile discoloration but no serosal tear. A subtotal cholecystectomy was completed without encountering a bile leak.

An intraoperative cholangiogram (IOC) demonstrated an unexpected streak of contrast just inferior to the cystic duct. The duodenum was flushed with saline and pressurized methylene blue via the cystic duct catheter, with no visible leak. Metal clips were placed on the discolored duodenal areas. A repeat IOC performed 10 minutes after the first showed no contrast leak and the disappearance of the previously noted streak.

A 75-year-old woman presented with acute severe dyspnea. Eight and thirteen years earlier, she had undergone coronary artery bypass grafting: the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) to the left anterior descending artery, the right internal mammary artery (RIMA) to an obtuse marginal branch, and a saphenous vein graft to the distal left circumflex artery. Her medical history included hypertension, diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 6.5%–6.7%), hyperlipidemia (LDL 100 mg/dL), and a bilateral neck bruit noted two years ago. MR angiography at that time showed <50% stenosis of both carotid arteries and 50% stenosis of both subclavian arteries. Ankle–brachial indices were elevated (ABI 1.62 on both sides), attributed to arterial stiffness, and she was asymptomatic without inter-arm blood pressure difference or arm claudication.

Six months before admission, she developed exertional chest discomfort. Two months later, her systolic blood pressure fell from 126/70 mmHg to 94/60 mmHg. ECG showed worsening ST-segment depression and QRS widening; echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 40% (previously >55%). Treatment with pimobendan led to slight improvement. One week before admission, her blood pressure measured 70/40 mmHg in the right arm and 80/50 mmHg in the left arm; antihypertensive medications were discontinued.

She was scheduled for cardiac catheterization but presented first with severe dyspnea. In the emergency department, respiratory rate was 30/min, heart rate 86/min, temperature 36.0°C, and bilateral arm blood pressures were difficult to measure. Chest radiography showed severe bilateral pulmonary edema. ECG demonstrated diffuse ST-segment depression with non-specific intraventricular conduction delay. Cardiac troponin I was positive; creatine phosphokinase rose from 66 U/L to 720 U/L. Renal and liver functions were normal.

She was intubated, admitted to intensive care, and started on intravenous dobutamine and furosemide. Dyspnea improved rapidly, and urine output was 950 mL in the first 4 hours and 50–100 mL/h thereafter. Despite vigorous treatment, systolic blood pressure remained low at 60–70 mmHg in both arms, but femoral pulses were easily palpable.

A 46-year-old woman presented with a 1.5-year history of progressive weakness in her left upper extremity that had impaired her work as a hairstylist. She had a background of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) and cervical intervertebral disc degeneration. Ten weeks earlier, she underwent left carpal tunnel release without symptomatic improvement.

Initial EMG/NCS (October 2020) showed moderate-to-severe left CTS, mild right CTS, and mild cervical radiculopathy. On examination, she had bilateral hyperreflexia in upper and lower extremities (3+ biceps, brachioradialis, triceps, patellar, Achilles), bilateral positive Hoffman signs, and weakness more pronounced on the left (deltoid 3/5 bilaterally; biceps 4/5 right, 3/5 left; triceps 4/5 right, 3/5 left; wrist extensors/flexors 4/5 left; hand intrinsics 3/5 left). Lower extremity strength was 4/5 in tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus bilaterally. Sensation was intact.

Cervical MRI revealed degenerative disc disease at C5–C6 and C6–C7 with a small C6–C7 disc herniation causing moderate bilateral foraminal stenosis, worse on the left, but no central canal stenosis.

Given the combination of marked bilateral weakness (left > right), hyperreflexia, positive Hoffman signs, and fasciculations, she was referred to neurology for repeat EMG/NCS and to a neurosurgeon for surgical consideration.

A 10‐year‐old girl with a history of SLE diagnosed at age 6 (initial features: polyarthralgia, facial rash, oral ulcers; ANA 1:320; anti-dsDNA 21.3 IU/mL; normal complement; SLEDAI 9) had been well on hydroxychloroquine. She presented with a 2-day history of fever up to 39.5°C, headache, and repeated vomiting. On examination, she was alert, without focal deficits or seizures; Brudzinski’s sign was positive. 

Noncontrast head CT showed an extensive hypodensity in the left temporal lobe without edema or hemorrhage. Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 29 cm H₂O, CSF WBC 485 cells/mm³ (91.7% polymorphs), protein 1526 mg/L, and glucose 3.6 mmol/L; gram stain and CSF cultures were negative. EEG demonstrated focal slowing with a sharp wave over the left posterior temporal region without epileptiform discharges. 

Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and antivirals were started, but fever and meningism persisted. Blood tests showed CRP 14.7 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/hr, C3 0.27 g/L, C4 < 0.1 g/L, ANA 1:2560, and anti-dsDNA > 300 IU/mL. Anti-NMDA, anti-NMO, and anti-MOG antibodies were negative, as were lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies. Multiplex PCR and antigen tests for common meningitis pathogens, plus specific viral, mycobacterial, and fungal studies, were all negative.

Brain MRI revealed T2-weighted hyperintensity in the left temporal subcortical and deep white matter with mild cortical swelling; susceptibility-weighted imaging showed petechial hemorrhages. MRA and MRV were normal, and MR spectroscopy showed no lactate peak.

A woman in her 50s with a 7-year history of methotrexate therapy (8 mg weekly) for rheumatoid arthritis underwent an annual health check and was found to have abnormal chest imaging. She reported no respiratory symptoms, no fever or cough, had never smoked, and had no known exposure to pigeons.

On chest radiography, there were infiltrative shadows in the right lower lung field. Noncontrast chest CT showed two small nodules and two areas of pulmonary infiltration in the right lower lobe; there was no pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies revealed:
• Leukocyte count 4.9 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 68.8%, lymphocytes 16.7%, eosinophils 5.1%)  
• C-reactive protein and glycosylated hemoglobin within normal limits  
• Tumor markers (CEA, SCC antigen, CYFRA 21-1, SLX, pro-GRP, NSE) within normal ranges  
• KL-6 237 U/mL  
• Interferon-γ release assay (T-SPOT.TB) negative  
• HIV antibody negative  
• Rheumatoid factor < 5 IU/mL; PR3-ANCA < 1.0; MPO-ANCA < 1.0; anti-ARS < 5.0; anti-SSA and anti-SSB negative; ANA titer 1:40  
• Soluble IL-2 receptor 547 U/mL  
• (1,3)-β-D-glucan 34.6 pg/mL (upper limit of normal 20 pg/mL)  
• Aspergillus antigen 0.3; Candida antigen < 0.02 U/mL

A 34-year-old man presents with three weeks of migratory generalized urticarial wheals that are intensely pruritic, last less than 24 hours each, and occur without relation to foods, drugs, physical stimuli, or exercise. Two months earlier, he had multiple wasp stings leading to acute hives treated with intravenous methylprednisolone and intramuscular chlorpheniramine, with symptom resolution in 24 hours; the next day he developed satellite lymphadenitis that resolved in 5 days with topical steroids. He has no history of allergic or autoimmune disease. Routine blood tests are normal except for a baseline mild leukopenia; basophil and eosinophil counts are normal. Workup excludes Helicobacter pylori antigen, beta-hemolytic streptococci, Chlamydia spp., Mycoplasma spp., hepatitis A/B/C, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and other herpesviruses. Thyroid peroxidase, TSH receptor, thyroglobulin, anti-endomysial, and anti–tissue transglutaminase antibodies are negative. D-dimer, ESR, CRP, fibrinogen, ferritin, and complement levels are normal; an autologous serum skin test is negative. Skin tests to common inhalant and food allergens, Apis mellifera, and Polistes dominula venoms are negative; intradermal tests to Vespula spp and Vespa crabro venoms are positive at 0.1 μg/mL. Serum specific IgE is elevated for Vespula spp (5.46 kU/L), Vespa crabro (0.47 kU/L), and Polistes dominula (0.69 kU/L); component-resolved diagnostics show rVes v 5 at 6.17 kU/L and rPol d 5 at 1.07 kU/L. Total IgE is 132 kU/L and baseline tryptase is 7 μg/mL. Despite high-dose antihistamines and prednisone tapered to 5 mg daily over three months, his urticaria remains poorly controlled with a high urticaria activity score.

A 7-month-old intact female Maine Coon kitten was evaluated for a 2-month history of severe regurgitation occurring seconds to minutes after eating or drinking, with episodes ranging from twice weekly to twice daily. Weight loss was noted over this period despite a normal appetite, water consumption, and activity level. Previous treatments—including maropitant, cimetidine, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, and gastrointestinal diets—had no effect. The kitten had a history of chronic vomiting of undigested food and bile from age 3–5 months and a self-resolving episode of acute vomiting at 5 months. No regurgitation or vomiting occurred before 3 months of age. On presentation, the kitten was bright, alert, weighed 2.5 kg with a body condition score of 2/9, and had stunted growth; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Thoracic radiographs obtained before and after oral contrast demonstrated severe and diffuse oesophageal dilatation consistent with generalized megaoesophagus, with persistent contrast and aeric distension of the oesophageal lumen and apparent loss of continuity between the distal oesophagus and the stomach. No aspiration pneumonia was evident.

A 12-year-old girl presented with a 2-week history of progressive weakness and generalized edema, which began in the feet and later involved the abdomen, and a 1-week history of progressively worsening dyspnea at rest. There was no fever, headache, rash, or other constitutional symptoms. She had no prior serious illness. 

On examination, she was in severe respiratory distress, markedly pale, with bilateral pitting pedal edema and mild dehydration. Respiratory rate was 40 breaths per minute. Chest examination revealed stony-dull percussion notes in the mid and lower lung zones bilaterally, decreased vocal and tactile fremitus, vesicular breath sounds of reduced intensity, and a few basal crepitations. 

Cardiovascular examination showed a low pulse volume, pulsus paradoxus, raised jugular venous pressure of 11 cm H₂O, tachycardia at 120 bpm, hypotension (60/30 mmHg), an impalpable apex beat, and very distant heart sounds. Abdominal examination revealed tender hepatomegaly 7 cm below the right costal margin and mild ascites. Other systems were normal. 

An initial diagnosis of congestive cardiac failure with bilateral pleural effusions and large pericardial effusion—possibly secondary to viral myocarditis or pericarditis, with tuberculosis to be ruled out—was made, and she was started on anti–heart-failure therapy. A chest radiograph confirmed bilateral pleural effusions and an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Bilateral pleural fluid aspirations yielded clear fluid with chemical analysis suggestive of a transudate. A Mantoux test was negative. Full blood count and film were unremarkable except for a packed cell volume of 23% (hemoglobin, 7.6 g/dL).

A 47-year-old woman with HIV-1 infection presented with a 10-day history of diffuse maculopapular rash, fever, myalgias, arthralgias, choluria, pruritus, and right upper-quadrant abdominal pain. Three days before admission she developed nausea, vomiting, and decreased oral intake. Her HIV had been well controlled on zidovudine, lamivudine, and lopinavir–ritonavir for the past three years, with CD4 counts consistently >500 cells/mm3. Forty-five days before presentation her regimen was changed to zidovudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine because of gastrointestinal intolerance. Twenty days after starting nevirapine the rash and jaundice began. 

On examination: temperature 39.0°C; blood pressure 95/66 mm Hg; marked conjunctival and skin icterus; diffuse maculopapular rash covering >50% of body surface; no lymphadenopathy; abdomen soft with tenderness in the right hypochondrium; no hepatosplenomegaly; neurologic examination normal.

Laboratory studies showed: normal complete blood count and differential; normal glucose, electrolytes, and pancreatic enzymes; elevated aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase; acute kidney injury with a threefold increase in serum creatinine and a 75% decrease in estimated glomerular filtration rate. Testing was negative for cytomegalovirus antigenemia, hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B and C antibodies. An electrocardiogram was normal. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a liver of normal size and shape with homogeneously increased echogenicity of the parenchyma.

A 7-year-old male Bichon Frise was evaluated for a 4-week history of progressive cough and recent anorexia. The cough began intermittently but increased in frequency over several days, and the dog’s appetite declined. There was no prior respiratory disease. Vaccinations were current; no parasite prophylaxis for 18 months. On exam, the dog was bright and alert, with normal heart and lung sounds, but had lost 20% of body weight since his last visit 18 months earlier. Mild otitis externa was noted; otherwise the physical examination was unremarkable.

Hematology on day 1 demonstrated marked eosinophilia (7.9 × 10^9/l; reference range 0.06–1.23) and moderate basophilia (0.27 × 10^9/l; reference range 0.00–0.1). Serum biochemistry was within reference limits. An antigen test for heartworm and fecal parasite analysis were negative.

Thoracic radiographs showed a large soft-tissue opacity in the left cranial lung lobe with a mild generalized bronchiolar pattern and no pleural effusion. After 10 days of antibiotics and bronchodilators, eosinophilia resolved but the mass on radiographs was unchanged. Pulmonary neoplasia was suspected, and the dog was referred for advanced imaging.

Contrast CT of the thorax revealed a lobulated mass in the left cranial lung lobe measuring 7.6 × 2.1 × 5.8 cm, compressing and distorting adjacent bronchi with heterogeneous enhancement and fluid pockets. Irregular nodular thickening infiltrated and nearly occluded airways in the right cranial and middle lobes. The sternal and cranial mediastinal lymph nodes were moderately enlarged. Abdominal CT was unremarkable.

A 70-year-old man presented with 2 weeks of abdominal pain, headache, and new melena after a family-physician trial of NSAIDs and a mucosal protectant. On arrival, he was hypotensive (80/56 mmHg), tachycardic (100 bpm), and severely anemic (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL). After blood-transfusion stabilization, esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) showed atypical esophagitis lesions in the lower esophagus and shallow ulcers and erosions throughout the stomach and duodenum. Colonoscopy (CS) revealed extensive, map-like shallow ulcers with well-defined margins and islands of residual mucosa in the terminal ileum; biopsy showed moderate lymphocytic infiltration without malignancy or cytomegalovirus. Biopsy of endoscopically normal ileal mucosa showed only mild lymphocytic infiltration. A proton‐pump inhibitor was started, and upper GI lesions healed on follow-up EGD one month later. Capsule endoscopy had previously demonstrated multiple small aphtha-like erosions in the ileum. Stool cultures were negative. The patient’s gastrin level was 100 pg/mL (normal <200 pg/mL). Serum MPO-ANCA, PR3-ANCA, and antinuclear antibodies were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable. Follow-up CS one month after presentation showed that the terminal ileal ulcers and erosions remained unchanged despite discontinuation of NSAIDs.

A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and moderate aortic regurgitation was referred for resection of a newly diagnosed left adrenal mass after 3 months of spells characterized by anxiety, agitation, headaches, pallor, palpitations, and hypertensive crises. An abdominal CT scan showed a left adrenal nodule compressing the splenic vein. Elevated urinary normetanephrines and metanephrines confirmed a catecholamine-producing tumor. He received 30 days of doxazosin and bisoprolol before surgery and was hemodynamically stable on admission. Preoperative ECG showed sinus tachycardia with T-wave inversions in lateral leads. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an LVEF of 55% without regional wall motion abnormalities.

He underwent laparoscopic left adrenalectomy. Gentle tumor manipulation elicited transient blood-pressure spikes to 180 mmHg until the main adrenal vein was ligated. Immediately after tumor removal, he became hypotensive to 50/30 mmHg and developed a new left bundle-branch block. Emergent coronary angiography showed no obstructive atherosclerotic disease (TIMI 2 flow, no vasospasm). Left ventriculography revealed circumferential midventricular akinesia. Repeat echocardiography demonstrated midventricular and apical akinesia with an LVEF of 25%. Cardiac biomarkers peaked on postoperative day 2 (troponin 21.9 ng/mL [URL 0.2 ng/mL]; NT-proBNP 7000 pg/mL [URL 300 pg/mL]).

A 40-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension presented in Pemba, Mozambique, with a 2-day history of fever, chills, malaise, general weakness and prostration. He denied headache, arthralgia or myalgia at onset. On admission, temperature was 38.2 °C, blood pressure 110/75 mmHg, and a diffuse, undifferentiated rash was noted without hemorrhages or edema. A rapid diagnostic test for Plasmodium falciparum was negative. Laboratory studies showed: white blood cell count 15.7 × 10^3/mm^3 (lymphocytes 6.9 × 10^3/mm^3), hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 33 × 10^3/mm^3, alanine aminotransferase 245 U/L, glucose 9.11 mmol/L, and urea 14.2 mmol/L. No blood cultures were available. He was started on ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin and ampicillin. Over the next two days, fever persisted and he developed headache, dizziness, symmetrical polyarthralgia and melaena. On hospital day 2, hemoglobin fell to 6.2 g/dL and platelets rose to 56 × 10^3/mm^3. On day 3 he was transferred to the ICU and received three units of whole blood. On day 4 he became comatose. Repeat malaria tests remained negative, and urinalysis was unremarkable. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were continued without improvement.

A 37-year-old man presented with headache, psychomotor retardation, and left hemiparesis. Laboratory evaluation revealed HIV infection (CD4+ T-cell count 20 cells/μL; plasma HIV RNA 301,000 copies/mL) and positive serology for Toxoplasma gondii. A brain CT scan showed multiple scattered parenchymal lesions with perilesional edema, mass effect, and ring contrast enhancement. He received anti-toxoplasma therapy without corticosteroids, with clinical and radiologic improvement, and initiated HAART one month after diagnosis (regimen as per institutional protocol). Toxoplasmosis therapy continued (followed by suppressive dosing), and MAC prophylaxis was maintained.

Three months after HAART initiation, he reported abrupt onset of right lower-limb numbness that progressed over one month to involve his entire right lower limb and right hemi-abdomen. He denied fever or other systemic symptoms and affirmed full adherence to all therapies. On examination, mental status and cranial nerves were normal. Apart from his prior left hemiparesis, there was a distinct sensory level at T9 on the right, with loss of touch and pain sensation below this level; strength, proprioception, and reflexes in the affected areas were preserved. 

A follow-up brain CT scan revealed that some prior lesions had improved, others had slightly worsened with ring enhancement and edema, and several new lesions had appeared. MRI of the dorsal spinal cord demonstrated T2-weighted hyperintense lesions extending from T3 to T9, with a probable posterolateral lesion at T7–T8. At this time, CD4+ T-cell count had risen to 128 cells/μL and plasma HIV RNA had fallen to 121 copies/mL. CSF analysis showed 5 cells/μL, protein 58 mg/dL, glucose 51 mg/dL; Gram and acid-fast stains, microbiological cultures, cryptococcal antigen, VDRL, and PCR assays for JC virus, BK virus, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, human herpesvirus 6, varicella-zoster virus, and enterovirus were negative. CSF PCR for T. gondii was not performed. EBV PCR was positive, but a normal CSF lymphocyte phenotype and a whole-body PET scan showed no hypermetabolic cerebral or medullary lesions. HTLV-I/II serology was negative.

A 79-year-old woman was admitted for a prolonged episode of confusion. Over the past months, she had recurrent episodes of confusion, disorientation, dysphasia, and fluctuating levels of consciousness; nonconvulsive seizures and status epilepticus had been considered, and antiseizure drugs including levetiracetam and gabapentin were ineffective. Intravenous valproic acid led to severe stupor that resolved after withdrawal. Her medical history included marginal zone lymphoma in remission (previous rituximab and bendamustine) and a pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy 5 years earlier for intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm.

On examination, she was disoriented and dysphasic without focal motor or sensory deficits. Electroencephalography showed generalized, irregular delta-theta activity with triphasic waves. Laboratory testing revealed a serum ammonia concentration of 121 μg/dl (reference 19–55 μg/dl) despite normal liver and kidney function. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and brain MRI were unremarkable. Hyperammonemic encephalopathy was suspected, and lactulose, rifaximin, and daily enemas were initiated. Serum ammonia levels decreased, and her clinical status improved under this regimen. Abdominal ultrasound with elastography and abdominal MRI showed only minor signs of chronic liver disease, without evidence of cirrhosis or significant portal hypertension.

A 63-year-old man presented with a 15-year history of various “foreign bodies” emanating from the superior fornices of both eyes, associated with blurred vision, burning, dryness, redness, and eye pain. His symptoms began in 2004 after colliding with a flowering “trumpet” plant; he reported flushing out visible plant and insect material with saline but continued to perceive persistent debris in a “permanent laceration” behind his eyes. In the days following the injury, he experienced insomnia, malaise, itching, eye pain, and, in a delirious state, rubbed his face against the floor. Over the years, he amassed a collection of self-extracted debris, including plant parts, acrylic fibers, cat hair, thread, metal filaments, and insects, retrieved through a ritual of filling and draining his kitchen sink and using a mascara brush to capture sediment.

He sought evaluation by multiple board-certified ophthalmologists and oculoplastic surgeons; records showed repeated eversion of lids and sweeping of the fornices with no evidence of retained foreign bodies. An orbital plain radiograph (March 2019) and an MRI of the orbits (June 2019) were both within normal limits.

In May 2019, corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/30 OS. External examination revealed floppy eyelid syndrome. Slit-lamp examination demonstrated trace conjunctival injection with corneal punctate staining bilaterally; no ophthalmic masses, lesions, or ulcers were seen, and pupils, motility, iris, and lenses were unremarkable.

On presentation to our clinic in February 2023, he reported a decrease in the volume of material and ocular symptoms. Examination with eyelid eversion again showed no lesions or foreign bodies. The patient was well-groomed and cooperative, with fluent speech, full orientation, intact memory, abstract thinking, insight, and judgment, and he denied suicidal ideation.

A 52-year-old man presented with a 5-year history of progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, pleuritic chest pain, abdominal distension, and peripheral edema. One year earlier, coronary angiography for chest pain was normal. Six months before admission, thoracentesis revealed a lymphocyte-predominant exudative right pleural effusion; cytology was nondiagnostic, and pleural biopsy was nondiagnostic.

Over the past 10 days, he noted worsening abdominal distension and pain. On examination, blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg, pulse 78/min, jugular venous pressure was markedly elevated, and heart sounds were muffled. Right lung base breath sounds were diminished. Abdominal examination showed mild hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral edema.

Laboratory tests were within normal limits. Analysis of ascitic fluid demonstrated protein 4.1 g/dL and serum–ascites albumin gradient 1.6 g/dL. Abdominal ultrasound showed congestive hepatomegaly, mild splenomegaly, ascites, and signs of portal hypertension; upper endoscopy revealed no esophageal varices, and viral hepatitis serologies were negative. Chest and abdominal CT demonstrated right pleural effusion, pericardial thickening with calcification, ascites, and inferior vena cava dilation.

A 15-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of painless, gradually progressive swelling of the upper and lower lips and of the gums.
She had no relevant medical history and no history of allergy to foods, drugs, or cosmetics; no asthma or eczema; and no family history of similar findings.
On extraoral examination, there was diffuse, soft, nontender swelling of both lips with normal temperature, with mild fissuring and a cobblestone appearance of the upper lip.
Intraoral examination revealed enlargement of the gingiva extending from tooth 13 to 23, involving marginal, interdental, and attached gingiva to the mucogingival junction; the gingiva was red, smooth, shiny, and lacked stippling. Probing revealed bleeding on probing, mild local deposits, and false pockets without clinical attachment loss.
Panoramic radiograph showed no alveolar bone loss in the maxillary or mandibular anterior region.
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, differential, platelet count, and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level, were within normal limits.
Chest radiograph was unremarkable, and the Mantoux test was negative.

A 29-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks’ gestation presented with a 4-day history of suprapubic pain and intermittent left flank pain, plus headache, nausea, and vomiting over the preceding 24 hours. She had no fever, vaginal bleeding, or changes in bowel habits and reported normal fetal movement. Her prenatal course was uncomplicated. She had a remote history of urolithiasis and a urinary tract infection two years earlier. 

On examination she was afebrile with normal vital signs and had mild left flank tenderness without peritoneal signs. A urine dipstick showed moderate leukocyte esterase, 6–10 squamous cells per high-power field, no blood, and no nitrites; urine culture later showed no growth. Her white blood cell count was 12 900 cells/mm3, creatinine was normal, and liver and biliary function tests were normal. Fetal fibronectin was negative, and cardiotocography showed rare contractions every 30 minutes with a reactive fetal heart rate. Betamethasone and a course of magnesium sulfate were administered for fetal lung maturity and neuroprotection, respectively, after which contractions resolved and flank pain improved.

On hospital day 3, she developed acute, colicky left flank pain with nausea and vomiting. Given the negative urine culture, absence of fever, and stable white blood cell count, infectious processes were considered less likely. A renal ultrasound showed mild left pelviectasis not out of proportion to normal pregnancy and small areas of echogenicity in the left kidney without shadowing; no definitive stones were visualized. Repeat urinalysis showed trace blood and trace leukocyte esterase. Gastrointestinal causes were deemed less likely given the location of the pain, good bowel sounds, lack of distention, and normal gastrointestinal and liver function tests. She was managed with intravenous fluids and analgesia, with symptom improvement. 

On hospital day 5, she experienced a recurrent episode of left flank pain, prompting urology consultation and a repeat renal ultrasound, which showed unchanged mild hydronephrosis without discrete stones or abscess. An MRI was obtained for further evaluation.

A 35-year-old African American woman with recently diagnosed, untreated HIV (CD4 count 19 cells/mm^3, viral load 1 000 000 IU/mL) presented with 2 days of fever (to 103°F), vomiting, diarrhea, and fatigue. She denied medication use. Examination showed oral thrush and lower abdominal tenderness; cardiovascular and pulmonary exams were benign; there was no lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, or lower-extremity edema. Laboratory evaluation revealed hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL, white-cell count 7000/µL with normal differential, platelet count 220 000/µL, and serum creatinine 9.0 mg/dL (baseline 1.2 mg/dL two weeks earlier). Urinalysis showed 53 WBCs per high-power field, leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative, and no proteinuria. She was started on IV ceftriaxone for presumed pyelonephritis but remained febrile; antibiotics were broadened to IV vancomycin and piperacillin–tazobactam. On hospital day 3, she had severe epistaxis and her platelet count fell to 26 000/µL. She had no history of heparin exposure, bleeding diathesis, or recent medication changes.

A 29‐year‐old woman presents with a 20‐year history of chronic anemia and progressive fatigue over the past 4 months. She reports no menstrual abnormalities, gastrointestinal bleeding, or nutritional deficits. Examination reveals pallor of the mucous membranes; no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy is noted.

Initial laboratory studies show: hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, hematocrit 31.6%, MCV 68.1 fL, MCH 21.1 pg, RDW 18.1%. Iron studies reveal serum iron 19 µg/dL (50–170), TIBC 430 µg/dL (250–450), ferritin 6 ng/mL (10–291). Peripheral smear shows anisopoikilocytosis and hypochromia. Reticulocyte count is 2%.

Autoimmune and infectious workup is negative, including ANA, anti–double‐stranded DNA, anti–MPO, anti–PR3, anti–gliadin, anti–transglutaminase, and anti–Helicobacter pylori antibodies. Hemoglobin A2 and F are normal; no circulating erythroblasts. Genetic testing for α‐ and β‐thalassemia is negative.

Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are unremarkable; duodenal biopsies show preserved villous architecture with a light intraepithelial lymphocytic infiltrate but no villous atrophy.

Therapy with daily oral ferrous sulfate (90 mg) and folic acid is initiated. At 6 months, symptoms improve but hemoglobin rises by only 0.4 g/dL to 10.2 g/dL. After 18 months, hemoglobin is 10.7 g/dL, MCV 75.4 fL, and serum iron 16 µg/dL with ferritin 11 ng/mL; the patient remains anemic and iron‐deficient.

A 68-year-old woman was admitted with a 2-week history of limb weakness and progressive difficulty walking. She had no relevant medical, family, or psychosocial history. On examination, temperature was 36.2 °C, heart rate 65 beats/min, and blood pressure 132/82 mmHg. She had a paucity of facial expression, normal cranial nerves, and muscle strength of 4/5 in all limbs. She exhibited an asymmetric resting tremor and rigidity in her limbs, diminished bilateral knee reflexes, and a positive right Babinski sign. Brain diffusion-weighted MRI showed obvious high-intensity signals around the bilateral lateral ventricles and corpus callosum.

Review of her records revealed that at age 62 she developed a resting tremor in her right hand, which extended to the left hand at 63, accompanied by bradykinesia, increased muscle tone, urinary incontinence, poor sleep quality with occasional shouting, and an MDS-UPDRS score of 88. She was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease and treated with levodopa and pramipexole, improving to 73 on the MDS-UPDRS. At age 65, selegiline was added without benefit (MDS-UPDRS 85), and she subsequently developed memory loss, visual hallucinations, and an MMSE score of 8/30.

A 69-year-old man with stage IV clear-cell renal carcinoma metastatic to the spine and brain presented with a 4-day history of gross hematuria, oliguria, fever (38.5 °C), fatigue, and decreased appetite. Two weeks earlier, he had started sunitinib 50 mg nightly. He had been on acetylsalicylic acid/dipyridamole for five years for stroke prevention. Hematuria persisted despite stopping aspirin/dipyridamole and a course of amoxicillin for presumed urinary tract infection. 

On arrival, blood pressure was 160/72 mmHg; digital rectal examination was negative for occult blood. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 68 000/mm3, sodium 120 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 41 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.7 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL). Coagulation studies were normal. A urine dipstick was positive for blood and protein. Urine sodium was < 10 mEq/L, and 24-hour urinary protein was 484 mg. Haptoglobin was normal, and peripheral smear showed no schistocytes. Inflammatory markers were elevated (CRP 55 mg/L, ESR 80 mm/hr). Serologies for p-ANCA, c-ANCA (MPO, PR3), complement levels, ANA, anti-dsDNA, rheumatoid factor, hepatitis B and C, and cryoglobulins were all negative.

A 63-year-old woman was referred for elevated serum liver enzyme levels. For the past six years she had eaten only small meals, and over the last two months her intake had decreased to <400 kcal/day, consisting of bread, cheese, raisins, walnuts, and tofu. She noted numbness in her extremities and on evaluation by her family physician was found to have AST 634 IU/L, ALT 462 IU/L, LDH 769 IU/L, ALP 764 IU/L, and γ-GTP 218 IU/L. She denied alcohol use, was a non-smoker, and had no significant medical history. 

On admission her vital signs were normal. Her height was 161 cm and weight 29.0 kg (BMI 11.2 kg/m2). Physical examination, including neurologic assessment, was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed WBC 5600/μL, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, platelets 198,000/μL, total protein 5.5 g/dL, albumin 3.3 g/dL, AST 267 IU/L, ALT 338 IU/L, LDH 557 IU/L, ALP 797 IU/L, γ-GTP 227 IU/L, transthyretin 8 mg/dL, transferrin 113 mg/dL, retinol-binding protein 0.7 mg/dL, vitamin B1 3.0 μg/dL, vitamin B12 >1500 pg/mL, and CRP 0.08 mg/dL. Serologic tests for hepatitis B and C and anti-mitochondrial antibodies were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography was unremarkable.
