Indirect calorimetry measured resting energy expenditure of 654 kcal/day.

Enteral nutrition was started at 300 kcal/day and increased to 500 kcal/day on day 4, with 100 mg intravenous vitamin B1 daily. Although she remained asymptomatic, her AST and ALT began to rise on day 8, raising concern for refeeding syndrome. Her serum electrolytes remained within normal limits throughout. By day 12, AST had increased to 1288 IU/L and ALT to 1043 IU/L, and her body weight had declined to 27.1 kg. Repeat abdominal ultrasonography again showed a normal-appearing liver.

A 65‐year‐old woman presented with two months of persistent left upper‐quadrant abdominal pain and multiple episodes of nonbilious, nonbloody vomiting of recently ingested food. The pain worsened with eating, leading to a 5 kg weight loss. She denied fever, night sweats, skin lesions, known allergies, atopy, or family history of similar illness. Initial evaluation elsewhere included an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy that revealed an antral ulcer; no biopsy was taken. Empiric clarithromycin‐based and then levofloxacin‐based Helicobacter pylori regimens were prescribed without improvement. 

On examination, she was hemodynamically stable, with conjunctival pallor and tenderness in the left upper quadrant; no lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or ascites were noted. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, total leukocyte count and differential within normal limits, and an absolute eosinophil count of 147/mm3. A fecal occult blood test was positive. 

A repeat upper endoscopy demonstrated a large ulcer on the lesser curvature of the antrum. Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen showed focal, asymmetrical thickening of the gastric wall (6.5 mm thickness over a 2.6 cm length) along the lesser curvature without perigastric lymphadenopathy.

A 40-year-old woman with a 17-month history of schizophrenia was admitted for adjustment of antipsychotic medication. Her regimen had been switched from risperidone to perospirone, and over three weeks the perospirone dose was increased to 40 mg/day. Shortly after reaching this dose, she developed tremor, muscle rigidity, akathisia, heavy sweating, difficulty swallowing and speaking, tachycardia, fluctuating blood pressure, a fever of 39.8 °C, restlessness, and confusion.  
Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 18.3 × 10^9/L, serum sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, creatine phosphokinase 813.2 U/L (normal 26–140 U/L), and myoglobin 486 µg/L (normal 12–76 µg/L). A lumbar puncture revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid. Neuroimaging was unremarkable. Electroencephalography demonstrated diffuse slow waves, consistent with metabolic encephalopathy.

A female neonate was delivered at 37 weeks’ gestation via planned cesarean section because of maternal gestational diabetes, intrauterine growth restriction, polyhydramnios, and a fetal echocardiogram that showed a hypoplastic left atrium and mildly dilated right atrium. Admission to the neonatal intensive care unit had been arranged for cardiac evaluation.

At birth, her APGAR scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes. She had moderate respiratory distress with subcostal retractions and was placed on noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation. Vital signs included a temperature of 36.9°C, respiratory rate of 57 breaths per minute, heart rate of 139 beats per minute, and an oxygen saturation of 99–100% on a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.30. On examination, she had craniotabes, a bell-shaped chest, mildly decreased muscle tone, and mild bowing of the bilateral femurs. A continuous machinery-type heart murmur was audible; pulses were normal. The remainder of the abdominal and skin examinations was unremarkable.

Echocardiography revealed a large patent ductus arteriosus and elevated right ventricular systolic pressure but normal cardiac structure. Chest radiography showed generalized demineralization of the bones and a bell-shaped rib cage. A skeletal survey demonstrated generalized osteopenia, metaphyseal lucencies, prominence of soft tissue over the parietal scalp, and mild bowing of the proximal humeri suggestive of healing fractures.

At 24 hours of life, laboratory studies were notable for a serum calcium concentration of 14.3 mg/dL (reference range, 8.4–10.6), ionized calcium of 2.32 mmol/L (reference range, 1.0–1.5), 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of 54.2 ng/mL (reference range, 31–80), and a parathyroid hormone level of 2116 pg/mL (reference range, 15–65). The infant was treated with intravenous fluids at 1.5 times maintenance, furosemide, and calcitonin, and transfer to a tertiary center was arranged for further evaluation.

A 50-year-old woman presented with persistent swelling of her lower lip for 2 years. She had no history of tuberculosis or contact with patients with tuberculosis or leprosy. Routine blood biochemistry and hematological parameters were within normal limits. A slit skin smear examination, Mantoux test, and chest radiograph were unremarkable. On the basis of these findings and the clinical presentation, a diagnosis of cheilitis granulomatosa Miescher (CGM) was made, and multiple intralesional corticosteroid injections were administered into the lower lip without improvement. Four weeks later, she developed erythematous, non-pruritic, non-scaling plaques above her upper lip and on the right lower chin, each measuring approximately 1 cm × 1.5 cm. Systemic examination was otherwise normal. Incisional biopsy specimens from the lower lip and an erythematous plaque revealed granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes with periadnexal and perineural lymphocytic infiltration on histopathological examination.

A 36-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of persistent cough and sputum production that worsened with the onset of a sore throat 1 day before admission. He works in a barbecue restaurant and has smoked approximately 20 cigarettes per day for 10 years. Initial treatment with an herbal cough remedy failed to relieve symptoms. On examination, vital signs were stable. Subcutaneous emphysema was palpable in the neck, and wet rales were auscultated over the left lung. Laboratory studies showed a leukocyte count of 25.74×10^9/L (neutrophils 21.04×10^9/L, 81.8%) and a C-reactive protein level of 1.63 mg/L. Chest radiography demonstrated obstructive atelectasis in the left lower lobe. Computed tomography of the chest confirmed pneumomediastinum and left lower lobe atelectasis. Flexible bronchoscopy revealed congested mucosa in the left main bronchus and in the basal and dorsal segments of the left lower lobe, along with copious white, viscous secretions, but no airway perforation, neoplasm, or active bleeding.

A 21-year-old man was brought to the emergency department by his aunt after first presenting with sudden-onset severe anxiety and the sensation that he was dying. He has high-functioning autism and obsessive-compulsive disorder; there is no other psychiatric or medical family history. He reported using cocaine that day, but collateral history denied this. He was diagnosed with a panic attack and discharged. A few hours later he returned, agitated, pacing, and nonverbal.  

Initial vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, liver function, renal profile, and inflammatory markers. A urine toxicology screen was negative. Notable findings included a low serum phosphate of 0.35 mmol/L and an elevated prolactin of 737 mu/L. Skull radiograph showed no fractures. MRI of the head was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture analysis returned with normal protein and glucose and was negative for bacteria or viruses.  

He was referred for psychiatric assessment and admitted to the acute psychiatric unit 9 days after initial presentation. On admission, he was severely disoriented to time, place, and person. He exhibited major thought block with markedly limited, stilted speech. He appeared dazed and had increased muscle tone, spastic movements, and preserved withdrawal to painful stimuli. His speech content was disjointed and bizarre; examples included “this is not the original,” “two people joined in the middle, different timelines,” and “I am not the soft science in the Jurassic thoughts.” He occasionally answered yes/no questions with great effort but could not recall his responses. Mental status examination showed a well-kept young man with poor eye contact and an intense stare, normal tone and volume of speech but extremely limited and incoherent content. Mood was euthymic, but thoughts were chaotic, and he lacked insight and capacity regarding his mental state.

A 67-year-old man presented in June 2013 with a swollen left hand after a laceration to his third finger sustained while working in soil. He also maintained three large hobby aquariums. He was treated with a 10-day course of cefprozil and clindamycin, with only marginal improvement. In October 2013, he returned with worsening stiffness and swelling of the left hand and digits. Rheumatology consultation led to a diagnosis of seronegative rheumatoid arthritis; all autoimmune serology was negative, and inflammatory markers were normal. A pulsed regimen of prednisone led to partial improvement, but swelling recurred. Sulfasalazine was added, with incomplete benefit and progression to involve the left elbow. Multiple aspirations and intra-articular steroid injections of the left elbow, wrist, and metacarpophalangeal joints yielded minimal improvement, and standard bacterial cultures were negative. Methotrexate and leflunomide were then initiated. By January 2014, firm nodules had developed along the extensor surfaces of the left arm and hand—including the ulnar aspect of the thumb, radial index finger, styloid process, and mid-shaft of the ulna. In February 2014, adalimumab was started and prednisone and sulfasalazine were discontinued; methotrexate and leflunomide were continued. After three months, he still had a swollen olecranon bursa and new lower extremity nodules. Aspirations of the wrist and knee remained microscopy-negative, with no bacterial growth. In December 2014, sulfasalazine and prednisone were restarted alongside a switch to etanercept, after which his nodular lesions dramatically worsened.

A 60-year-old woman underwent surgical tricuspid valve replacement for symptomatic tricuspid regurgitation. Ten days later, she developed acute left-sided hemiplegia, dysarthria, right-gaze preference, and a left facial droop. Her history included idiopathic hypertrophic subaortic stenosis with prior pacemaker placement and postoperative atrial fibrillation treated with apixaban. Noncontrast CT and CT angiography of the head showed an occlusion of the right distal internal carotid artery and an acute right middle cerebral artery infarct in the insula and temporal lobe. She did not receive IV thrombolysis because of anticoagulation and underwent mechanical thrombectomy via stent retriever and suction, achieving complete revascularization.

The day after thrombectomy, she reported right eyelid droop, binocular diplopia, and loss of peripheral vision in both eyes. On examination, near visual acuity was 20/60 in each eye. There was no anisocoria or relative afferent pupillary defect. The right eyelid had 1 mm of ptosis, and there was mild limitation of abduction and supraduction of the right eye. Anterior segment examination showed mild conjunctival chemosis OD, and dilated funduscopic examination was normal bilaterally. Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits was unremarkable. Noncontrast CT of the head showed no change in the known infarct and no lesion involving the optic chiasm. MRI was not obtained because of her non-MRI–compatible pacemaker.

A 19-year-old man with no prior medical history presented in October 2023 with sudden onset of speech difficulties, right arm weakness, and paresthesia of the right side of his body. On arrival, he was alert and oriented but had expressive aphasia and difficulty moving his right upper and lower limbs. Vital signs were within normal limits. A noncontrast CT scan of the head showed a hypodense area in the left corona radiata. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Two days after admission, MRI of the brain and cervical spine with and without gadolinium revealed multiple demyelinating lesions both supra- and infratentorially and in the cervical and dorsal spinal cord, some of which enhanced with contrast—findings suggestive of multiple sclerosis. On hospital day 5, serum studies for MOG antibody, anti–aquaporin 4 antibody, HIV types 1 and 2, VDRL, Borrelia burgdorferi antibody, Toxoplasma antibody, cytomegalovirus antibody, anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies, and an extended ANA blot profile were obtained, and all results were negative.

A 29-year-old Taiwanese woman with a family history of Sjögren’s syndrome presented with two weeks of daily fevers, arthralgias, sore throat, and a macular rash. Initial evaluation at a district hospital included negative viral tests and bacterial cultures. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (13 060/μL with 85.5% neutrophils) and marked hyperferritinemia (12 585 ng/mL). Antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor were negative. Gallium-67 inflammation scanning and abdominal CT demonstrated multiple enlarged lymph nodes; an excisional lymph node biopsy excluded lymphoma. She met Yamaguchi criteria for adult-onset Still’s disease. 

Because of a history of NSAID allergy, on hospital day 8 she received intravenous betamethasone (8 mg/day), which was transitioned to oral prednisolone (20 mg/day) two days later. Her fevers and arthralgias resolved. On day 10, ALT was 150 U/L and AST was 119 U/L; by day 15, levels peaked at ALT 1473 U/L and AST 722 U/L. Under suspicion of drug-induced liver injury, all medications were stopped. Viral and autoimmune hepatitis were excluded by serological tests, and liver enzymes declined. Corticosteroids were resumed on day 17, and she was discharged on prednisolone 20 mg/day. 

Five days after discharge, she was readmitted with acute severe hepatitis (ALT 1652 U/L; AST 766 U/L). Prednisolone was halted immediately while silymarin and lactulose were maintained.

A 35-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of mobile teeth in the lower left molar region and progressive difficulty chewing associated with pain and reduced mouth opening. She had hypothyroidism managed with medication; no history of trauma, familial bone disease, or systemic symptoms. On panoramic radiography, an initial patchy osteolysis of the left mandibular condyle was noted. Over 18 months, serial orthopantomograms demonstrated slowly progressive osteolysis extending from the condyle through the angle toward the mandibular body on the left side. Laboratory studies showed hypocalcemia (serum calcium 4.9 mg/dL), low vitamin D (52.14 nmol/L), and low intact parathyroid hormone (14.81 pg/mL). Investigations—including serologies and imaging—were performed to exclude rheumatoid arthritis, multiple myeloma, eosinophilic granuloma, and other systemic diseases. A whole-body PET scan revealed no additional lytic lesions. Cone-beam CT with three-dimensional reconstruction confirmed the extent of mandibular bone loss confined to the left hemi-mandible.

A 24-year-old woman presented with acute onset of severe left lower-quadrant abdominal pain that quickly became intermittent and mild (3/10). She denied fevers, vomiting, vaginal discharge or bleeding, dyspareunia, urinary symptoms, and changes in bowel habits. Her menstrual cycles were regular; her last period was 3 weeks prior. She had no history of sexually transmitted infections, pelvic masses, or prior pelvic surgery. Medical history was significant only for celiac disease.

On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination revealed a soft abdomen with mild left lower-quadrant tenderness without guarding or rebound. Speculum and pelvic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 11.4×10^9/L, neutrophils 8.9×10^9/L, and C-reactive protein <2 mg/L. A pregnancy test was negative (β-hCG <2 IU/L). Urinalysis and vaginal cultures were negative.

Transabdominal and transvaginal pelvic ultrasonography demonstrated a left ovarian volume of 4 mL (right ovary 1.9 mL), both within normal limits. There was no discrete mass or cyst. The distal left fallopian tube appeared bulky but with normal vascularity and no tubo-ovarian collection. Color Doppler flow was normal in both ovaries. The report noted that the patient was unable to empty her bladder during the study.

The gynecology team admitted her for observation and analgesia. Analgesic requirements remained minimal until day 4, when she became febrile to 38.4 °C and required more analgesia. Empiric intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics were started. On day 6, her C-reactive protein rose to 207 mg/L. The decision was made to perform an exploratory laparoscopy.

A 30-year-old man first noted right calf muscle cramps in 2013. Twelve months later, he developed right foot drop, fasciculations in the right leg, and wasting of the right anterior compartment. Neurological examination in 2014 showed 2/5 strength of the right ankle extensors, right leg amyotrophy, brisk reflexes in the lower limbs, a positive right Babinski sign, and no sensory deficits.

By 2015, fasciculations were present throughout the body, painful cramps and weakness appeared in the left shin, and thigh muscle atrophy developed. Deep tendon reflexes remained brisk except for absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally; Hoffmann sign was positive. There were no bulbar or respiratory symptoms.

In 2015, T2-weighted MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a slitlike syrinx (central canal dilation) extending from T3 to T9 without Chiari malformation or extramedullary compression; brain and cervical MRI were normal. EMG in 2015 revealed fibrillation potentials, fasciculations, and large‐amplitude, long‐duration motor–unit potentials in both upper and lower limbs without conduction block. GM-1 and GM-2 antibody titers were negative, and routine blood and CSF studies were normal. Follow-up spinal MRI in 2016 and 2019 showed no change in the cavity size.

36-year-old gravida 2 para 1 woman at 30 weeks’ gestation presented with fever, productive cough, and central cyanosis for 2 days. Two weeks earlier, she was diagnosed with multibacillary leprosy based on hypoaesthetic annular plaques on the trunk and limbs, a positive slit-skin smear (morphological index 3.2%; bacteriological index 4.3%), and was started on clofazimine, rifampicin, and dapsone 100 mg daily. She denied headache, chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis, chemical exposures, or unprescribed medications. On examination, her temperature spiked once on admission; vital signs were otherwise stable without respiratory distress. Oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry was 84–88% on room air, and both radial arterial and venous blood appeared dark. Arterial blood gas on room air showed PaO₂ 111 mmHg and calculated SaO₂ 98%. Laboratory tests revealed normal hemoglobin, bilirubin, LDH, and leukocyte count. G6PD activity was normal. Chest radiograph and sputum studies for bacterial culture and acid-fast bacilli were unremarkable. Administration of 100% oxygen failed to correct the cyanosis, and repeat arterial blood gas values remained unchanged.

A 41‐year‐old man presented with progressive lower leg edema and dyspnea at rest. He reported two years of exertional dyspnea on light exercise but denied subjective limb weakness. His medical history was unremarkable, with no statin use or family history of cardiac or neuromuscular disease.

On examination, he had jugular venous distention and bilateral pitting edema. Lung auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds without crackles. Cardiac auscultation was unremarkable. He demonstrated proximal limb weakness (manual muscle testing score 3/5) and an unsteady gait.

Laboratory studies showed a serum creatine kinase level of 4409 U/L, CK-MB of 229 U/L (normal <12 U/L), brain natriuretic peptide 896.6 pg/mL (normal <18.4 pg/mL), and cardiac troponin I 240 pg/mL (cut-off 26.2 pg/mL). Chest radiography revealed cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio 64%), pulmonary congestion, and pleural effusion. Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus rhythm at 133 beats per minute, poor R-wave progression, and T-wave inversions in leads II, III, and aVF.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a dilated left ventricle (end-diastolic volume 120 mL, end-systolic volume 93 mL), diffuse hypokinesis, an ejection fraction of 20%, and moderate tricuspid and mild mitral regurgitation without regional wall motion abnormalities. He was diagnosed with acute heart failure, received intensive care (including catecholamines, intubation, and intra-aortic balloon pumping), and was treated with ACE inhibitors, β‐blockers, and amiodarone. He was discharged after 136 days, but his low ejection fraction and elevated CK, BNP, and troponin levels persisted, and his proximal muscle weakness progressed.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated endocardial late gadolinium enhancement in the anterolateral and inferior walls, with spotty transmural enhancement in the inferior wall. Coronary angiography revealed only moderate stenosis of the left anterior descending artery. Muscle MRI of the arms showed high-intensity signals in the biceps and triceps on short-inversion-time inversion recovery sequences.

A 52-year-old man (weight 90 kg) with a history of obstructive sleep apnea, hypothyroidism, and mild gastroesophageal reflux underwent elective right shoulder arthroscopy for rotator cuff repair. He had tolerated three prior surgeries without anesthetic complications. 

At 11:10 AM, an ultrasound- and nerve stimulation–guided interscalene block was performed with 30 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine containing epinephrine (1:300 000) without incident. At 11:46 AM, general anesthesia was induced with fentanyl (75 µg), lidocaine (80 mg), and propofol (200 mg); tracheal intubation was facilitated with rocuronium (50 mg). Anesthesia was maintained with isoflurane (0.8–1%) in oxygen and air. Immediately after induction, his blood pressure was in the 150s/70s mm Hg and heart rate in the 80s bpm.

Surgical incision at 12:36 PM was followed by a drop in blood pressure to the 70s/30s mm Hg and heart rate to 40–50 bpm. Two doses of intravenous ephedrine (10 mg and 5 mg) and glycopyrrolate (0.4 mg) failed to restore normotension. At 13:02 PM, a phenylephrine infusion (0.2 µg/kg/min) was started, and by 13:05 PM, he returned to baseline blood pressure and heart rate.

At 13:20 PM, with an end-tidal isoflurane concentration of 0.87%, arthroscopic irrigation was initiated. His blood pressure abruptly increased to 229–234/111–116 mm Hg with a sinus tachycardia of 115–125 bpm. The phenylephrine infusion was discontinued. He received midazolam (total 2 mg), two boluses of propofol (30 mg and 40 mg), two boluses of esmolol (30 mg each), and the end-tidal isoflurane concentration was increased to 1.4%, but his blood pressure and heart rate remained elevated with minimal change.

A 25-year-old woman with a history of severe childhood abuse believed, based on cultural teachings, that marriage would heal her past wounds. She married at age 21. After one year, her husband was emotionally and physically abusive, and she underwent an abortion related to the abuse. Shortly thereafter, she experienced persistent stomach pain, severe headache, neck pain, sleeping difficulties, and profound bitterness and loss of trust in others. One month later, she developed sudden, temporary paralysis of both legs and was unable to walk. She remained fully conscious and communicated through gestures, having lost her voice.

On return to her biological family, she underwent extensive evaluations: radiography of the legs, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, and routine blood tests (including a complete blood count), all of which were normal. She was treated with prednisolone 5 mg daily, tramadol for pain, and physiotherapy, with only minimal improvement. After two weeks of hospitalization and inpatient physiotherapy, she was discharged with the understanding that her symptoms might resolve spontaneously in the absence of identifiable neurological pathology. Her family then sought traditional healing when her condition failed to improve and subsequently worsened. She was brought back to the hospital, and, given her inability to speak, was referred to a psychotherapist for further assessment.

A 16-year-old female high–level soccer player twisted her right ankle during a match and immediately noted pain, swelling, and difficulty bearing weight. She had no prior history of tibial, tarsal, or ankle disease or injury. In the emergency department, radiographs of the right ankle were interpreted as a displaced medial malleolus fracture and demonstrated an os subfibularis. 

On transfer to our department, examination of the right ankle confirmed swelling, functional impairment, and intense medial malleolar pain but revealed no ankle laxity, instability, or pronation pain, and flexion-extension was preserved with only slight discomfort. Twenty-four hours later, she reported a marked reduction in pain and swelling and improved range of motion. 

To investigate the discrepancy between the initial radiographic interpretation and the unexpectedly benign clinical course, a comparison radiograph of the left (uninjured) ankle was obtained and showed a similarly shaped medial malleolus fragment without an os subfibularis. 

Because the clinical findings and bilateral radiographs were incongruent with a typical acute fracture, a bilateral CT scan was ordered.

A 47-year-old previously healthy woman presented with four months of generalized body swelling, disproportionate ascites, loss of appetite, and weight loss. She denied fever, night sweats, jaundice, bleeding, cough, or TB exposure. There was no history of cardiac, renal, or liver disease; no alcohol use; and an HIV test was negative. On exam she was emaciated (BMI 18), afebrile, with moderate ascites, mild ankle edema, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, and no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed normochromic normocytic anemia, thrombocytosis, normal liver enzymes except mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT, normal INR, normal renal function, and a serum CA-125 of 175 U/ml (normal <46). Chest radiograph was normal; echocardiography showed normal cardiac structure and function without constrictive pericarditis. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed no ovarian pathology. Abdominal ultrasound and contrast-enhanced CT suggested heterogeneous liver parenchyma, minimal surface nodularity, and moderate ascites without portal vein thrombosis or lymphadenopathy, raising concern for decompensated chronic liver disease. Workup for cirrhosis was unrevealing, and upper endoscopy showed no varices or portal gastropathy. Diuretics were started. Diagnostic paracentesis revealed exudative ascites with elevated inflammatory markers; cultures (bacterial, fungal), acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear, TB culture, and GeneXpert on fluid were negative, and cytology was negative for malignant cells. The tuberculin skin test measured 17 mm induration.

A 37 year-old man with HIV infection and a recent history of cryptococcal meningitis, treated with amphotericin followed by fluconazole, began ART (zidovudine, lamivudine, efavirenz) 21 days after meningitis treatment completion. His baseline CD4 count was 5 cells/µL, rising to 29 cells/µL by day +21 of ART. On day +21, he noted hypogastric abdominal pain and was treated empirically for urinary tract infection with ciprofloxacin, with some improvement. By day +35, the pain recurred, now associated with low-grade fevers and a dry cough; physical examination showed tachypnea (28 breaths/min) and right iliac-fossa tenderness. A complete blood count, chest radiograph, and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. He was treated for possible atypical pneumonia with doxycycline; his respiratory symptoms improved, but abdominal pain persisted with occasional vomiting. On day +84, a repeat chest radiograph to exclude tuberculosis was unremarkable. His CD4 count had fallen to 14 cells/µL, and HIV-1 viral load was 22,000 copies/mL despite verified adherence. On day +112, abdominal ultrasound showed an appendicular mass and para-aortic lymphadenopathy; CD4 was 8 cells/µL and viral load 15,475 copies/mL. He consented to ultrasound-guided biopsy on day +140, and a second ultrasound demonstrated ileal wall thickening (6 mm) with adjacent 1 cm lymph nodes. Two lymph-node biopsy specimens showed no abnormality on histology. By day +168, abdominal pain and vomiting persisted, CD4 was 24 cells/µL, viral load 23,755 copies/mL, and he was presumed to have ART failure possibly due to malabsorption from thickened gut. An empiric trial of anti-tuberculosis therapy was started.

A 21-year-old woman presented with 7 days of abdominal pain. She had no recent travel, no history of asthma or allergies, and no family history of similar symptoms. On examination, she had tenderness in the right lower abdomen; cardiopulmonary findings were normal. Vital signs were: temperature 36.7°C, heart rate 102 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 124/90 mmHg. Laboratory tests showed white blood cells 60.64×10^9/L, neutrophils 10.06×10^9/L, lymphocytes 6.84×10^9/L, eosinophils 42.80×10^9/L, and total IgE 1109.3 IU/mL. A stool routine examination was normal, and allergen testing for 20 common allergens was negative. Abdominal CT revealed bowel-wall thickening and pelvic and abdominal ascites. Diagnostic paracentesis yielded yellowish fluid with a high eosinophil count; bacterial and tuberculosis cultures were negative and cytology showed no malignant cells. Bone marrow aspiration demonstrated active myelopoiesis with an abnormally high percentage of eosinophils. Gastroscopy revealed mild gastric mucosal erythema, and colonoscopy showed mucosal edema, erythema, erosions, and a villous appearance of the terminal ileum.

A 49-year-old amateur athlete presented with 3 weeks of exercise intolerance manifesting as exertional dyspnoea and dizziness. He denied syncope, had no family history of sudden cardiac death, and took no medications. He had traveled to Iran and, 3 months earlier, had an inguinal bullous skin lesion treated briefly with topical steroids without recurrence.

On examination: heart rate 61 bpm, blood pressure 122/77 mmHg, temperature 36.5 °C; cardiac and pulmonary exams were normal. Laboratory tests showed normal leukocytes (4.89 g/L) and CRP (0.8 mg/L). Resting ECG revealed an incomplete right bundle branch block and first-degree AV block; rhythm monitoring showed intermittent 2:1 AV block. During spiroergometry, exercise-induced high-degree AV block was documented.

Transthoracic echocardiography raised suspicion of inferobasal septal wall-motion abnormalities and, retrospectively, a mass; left ventricular ejection fraction was normal. Coronary angiography excluded coronary artery disease, and chest CT revealed no pulmonary pathology. Cardiac MRI demonstrated a 5 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm mass in the inferobasal septum with late gadolinium enhancement but no active perfusion. FDG-PET showed intense uptake in the inferobasal septum and no extracardiac uptake.

Further evaluation revealed normal sIL-2 receptor, ANA, ANCA, serum calcium, and ACE levels. Blood cultures (aerobic, anaerobic, mycobacterial) and serologies for Brucella, Bartonella henselae, Treponema pallidum, Borrelia burgdorferi, Coxiella burnetii, and HIV were negative. PCR for tuberculosis and mycobacterial cultures were negative. Dermatologic full-body exam showed only non-specific skin changes.

Because there were no extracardiac manifestations, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography-guided endomyocardial biopsies were performed, but all samples were non-specific.

A 68-year-old woman was diagnosed with sigmoid colon cancer and was scheduled for laparoscopic colectomy the next day. On the evening before surgery, she reported left preauricular pain and difficulty opening her mouth. On examination, the maximum interincisal opening was 13 mm. Palpation of the temporomandibular joints revealed no pain or erythema, and there was no joint clicking. Schuller’s radiographic views of the left temporomandibular joint showed that the mandibular condyle did not translate anteriorly in the open position; there was no evidence of bony ankylosis or mandibular fracture. Dental examination revealed tooth mobility and loss from periodontal disease, with deviation of the occlusal plane.

A 24-year-old Indigenous Australian woman from a remote community presented with a 3-month history of left thigh swelling and pain associated with limitation of movement. She had type 1 diabetes mellitus diagnosed at age 14 years with chronically poor glycaemic control (HbA1c, 12.4% on admission; historically as high as 20.9%) and multiple microvascular complications, including proliferative retinopathy, nephrotic-range proteinuria, peripheral neuropathy, and autonomic neuropathy. Other history was notable for acute rheumatic fever, syphilis, recurrent urinary tract infections, active smoking (20 cigarettes per day), and prior right femoral neck fracture with internal fixation. Her only medication was premixed insulin (degludec and aspart 14 units twice daily).

On examination she was pale, cachectic (weight 32.5 kg; BMI 12.9 kg/m2), and sinus tachycardic at 120 bpm. She had significant tender swelling of the left thigh without erythema, warmth, or skin changes; peripheral pulses were intact. Neurologic assessment was limited by pain but revealed stocking-distribution sensory neuropathy and reduced proximal left lower-limb strength. Visual acuity was counting fingers bilaterally; funduscopic exam showed severe proliferative diabetic retinopathy with macular oedema.

Laboratory studies revealed normocytic anaemia (Hb 90 g/L), thrombocytosis (649 × 10^9/L), leukocytosis (20.3 × 10^9/L), elevated neutrophils (17.43 × 10^9/L), ESR 120 mm/h, CRP 185 mg/L, ferritin 1290 µg/L, and creatinine clearance 50 mL/min. Creatine kinase and liver function tests were normal. Thyroid function was normal; morning cortisol was 528 nmol/L. Nutritional studies showed hypoalbuminaemia (<15 g/L), vitamin D 10.3 nmol/L, and vitamin C 12 µmol/L; coeliac serology was negative. Urinalysis indicated a urinary tract infection and albumin/creatinine ratio 840 g/mol. Renal ultrasound demonstrated cystitis; renal biopsy confirmed class III diabetic nephropathy. 

CT of the pelvis and left leg showed ill-defined diffuse low attenuation in the left mid-thigh muscle measuring 36 × 34 × 150 mm without masses or collections. A Doppler ultrasound excluded deep vein thrombosis. MRI revealed marked oedema of the left anterior thigh musculature (rectus femoris, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, and adductor muscles) with muscle atrophy, fatty and fluid replacement, and subcutaneous tissue oedema; the posterior compartment was spared.

A 60‐year‐old man with no history of liver disease, pancreatitis, or abdominal trauma was admitted for severe anemia (hemoglobin, 4.8 g/dL) after one episode of hematemesis and two episodes of melena over the prior 24 hours. He was hemodynamically unstable (pulse, 110 bpm; blood pressure, 100/50 mmHg) but afebrile, with an unremarkable abdominal examination and no stigmata of portal hypertension. Digital rectal examination revealed melanic stool. Other laboratory tests, including coagulation, liver, and renal function, were normal.

After resuscitation with transfusion and high‐dose proton‐pump inhibitor, emergent esophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed. A moderate amount of fresh blood was aspirated from the stomach. In retroflexion, the gastric fundus showed varicose‐shaped, pulsating, tortuous submucosal vessels without active bleeding, and a small erosion over one vessel suggested recent rupture. There were no endoscopic signs of portal hypertension.

To further characterize the lesion, computed tomography angiography was obtained. There was complete thrombosis of the splenic artery and tortuous arterial structures arising from the left gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries and coursing into the gastric fundus. No active contrast extravasation was seen.

A 62-year-old woman with a history of childhood angioedema, episodic migraines treated with triptans, and gastroesophageal reflux presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset dyspnea. The symptoms began less than 30 minutes after an otherwise unremarkable MRI with gadolinium contrast. On examination, her oxygen saturation was 87% on room air, heart rate 106/min, blood pressure normal, and temperature 37.5 °C. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral crackles; there were no signs of heart failure or systemic rheumatologic disease.

D-dimer was elevated at 7593 ng/mL. CT pulmonary angiography showed no pulmonary embolism but demonstrated diffuse ground-glass opacities with a perihilar distribution. Hemoglobin was 15.2 g/dL, leukocytes 4.0 G/L (neutrophils 3.2 G/L), and creatinine 77 μmol/L. Multiplex PCR for respiratory viruses and atypical bacteria was negative, and urine antigens for Legionella pneumophila and Streptococcus pneumoniae were negative. Cardiac evaluation revealed a normal troponin level (<3 ng/L), NT-proBNP 380 ng/L, unremarkable ECG, and echocardiography with LVEF 56% and no pulmonary hypertension. Serologic testing for ANCA, ANA, rheumatoid factor, and anti–citrullinated peptide antibodies was negative; protein electrophoresis and serum calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D levels were normal. In light of diffuse ground-glass opacities without an identified cause, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed.

A 49-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 11.1% one month earlier), untreated hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, morbid obesity (BMI 42 kg/m^2), and obstructive sleep apnoea presented with 4 days of diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever, and chills. He denied respiratory or chest symptoms. On first presentation, he was tachycardic (102 b.p.m.) but otherwise afebrile and normotensive; chest radiograph showed mild pulmonary congestion. He was tested for SARS-CoV-2 and discharged after intravenous fluids. 

One day later, he returned with fever (39.5°C), diarrhoea, dyspnoea, and severe cough. SARS-CoV-2 testing was positive. On examination, he was tachypnoeic (26 breaths/min), tachycardic (108 b.p.m.), with coarse bilateral breath sounds; cardiac exam was normal. Repeat chest radiograph showed patchy alveolar opacities superimposed on diffuse interstitial changes.

Laboratory results:
- WBC 5.8×10^3/µL, lymphocytes 0.6×10^3/µL  
- CRP 9.79 mg/dL, LDH 296 U/L, ferritin 482 ng/dL, IL-6 83.75 pg/mL  
- D-dimer <150 µg/L  
- Troponin I 0.018 ng/mL, BNP 25 pg/mL  

Arterial blood gas on nasal cannula showed pH 7.38, PaO₂ 66.2 mmHg, PaCO₂ 38.5 mmHg. Electrocardiogram on admission was normal sinus rhythm at 78 b.p.m.

He was admitted to the ICU for respiratory failure and treated with hydroxychloroquine. Despite therapy, inflammatory markers and oxygen requirements worsened, and he was intubated on hospital Day 6. Cardiac monitoring demonstrated episodes of premature ventricular complexes with ventricular bigeminy. 

On Day 7, transthoracic echocardiography revealed global left ventricular hypokinesis with an ejection fraction of 37% (previously 60–65% two months earlier) and markedly impaired global longitudinal strain averaging –1%.

An 8-year-old autistic boy presented with severe bilateral leg pain and difficulty walking of recent onset. He also had gum swelling and bleeding, a low-grade fever, and a maculopapular rash on both upper and lower extremities. Routine blood tests, tick titers, and an autoimmune workup were all normal. A whole-body bone scintigraphy examination showed increased radiotracer activity in the bilateral shoulders, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles, most severe in the knees. Radiographs of these areas were normal. Differential considerations included infiltrative processes such as leukemia, neuroblastoma metastases, and multifocal osteomyelitis; multifocal fractures were felt to be unlikely. Contrast-enhanced MRI of both femurs demonstrated intense metaphyseal signal abnormality and enhancement in the bilateral proximal and distal femurs and proximal tibiae, as well as subperiosteal signal abnormality and enhancement along the metaphyses.

A 41-year-old woman was referred for therapy-resistant dyspnea and angioedema of unknown origin. Six weeks earlier, she had developed progressive dyspnea and coughing, culminating in a severe coughing attack with syncope. She was initially treated for presumed allergic asthma with inhaled bronchodilators, oral glucocorticoids, and antihistamines without improvement and spent 14 days in a local hospital before referral.

On examination, she was obese (160 cm, 85 kg) with significant swelling of the face and neck, bilateral subconjunctival hemorrhages, and basal rhonchi; there were no urticarial hives. She had a five pack-year smoking history (quit at symptom onset) and reported allergies to dust mites, pollen, hay, straw, cats, and dogs. Her medications included prednisolone 25 mg daily, levocetirizine as needed, inhaled budesonide, fenoterol/ipratropium bromide as needed, dihydrocodeine, transdermal nicotine, and local antifungal therapy for laryngeal thrush.

Initial laboratory studies showed CRP 0.71 mg/dL (normal <0.5) and a leukocytosis of 30–40 ×10^9 cells/L with 44% lymphocytes. Chest radiography and CT of the head, neck, and chest were unremarkable except for an enlarged thyroid gland; thyroid function tests confirmed a euthyroid multinodular goitre without antibodies. Morning cortisol and ACTH levels were normal. A RAST panel was negative for common inhalant and food allergens, though total IgE was elevated at 310 kU/L (normal <100). Multiple lung function tests excluded obstructive ventilatory disease. Complement C4 and C1-INH levels were normal. Echocardiography was unremarkable.

Because of the marked lymphocytosis, hematology evaluated for lymphoproliferative disease: immunophenotyping showed increased T cells but no clonal population; serum electrophoresis, abdominal sonography, and CT of the head, neck, chest, and abdomen revealed no malignancy. Repeat chest CT 13 days later showed peribronchovascular ground-glass opacities in the mediobasal segment of the left lower lobe and minimal tree-in-bud opacities in the left upper lobe. An interferon-γ release assay for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative. Extensive autoantibody testing was negative. Oropharyngeal swab cultures and pneumococcal urine antigen testing yielded no new findings. Serologies for respiratory syncytial virus, coxsackievirus, echovirus, adenovirus, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae were negative.

A 21-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of dry skin and generalized spiny skin lesions. She had been treated empirically for eczema with a medium-strength topical corticosteroid without improvement. She had no other medical problems, medications, atopy, allergies, or family history of similar skin findings.

On examination, she had multiple minute, digitate, folliculocentric hyperkeratotic papules symmetrically involving the face, neck, trunk, and upper extremities. There was no perilesional erythema, palmoplantar keratoderma, scarring, alopecia, or signs of nutritional deficiency.

A 3-mm punch biopsy from the back showed keratin plugs in hair follicle infundibula, sparse perifollicular lymphocytes, and cystic spaces in the outer root sheath of hair follicles and sebaceous glands. Alcian blue–periodic acid–Schiff stain highlighted mucin within these spaces. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated CD3- and predominantly CD4-positive small T lymphocytes, few CD8-positive T cells, and inconspicuous CD20-positive B cells and CD30-positive cells. T-cell receptor gene-rearrangement testing failed for technical reasons.

An 8-year-old girl presented with a 1-year history of clonic seizures involving the right upper and lower limbs, each lasting 2–5 minutes, with prolonged postictal states but no loss of consciousness; she had occasional bladder incontinence. The first seizure occurred at age 7, after which seizure frequency rose to 10–15 episodes per day, and she developed slurred speech, cognitive delay, and an abnormal gait. Her perinatal history was unremarkable, with no neonatal seizures, transfusions, neurosurgery, head trauma, allergies, or family history of epilepsy.

Initial routine electroencephalography (EEG) and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were normal. She was treated sequentially with oxcarbazepine, valproate sodium, and clonazepam without full seizure control. One month before admission, she developed paresthesia and twitching of the right arm. She was admitted with focal status epilepticus and generalized seizures refractory to antiepileptic drugs.

On neurologic examination, there was constant twitching of the right hand, intermittent stiffening of the right leg and pelvis, and right hemiparesis (Medical Research Council grade 3 on the right, grade 5 on the left); tendon reflexes were exaggerated on the right. She had severe global developmental delay; there were no meningeal signs and cranial nerves were intact.

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal, and polymerase-chain-reaction assays for herpes simplex virus, Epstein–Barr virus, measles, rubella, and cytomegalovirus were negative. EEG showed slow activity with focal left frontal biphasic spikes and paroxysmal discharges. MRI of the brain revealed left hemispheric atrophy, including atrophy of the left insular cortex on T1-weighted images and atrophy of the left caudate and putamen nuclei on T2-weighted images.
